classes.title: Black-Hole Interiors, Remnants and Evaporation under the Aldred Limit

papers.t: Accretion onto a Limit Remnant: Bondi Capture and Eddington Output of a Heavy Relic
papers.r: The Bondi radius is 1.156e-07 metres, about a tenth of a micrometre, and the capture rate is 7.021e-31 kilograms per second. The Eddington ceiling of 5.474e+11 watts is formally large but irrelevant, because the luminosity at ten percent efficiency on the Bondi supply is only 6.310e-15 watts, some twenty-six orders below the ceiling; the growth time is 3.908e+33 years, vastly exceeding the cosmic age.

papers.t: Charged Black Holes and the Density Cap: Where the Inner Horizon Meets the Capped Core
papers.r: The capped radius is 7.876e-10 metres. At half the extremal charge the inner horizon already sits at 1.978e+03 metres, far outside the cap, and the two structures meet only at a charge fraction of 3.264e-07, extremely close to uncharged. The extremal charge itself is 1.714e+21 coulombs.

papers.t: A Cold-Remnant Temperature Law: Where the Specific Heat of an Evaporating Hole Changes Sign
papers.r: The turnover sits at 1.500e+11 kilograms by the analytic route and 1.499e+11 kilograms by the numerical scan, agreement at the quoted precision. The maximum temperature is 5.454e+11 kelvin. At ten remnant masses the model gives 1.403e+11 kelvin against the uncorrected Hawking value 1.417e+11 kelvin, a one-percent correction, so the law is invisible until the end-stage and decisive only there, exactly the behaviour a

papers.t: Time to the Cap: Free-Fall Duration from Nuclear Density to the Aldred Limit
papers.r: From nuclear saturation density the characteristic time is 1.255e-04 seconds; at the cap itself it is 6.739e-25 seconds; from a white-dwarf-like starting density it is 2.101e+00 seconds. The density ratio traversed from nuclear matter to the cap is 3.471e+40, forty orders of magnitude, yet the clock changes by only twenty orders because of the square root.

papers.t: Crossover Masses by Carrier: Which Branch Sets the Smallest Possible Black Hole
papers.r: The electron branch gives a crossover of 1.592e+14 kilograms, the proton branch 8.671e+10 kilograms, and the neutron branch 8.659e+10 kilograms. The electron-to-neutron ratio is 1.839e+03, matching the inverse mass ratio as the scaling law requires.

papers.t: Density-Capped Interiors: The Radius at Which a Black Hole Reaches the Aldred Limit
papers.r: For ten solar masses the horizon sits at 2.953e+04 metres while the capped radius is only 7.876e-10 metres, a ratio of 2.667e-14. The mean density inside that horizon is 1.843e+17 kilograms per cubic metre, below the bound by a factor 5.273e+40, so the horizon itself is nowhere near the ceiling: the cap is a deep-interior statement.

papers.t: End-States of Evaporation Under a Density Cap: A Classification by Initial Mass
papers.r: The remnant boundary sits at 8.659e+10 kilograms and the expiring-today boundary at 1.730e+11 kilograms. An object starting at the second boundary radiates 7.766e+27 joules over its life and returns a fraction 4.995e-01 of its mass, retaining only the remnant.

papers.t: Evaporation Time to the Remnant: How the Density Cap Shortens the Hawking Lifetime
papers.r: For an initial mass of 1e12 kilograms the full lifetime is 8.411e+19 seconds and the time to reach the remnant is 8.406e+19 seconds; the saved fraction is 6.493e-04, utterly negligible, because the remnant mass of 8.659e+10 kilograms is about one order of magnitude below the initial mass and the cube of that ratio suppresses the saved tail. Even at 1e15 kilograms the saved fraction is only 6.494e-13.

papers.t: The Energy Ceiling of Hawking Radiation Implied by a Finite Remnant Temperature
papers.r: The ceiling temperature of 1.417e+12 kelvin gives a characteristic energy of 1.221e-01 giga-electronvolts and a spectral peak at 3.443e-01 giga-electronvolts, corresponding to a wavelength of 3.601e-15 metres. The endpoint therefore sits in the high-energy gamma-ray band, some nineteen orders of magnitude below the Planck energy.

papers.t: Counting Cells in a Capped Interior: Planck Volumes Versus Horizon Entropy
papers.r: For ten solar masses the interior holds 4.846e+77 Planck cells against 1.513e+79 horizon bits, a ratio of only 3.203e-02. For one solar mass the ratio is 3.203e-01 and for a million solar masses it drops to 3.203e-07. The capped interior therefore contains fewer Planck cells than the horizon has bits, at every mass in the scan, and the shortfall grows linearly with mass.

papers.t: The Volume of a Capped Interior: Linear Growth in Mass Instead of Cubic Growth in Radius
papers.r: For ten solar masses the capped volume is 2.046e-27 cubic metres against a horizon ball of 1.079e+14 cubic metres, a ratio of 1.896e-41. For a billion solar masses the capped volume reaches 2.046e-19 cubic metres yet the ratio falls to 1.896e-57.

papers.t: A Bound on the Ringdown Shift from a Capped Interior in a Sixty-Solar-Mass Merger Remnant
papers.r: The ringdown frequency is 2.012e+02 hertz with a damping time of 6.327e-03 seconds. The capped radius is 1.431e-09 metres against a horizon of 1.772e+05 metres, a volume fraction of 5.268e-43, bounding any shift at 1.060e-40 hertz. Present detectors resolve ringdown frequencies to about a hertz at these masses, so the bound lies some forty orders of magnitude below resolution.

papers.t: Primordial Remnants as Dark Matter: Number Density and Mean Separation Implied by the Limit Remnant
papers.r: The remnant mass is 8.659e+10 kilograms and the required number density is 8.235e-33 per cubic metre, giving a mean separation of 4.952e+10 metres, about 4.952e+07 kilometres, and a flux of 1.812e-27 remnants per square metre per second.

papers.t: Entropy of the Limit Remnant: How Much Disorder Survives Evaporation
papers.r: At the remnant mass of 8.659e+10 kilograms the entropy is 1.989e+38 in units of Boltzmann's constant, or 2.870e+38 bits. A hole one hundred times heavier carries 1.989e+42 in the same units, ten thousand times more, displaying the quadratic law.

papers.t: The Remnant Mass Implied by the Aldred Limit: Where the Horizon Meets the Density Cap
papers.r: The remnant mass is 8.659e+10 kilograms, or 8.659e+13 grams, which is 3.979e+18 times the Planck mass. Its horizon radius at the meeting point is 1.286e-16 metres, and the radius check returns 1.000e+00, unity to the precision shown, confirming the algebra.

papers.t: A Temperature Ceiling for Evaporating Black Holes Set by the Density Cap
papers.r: The ceiling is 1.417e+12 kelvin at the remnant mass of 8.659e+10 kilograms. For orientation, a ten-solar-mass hole radiates at 6.170e-09 kelvin and a solar-mass hole at 6.170e-08 kelvin, while a hole of 1e12 kilograms reaches 1.227e+11 kelvin.

papers.t: Rotating Black Holes and the Density Cap: Spin Dependence of the Capped Core's Horizon Fraction
papers.r: At zero spin the capped radius is a fraction 2.667e-14 of the horizon radius. At a spin parameter of 0.998 the horizon has contracted to 1.570e+04 metres and the fraction rises to 5.016e-14, nearly doubling, while the equatorial static limit stays at 2.953e+04 metres and the core itself remains at 7.876e-10 metres.

classes.title: Nucleosynthesis and Structure Formation in a Bounced Cosmology

papers.t: The Baryon-to-Photon Ratio in a Bounced Cosmology: A Consistency Window from Two Independent Eras
papers.r: The allowed entropy production at the bounce is limited to about 2 percent, corresponding to a dilution factor no larger than 1.02 at the stated confidence. At a factor of 1.2 the deuterium prediction would already fall to 1.89e-05.

papers.t: Microwave Background Spectral Distortions from Bounce-Era Dissipation: A Limit on Small-Scale Power
papers.r: For a cutoff at one thousand per megaparsec the predicted distortion falls to 1.02e-08, with a surviving power fraction of 0.511; at two hundred per megaparsec it falls further, to 4.34e-09; the standard value is 2.00e-08, and the firm observational limit from past measurement is 9 in a hundred thousand.

papers.t: A Combined Light-Element Fit to the Bounce Temperature: Helium, Deuterium and Helium-3 Together
papers.r: The combined statistic is decisive at low bounce temperatures: at 0.5 MeV the chi-square reaches 86.0, and at 1 MeV it is 56.65, both far beyond any acceptable fit for three data points, while the best region, around 15 MeV and above, returns a chi-square of 0.0.

papers.t: Deuterium Survival Through the Bottleneck in a Bounced Cosmology: A Yield and a Sensitivity Coefficient
papers.r: The scan gives a logarithmic sensitivity of 0.15 for the deuterium abundance with respect to the bounce temperature in the range examined. A bounce at 0.2 MeV would leave a residue of 2.16e-05, well below the observed value, while a bounce at 1 MeV leaves 2.52e-05, close to the standard 2.53e-05.

papers.t: Photon Diffusion Damping with a Modified Pre-Recombination History: A Bound from the Damping Tail
papers.r: A residual expansion change of one percent at recombination would move the damping wavenumber from 0.140 to 0.1407 per megaparsec, a shift of 0.5 percent, at the edge of present precision. The damping tail therefore limits any residual effect to about 2.0 percent.

papers.t: Effective Relativistic Species Through a Bounce: A Bound on Additional Radiation from the Expansion History
papers.r: At a bounce temperature of 3 MeV the equivalent shift is 0.122, giving an effective count of 3.166 against the observed 2.99 with an uncertainty of 0.17; at 10 MeV the shift falls to 0.011. The species count thus independently disfavours a bounce lying within a small factor of the nucleosynthesis temperature, reinforcing the abundance bounds through a channel that depends on the expansion rate alone rather than on an

papers.t: The Matter-Radiation Equality Epoch with a Stiff Spin Component: A Redshift Bound
papers.r: At a bounce temperature of 1 MeV the spin fraction at equality is 6.40e-13, utterly negligible; even at a bounce temperature of 0.01 MeV, already excluded by nucleosynthesis, the fraction is only 6.40e-09 and the equality redshift moves to 3400.0.

papers.t: Growth of Structure with a Bounce-Imposed Initial Cutoff: The Suppression of the Linear Growth Factor
papers.r: For a cutoff at 1 per megaparsec the variance on the integrated galaxy-scale band falls by 43.46 percent, an effect far larger than current uncertainties and therefore already excluded; at 10 per megaparsec the loss is 0.6 percent, and at 50 per megaparsec it is 0.02 percent, below present sensitivity.

papers.t: A Minimum Halo Mass from the Bounce: The Low-Mass End of the Halo Mass Function
papers.r: A cutoff at 10 per megaparsec implies a minimum halo mass of 5.16e+09 solar masses; at 50 per megaparsec the minimum falls to 4.13e+07 solar masses; and at 5 per megaparsec it rises to 4.13e+10 solar masses, a value that would already struggle to accommodate the smallest observed dwarfs.

papers.t: Helium-4 Yield in a Torsion-Regulated Bounce: A Lower Bound on the Bounce Temperature
papers.r: The calculation finds that a bounce temperature of 3.0 MeV or higher keeps the predicted yield within the stated observational tolerance around 0.245, while a bounce at 2 MeV would give 0.2365 and a bounce at 8 MeV would give 0.2449, against the standard value 0.245.

papers.t: The Jeans Mass at First Collapse with Bounce-Set Initial Conditions: Timing the First Stars
papers.r: For a cutoff at 10 per megaparsec the first collapse moves to redshift 15.5, a delay of 4.5 units of redshift from the standard expectation near twenty; for a cutoff at 50 per megaparsec the timing is essentially standard, at redshift 18.1.

papers.t: The Lithium-7 Discrepancy as a Test of Bounce Timing: Why a Slowed Expansion Moves the Yield the Wrong Way
papers.r: The computation shows the bounce moving the predicted abundance in the wrong direction for this discrepancy: at a bounce temperature of 0.15 MeV the prediction rises to 5.29e-10, a factor 3.3 above the plateau value, compared with the standard factor of 2.94.

papers.t: The Matter Power Spectrum Turnover in a Bounced Cosmology: Equality Scale Against a Bounce Scale
papers.r: The equality scale comes out at 0.010 per megaparsec. A cutoff at 0.1 per megaparsec would suppress power at 0.05 per megaparsec by 22.12 percent, which surveys would not have missed; a cutoff at 0.5 per megaparsec suppresses the same point by only 1.0 percent.

papers.t: Neutron-Proton Freeze-Out Under a Reduced Expansion Rate: The Shift in Temperature and Neutron Fraction
papers.r: The shift is systematic and grows as the bounce approaches: a bounce temperature of 1.2 MeV moves freeze-out to 0.739 MeV, a change of -7.6 percent from the standard 0.80 MeV, and the neutron fraction falls from 0.199 to 0.1738; at 3 MeV the freeze-out temperature is 0.791 MeV.

papers.t: The Redshift of Recombination Under a Bounce-Modified Expansion History: A Sub-Percent Calculation
papers.r: With the stated sensitivity, a one percent residual change in the expansion rate would move the last-scattering redshift to 1093.2, a shift of 3.3 units, more than ten times the observational uncertainty of 0.25. Conversely, the spin term predicted at recombination for bounce temperatures above the nucleosynthesis bound corresponds to a shift orders of magnitude below the uncertainty.

papers.t: The Sound Horizon and Baryon Acoustic Oscillations with a Modified Early Expansion Rate
papers.r: A sustained one percent change in the early expansion rate would move the ruler to 146.43 megaparsecs, a shift of -0.45 percent, several times the stated uncertainty of 0.26 megaparsecs. The bounce contribution on the branch allowed by nucleosynthesis is far smaller, because the sound integral is dominated by epochs long after the spin term has faded.

papers.t: The Global 21-Centimetre Signal with a Bounce Cutoff: A Shift in the Absorption Trough
papers.r: For a cutoff at 10 per megaparsec the trough centre moves to redshift 12.5, corresponding to an observed frequency of 104.8 megahertz, against the standard centre near redshift 17 and 79 megahertz. Future global-signal experiments aiming at few-megahertz precision on the trough position will therefore test the same cutoff range as the dwarf and variance probes, in an entirely different observational band, which is pr

classes.title: Quantum Fields and Particle Creation Through a Bounce

papers.t: Adiabatic Order and the Ambiguity of the Particle Concept at the Bounce Point
papers.r: At wavenumber 2 the zeroth-order definition assigns the mode an instantaneous occupation of 5.583e-04 at the bounce point, while the second-order definition assigns 6.243e-04; the spread between them is part of the pattern whose largest value across the three wavenumbers is 3.082e-02.

papers.t: Adiabatic Subtraction and the Vacuum Energy Density at the Bounce Point
papers.r: The unrenormalised density on the grid is 5.493e+01. Subtracting at zeroth order leaves a remainder of 2.015e-03; subtracting at second order leaves 3.897e-02. The relative movement between the two remainders is 1.83e+01, and the zeroth-order subtraction term itself is 5.492e+01.

papers.t: An Effective Temperature for Particles Created at a Bounce
papers.r: The low-wavenumber fit gives an effective temperature of 0.721 in bounce units, with a coefficient of determination of 0.8062 and an intercept of -0.320, measurably offset from the zero a true thermal form requires. At the highest computed wavenumber the actual occupation is 6.051e-18, while the thermal extrapolation predicts 9.553e-07.

papers.t: Backreaction of Created Particles on the Bounce: A Self-Consistency Bound
papers.r: The created-particle energy density at the final time is 1.242e-07. The background density scale set by the maximum expansion rate, whose value is 3.849e-01, is 1.768e-02. Their ratio is 7.025e-06.

papers.t: The Bogoliubov Spectrum of a Massless Scalar Field in a Bounce
papers.r: Over the fitted decade the spectrum falls with a logarithmic slope of -16.694. The integrated number density is 1.379e-01 particles per unit volume in bounce units. The longest mode computed carries occupation 1.012e+03, and by the top of the grid the occupation has fallen to 1.446e-20; at the middle of the fitted decade the occupation is 2.887e-06.

papers.t: Dirac Fermion Creation Through a Bounce and the Pauli Bound
papers.r: The largest occupation found anywhere in the scan is 2.474e-02, at wavenumber 0.3 and mass 0.5. At wavenumber 1 and mass 2 the occupation falls to 1.874e-04, and at wavenumber 1 and mass 0.5 the occupation is 4.607e-03. At wavenumber 3 and mass 0.5 the occupation is 2.860e-07.

papers.t: Mass Suppression of Particle Creation at a Cosmological Bounce
papers.r: The massless field at this wavenumber is created with occupation 3.281e-01. At mass 10 the occupation has fallen by a factor 4.839e-09 relative to that value, reaching 1.588e-09 in absolute terms. At the intermediate mass of 2 the occupation is 4.900e-03.

papers.t: Mode Evolution of a Scalar Field Through a Cosmological Bounce
papers.r: The longest mode, at wavenumber 0.1 in bounce units, emerges with occupation 1.012e+03, while the mode at wavenumber 1 carries 3.281e-01 and the shortest mode examined, at wavenumber 10, carries only 6.051e-18. The ordering is monotone in wavenumber across all five cases.

papers.t: Neutrino Oscillation Phases Accumulated Through a Bounce
papers.r: At momentum 1 the phase accumulated through the bounce is 2.055 radians, against 0.020 radians for the fixed-scale-factor comparison over the same interval: the bounce changes the accumulated phase by a substantial factor, it does not merely rescale the clock. The point oscillation probability at that momentum is 0.623, and averaging over the packet reduces it to 0.622.

papers.t: Non-Minimal Coupling and Particle Creation Through a Bounce
papers.r: At the conformal value the occupation is 1.233e-32, again at the numerical floor, confirming the algebraic prediction inside the computation. Minimal coupling, xi equal to zero, gives 3.281e-01. The largest occupation in the scan is 1.960e+02, found at xi equal to -0.50, and at xi equal to one the occupation is 9.095e-04.

papers.t: Parametric Resonance in the Expanding Branch After a Bounce
papers.r: The largest growth exponent found is 0.1339, at wavenumber 0.90. The far off-band mode at wavenumber 3 has exponent 0.0000, consistent with no growth, while the longest mode computed has exponent -0.0008. The resonant mode's amplitude reaches a maximum of 1.30e+03 times its initial value over the integration.

papers.t: Particle Creation in an Asymmetric Bounce: Unequal Contraction and Expansion
papers.r: At wavenumber 1 the asymmetric bounce creates occupation 4.811e-01 against 3.281e-01 for the symmetric bounce, a ratio of 1.466. At wavenumber 0.3 the ratio is 0.458, and at wavenumber 3 it is 218.902. The asymmetry therefore does not act as a simple overall rescaling: its imprint varies strongly with wavenumber, from suppression at the longest wavelength computed to a very large ratio at wavenumber 3, where both occ

papers.t: Photon Creation by a Torsion-Coupled Gauge Field at a Bounce
papers.r: The control run returns an occupation of 1.233e-32, which is the size of the numerical residue and sets the floor below which no claimed creation in this paper should be believed. Switching the coupling on, the occupation at alpha equal to one half is 4.087e-02, at alpha equal to one it is 3.281e-01, and at alpha equal to two it reaches 4.804e+00.

papers.t: Squeezing and Entanglement of Vacuum Modes Across a Bounce
papers.r: The longest mode computed, at wavenumber 0.1, is squeezed by 4.153 units and carries an entanglement entropy of 7.921 natural units per pair. At wavenumber 1 the squeezing parameter is 0.545 and the occupation is 3.281e-01. By wavenumber 10 the entropy per pair has fallen to 2.399e-16.

papers.t: Tensor Mode Creation and the Graviton Background Produced by a Bounce
papers.r: The integrated tensor energy density at the evaluation time is 2.433e-07 in bounce units. The spectrum per logarithmic interval peaks at wavenumber 0.58, where it reaches 1.375e-07. The longest mode on the grid carries occupation 1.012e+03, while at the top of the grid the energy per interval has fallen to 5.926e-22.

papers.t: The Null Energy Condition Budget of a Cosmological Bounce
papers.r: The violation lasts 1.507 units of cosmic time centred on the turning point. Its deepest point is -7.956e-02, reached at the centre, and its time integral is -6.126e-02. The largest expansion rate reached on either side of the bounce is 3.85e-01, and at the turning point itself density plus pressure takes the value -7.956e-02.

papers.t: The Power Spectrum of Vacuum Fluctuations After a Bounce
papers.r: The fitted slope of the dimensionless power over that decade is 0.659. The largest amplification relative to the flat-space reference is 2.05e+03, reached at wavenumber 0.10. At wavenumber 0.24 the dimensionless power is 1.759e-04, and at the top of the grid the ratio to the flat-space reference has settled to 1.00e+00.

classes.title: Second-Generation Propulsion and Energy Designs from the Transit Law and Torsion

papers.t: A Bounce-Recoil Engine: Cyclic Thrust from Repeated Compression Against the Density Bound
papers.r: At a cycle frequency of 10 Hz the engine delivers a mean thrust of 24.0 N at a mean power of 180.0 kW, consuming 432.0 kg of hydrogen per hour. At 50 Hz the thrust rises to 120.0 N and the power to 900.0 kW, while at 1 Hz the thrust is 2.4 N.

papers.t: A Bounce-Spring Docking Recycler: Energy Recovered from Spacecraft Capture by a Bound-Limited Spring
papers.r: At an approach speed of 0.20 m per second the capture energy is 0.16 kJ, of which 0.10 kJ is recovered at a recovery fraction of 0.64, with a peak deceleration of 0.017 m per second squared. At half a metre per second the recovered energy rises to 0.70 kJ from a capture energy of 1.00 kJ, and three hundred reference captures in a year return 30.0 kJ in total.

papers.t: A Fifth-Coordinate Heat Pump: Coefficient of Performance for Phase-Assisted Heat Transport
papers.r: At a temperature lift of 45 K the combined coefficient of performance is 3.65 against 3.08 for the fluid cycle alone. At a lift of 60 K the figures are 2.90 combined against 2.31 fluid-only, while at a small lift of 15 K the combined machine reaches 7.50 against 9.24 for the fluid cycle, so the advantage concentrates at large lifts.

papers.t: A Phase-Step Linear Motor: Force and Speed of a Translator Driven by Incremental Phase Advance
papers.r: The step energy divided by the step increment gives a mean force of 425 N, sufficient to accelerate the reference load at 0.106 m per second squared. At a step rate of one thousand per second the translator moves at 2.00 mm per second and draws 1.0 W; at ten thousand steps per second it reaches 20.00 mm per second at 10.0 W.

papers.t: A Phase-Transit Cargo Ferry: Energy and Crossing Time for a Five-Tonne Payload
papers.r: A crossing specified at eight full turns of the phase coordinate costs 4800.0 MJ of electrical energy, drawn at a mean power of 1333.3 kW over a one-hour crossing. A single turn costs 600.0 MJ and a sixteen-turn route costs 9600.0 MJ.

papers.t: A Polarised Pellet Ignitor: Driver Energy and Gain for Spin-Aligned Fusion Fuel
papers.r: At a polarised fraction of one half, the ignition energy falls to 9.60 kJ, the yield at fixed compression rises to 225.0 kJ, and the gain reaches 23.44, against a gain of 15.00 for unpolarised fuel. At full polarisation the ignition energy is 8.00 kJ and the gain is 33.75.

papers.t: A Shear-Capped Fusion Reactor: Power Balance for a Deuterium-Tritium Plant Limited by Torsion Shear
papers.r: At a temperature of 20 keV and the capped density, the plant produces 1588.1 MW of fusion power, of which 315.8 MW appears in alpha particles, against 12.3 MW of bremsstrahlung loss. Gross electric output is 630.3 MW and net output after recirculation is 472.7 MW.

papers.t: A Spin-Polarisation Battery: Stored Energy and Discharge Power of an Aligned-Spin Cell
papers.r: A cell of one litre stores 0.18 kJ, discharges at 0.3 W over the stated discharge interval, and returns a round-trip efficiency of 36.0 percent over a day of storage; the same litre in conventional lithium chemistry stores 900.0 kJ. A ten-litre cell stores 1.80 kJ at a round-trip efficiency of 36.0 percent.

papers.t: A Spin-Polarised Interstellar Ramjet: Collection, Thrust and the Drag Balance at Cruise
papers.r: Polarisation raises the exhaust velocity to 0.054 of light speed, and the thrust-drag balance changes sign at that speed: below it the ship gains, above it the collected stream costs more momentum than the exhaust returns.

papers.t: A Torsion-Assisted Electrolysis Plant: Cell Voltage and Hydrogen Output for Polarised Feed Water
papers.r: The plant produces 1.44 kg of hydrogen per hour. At a polarised fraction of 0.6 the cell voltage falls to 1.691 V from 1.830 V unpolarised, and the specific energy falls to 46.85 kWh per kilogram from 50.68, a saving of 7.6 percent, against a reversible-voltage floor of 34.07 kWh per kilogram that no polarisation can move.

papers.t: A Torsion-Coupled Gridded Ion Engine: Beam Voltage, Thrust and Power for a Xenon Drive
papers.r: At a grid voltage of 1200 V and a polarised fraction of one half, the beam velocity reaches 51446 m per second against 41997 m per second unpolarised, a gain of 22.5 percent, giving a specific impulse of 5246 s, a thrust of 257.23 mN at the reference mass flow, and a jet power of 6616.7 W. At full polarisation and 2000 V the beam velocity reaches 78615 m per second.

papers.t: A Torsion Dynamo: Electrical Output of a Generator Driven by a Spinning Polarised Rotor
papers.r: At 3000 revolutions per minute the conventional term gives 144.0 V and the torsion term adds 12.0 V, a share of 7.7 percent of the total, for a gross output of 2028.0 W and a net output of 1849.8 W after stated losses. At 6000 revolutions per minute the gross output reaches 8112.0 W.

papers.t: A Torsion Heat Engine: Cycle Work Between Two Spin-Density States of a Polarised Working Body
papers.r: At a hot reservoir of 500 K against a cold reservoir of 300 K, the cycle delivers 552.0 J of work per cycle at an efficiency of 46.00 percent, against a plain Carnot efficiency of 40.00 percent at the same temperatures; the spin term contributes 72.0 J of the work. Efficiency rises from 20.29 percent at a hot temperature of 350 K to 68.5 percent at 800 K.

papers.t: A Torsion-Seeded Plasma Heater: Heating Rate for a Fusion Fuel Stream from Spin Relaxation
papers.r: At a density of 1.0e+20 per cubic metre the deposited power density is 0.120 MW per cubic metre and the stream heats at 2.50 keV per second, needing a residence time of 0.8011 s to climb the stated interval.

papers.t: A Transit-Assisted Orbital Tug: Propellant Saved on Standard Transfers by Partial Phase Advance
papers.r: On a transfer of 900 m per second with four tenths assigned to the transit system, the tug saves 1691.5 kg of propellant at an electrical cost of 38.88 GJ. The saving is 663.2 kg on a 400 m per second transfer and 3586.3 kg on a 1600 m per second transfer at the same assigned fraction, and raising the assigned fraction on the reference transfer to eight tenths saves 3203.1 kg for 77.76 GJ.

papers.t: A Transit Refrigerator: Cooling Power and Coefficient of Performance for a Phase-Cycle Cold Box
papers.r: At a cold temperature of 4 K the box draws 112.1 W at the wall against 349.2 W for a fluid stage alone at the same duty, a saving of 67.9 percent. At 2 K the combined box draws 231.6 W and the saving reaches 67.1 percent, while at 10 K the box draws 42.9 W and the saving narrows to 68.6 percent.

papers.t: A Vacuum-Gradient Energy Harvester: Casimir Stroke Work and Power at Micrometre Gaps
papers.r: At a closed gap of 0.50 micrometres the net work is 1.38 nanojoules per cycle and the net power at the stated cycling rate is 1.38 microwatts for a plate array of one square metre. Closing the gap to 0.10 micrometres raises the net work per cycle to 173.34 nanojoules and the net power to 173.34 microwatts, while a 2.0 micrometre gap yields only 0.02 microwatts.

classes.title: The Dark Sector in the Limit Frame

papers.t: Effective Dark-Energy Density from Residual Shear After a Bounce: Two Normalisations, Two Verdicts
papers.r: Propagating a one-percent bounce shear fraction forward gives only 7.431e-114 kg per cubic metre today, while normalising shear to the dark-energy density today makes it larger than the radiation density at nucleosynthesis by a factor 7.442e+21. With equation of state 1.0, residual shear is excluded as dark energy on both counts.

papers.t: A Dark-Matter Candidate Mass from the Carrier Ladder: Torsion-Only Annihilation Against the Relic Density
papers.r: The canonical thermal-relic rate is 3.000e-32 cubic metres per second. Torsion contact estimates fall short so severely that the tau would still be overproduced by a factor 1.809e+67, the neutron by 6.468e+67, and the electron by 2.187e+74; no ladder carrier reaches the observed abundance by this route alone.

papers.t: A Combined Dark-Sector Density Budget for the Limit Frame Against Planck Values
papers.r: Adding the computed spin and shear contributions, together 7.505e-112 kg per cubic metre, leaves the Planck budget unchanged. Replacing the geometric term with the sixth-power neutron residue, 1.071e-18 kg per cubic metre, gives a dark-energy fraction of 1.000e+00, a deviation of 4.504e+01 standard deviations, while the fifth-power residue at 1.391e+01 would overshoot the total.

papers.t: A Clustering Bound for Dark Energy in the Fifth-Coordinate Picture: Sound Speed and the Clustering Length
papers.r: The Hubble radius is 4.451e+03 megaparsecs, so a dark-energy component travelling at light speed clusters only on that scale. Clustering on ten-megaparsec scales would require a sound speed of only 2.247e-03 of light speed, far below the value a geometric component naturally carries.

papers.t: Free-Streaming of Dark Matter in the Limit Frame: Masses That Preserve Observed Small-Scale Structure
papers.r: A thermal 0.1-electronvolt carrier would free-stream 5.000e+03 megaparsecs, erasing observed structure, while at the Lyman-alpha floor of 5.3 kiloelectronvolts the length is 9.434e-02 megaparsecs and for the electron it falls to 9.785e-01 kiloparsecs. The mass floor in this frame is the standard one.

papers.t: A Bound on the Dark-Sector Interaction Rate from Structure Formation
papers.r: A coupling of one tenth of the Hubble rate would transfer a fraction 2.172e-01 of today's matter density per Hubble time. The approximate compatibility edge in this accounting lies near a coupling of 1.0e-02, a rate of 2.183e-20 per second, against a present expansion rate of 2.183e-18 per second.

papers.t: Distance-Modulus Shift from Fifth-Coordinate Dark Energy: A Supernova Test of the Radius Drift
papers.r: The maximally allowed radius drift changes the distance modulus by -2.002e-02 magnitudes at redshift one half, -2.520e-02 at redshift one, and -2.486e-02 at redshift two. Those shifts sit at the level of current binned supernova precision and define what improved samples must resolve.

papers.t: Dark Radiation from the Fifth Coordinate Bounded by the Effective Number of Relativistic Species
papers.r: One bosonic degree of freedom at the photon temperature would add 2.202e+00 to the effective species count, against the Planck value 2.99 +/- 0.17 and an allowed addition of about three tenths. The temperature ratio must therefore be below 6.076e-01 for a boson, 6.282e-01 for a fermion, and 3.417e-01 for ten bosonic modes.

papers.t: An Effective Cosmological Constant from a Fifth Coordinate: Size of the Extra Dimension Implied by Observation
papers.r: Matching the observed dark-energy density 5.836e-27 kg per cubic metre with a fifth-coordinate curvature term requires a radius of 1.660e+26 metres (5.379e+00 Gpc), comparable to the Hubble radius 1.373e+26 metres, while a Planck-length radius overproduces the density by a factor 1.054e+122.

papers.t: Quintessence-Like Dynamics of the Fifth Coordinate: The Allowed Drift of the Dark-Energy Equation of State
papers.r: A fifth-coordinate radius drifting as a power alpha of the scale factor gives a dark-energy equation of state of minus one plus two thirds alpha. Combined-data limits put alpha below about 9.0e-02, where the equation of state is -9.400e-01; a radius that had doubled since redshift one would give -7.200e-01, well outside the allowed range.

papers.t: Growth-Rate Prediction of the Frame Dark Sector: f-Sigma-Eight Against Redshift-Space Distortion Measurements
papers.r: The integrated constant case gives a growth product of 4.742e-01 at redshift one half, and the maximally allowed drifting case gives 4.676e-01, a change of -1.380e+00 percent. Both sit within current measurement uncertainties, and the drift case defines a concrete target for combined surveys.

papers.t: Isocurvature Bound on a Bounce-Produced Dark Component
papers.r: Against an isocurvature power bound of 3.8e-02, a bounce-produced component carrying all of the cold density may carry an independent contrast of at most 1.987e-01 of the adiabatic amplitude, while a component carrying a tenth of the density is allowed 1.987e+00. An order-unity independent imprint on the full component would give an isocurvature fraction of 5.000e-01, far above the bound.

papers.t: Phantom-Divide Crossing Test for the Spin Fluid: Where the Effective Equation of State Would Cross Minus One
papers.r: With a present spin magnitude of 7.431e-112 kg per cubic metre, the effective equation of state deviates from minus one by only 1.630e-83 at redshift one, and the phantom crossing occurs at redshift 1.410e+14, about ten to the power 1.415e+01. Low-redshift crossing, if confirmed, would exclude this combination.

papers.t: Clustering Scale of a Spin-Fluid Dark Component: Where Torsion Pressure Would Smooth Structure
papers.r: At a galaxy-halo density the spin correction ratio is 1.029e-79 and the corresponding smoothing length is 6.598e-16 metres, a fraction 1.100e-36 of the halo size. Torsion pressure would affect clustering only near 9.718e+57 kg per cubic metre, far above astrophysical densities.

papers.t: Halo Density Profiles with a Torsion Correction: The Radius Where the Correction Would Cap a Cusp
papers.r: A Milky Way-like profile reaches 9.070e-21 kg per cubic metre at one kiloparsec, where the torsion correction is 9.334e-79. The formal cap radius is 3.175e-59 metres on the neutron branch and 1.073e-52 metres on the electron branch, so the correction cannot produce observed dwarf-galaxy cores.

papers.t: Equation of State of the Torsion Spin Fluid at Late Times
papers.r: The bounce-normalised torsion spin correction today is 7.431e-112 kg per cubic metre, a fraction 1.273e-85 of the observed dark-energy density 5.836e-27 kg per cubic metre, and the effective dark-sector equation of state at redshift one is -1.000e+00. The spin fluid in this form is therefore not a viable dark-energy component, a negative result stated at full size.

papers.t: Vacuum Dissolution Residue as a Dark-Energy Density: Computed Value Against the Observed Value
papers.r: The observed dark-energy density is 5.836e-27 kg per cubic metre, about 10 to the power 1.229e+02 below the Planck density. Reproducing it as a mass-ratio power requires exponent 6.432e+00 for the neutron carrier and 5.494e+00 for the electron, neither of which is an integer, so the simple residue family does not explain the value.

(a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

classes.title: Entropy, Thermodynamics and the Arrow of Time in a Bounced Cosmology

papers.t: The Arrow of Time Across a Symmetric Bounce: A Computed Two-Branch Test
papers.r: The construction is exactly symmetric at the precision computed: observers on the far branch would record entropy increasing away from the bounce, which from our side reads as increasing toward the past. Each branch has a consistent internal arrow, and neither branch's inhabitants could use thermodynamics alone to determine which side of the bounce they occupy.

papers.t: Black-Hole Entropy as a Fraction of the Total Budget Across a Bounce
papers.r: The black-hole fraction of the contents budget is effectively unity at the precision of the census. Most of what would need to cross a bounce is therefore black-hole entropy, concentrated in objects whose density lies far below the limit and which the bounce geometry has no obvious mechanism to dissolve. The entropy problem of the bounce is, quantitatively, a black-hole problem.

papers.t: Microwave Background Entropy Compared with the Temperature Ceiling at the Bounce
papers.r: The ratio is unity at the precision of the arithmetic, confirming that adiabatic transport through a density-limited bounce neither creates nor destroys photon entropy. Whatever entropy change a bounce produces must therefore come from explicitly non-adiabatic channels, such as the particle creation estimated separately, whose size is already known to be small.

papers.t: Entropy Density at the Density Limit: A Radiation and Spin-Fluid Estimate
papers.r: At the limit, the thermal energy exceeds the Fermi energy of the neutron fluid, so the spin carriers are not a cold degenerate gas at the turnaround; they are thermally disordered. The entropy density is enormous by laboratory standards yet finite, and its finiteness traces directly to the finiteness of the temperature ceiling.

papers.t: Entropy Carried by the Torsion Spin Fluid at the Density Limit
papers.r: The unpolarised spin fluid carries an entropy density comparable to the radiation value at the same temperature, so the matter sector is not a negligible appendix to the radiation ledger at the bounce, whatever is true at late times. Polarisation, which coherent torsion scenarios require, carries a definite per-particle entropy price that must be paid by whatever aligns the spins.

papers.t: A Fluctuation-Theorem Estimate for Entropy Decrease During Contraction
papers.r: For microscopic decreases the suppression is mild and such events are routine. For anything macroscopic it becomes overwhelming, and for a cosmological decrease the logarithm of the probability is itself a cosmological-scale negative number. A fluctuation origin for a low-entropy branch is not merely unlikely; it is suppressed beyond any scale at which the word improbable retains meaning.

papers.t: Entropy of Gravitational Waves Produced at a Bounce
papers.r: The gravitational-wave entropy is a fixed, substantial fraction of the photon entropy rather than a negligible trace, because a decoupled relativistic background cools only by the degrees-of-freedom factor. Any complete budget that omits it understates the radiation-sector entropy by that fraction.

papers.t: Horizon Entropy at the Bounce Point Compared with the Present Epoch
papers.r: The bounce horizon entropy is smaller than the present value by an enormous factor, and the minimum radius is microscopic by cosmological standards while remaining far above the Planck length. The bounce temperature is correspondingly high but finite, which is the thermodynamic content of a density limit: no divergence appears in any of the three quantities.

papers.t: Information Capacity in Bits of the Pre-Bounce Phase
papers.r: The capacity at the bounce is finite and far below the present horizon capacity, yet still large compared with the information content of the radiation background. The two bounds agree at order-of-magnitude level, which supports the internal consistency of the minimum patch derived from the density limit.

papers.t: A Landauer-Type Bound on Information Erasure at a Bounce
papers.r: Erasure at the bounce is extraordinarily expensive per bit because the temperature is so high, yet the patch energy is also enormous, and the computation gives the precise fraction that results. The fraction is below unity: even consuming all available energy, a bounce cannot erase everything it contains, so complete information reset is forbidden by thermodynamics rather than merely unmodelled.

papers.t: Maximum Entropy Reachable Before the Next Turnaround in a Recollapsing Branch
papers.r: The reachable entropy falls far short of the maximum. A recollapsing branch turns around while still, thermodynamically, in its youth: heat death in the strict sense of saturating the bound is not achieved even given the full expansion lifetime, because the production rate is too slow compared with the size of the bound.

papers.t: Entropy Produced by Particle Creation During a Single Bounce
papers.r: The created entropy is a small fraction of the radiation entropy already present. Particle creation at the bounce is therefore a perturbation of the entropy budget, not its source. A bounce that needed creation to explain the observed entropy would fall short by orders of magnitude, and that shortfall is a quantitative result rather than a preference among models.

papers.t: The Past-Hypothesis Cost of a Bounce: How Special the Pre-Bounce State Must Be
papers.r: The required phase-space fraction is so small that its decimal logarithm is itself an astronomically large negative number. A bounce does not soften the past hypothesis; it relocates it. The contracting branch must arrive at the turnaround in a state every bit as atypical as the expanding branch is usually assumed to start in.

papers.t: Entropy of the Relic Neutrino Background Carried Through a Bounce
papers.r: The neutrino entropy is comparable to, and slightly below, the photon entropy today, and adiabatic transport preserves the ratio through the bounce. If re-coupling occurred at the bounce temperature the background would be reprocessed rather than preserved, which would erase the decoupling signature; the preservation result therefore doubles as a statement about which bounce temperatures are compatible with an intact

papers.t: Coarse-Graining and the Second Law in the Contracting Branch of a Bounce
papers.r: Clumping produces coarse-grained entropy in contraction at a scale that is a substantial fraction of the present radiation entropy, and nothing in the estimate changes sign when the expansion reverses. Contraction is not a rewind: structures that form while the universe contracts dissipate and virialise in the ordinary direction, generating entropy as they do so.

papers.t: Entropy Growth per Cycle in a Cyclic Bounce and the Heat-Death Avoidance Test
papers.r: The claim of identical eternal cycles fails the arithmetic. With any positive production per cycle, successive cycles are larger and longer, the sequence terminates against the entropy maximum after a finite computed number of cycles, and running the sequence backward reaches implausibly small cycles after a finite count as well.

papers.t: Total Entropy Budget of the Observable Universe Before and After a Density-Limited Bounce
papers.r: Black holes dominate the contents budget by many orders of magnitude, while photons and neutrinos, which dominate textbook discussions of cosmic entropy, are a minor share. The horizon bound sits far above even the black-hole total, so the present contents are nowhere near the maximum the geometry allows.

classes.title: Precision Instruments and Sensors from the Physics

papers.t: A Bounce-Signature Timing Discriminator for a Distributed Detector Network with Computed Coincidence Performance
papers.r: A bounce, if one occurs in an observable channel, announces itself as a short, chirp-like signature whose most robust feature is its timing pattern across a distributed network. This paper specifies the timing discriminator for such a network of four stations: the unit that decides, from arrival times alone, whether a set of triggers is one event seen four times or four unrelated accidents.

papers.t: A Density-Threshold Pressure Standard: Pressure Realisation from a Polarised-Gas Density Threshold
papers.r: Primary pressure standards are few: the mercury column, the piston gauge, and ultrasonic interferometry exhaust the usual list, and each carries artefacts of its own. This paper proposes a standard anchored to a threshold rather than to an artefact: the density at which the spin-relaxation rate of a polarised helium-3 sample changes regime, a kink whose location is fixed by the spin-density physics of the sample rath

papers.t: A Fifth-Coordinate Gravimeter: Absolute Gravity Measurement by Extra-Coordinate Phase Readout
papers.r: Absolute gravimeters measure the local gravitational acceleration by timing a falling mass or, in atom-interferometric form, by reading the phase accumulated by falling atoms. This paper specifies a gravimeter that reads the same acceleration through the extra-coordinate phase channel, in which the scale factor is set by the product of the optical wavevector, a stated fifth-coordinate coupling of five per cent, and t

papers.t: A Fifth-Coordinate Phase Interferometer: Atom-Optical Readout of Extra-Coordinate Displacement with Computed Resolution
papers.r: An interferometer whose arms are arranged to cancel ordinary displacement can retain sensitivity to displacement along a compact fifth coordinate, which appears as a residual phase that common-mode rejection does not remove. This paper specifies such an instrument on the platform of a Raman atom interferometer, with a stated extra-coordinate coupling of five per cent of the optical wavevector product.

papers.t: A Phase-Step Position Encoder with Nanometre-Scale Computed Resolution and a Full Accuracy Budget
papers.r: Resolution is the cheapest specification in position encoding and accuracy is the expensive one; data sheets quote the first and bury the second. This paper specifies a position encoder whose readout follows the transit phase-step structure, subdividing a forty-micrometre scale pitch into 8192 phase steps, and it reports both numbers with equal prominence. The computed resolution is 4.88 nanometres.

papers.t: A Polarised-Film Radiation Dosimeter: Computed Dose Response, Minimum Detectable Dose and Range of a Spin-Polarised Film Badge
papers.r: Radiation dose in a polarised material leaves a permanent record: ionising events destroy polarisation in proportion to dose, and a polarimetric readout afterwards recovers the accumulated exposure. This paper specifies a badge dosimeter on that principle and computes its dosimetric characteristics.

papers.t: A Polarised-Target Neutron Flux Monitor Using a Spin-Polarised Helium-3 Cell
papers.r: Beamline neutron flux is usually monitored by fission chambers or activation foils, instruments that report a count but carry no spin information. A spin-polarised helium-3 cell monitors flux and polarisation together, because its capture cross section depends on the relative spin orientation of neutron and nucleus.

papers.t: A Shear-Capped Centrifuge Governor with a Computed Trip Speed, Overshoot Budget and Containment Margin
papers.r: Centrifuge overspeed is a low-frequency, high-consequence failure: rotors store enough energy to destroy their housings, and the protection is usually a speed switch whose setting is a matter of procedure.

papers.t: A Shear-Threshold Impact Sensor with a Computed Trip Level, Response Time and False-Trigger Behaviour
papers.r: Threshold sensors fail in two ways: they trip late, or they trip when nothing happened. This paper specifies an impact sensor whose trip level is set by a shear-cap analogue drawn from the density-limit framework, and computes both failure modes.

papers.t: A Spin-Current Detector Based on the Inverse Spin Hall Effect in a Platinum Strip with Computed Voltage Sensitivity
papers.r: Spin currents carry angular momentum without net charge flow, and in a torsion-sourced framework they are also the form in which spin information moves between a source and a sensor. Detecting them electrically is done through the inverse spin Hall effect, which converts a spin current into a transverse voltage in a heavy metal.

papers.t: A Spin-Polarisation Magnetometer: Computed Sensitivity of a Dense Polarised Alkali Ensemble
papers.r: A dense, highly polarised alkali vapour is a magnetic sensor whose fundamental noise limits lie far below what practical instruments achieve, and the gap between the two is where magnetometer design actually happens.

papers.t: A Torsion-Coupled Seismometer for Rotational Ground Motion with a Computed Angular Noise Floor
papers.r: Rotational ground motion is the neglected half of seismology: conventional seismometers record translation, and rotation is recovered, if at all, by differencing separated instruments. A torsion pendulum records rotation directly, and in the framework used here it carries a second coupling, to torsion itself, through its suspension fibre.

papers.t: A Torsion Gradiometer Array: Differential Spin-Precession Sensing of Torsion Gradients with a Computed Noise Floor
papers.r: A torsion gradient is the spatial rate of change of the torsion field, and in the Einstein-Cartan framework it is the quantity that a laboratory instrument can hope to register without waiting for astrophysical densities. This paper specifies an array of sixteen spin-ensemble pairs on a 0.40 m baseline that reads the gradient through differential spin precession.

papers.t: A Torsion-Modulated Atomic Clock Comparison Unit: Differential Optical Clock Readout of a Torsion Coupling
papers.r: Optical clocks now compare frequencies at levels where a new coupling, if it exists, has nowhere to hide except below the systematic floor. This paper specifies a differential comparison unit that looks for a torsion coupling in the one place it could appear cleanly: as a modulation of the frequency ratio between two clocks of different species, driven by a rotating polarised source whose torsion field at the clocks

papers.t: A Transit-Beacon Receiver: Link Budget, Sensitivity and Acquisition Behaviour for Phase-Step Beacon Signals
papers.r: A beacon organised by the transit law's phase steps is only as useful as the receiver that can find it: a narrowband, structured signal that must be acquired against Doppler uncertainty and noise. This paper specifies the companion receiver to such a beacon and computes its link performance end to end.

papers.t: A Transit-Phase Ranging Unit: Distance Measurement by Phase-Step Counting with Computed Resolution and Ambiguity Range
papers.r: Ranging by phase has a characteristic two-scale structure: a fine interpolation within one period and a coarse ambiguity across periods, and most practical systems bolt the two together from separate waveforms. A waveform organised by the transit law's phase steps carries both scales natively, whole steps for the coarse count and intra-step phase for the fine interpolation.

papers.t: A Vacuum-Gradient Microbalance: Torsion Readout of Vacuum Energy Density Gradients with a Computed Force Floor
papers.r: If vacuum energy density varies in space, its gradient exerts a force on matter, and the instrument for that force is a torsion balance pushed to its thermal limit. This paper specifies a vacuum-gradient microbalance: a torsion pendulum of constant 1.0e-8 newton metres per radian whose test body is cycled between two vacuum landscapes defined by movable boundary plates.

homework.q: Take the paper “A Bounce-Signature Timing Discriminator for a Distributed Detector Network with Computed Coincidence Performance”. Its stated result is: A bounce, if one occurs in an observable channel, announces itself as a short, chirp-like signature whose most robust feature is its timing pattern across a distributed network. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

classes.title: Primordial Perturbations, Non-Gaussianity and the Power Spectrum Through a Bounce

papers.t: Equilateral Non-Gaussianity and the Effective Sound Speed of Perturbations at the Bounce
papers.r: Equilateral non-Gaussianity arises from derivative interactions among perturbations of comparable wavelength, and in most early-universe models it is controlled by the sound speed of the scalar perturbations. This paper computes it for perturbations crossing a torsion-regulated bounce, where the torsion contribution modifies the effective sound speed during the crossing epoch.

papers.t: Isocurvature Perturbations Through a Bounce: Amplification of Entropy Modes and the Planck Fraction Bound
papers.r: Isocurvature perturbations, fluctuations in the relative composition of the cosmic fluids at fixed total density, are generated whenever more than one field or fluid carries the primordial fluctuations. This paper computes their amplification through a torsion-regulated bounce and the resulting isocurvature fraction. Entropy modes grow by a power factor G = 1.36 across the transition.

papers.t: Suppression of Large-Scale Scalar Power by the Bounce Scale: Quadrupole and Low-Multipole Consequences
papers.r: Modes much larger than the bounce horizon scale are not transmitted through a bounce perfectly; part of their amplitude is reflected by the rapid transition. This paper computes the resulting suppression of the primordial power spectrum at large scales and its consequences for the lowest microwave multipoles.

papers.t: Local Non-Gaussianity Generated at a Bounce: The Sharpness Bound Imposed by the Planck fNL Measurement
papers.r: Primordial non-Gaussianity of the local type is a sensitive probe of how many degrees of freedom were active when the perturbations were made. This paper computes the local non-Gaussianity parameter generated when perturbations pass through a bounce whose duration is finite, and converts the Planck constraint into a bound on that duration.

papers.t: Two Matching Prescriptions at the Bounce Give Two Spectral Tilts: A Difference Planck Can Resolve
papers.r: Calculations of perturbations through a bounce require a prescription for matching the perturbations across the transition, and the literature uses more than one. This paper computes the spectral index under the two standard prescriptions and finds that the choice is not a technicality: it moves the prediction by more than the observational error.

papers.t: The Orthogonal Non-Gaussian Shape at a Bounce and Its Correlation With the Standard Template
papers.r: Data analyses search for primordial non-Gaussianity with a small set of standard templates, so a model's bispectrum matters observationally only through its overlap with those templates. This paper computes the overlap of the bounce-generated bispectrum with the orthogonal template and the amplitude the orthogonal search would report.

papers.t: Oscillatory Features in the Primordial Spectrum From the Phase Accumulated Through a Bounce
papers.r: A bounce imprints a phase on every perturbation mode that passes through it, and a phase that varies with wavenumber appears in the power spectrum as an oscillation. This paper computes the amplitude and frequency of that ringing for a torsion-regulated bounce and states the size of the signal that feature searches should look for.

papers.t: The Post-Bounce Thermal History as a Source of Tilt Uncertainty: Reheating Temperature Bounds From the Spectral Index
papers.r: The spectral index measured today depends, in a bounce cosmology, on the thermal history after the bounce, because that history decides how much expansion separates the bounce from the crossing of the pivot mode. This paper quantifies the dependence and inverts it into a bound on the reheating temperature.

papers.t: Second-Order Running of the Primordial Spectrum Through the Bounce: A Prediction Below the Planck Central Value
papers.r: This paper computes the second-order running of the scalar spectrum, beta, for a bounce in which the scale dependence of the shear fraction itself changes across the observable window. Allowing the scaling exponent to vary linearly in the logarithm of wavenumber, with slope delta = -0.60, gives alpha = -0.002109 and beta = 0.01042 at the pivot, the beta value confirmed by an independent finite-difference evaluation i

papers.t: Running of the Scalar Spectral Index From a Scale-Dependent Shear Fraction at the Bounce
papers.r: If the conditions at a bounce vary with the scale crossing it, the spectral index runs. This paper computes the running produced when the shear fraction at crossing scales with wavenumber as a power law, f(k) = f* (k/k*)^gamma, and compares it with the Planck measurement. At the fiducial scaling exponent gamma = 0.12, the running at the pivot is alpha = -0.002109 and the running of the running is beta = -0.00012656.

papers.t: The Scalar Amplitude Cannot Be Generated at the Bounce Itself: A Shortfall of Twenty-Seven Orders of Magnitude
papers.r: This paper tests a specific and widely assumed claim: that the observed scalar perturbations could have been generated as vacuum fluctuations at the moment of a torsion-regulated bounce. The arithmetic says they could not.

papers.t: The Scalar Spectral Index Through a Torsion-Regulated Bounce: The Shear Fraction Required by the Planck Tilt
papers.r: This paper computes the primordial scalar spectral index produced when curvature perturbations cross the horizon through a torsion-regulated bounce, and inverts the calculation to find the bounce shear fraction that the observed tilt requires. In the model studied, the tilt obeys ns = 1 - 2 sqrt(f), with f the ratio of shear energy density to total density at crossing.

papers.t: The Scalar Spectral Index Across Ten Decades of Wavenumber in a Bounce Spectrum
papers.r: A single spectral index quoted at a pivot scale conceals how much the index itself varies across the full range of scales that different observations probe. This paper tabulates the scalar index of the bounce spectrum from k = 1e-4 to 50 per megaparsec, ten decades short of the full range in logarithmic terms covered by microwave, large-scale-structure, Lyman-alpha, and spectral-distortion probes taken together.

papers.t: The Tensor Power Spectrum Through the Bounce and the Expected B-Mode Signal at the Recombination Peak
papers.r: This paper assembles the tensor power spectrum implied by the bounce calculations of the tensor amplitude and tilt, and converts it into the B-mode polarisation signal an observer would measure. With a tensor-to-scalar ratio of 0.011 at the pivot and a blue tensor tilt of 0.018, the ratio at the microwave scale k = 0.002 per megaparsec is r = 0.009272, because the ratio itself runs with the exponent 0.0531 set by the

papers.t: A Blue Tensor Tilt Through the Bounce: Deviation From the Inflationary Consistency Relation and Its Detectability
papers.r: The single-field inflationary consistency relation, nt = -r/8, is one of the few exact statements in primordial cosmology. This paper computes the tensor spectral index predicted when tensor modes pass through a torsion-regulated bounce, and quantifies how far the prediction sits from that relation and whether the difference can be measured.

papers.t: Tensor-to-Scalar Ratio Through a Bounce: How Many E-Folds of Post-Bounce Expansion the BICEP Bound Requires
papers.r: This paper computes the tensor-to-scalar ratio that survives a torsion-regulated bounce as a function of the post-bounce expansion history, and finds the minimum expansion the current gravitational-wave bound demands.

papers.t: The Primordial Trispectrum Through a Bounce: tauNL and gNL Against the Planck Bound
papers.r: The four-point function of the primordial perturbations tests the structure of the generating mechanism in ways the bispectrum cannot, because its two standard amplitudes respond differently to single-source and multi-source generation. This paper computes both for perturbations transmitted through a torsion-regulated bounce. The single-source consistency value implied by the local bispectrum is tauNL = 4.72.

classes.title: Laboratory Analogues: Spin, Torsion and Vacuum Effects in Condensed Matter and Tabletop Systems

papers.t: Spin-Dependent Phase Shifts in Atom Interferometry and Limits on Torsion Gradients
papers.r: This paper examines what differential phase sensitivity in a caesium atom interferometer implies for a spatial gradient of axial torsion across the two arms. The system considered is a caesium interferometer with half-second interrogation and 10^-4 radian phase sensitivity, and the observable is interferometric phase and the torsion-gradient limit it supports.

papers.t: Acoustic Horizon Temperature in a Bose-Einstein Condensate Analogue and Its Relation to a Bounce Temperature Scale
papers.r: This paper examines what horizon temperature a condensate acoustic black hole analogue reaches for realistic velocity gradients, and how that scale should and should not be compared with cosmological bounce temperatures. The system considered is a condensate flow with velocity gradients of 100 to 10,000 per second at the acoustic horizon, and the observable is analogue horizon temperature in nanokelvin.

papers.t: Bose-Einstein Condensate Analogue of a Density Bounce: Healing Length at Peak Compression
papers.r: This paper examines how far a rubidium condensate can be compressed before the healing length reaches the cloud size, as a laboratory analogue of a density turnaround. The system considered is a rubidium-87 condensate with scattering length 5.3 nm compressed through four decades of density, and the observable is healing length, chemical potential and the compression endpoint.

papers.t: Casimir Energy Density Between Conducting Plates Compared with the Aldred Limit Density
papers.r: This paper examines how the negative Casimir energy density at nanometre separations compares in magnitude with the positive density bound set by spin torsion. The system considered is conducting plates at separations of 100, 10 and 1 nanometres, and the observable is Casimir energy density and its ratio to the torsion density bound.

papers.t: Torsion Bounds from Casimir Pressure Measurements Between Metallic Plates
papers.r: This paper examines whether precision Casimir pressure measurements already limit a uniform axial torsion background through its vacuum pressure contribution. The system considered is parallel metallic plates separated by 100 nm to 5 micrometres, and the observable is Casimir pressure and its fractional measurement uncertainty.

papers.t: Strain-Induced Axial Fields in Graphene as a Condensed-Matter Analogue of Torsion Coupling
papers.r: This paper examines how strain in graphene generates an axial gauge field for Dirac carriers that mimics, in form, a torsion coupling, and what energy scales the analogue reaches. The system considered is graphene under uniform strains of one to twenty percent, and the observable is momentum shift and axial energy scale in the strained Dirac spectrum.

papers.t: Wall Relaxation of Polarised Helium-3 in Storage Cells as a Bound on Spin-Dependent Gradients
papers.r: This paper examines how the hundred-hour storage lifetime of polarised helium-3 in coated cells limits any spin-dependent gradient that would relax the polarisation. The system considered is polarised helium-3 stored for of order one hundred hours in a five-centimetre coated cell, and the observable is relaxation rate, per-spin energy sensitivity and gradient limit.

papers.t: Axial Torsion Bounds from the Hydrogen Hyperfine Interval and Its Measurement Precision
papers.r: This paper examines what the precisely known hydrogen hyperfine interval implies for a spin coupling to a uniform axial background. The system considered is ground-state hydrogen and the 21-centimetre hyperfine transition at 1420.405751768 MHz, and the observable is hyperfine frequency precision translated into an energy and torsion limit.

papers.t: Spin Density in a Polarised Liquid Xenon Target Compared with Solid-State Polarised Media
papers.r: This paper examines what polarised spin density a liquid xenon target actually delivers once isotopic abundance and achievable polarisation are included, set against solid polarised media. The system considered is liquid xenon at 3 grams per cubic centimetre with xenon-129 enrichment and thirty percent polarisation, and the observable is isotopic, polarisation-corrected spin density and the comparison with solids.

papers.t: Muon Spin Relaxation Rates as a Limit on Fluctuating Torsion Fields in Solids
papers.r: This paper examines how precisely muon spin relaxation in a solid sample limits fluctuating spin couplings at the muon site. The system considered is positive muons implanted in a solid with field sensitivity near 10 microtesla, and the observable is relaxation rate, local-field sensitivity and the implied coupling limit.

papers.t: Neutron Spin Rotation in Polarised Xenon as a Bound on Spin-Torsion Coupling
papers.r: This paper examines how neutron spin rotation through polarised xenon gas limits a spin-dependent interaction that would rotate the neutron spin plane. The system considered is cold neutrons traversing polarised xenon at a density near 5 x 10^26 per cubic metre, and the observable is spin rotation angle per unit length and its implied energy scale.

papers.t: Optomechanical Force Noise and the Detectability of a Torsion-Induced Vacuum Force
papers.r: This paper examines whether cryogenic optomechanical force sensitivity is sufficient to resolve vacuum forces at micrometre separations and limit an additional torsion-related component. The system considered is a picogram-scale cryogenic optomechanical resonator at 10 millikelvin, and the observable is thermal force noise, Casimir force magnitude and integration time.

papers.t: Tabletop Equivalence Tests with Spin-Polarised Test Masses: Differential Acceleration Bounds
papers.r: This paper examines what differential-acceleration sensitivity for a spin-polarised test mass implies for a spin-dependent component of free fall. The system considered is a 10 gram polarised test mass carrying 10^23 aligned spins in a tabletop equivalence test, and the observable is Eotvos parameter, differential acceleration and the spin-fraction normalisation.

papers.t: Energy Shifts of a Spin-Polarised Torsion Pendulum in an Axial Background
papers.r: This paper examines how a macroscopic spin-polarised pendulum converts a torque sensitivity into a per-spin energy limit and an axial torsion limit. The system considered is a torsion pendulum carrying of order 10^23 polarised electron spins, and the observable is pendulum torque and the corresponding energy shift per spin.

papers.t: Cooper Pair Spin Density in Niobium and Suppression of Torsion Effects in the Superconducting State
papers.r: This paper examines why singlet pairing in niobium suppresses the spin source for torsion even though the electron density is among the highest available in a solid. The system considered is niobium with a conduction-electron density near 5.6 x 10^28 per cubic metre, and the observable is pair density, singlet suppression and residual triplet torsion energy.

papers.t: Spin Density and Torsion Energy in Superfluid Helium-3 Compared with Condensation Energy
papers.r: This paper examines whether spin-torsion energy in fully polarised superfluid helium-3 could compete with the condensation energy that stabilises the superfluid phases. The system considered is liquid helium-3 at a number density near 1.6 x 10^28 per cubic metre, and the observable is torsion energy density set against condensation energy density.

papers.t: Vacuum Birefringence Ellipticity as a Tabletop Limit on Torsion-Induced Optical Anisotropy
papers.r: This paper examines whether cavity-enhanced vacuum birefringence searches already constrain optical anisotropy that an axial torsion background would induce. The system considered is a 1064 nm laser in a high-finesse cavity with an effective path near 100 km, and the observable is ellipticity, refractive-index difference and the corresponding torsion scale.

classes.title: Axions, Axion-Like Particles and Light Relics Against the Limit and Bounce Bounds

papers.t: Haloscope Mass Coverage of the ADMX Search and the Prior a Bounce Places on the Axion Mass
papers.r: The band from 6.50e-01 to 8.00e+00 GHz corresponds to masses from 2.69e+00 to 3.31e+01 micro-electronvolts. At 1 GHz the implied decay constant is 1.38e+12 GeV, with a DFSZ coupling of 6.29e-16 per GeV and a KSVZ coupling larger by a factor of 2.57e+00, at 1.62e-15 per GeV.

papers.t: Axion-Like Particle Conversion in Cluster Magnetic Fields: Probabilities Against the CAST Bound and the Bounce Scale
papers.r: For a massless particle at a coupling of 10^-12 per GeV the single-domain probability is 2.33e-04; at 10^-11 per GeV it rises to 2.33e-02, scaling as the square of the coupling, and at 10^-13 per GeV it falls to 2.33e-06. A mass of 10^-9 eV at the middle coupling suppresses the probability to 1.53e-15, because the oscillation phase across the domain becomes large and the sine factor averages down.

papers.t: The Axion-Electron Coupling from White Dwarf Cooling Set Against DFSZ Scales in the Bounce Frame
papers.r: The coupling falls from 1.70e-13 at a decay constant of 10^9 GeV to 1.70e-16 at 10^12 GeV. Requiring it to stay below 2.80e-13 forces the decay constant above 6.08e+08 GeV, corresponding to a QCD axion mass below 9.37e+03 micro-electronvolts. These are strong statements about the DFSZ line specifically; a KSVZ axion, whose tree-level electron coupling vanishes, is untouched by them.

papers.t: The Axion Minicluster Mass Scale Set by the Horizon at Oscillation, Evaluated in a Bounced History
papers.r: At an oscillation temperature of 1 GeV the Hubble rate is 2.92e+05 per second, the total mass within the horizon is 3.47e-01 solar masses, and the scaled minicluster mass is 1.00e-12 solar masses. If oscillation is delayed to 0.15 GeV the minicluster mass rises to 2.96e-10 solar masses, following the inverse-cube scaling.

papers.t: Axion Misalignment Abundance When the Bounce Caps the History Before Oscillation
papers.r: The required initial angle is 13.80 at a decay constant of 10^10 GeV, 0.94 at 10^12 GeV, and 0.25 at 10^13 GeV. An angle of unity at 10^13 GeV would overproduce dark matter by the factor shown in the deposited table, with Omega h^2 reaching 1.99e+00.

papers.t: The Axion-Nucleon Coupling and Cooling Bounds from Neutron Stars, Read Against the Limit Density
papers.r: The coupling runs from 4.69e-10 at a decay constant of 10^9 GeV down to 4.69e-13 at 10^12 GeV. The adopted bound of 1.00e-09 corresponds to a minimum decay constant of 4.69e+08 GeV. The ratio of a neutron star's central density to the bound density is 1.03e-40: the star operates forty orders of magnitude below the density at which torsion would reorganise its structure, on the bound density of 9.72e+54 g per cubic ce

papers.t: The Axion-Photon Coupling in Two Benchmark Models Against the CAST Bound, Read in a Bounced Cosmology
papers.r: At a decay constant of 10^10 GeV the KSVZ coupling is 2.23e-13 per GeV and the DFSZ coupling is 8.67e-14 per GeV; the DFSZ value is a factor of 3.89e-01 of the KSVZ value, entirely because of the E/N term. Setting each coupling equal to the CAST value of 6.60e-11 per GeV gives minimum decay constants of 3.38e+07 GeV for KSVZ and 1.31e+07 GeV for DFSZ.

papers.t: Dark Photon Light Relics: Resonant Conversion Epochs in a Plasma History with a Temperature Ceiling
papers.r: Resonance temperatures are 1.00e-05 eV for a mass of 10^-6 eV, 1.00e-01 eV for 10^-2 eV, and 1.00e+03 eV for 100 eV. Even the largest of these is only a fraction 3.54e-20 of the ceiling at the middle mass, and the ceiling itself is 2.82e+18 eV, set by the bound density of 9.72e+54 g per cubic centimetre.

papers.t: Extra Relativistic Species at a Bounce: The Minimum Delta N eff Imposed by a Capped Thermal History
papers.r: At the largest Standard Model value, g_* = 106.75, the floors are 2.68e-02 for a scalar, 4.69e-02 for a Weyl fermion and 5.35e-02 for a vector. A scalar that instead stayed coupled until the MeV era would contribute 5.71e-01, more than twenty times its floor.

papers.t: Fuzzy Dark Matter: The de Broglie Scale of an Ultralight Axion Against Lyman-Alpha Forest Bounds
papers.r: At 10^-22 eV the wavelength is 0.60 kpc, the scale that made the idea attractive for dwarf-galaxy cores. At the forest bound of 2 x 10^-21 eV it shrinks to 0.030 kpc, smaller by a factor of 20.0, and at 10^-23 eV it would extend to 6.0 kpc.

papers.t: The Abundance of a Light Thermal Relic Computed Against the Limit Density and the Observed Radiation Budget
papers.r: A relic decoupling at g_* = 106.75 reaches Omega h^2 = 0.12 only at a mass of 1.11e+02 eV, while one decoupling at g_* = 10.75 reaches the same density at 1.12e+01 eV; the protective factor from early decoupling is 9.93e+00. To stay below a hot-component ceiling of 0.001 in Omega h^2, the earliest-decoupled case must be lighter than 9.25e-01 eV.

papers.t: Majoron Light Relics: Lifetimes, Decay Radiation and Production in a Capped Thermal Bath
papers.r: For a breaking scale of 10^5 GeV and a mass of 1 keV the lifetime is 4.41e+13 seconds, well inside the early universe, so such a majoron decays while its decay products can still affect the radiation history and nucleosynthesis.

papers.t: Multiple Goldstone Relics: How Many Early-Decoupled Bosons the Observed Radiation Budget Allows
papers.r: A boson decoupling at the top of the ladder contributes 2.68e-02 and up to 11.2 such bosons fit under the ceiling. At 1 GeV the single contribution rises to 5.55e-02, and at 5 MeV it reaches 5.71e-01, where the ceiling admits only 0.53 of a boson, meaning a single MeV-decoupled Goldstone already overshoots the adopted bound by itself.

papers.t: The QCD Axion Mass Window Set Against the Bounce Temperature of a Torsion-Regulated Cosmology
papers.r: Across the grid the axion mass runs from 5.70e+04 micro-electronvolts at the lowest decay constant to 5.70e-02 micro-electronvolts at the highest. At the reference decay constant of 10^12 GeV the mass is 5.70e+00 micro-electronvolts and the constant-mass oscillation temperature is 1.88e+01 GeV.

papers.t: Sterile Neutrino Light Relics: The Production Window Set by Mixing, Set Against X-Ray and Bounce Scales
papers.r: The required mixing falls steeply with mass, from 2.70e-10 at 1 keV through 5.51e-12 at 7 keV to 1.08e-13 at 50 keV, a span of 2.50e+03. At low masses the required mixing is comparatively large and sits in territory that X-ray non-detections exclude; at high masses structure-formation limits on warm dark matter take over from below.

papers.t: Thermal Axion-Like Particle Dark Radiation: Decoupling Temperatures Implied by the Photon Coupling
papers.r: At a coupling of 10^-10 per GeV the decoupling temperature is 1.93e+04 GeV and the residual contribution is 2.68e-02. At 10^-12 per GeV decoupling moves to 1.93e+08 GeV, still above the electroweak scale, so the contribution sits at the same floor value of 2.68e-02, the smallest a thermalised scalar can contribute. At 10^-9 per GeV the decoupling temperature is 1.73e+02 GeV.

papers.t: Thermal Axions as Hot Dark Matter: The Mass Ceiling from Abundance and Radiation Limits Combined
papers.r: For decoupling at g_* = 61.75, the radiation contribution is 5.55e-02, the mass that saturates the hot-component ceiling is 7.52e-01 eV, and the mass that would account for all the dark matter by abundance is 9.03e+01 eV. At the top of the ladder the corresponding masses rise to 1.30e+00 eV and 1.56e+02 eV.
