classes.title: Relativistic Jets and Synchrotron Outflows from Compact Objects Against Energy and Density Bounds

papers.t: Testing the Blazar Sequence: Synchrotron Peak Frequency Against Bolometric Luminosity in a Representative Sample
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: whether more luminous blazars really peak at lower synchrotron frequencies, as the blazar sequence proposes, when the trend is fitted to a representative set of published spectral energy distributions.

papers.t: Jet Kinetic Luminosity from X-Ray Cavities: The Calorimetry of Radio Bubbles in Cluster Gas
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: how much kinetic power a jet must have supplied, averaged over a bubble's life, to inflate the cavities it is observed to have excavated in hot cluster gas.

papers.t: Collimation and the Causal Bound: Opening Angles, Lorentz Factors and the Shape of the M87 Jet
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: whether the measured opening angles of relativistic jets are narrow enough, given their Lorentz factors, for the flow to remain in causal contact across its own width.

papers.t: Compton Dominance as a Location Finder: Where Blazar Gamma Rays Are Made
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: what the ratio of gamma-ray to synchrotron luminosity in a blazar implies about the external photon field at the emission site, and hence about where along the jet the gamma rays originate.

papers.t: Removing the Doppler Amplifier: Intrinsic Luminosities of Beamed Jets After De-Boosting
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: how luminous a beamed jet source really is once the relativistic amplification that makes it conspicuous is divided out.

papers.t: Equipartition Magnetic Fields in Radio Lobes: A Calibrated Estimate and Its Energy Content
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: what magnetic field minimises the total energy of a radio lobe for its observed synchrotron luminosity and size, and how much energy that minimum represents.

papers.t: The Fanaroff-Riley Break Revisited: Jet Power, Host Light and the Deceleration Divide
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: whether the luminosity dividing the two Fanaroff-Riley morphologies is a fixed radio power or a moving threshold set by the host galaxy, as a jet-deceleration picture requires.

papers.t: Testing Knot Magnetic Fields with the Inverse-Compton to Synchrotron Ratio in Large-Scale Jets
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: whether the X-ray emission of large-scale jet knots can be inverse-Compton scattering of the cosmic microwave background by the radio-emitting electrons, or whether the flux ratio forbids it at equipartition fields.

papers.t: What Jets Are Made Of: The Energy Budget of Proton Loading in Relativistic Outflows
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: how much heavier the energy bill for a jet becomes if charge neutrality is supplied by protons rather than by positrons, for a fixed observed synchrotron output.

papers.t: One-Sidedness as a Speedometer: Bulk Velocity from Jet to Counterjet Brightness Ratios
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: what the absence or faintness of a counterjet, quantified as a brightness ratio, implies for the product of speed and viewing geometry in a two-sided outflow.

papers.t: Jet Power Against the Eddington Limit: A Budget for Six Well-Measured Radio Galaxies and Quasars
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: whether the kinetic power carried by a relativistic jet can exceed, approach, or must remain far below the Eddington luminosity of the black hole that launches it.

papers.t: Stellar-Mass Jets at Full Stretch: Kinetic Power in Microquasars Against Their Own Eddington Limit
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: whether the jets of stellar-mass black holes, scaled by their own Eddington limits, reach the same extreme states as the jets of supermassive black holes, or occupy a different regime altogether.

papers.t: The Cost of Leaving Equipartition: How Total Lobe Energy Grows When the Field Departs from Its Minimum
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: by how much the total energy of a synchrotron source inflates if its magnetic field is not at the energy-minimising value, as direct field measurements increasingly suggest for some sources.

papers.t: A Magnetic-Field Bound from the Synchrotron Self-Absorption Turnover in Compact Jet Cores
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: what magnetic field follows, with almost no free parameters, from the frequency at which a compact jet core becomes opaque to its own synchrotron radiation.

papers.t: Spectral Ageing in Radio Lobes: An Upper Bound on Source Age from the Break Frequency
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: how old a radio lobe can be, at most, before synchrotron and inverse-Compton losses move its spectral break below the frequency where a break is observed.

papers.t: Superluminal Motion as a Lower Bound: Lorentz Factors and Viewing Angles for Fast Jet Components
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: what an observed apparent transverse speed, by itself and without any flux information, forces the true Lorentz factor and viewing angle of a jet component to be.

papers.t: Synchrotron Cooling Times in Jet Knots: Which Electrons Survive the Trip Downstream
papers.r: This paper addresses a single accounting question in the physics of relativistic jets: whether electrons energetic enough to emit optical and X-ray synchrotron radiation can survive transport over kiloparsec distances in a jet, or must be accelerated where they radiate.

papers.t: A Crab Pulsar Energetics Check: From Spin-Down Power to Nebular Output
papers.r: The Crab audit passes on power (spin-down exceeds nebular output by a factor of about four to five), fails the pure dipole on age by about 290 years and on braking index by half a unit, and excludes torsion as the cause of either failure by forty orders of magnitude — leaving magnetospheric torque physics as the quantitatively indicated explanation.

papers.t: Magnetar Giant Flare Energetics Against the Density Ceiling
papers.r: The 2004 giant flare spent about three percent of its star's stored magnetic energy, confirming the magnetar account's basic affordability, while its energy density fell short of the bounce ceiling by some forty-nine orders of magnitude, with a field near ten to the thirty-seventh gauss required for magnetism ever to approach that ceiling.

papers.t: Pulsar Glitch Energetics and the Density Ceiling
papers.r: Vela-class glitches release up to roughly ten to the forty-third ergs from material whose mean density sits forty orders of magnitude below the bounce ceiling, so glitch phenomenology is exactly as torsion-free as the framework predicts, while the recurring glitch power remains a sharp quantitative constraint on internal reservoir models.

papers.t: Pulsar Spin-Down Against the Torsion Bound
papers.r: Uniform dipole arithmetic returns fields near ten to the twelfth gauss and powers spanning a millionfold range for the sample pulsars, while the torsion correction to spin-down at stellar central densities is of order ten to the minus forty — conclusively undetectable, and sufficient to exclude spin-torsion explanations of observed spin-down anomalies.

papers.t: A Pulsar Timing Array Network: Pulsar Count, Timing Precision and Span Required for a Stated Nanohertz Background Amplitude
papers.r: A pulsar timing array is designed backwards from a target: the smallest nanohertz gravitational-wave background amplitude it must detect. With 68 millisecond pulsars timed to 80 ns root-mean-square every 14 days for 20 years (522 observations per pulsar), the computed detectable characteristic-strain amplitude at a reference frequency of one per year is 6.80e-16.

classes.title: Laboratory and Astrophysical Tests of Einstein-Cartan Torsion

papers.t: Atom Interferometry Beside a Spin-Polarised Source: The Torsion Phase and Its Detectability
papers.r: Atoms crossing a magnetised iron foil (polarised electron density 1.9e29 per cubic metre, torsion 6.24e-40 per metre, spin shift 1.23e-46 eV) accumulate an Einstein-Cartan phase of 1.87e-39 radians in a 10 micrometre transit, which lies 29.7 orders of magnitude below an averaged interferometric sensitivity of 1e-09 radians; the configuration bounds any multiplier of the torsion coupling at 5.35e+29 and would need a p

papers.t: Binary Pulsar Timing and the Non-Propagating Character of Einstein-Cartan Torsion
papers.r: Einstein-Cartan torsion is algebraic and radiates nothing, so the double pulsar's agreement with general relativity at a fractional excess below 1e-04 is exactly the minimal theory's prediction; for propagating-torsion extensions the same timing bounds the torsion charge-to-mass ratio at kappa below 6.60e-05 (orbital beta 2.09e-03, asymmetry factor 0.1), with a Hulse-Taylor-class system giving 2.95e-04.

papers.t: Comagnetometer Bounds on a Background Axial Torsion Field
papers.r: A potassium / helium-3 comagnetometer resolving anomalous spin energies of 1e-26 eV bounds a homogeneous axial torsion background at 5.07e-20 per metre (neutron / mercury: 5.07e-19 per metre), only a factor of about 151 above the 3.36e-22 per metre that Earth's rotation would source if bulk rotation counted as spin density — which it does not, the genuine Einstein-Cartan background at an unpolarised Earth being zero.

papers.t: The Electron Anomalous Magnetic Moment as a Bound on Torsion Couplings
papers.r: The electron anomaly's absolute uncertainty of 3e-13 against a 1.5e11 Hz cyclotron carrier converts to a spin-precession ceiling of 0.283 radians per second and bounds an axial torsion background at 9.43e-10 per metre (muon anomaly: 6.29e-09 per metre) — ten orders weaker than comagnetometer bounds, because the anomaly's precision attaches to a ratio whose large denominator dilutes an absolute-frequency coupling.

papers.t: Equivalence-Principle Tests with Spin-Polarised Test Bodies
papers.r: Einstein-Cartan theory predicts an exactly zero spin-dependent Eotvos parameter, since its torsion never leaves the source matter; for propagating axial extensions, a 10-gram body carrying 1e23 polarised spins falling toward a generously charged Earth converts eta bounds of 1e-13 and 1e-15 into coupling limits g squared over 4 pi below 1.26e-40 and 1.26e-42 — within about five and about three orders of magnitude of t

papers.t: Orbiting Gyroscopes as Torsion Sensors: Frame Couplings and the Gravity Probe B Bound
papers.r: Gravity Probe B's residuals bound an axial torsion background, for theories coupling torsion to total angular momentum, at 4.00e-24 per metre from the frame-dragging channel (7.8 milliarcseconds per year, an anomalous precession of 1.20e-15 radians per second) and 1.02e-23 per metre from the geodetic channel — a factor of about 84 below the 3.36e-22 per metre a rotating Earth would source if bulk rotation counted as

papers.t: Clock-Anisotropy Limits on Spatial Torsion from Hughes-Drever Experiments
papers.r: Clock-anisotropy sensitivities convert to bounds on spatial torsion background components of 5.07e-19 per metre (neutron spin, 1e-25 eV) and 5.07e-18 per metre (electron spin, 1e-24 eV), sitting 34.4 orders of magnitude below the Aldred-bound torsion of 1.35e+16 per metre in neutron matter and nineteen orders above the 1.08e-38 per metre that even a wholly spin-polarised Earth could source — so these experiments fenc

papers.t: Hydrogen Hyperfine and 1S-2S Spectroscopy Bounds on Spin-Contact Torsion Terms
papers.r: Einstein-Cartan torsion shifts the hydrogen hyperfine interval by 6.96e-46 eV (about 1.7e-31 Hz on the 21-centimetre line), computed from the contact term with |psi(0)| squared = 2.15e+30 per cubic metre — 27.9 orders of magnitude below the maser comparison sensitivity of 5.87e-18 eV, which bounds the torsion contact coupling at 8.44e+27 times its Einstein-Cartan value, with muonium giving the weaker independent fenc

papers.t: Muon Spin Rotation in Ferromagnetic Hosts as a Probe of Electron-Sourced Torsion
papers.r: A muon implanted in magnetised iron sits in a torsion of 6.24e-40 per metre and precesses under it at 1.87e-31 radians per second, gathering 4.11e-37 radians in its lifetime — an equivalent field of 4.39e-40 tesla — so muon spin rotation bounds the muon's torsion coupling multiplier at 1.34e+33, thirty-three orders from the Einstein-Cartan value despite a perfectly polarised probe inside the source matter itself.

papers.t: A Torsion Potential for Neutrino Oscillations in Polarised Terrestrial Matter
papers.r: The geomagnetic field aligns only 1.12e-07 of crustal electron spins, so the torsion potential for terrestrial neutrinos is 7.25e-53 eV — a fraction 5.72e-40 of the standard matter potential of 1.27e-13 eV — and even a saturated-iron target reaches only 1.23e-46 eV, 31.9 orders below the oscillation sensitivity floor; torsion may be omitted from terrestrial oscillation physics permanently and exactly.

papers.t: Neutron Spin Rotation in Polarised Matter as a Direct Torsion Measurement
papers.r: A thermal neutron crossing one centimetre of magnetised iron (torsion 6.24e-40 per metre, spin splitting 1.23e-46 eV) rotates by 8.50e-37 radians, and by 6.20e-39 radians in a polarised helium-3 cell, against a spin-rotation sensitivity of 1e-07 radians — shortfalls of 29.1 and 31.2 orders of magnitude that bound any multiplier of the Einstein-Cartan torsion coupling at 1.18e+29 for this geometry.

papers.t: Two-Solar-Mass Neutron Stars as an Exclusion Test of Low Torsion Bound Densities
papers.r: The observed two-solar-mass neutron stars exclude any operative torsion bound density below 2e+18 kg per cubic metre, while the standard neutron branch at 9.72e+57 kg per cubic metre produces a fractional structural correction of only 1.03e-40 at realised central densities — ordinary stars are exactly what the framework predicts; translated to carriers the exclusion requires only masses above 1.35e-11 eV per c square

papers.r: In Einstein-Cartan theory torsion is algebraic and does not propagate into vacuum, so a polarised torsion balance with separated source and test bodies has an exactly zero predicted signal; its scientific reach is against propagating axial extensions, which it bounds at g squared over 4 pi below 1.79e-37 for long range (per-spin energy sensitivity 6.64e-20 eV with 9.4e22 polarised spins), about eight orders of magnit

papers.r: A proton frozen-spin storage ring with a precession sensitivity of 1e-09 radians per second bounds an axial torsion background at 3.34e-18 per metre (spin-energy equivalent 6.58e-25 eV), second only to comagnetometers among laboratory background probes and with wholly independent systematics, while the deuteron configuration gives 3.34e-16 per metre and the beam's self-sourced torsion of 3.28e-54 per metre sits thirt

papers.t: Torsion-Induced Neutrino Spin Conversion in a Supernova Core and the SN 1987A Constraint
papers.r: At a generous neutron-spin aligned fraction of 1e-03, a supernova core's torsion of 5.91e-28 per metre splits neutrino helicities by 1.17e-34 eV and converts them with probability 1.40e-46 across the core; the polarisation required for an observable 0.3 conversion computes to 4.90e+19, greater than unity and therefore impossible, so SN 1987A places no constraint on Einstein-Cartan core torsion and the channel reopens

papers.t: Torsion Corrections to the Chandrasekhar Mass from Partially Polarised Electron Matter
papers.r: On the electron branch of the Aldred bound (2.87e+51 kg per cubic metre), torsion corrects the Chandrasekhar mass by only 3.48e-45 at a central density of 1e11 kg per cubic metre even with a generous polarised fraction of 0.01, and the observed fidelity of white dwarfs to the standard limit excludes electron-branch bound densities below 1.00e+10 kg per cubic metre — forty-one orders below the branch itself.

classes.title: Cosmic Rays and the Highest-Energy Particles Against Density and Shear Bounds

papers.t: A Lower Bound on Local Source Density from the Observed Flux and the Propagation Horizon
papers.r: The observed flux of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, combined with the propagation horizon, fixes the power the local universe must supply. Taking the energy density above 1e19 eV as 5.5e-22 erg per cubic centimetre and the loss time as the light-travel time across a 100 megaparsec horizon, 3.262e+08 years, the required luminosity density is 4.956e+43 erg per cubic megaparsec per year.

papers.t: Blazar Jet Particle Energies Against the Hillas Limit and the Critical Shear
papers.r: Blazar jets are among the few environments whose observed variability, field strength, and beaming place them near the Hillas requirement for the highest-energy cosmic rays, and they are tested here against both that requirement and the critical shear of the density bound.

papers.t: Acceleration Time Against Loss Time: Where the Race Is Won in Candidate Sources
papers.r: Acceleration is a race: a particle must gain energy faster than every loss channel drains it, and the finishing line of that race, not geometry alone, sets many real maximum energies. For an active-galactic-nucleus jet knot with a field of 5e-9 tesla and a flow speed of 0.9 c, the diffusive acceleration time at 1e20 eV is 2.747e+12 seconds against a proton synchrotron loss time of 5.680e+12 seconds, a ratio of 4.836e

papers.t: Air-Shower Maximum Depth for a 10^20 eV Proton Under a Density Ceiling
papers.r: When a 1e20 eV proton strikes the top of the atmosphere, the cascade it initiates reaches its largest particle count at a slant depth that fluorescence telescopes can photograph. A Heitler-model calculation anchored to published shower-model values gives a proton maximum depth of 8.100e+02 g per square centimetre at 1e20 eV, against 7.138e+02 g per square centimetre for iron at the same total energy, a separation of

papers.t: Arrival-Direction Isotropy: Dipole Sensitivity as a Function of Event Count
papers.r: How isotropic is the ultra-high-energy sky, and how strongly do the event counts let anyone say so? For N events the dipole amplitude carries a statistical uncertainty of about two over the square root of N, so samples of one thousand, ten thousand, and one hundred thousand events resolve dipoles of 6.325e-02, and correspondingly finer scales.

papers.t: Composition Inference from Published Shower-Maximum Distributions by the Superposition Method
papers.r: Published mean shower-maximum depths are converted into a mean logarithmic mass by the superposition method, using a proton reference line rising at 55 g per square centimetre per decade and an iron line 96.2 g per square centimetre shallower. The conversion constant is 2.389e+01 g per square centimetre per unit of natural-log mass.

papers.t: Energy Calibration Cross-Check: How a Fourteen Percent Scale Shift Moves the Measured Flux
papers.r: Ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray energies are assigned by two techniques, fluorescence calorimetry and surface-detector estimation, whose cross-calibration carries a systematic scale uncertainty of order fourteen percent. Because the spectrum falls steeply, a scale shift moves the measured flux far more than it moves the energies.

papers.t: Energy Lost by a 10^20 eV Proton Crossing 50 Megaparsecs of Microwave Background
papers.r: A proton launched at 1e20 eV toward an observer 50 megaparsecs away does not arrive at 1e20 eV. Combining photopion losses, Bethe-Heitler pair production, and adiabatic expansion in a continuous-loss approximation gives an effective loss length of 2.419e+01 Mpc at that energy and an arrival energy of 1.265e+19 eV, a retained fraction of only 1.265e-01.

papers.t: The Greisen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin Threshold Recomputed with a Density-Bound Correction
papers.r: The photopion threshold that sets the Greisen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin suppression is recomputed from the Delta(1232) resonance condition and from the direct pion-production threshold, and a density-bound correction drawn from the neutron-branch limit of 9.72e+54 g per cubic centimetre is then applied to the cosmic microwave background photon field.

papers.t: Magnetic Deflection of 10^20 eV Particles in Galactic and Extragalactic Fields
papers.r: Charged particles do not point back to their sources exactly; magnetic fields bend them en route, and the bending is computed here for the extreme events. A 1e20 eV proton crossing one kiloparsec of a two-microgauss galactic field is deflected by 1.060e+00 degrees, while iron at the same energy bends by 2.756e+01 degrees, and iron at 6e19 eV over three kiloparsecs bends by 1.378e+02 degrees, effectively erasing sourc

papers.t: Maximum Acceleration Energy When a Hillas Criterion Meets a Critical Shear
papers.r: The highest energy a source can impart to a charged particle is bounded geometrically: the particle must remain inside the accelerator while it gains energy. Applying the Hillas criterion E = Z e B R beta c to six representative source classes gives proton maxima ranging from 9.252e+14 eV for a supernova remnant to 2.498e+19 eV for an active-galactic-nucleus jet knot, with iron at the same site reaching 6.495e+20 eV.

papers.t: Neutron Decay Length at 10^20 eV and the Question of Galactic Escape
papers.r: A free neutron is unstable, but at ultra-high energy time dilation turns it into a long-range messenger. With a rest-frame lifetime of 879.4 seconds and a Lorentz factor of 1.064e+11 at 1e20 eV, the mean decay length is 9.093e-01 megaparsecs, or 9.093e+02 kiloparsecs: a neutron at this energy crosses the entire Milky Way, whose disk spans some twenty kiloparsecs, with a decay probability of only 2.175e-02 along the w

papers.t: Photodisintegration of Iron Nuclei on Background Photons: Threshold Lorentz Factors and Survival Distances
papers.r: An iron nucleus crossing intergalactic space is dismantled, nucleon by nucleon, when background photons are blueshifted in its rest frame past the giant-dipole threshold. Setting that threshold at 10 MeV gives a required Lorentz factor of 7.886e+09 against a mean microwave photon, corresponding to a total iron energy of 4.144e+20 eV; against a Wien-tail photon the energy falls to 1.642e+20 eV, and against an optical

papers.t: The Ankle of the Cosmic-Ray Spectrum as a Pair-Production Feature: Threshold Arithmetic
papers.r: The hardening of the cosmic-ray spectrum near 5e18 eV, the ankle, is tested against the pair-production interpretation by direct threshold arithmetic. For a proton colliding head-on with a microwave-background photon, the Bethe-Heitler threshold for producing an electron-positron pair is 7.567e+17 eV at the mean photon energy and 2.998e+17 eV for a Wien-tail photon, with 4.797e+17 eV at 1e-03 eV.

papers.t: The Cosmogenic Neutrino Flux Implied by the Observed Cosmic-Ray Spectrum and Composition
papers.r: Every photopion interaction that taxes a cosmic-ray proton also mints neutrinos, so the observed cosmic-ray spectrum implies a diffuse neutrino flux whose size can be estimated from the same luminosity density that the source census requires.

papers.t: The Muon Excess in Air Showers: Size of the Discrepancy and What Could Close It
papers.r: Air showers contain more muons than the best hadronic interaction models predict, and the size of that statement can be made precise. In the Heitler hadronic picture the muon number grows with energy to the power beta of 0.93, and iron primaries yield 1.325e+00 times the muons of protons at fixed energy.

papers.t: The Spectrum Above the Suppression: Extrapolation, Horizon Filtering, and What a Recovery Would Mean
papers.r: What should the spectrum do above the suppression if standard propagation is the whole story? Continuing the ankle-region power law upward and then applying horizon filtering from the photopion loss lengths gives a definite shape: relative to the unfiltered extrapolation, the flux at 5e19 eV stands at a factor 4.346e-01, at 1e20 eV at 1.889e-01, and at 2e20 eV at 1.084e-01, with the filtered relative flux at 2e20 eV

Its stated result is: The observed flux of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, combined with the propagation horizon, fixes the power the local universe must supply. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

classes.title: Compact Objects Against the Density and Shear Limits

papers.t: Carbon Ignition in an Accreting White Dwarf Occurs Far Below the Electron-Branch Bound
papers.r: In the single-degenerate channel for Type Ia supernovae, a carbon-oxygen white dwarf gains mass from a companion until carbon ignites in its centre and the star is destroyed. This paper compares the densities at which ignition occurs, 1e12 to 5e12 kg per cubic metre, with the electron-branch density bound of 2.87e+48 g per cubic centimetre, and computes the growth times involved.

papers.t: Critical Shear in Stellar Collapse: The Asymmetry Required to Defeat a Torsion Bounce
papers.r: A density bound halts spherical collapse, but real stellar cores are not spherical, and shear contributes to the expansion equation with the opposite effect. This paper computes the critical shear at which that halt would fail, on three carrier branches, and compares it with the shear a collapsing core can plausibly carry.

papers.t: Electron-Capture Collapse of Oxygen-Neon-Magnesium Cores and Its Shift Under the Electron-Branch Bound
papers.r: Some supernovae begin not with an iron core but with an oxygen-neon-magnesium core that collapses when electron captures remove its pressure support at a sharply defined density. Because the trigger is an electron process with a density threshold, it is a natural candidate for modification by the electron-branch density bound.

papers.t: Horizon Formation in Stellar Collapse Occurs at Densities Far Below the Density Bound
papers.r: Whether a density bound can prevent black hole formation in stellar collapse depends on a race: the collapsing matter must reach the bound before its radius falls inside its Schwarzschild radius. This paper computes the density of a collapsing mass at the moment of horizon formation, rho_H = 3 c^6 / (32 pi G^3 M^2), for progenitors from 3 to 100 solar masses, and finds the mass at which the race would be tied.

papers.t: Hybrid Stars and Twin Configurations: Phase-Transition Densities Tested Against the Density and Shear Bounds
papers.r: A strong first-order transition from hadronic to quark matter inside a neutron star can produce hybrid stars, and in some models a second, disconnected family of twin stars with the same mass but smaller radii. This paper tests the transition region, two to five times saturation density, against every branch of the density bound that could apply to it, and against the critical shear.

papers.t: Magnetic Stress in Magnetars Compared with the Critical Shear Density of the Bound
papers.r: Magnetars carry the strongest known magnetic fields, and magnetic stress is a genuine source of anisotropy in a neutron star, which makes it the one stellar agent that speaks the same language as shear.

papers.t: Prompt Collapse Thresholds in Binary Neutron Star Mergers and Their Shift Under the Density Bound
papers.r: When two neutron stars merge, the remnant either collapses promptly to a black hole, survives briefly as a hypermassive star held up by differential rotation, or endures, and the boundary between those fates is a threshold total mass near 2.9 solar masses that gravitational-wave astronomy now uses as an equation-of-state probe.

papers.t: Neutrino Trapping in a Collapsing Core and the Conditions for a Neutrino Branch to Become Operative
papers.r: Whether a fermion species can set a density bound in collapsing matter depends on whether it is trapped with the matter, and neutrinos are the borderline case: they stream freely early in the collapse and are trapped once the core grows dense enough. This paper computes the trapping transition with a standard mean-free-path scaling and evaluates the fractions of both candidate bounds at trapping.

papers.t: A Bound on the Correction to the Neutron Star Maximum Mass from the Density Limit
papers.r: The maximum mass of a neutron star is set by the behaviour of matter at several times nuclear saturation density, the highest densities known to occur in stable objects. This paper asks how large a correction the neutron-branch density bound of 9.72e+54 g per cubic centimetre can make to that maximum.

papers.t: Mass Shedding, Observed Spin and the Rotation Rate Implied by the Density Bound in Neutron Stars
papers.r: The fastest neutron stars rotate hundreds of times per second, close enough to their mass-shedding limit that spin is a real structural constraint. This paper sets three rotation scales side by side: the observed spins of millisecond pulsars up to 716 Hz, the Kepler frequency of 1.650e+03 Hz for a canonical 1.4-solar-mass, 12 km star, and the rotation rate of 2.62e+23 Hz that a star compressed to the neutron-branch d

papers.t: Pair-Instability Collapse and Explosion Are Decided at Densities Far Below the Density Bound
papers.r: The most massive stars meet an instability with no counterpart at lower masses: their cores grow hot enough that photons convert to electron-positron pairs, pressure support softens, and the core contracts or disrupts depending on its mass.

papers.t: The Radius Floor for a Protoneutron Star Implied by the Neutron-Branch Bound
papers.r: A density bound implies a smallest possible radius for a given mass: compress a star to the bound density and it can shrink no further. For a newborn protoneutron star this paper evaluates that floor and places it beside the star's actual radius and its Schwarzschild radius.

papers.t: Strange Quark Matter Densities Compared with the Up- and Down-Quark Branches of the Bound
papers.r: If strange quark matter is the true ground state of dense matter, self-bound quark stars could exist with central densities modestly above nuclear saturation and surfaces at nearly constant density. Because their spin carriers would be quarks rather than nucleons, the operative density bound for such objects sits on the quark branches.

papers.t: The Density Gap Between Supernova Core Bounce and the Neutron-Branch Density Bound
papers.r: In a core-collapse supernova the infalling iron core halts at nuclear density, rebounds, and launches the shock whose revival remains the central problem of supernova theory. Because the halt is called a bounce, it invites confusion with the turnaround that a spin-torsion density bound would produce. This paper separates the two events numerically.

papers.t: The Spin-Torsion Energy Available at Supernova Bounce Is Too Small to Power Any Part of the Explosion
papers.r: This paper addresses a specific claim by arithmetic: that spin-torsion energy released at the density bound could contribute to exploding a collapsing star. At the density where a real core bounces, 3e17 kg per cubic metre, the torsion energy density on the neutron branch is 8.324e-07 joules per cubic metre, and integrated over a 10 km core it totals 3.487e+06 joules.

papers.t: The Chandrasekhar Mass Corrected by the Electron-Branch Density Bound
papers.r: The Chandrasekhar mass is the best-known density-related bound in stellar astrophysics, so it is the natural first place to ask whether a spin-torsion density ceiling changes a stellar limit. This paper recomputes the limiting mass of 1.456 solar masses for a mean molecular weight per electron of two, places finite central densities for near-limit white dwarfs between 1e9 and 1e13 kg per cubic metre against the elect

papers.t: Central Densities Along the White Dwarf Sequence Compared with the Electron-Branch Bound
papers.r: White dwarfs span a wide range of central densities along their mass sequence, and the most massive of them are the densest stable stars short of neutron stars. This paper computes radii from the standard mass-radius relation, estimates central densities with a polytropic concentration factor, and places six masses from 0.4 to 1.35 solar masses against the electron-branch density bound.

classes.title: Stellar Death: Supernovae, Kilonovae and Gamma-Ray Bursts Against the Density and Shear Limits

papers.t: Cooling Duration of the Supernova Neutrino Signal as a Remnant Mass Measure
papers.r: Cooling duration grows from 7.0 s at 1.4 solar masses (binding energy 1.53e53 erg) to 14.2 s at 2.0 solar masses in the adopted scaling, a separation large compared with timing precision for a Galactic event, giving a remnant-mass inference good to roughly a tenth of a solar mass after the radius systematic.

papers.t: Core Bounce Density in Massive Progenitors Compared with the Torsion Density Ceiling
papers.r: Across progenitors from 12 to 40 solar masses, bounce densities of 2.8e14 to 6.1e14 g/cm3 remain 40.2 to 40.5 orders of magnitude below the torsion density ceiling of 9.72e54 g/cm3; no plausible equation-of-state or rotation variation closes that separation, so ordinary core bounce does not directly probe the ceiling.

papers.t: Densities and Temperatures in Collapsar Accretion Disks Compared with Nuclear and Ceiling Scales
papers.r: At 100 km the collapsar disk reaches 2.0e11 g/cm3 and 3.0e10 K, some 43.7 orders of magnitude below the torsion ceiling and three orders below nuclear saturation, certifying that collapsar jet physics is governed by neutrino and magnetic processes with negligible torsion corrections at any disk radius.

papers.t: Edges of the Pair-Instability Mass Gap from Helium Core Burning
papers.r: Pulsational pair instability begins at helium-core masses near 40 solar masses and full disruption spans 65 to 130 solar masses, leaving a remnant black-hole mass gap from about 45 to 130 solar masses; a black hole inside the gap, such as the primary of GW190521, requires a formation channel beyond isolated collapse or a substantial shift in the carbon-oxygen reaction rate.

papers.t: Ejecta Mass Budget of GW170817: Dynamical, Wind and Secular Components
papers.r: The three-component budget for GW170817 totals 0.053 solar masses of ejecta (0.008 dynamical, 0.020 wind, 0.025 secular disk), with the dynamical component contributing about 15 percent of the mass but the highest kinetic energy per unit mass; the wind and secular components require a remnant that survived at least briefly rather than collapsing promptly.

papers.t: Electron Fraction Windows for Weak and Main r-Process Production in Neutrino-Driven Winds
papers.r: The neutron-to-seed proxy reaches 28.6 at electron fraction 0.42 and falls to 15.4 at 0.48; main r-process production requires electron fractions below about 0.45 and weak production extends to about 0.50, a window modern neutrino-driven winds reach only briefly — a negative result for winds as the dominant main-process site.

papers.t: Extended Emission in Short Gamma-Ray Bursts: Energy and Duration Constraints on the Remnant
papers.r: Extended emission carries 5e49 to 2e51 erg over durations up to 100 s, giving a typical mean luminosity near 6.3e48 erg/s; the durations exceed compact disk viscous times by two orders of magnitude and favour a surviving magnetar remnant, while energies alone would not discriminate between engines.

papers.t: Fallback Accretion Rates and Late Remnant Growth After Core Collapse
papers.r: With fallback normalised to 0.02 solar masses per second at 10 s and a t^-5/3 decay, the rate falls to 9.0e-6 solar masses per second by 1000 s and the total late fallback integrated to infinity is 0.30 solar masses — enough to matter for remnants born near the mass ceiling but not to convert a typical remnant on its own.

papers.t: Lanthanide Fraction and Opacity Control of Kilonova Colour Evolution
papers.r: At a lanthanide fraction of 1 percent the ejecta opacity reaches 63.83 cm2/g, about 128 times the iron-like value of 0.5 cm2/g, so even modest neutron richness reddens a kilonova strongly and the blue component of AT 2017gfo required a genuinely lanthanide-poor ejecta component.

papers.t: Magnetar Spin-Down Energy as a Cap on Gamma-Ray Burst Plateau Luminosities
papers.r: A 1 ms magnetar stores 2.0e52 erg of rotational energy with an initial spin-down luminosity of 1.0e49 erg/s and a spin-down time of 2000 s; most plateaus sit comfortably below this cap, but the brightest would require sub-breakup periods and are better explained by continued accretion, so the cap sorts the plateau population.

papers.t: Neutrino Luminosity at Bounce and the Energy Partition of a Collapsing Core
papers.r: Partitioning a representative neutrino light curve gives a total radiated energy of 3.19e53 erg, in which the brilliant bounce burst (peak 3.5e53 erg/s) contributes only about 1.1 percent while the long cooling phase contributes 84.5 percent — burst statistics and total counts therefore probe different physics and must not be conflated.

papers.t: Proto-Neutron Star Mass Growth and the Threshold for Failed Supernovae
papers.r: With accreted mass growing linearly with progenitor mass and a 0.35 solar-mass fallback allowance against a cold ceiling of 2.16 solar masses, the first failing progenitor appears at 28 solar masses and a 40 solar-mass progenitor accretes 2.63 solar masses, overshooting the ceiling substantially; the threshold shifts by several progenitor solar masses with the fallback allowance.

papers.t: SN 1987A as a Calorimeter: Neutrino Counts, Explosion Energy and Remnant Binding
papers.r: The 19 detected neutrinos from SN 1987A at 50 kpc support a total radiated energy consistent with a remnant binding energy of 2.6e53 erg (inferred neutrino energy about 2.2e53 erg) against an ejecta kinetic energy of 1.1e51 erg — a kinetic share of only 0.42 percent — while the sparse counts do not support precise cooling-timescale or equation-of-state claims.

papers.t: Shear and Pressure Collimation of Relativistic Jets Inside a Stellar Envelope
papers.r: For a jet power of 1e50 erg/s the collimated half-opening angle is about 5.16 degrees with a beaming factor of 247, reducing a 1e53 erg isotropic-equivalent event to a true energy near 4.0e50 erg; corrected energies cluster near the canonical supernova scale, supporting beaming rather than an extraordinary engine as the main source of apparent energy spread.

papers.t: Shock Revival Energy Budget and the Fraction of Binding Energy Available to Explode a Star
papers.r: A typical core-collapse explosion converts only about 0.33 percent of the remnant binding energy (3.0e53 erg) into kinetic energy, and even a hypernova converts only about 2.6 percent; the explosion problem is therefore one of energy coupling to the shock, not of total energy supply.

papers.t: The Compactness Bound on Jet Lorentz Factors in Gamma-Ray Bursts
papers.r: The compactness argument requires a bulk Lorentz factor of about 110 for a typical long burst, rising to several hundred for bright, rapidly varying bursts; afterglow-inferred Lorentz factors sit above these floors, so the bound is satisfied but not saturated and low-Lorentz-factor emission models must move the emission radius outward.

papers.t: Time to Black Hole Formation in Failing Cores as a Neutrino Signal Diagnostic
papers.r: Under a hot maximum mass of 2.35 solar masses, the time from bounce to black hole formation ranges from about 0.31 s at the highest accretion rate (2.6 solar masses per second, 50 solar-mass progenitor) to 2.0 s at the lowest (0.4 solar masses per second, 20 solar-mass progenitor), so a Galactic failing event would show an abrupt neutrino-signal cutoff that directly measures the hot mass ceiling.

homework.q: Take the paper “Cooling Duration of the Supernova Neutrino Signal as a Remnant Mass Measure”. Its stated result is: Cooling duration grows from 7.0 s at 1.4 solar masses (binding energy 1.53e53 erg) to 14.2 s at 2.0 solar masses in the adopted scaling, a separation large compared with timing precision for a Galactic event, giving a remnant-mass inference good to roughly a tenth of a solar mass after the radius sy (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

classes.title: Protoplanetary and Debris Discs: Dust Evolution, Planetesimal Formation and Disc Dispersal Against the Frame's Bounds

papers.t: The Dust You Cannot See: Millimetre Optical Depths in Protoplanetary Discs and the Resulting Mass Underestimate
papers.r: Millimetre continuum fluxes are routinely converted into dust masses on the assumption that the emission is optically thin, so that every grain contributes. In the inner regions of a disc of ordinary mass that assumption fails badly.

papers.t: The Slow Grinder: Collisional Cascade Timescales for Debris Belts From First Principles
papers.r: Debris discs are collisional cascades: belts of planetesimals grinding themselves to dust over billions of years, with the dust we see continuously resupplied and removed. The cascade's pace is set by the collision time of its largest bodies.

papers.t: Waking the Belt: Self-Stirring Times, the Case for Planetary Stirrers, and the Maximum Luminosity a Debris Disc Can Show
papers.r: A planetesimal belt is dark until something stirs it: collision velocities must be raised to disruptive levels before the cascade can begin. This paper computes when a belt can stir itself — by growing its own Pluto-sized stirrers — and what luminosity it can then show, for belts at 45 AU. The self-stirring time is 2851 Myr for a one-Earth-mass belt, 285 Myr for ten Earth masses and 95 Myr for thirty.

papers.t: Shrinking Discs: How Fast Radial Drift Erodes the Dust Disc's Outer Edge, and What the Observed Sizes Require
papers.r: A dust disc should eat itself from the outside in: the grains at its outer edge drift inward at a speed that, on a standard profile, does not depend on radius, so the edge marches inward at a constant rate and the disc's dust radius is a clock. This paper winds the clock.

papers.t: Flat Layers: Dust Settling Equilibrium, Settling Times, and the Turbulence That ALMA's Thin Discs Require
papers.r: Dust settles toward the midplane until turbulence stirs it back up, and the equilibrium layer thickness is a direct gauge of the turbulence. This paper computes the gauge and reads the observations with it. The settling equilibrium H_d/H = sqrt(alpha/(alpha + St)) gives layer thicknesses of 0.10 for alpha = 1e-3 and Stokes 0.1, 0.30 for alpha = 1e-2, and 0.032 for alpha = 1e-4.

papers.t: How Large Can a Grain Grow Before Collisions Break It? Fragmentation and Drift Size Limits Across the Disc
papers.r: Turbulent collisions set a ceiling on grain size: grow too large, and relative velocities exceed the fragmentation threshold and collisions shatter instead of stick. Using the standard fragmentation-limit formula with turbulence alpha = 1e-3, this paper computes the ceiling across the disc for bare silicate grains (fragmentation velocity 1 m per second) and icy grains (10 m per second), and compares it with the size

papers.t: How Far Below the Ceilings? Protoplanetary Disc Midplane Densities and Keplerian Shear Against a Torsion Density Bound
papers.r: A torsion-regulated gravitational bound sets a maximum density of 9.72e+57 kg per cubic metre and a critical shear rate of 8.56e+32 per second. This paper asks a deliberately narrow question: by what factor do the midplane densities and Keplerian shear rates of an ordinary protoplanetary disc fall below those two ceilings? For a Hayashi-type disc around a solar-mass star, the midplane density at 1 AU is 1.36e-06 kg p

papers.t: The Race at the Heart of Planet Formation: Grain Growth Times Against Radial Drift Times From 1 to 100 AU
papers.r: Dust in a protoplanetary disc must grow from micrometre grains to planetesimals before the gas drag that enables growth also drags it into the star. This paper computes both clocks on the same disc model.

papers.t: Feeding on Pebble Rain: Accretion Rates and Core Growth Times for Embryos at 5 and 10 AU
papers.r: Once a planetesimal is large enough, it grows not by colliding with its peers but by sweeping up the pebbles that drift past it — pebble accretion, the fastest growth mode known in discs. This paper computes the rates in the two-dimensional Hill regime for pebbles of Stokes number 0.1 in a reference disc.

papers.t: Starlight as a Solvent: EUV and X-Ray Photoevaporation Rates, Launch Radii and Disc Dispersal Times
papers.r: A young star irradiates its own disc with ultraviolet and X-ray photons energetic enough to heat surface gas until it escapes. This paper computes the launch geometry and the mass-loss rates for the two main drivers and converts them into dispersal times.

papers.t: Born Big: The Characteristic Size of Planetesimals Formed by Gravitational Collapse of Pebble Clouds
papers.r: If pebble clouds collapse gravitationally, the planetesimals they make are not pebble-sized or kilometre-sized by accident: their mass is set by the density at which self-gravity beats tidal shear (the Roche density) and by the size of the collapsing patch. This paper computes the characteristic product across the disc.

papers.t: Fluff as a Strategy: How Porosity Holds the Stokes Number Down and Lets Aggregates Grow Past the Drift Barrier
papers.r: The drift barrier exists because compact grains couple to the gas in proportion to their size: grow, and the Stokes number — hence the drift speed — grows with you. Porous aggregates break that proportionality. This paper computes the Stokes number of fractal aggregates with dimensions D = 2.0, 2.5 and 3.0 (compact) at 5 and 30 AU.

papers.t: Holding Back the Drift: The Minimum Pressure-Bump Amplitude That Traps Pebbles, and How Long the Trap Must Hold
papers.r: Radial drift stops where the pressure gradient vanishes, so a local pressure maximum — a bump — is a trap for pebbles. This paper computes, for a bump at 30 AU in a reference disc, the minimum bump amplitude at which a pressure maximum actually exists, and the retention budget of the trap once it exists.

papers.t: Moving Frost Lines: Snowline Positions for Water, Carbon Dioxide and Carbon Monoxide in Passive and Accreting Discs
papers.r: Where a volatile freezes out onto grains — its snowline — the solid mass, the grain stickiness and the gas composition all change at once, so snowline positions organise planet formation. This paper computes them for water, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide on the reference disc, first for passive irradiation heating alone and then with viscous accretion heating added at three accretion rates.

papers.t: How Much Dust Is Enough? A Settling-Based Threshold for Streaming Concentration, Tested Against Measured Disc Dust Abundances
papers.r: Streaming instability is the leading mechanism for concentrating pebbles into gravitationally collapsing clouds, but it engages strongly only when the midplane dust-to-gas ratio approaches unity. This paper derives the required vertically integrated dust abundance from that condition and the standard settling equilibrium, Z_req = sqrt(alpha/(alpha + St)), and tests it against measured disc dust abundances.

papers.t: The Endgame in Numbers: When the Wind Overtakes Accretion, How Long the Inner Disc Survives, and Why a Tenth of Discs Have Holes
papers.r: Disc dispersal has two timescales — a long life and a rapid death — and the standard explanation is a handover: once the accretion rate through the disc falls to the photoevaporative wind rate, the wind opens a gap, the inner disc drains, and the outer disc follows. This paper computes the handover with a similarity-solution accretion decline and the wind rates of the companion calculation.

papers.t: The Turbulence Budget: What Alpha Must Do to Drain a Disc in Three Million Years, and Why Measurements Refuse
papers.r: If discs evolve viscously, a single number — the turbulence parameter alpha — must simultaneously set the disc lifetime, the accretion rate onto the star, and the turbulent velocities that observations measure. This paper prices all three demands on the reference disc, and reports where they agree and where they refuse to.

classes.title: Globular Clusters, Stellar Populations and the Age Problem as Tests of the Frame

papers.t: A Bound on Convective Overshoot as an Error Source in Low-Mass Turnoff Ages
papers.r: Convective overshoot — the penetration of convective motions beyond the formal boundary of a core — is a leading uncertainty in the ages of intermediate-age stellar populations, where turnoff stars have substantial convective cores Whether it also threatens the ages of old globular clusters, whose turnoff stars are far less massive, is a question with a quantitative answer This study bounds the effect using the respo

papers.t: Alpha Enhancement, Global Metallicity, and the Resulting Shift in Cluster Ages
papers.r: Globular cluster stars are not scaled copies of the Sun's mixture Their alpha elements — oxygen, magnesium, silicon, calcium — are enhanced relative to iron by factors of two or more, and it is the total metal content, not iron alone, that governs opacity and therefore evolution This study applies the standard global-metallicity equivalence to five clusters and converts the result into age terms.

papers.t: Atomic Diffusion and Gravitational Settling as a Systematic Correction to Cluster Ages
papers.r: Stars are not chemically frozen In the quiet radiative interiors of old, metal-poor stars, helium and heavy elements slowly sink under gravity while radiation levitates selected species, altering surface composition and, more importantly for chronology, the rate at which the core evolves This study sizes the resulting age correction for five clusters using published diffusion-inclusive modelling.

papers.t: Detached Eclipsing Binaries as Mass Anchors for the Age of 47 Tucanae
papers.r: An eclipsing binary weighs its stars In a detached system near the turnoff, the dynamical mass of the brighter component, combined with its luminosity, confronts stellar models with a test that distance and reddening cannot evade in the usual way, because mass enters the models as directly as age does This study converts the published component masses of the 47 Tucanae system V69 into age terms through a stated local

papers.t: Does a Bounced Cosmology Supply a Maximum Cluster Age? A Formal Test With a Negative Result
papers.r: A framework earns the name testable by supplying the quantity a measurement could contradict This study asks whether a bounced cosmology supplies a maximum age for a globular cluster — a number an observed age could exceed It does not.

papers.t: How Internal Helium Spreads Bias Turnoff Ages in Clusters With Multiple Populations
papers.r: Most globular clusters host sub-populations enriched in helium by amounts that would have been dismissed as impossible a generation ago Because a helium-rich star burns faster, fitting such a star with primordial-helium models overstates its age This study converts published helium spreads into age biases for five clusters.

papers.t: Main-Sequence Turnoff Ages of the Oldest Globular Clusters Against the Time a Bounced Cosmology Allows
papers.r: The oldest globular clusters are the sharpest local clock available for testing any cosmology that replaces an initial singularity with a bounce Using published main-sequence turnoff ages for six well studied clusters and the Planck cosmic age of 13.787 billion years, this study computes the time left between cluster formation and the beginning of the current expansion for each system The oldest system in the sample,

papers.t: Propagating Gaia-Era Distance Errors Into Globular Cluster Ages
papers.r: A turnoff age is only as good as the distance that converts apparent brightness into luminosity The Gaia mission changed cluster distances from a patchwork of methods into a homogeneous, parallax-anchored scale, but homogeneous is not the same as exact This study propagates representative Gaia-era distance-modulus uncertainties for six clusters through the turnoff age sensitivity.

papers.t: RR Lyrae Period Shifts as an Independent Age Scale for Metal-Poor Clusters
papers.r: RR Lyrae variables pulsate with periods set by their mean density, luminosity, and temperature, which makes their period distribution a clock that owes nothing to isochrone fitting This study recomputes the period and luminosity systematics of five metal-poor clusters from catalogue values The mean period gap between the two Oosterhoff groups in the sample is 0.070 days, and the adopted luminosity-metallicity relatio

papers.t: Red-Giant Mass Loss and Its Degeneracy With Age on the Horizontal Branch
papers.r: Before a cluster star can sit on the horizontal branch, it must climb the red giant branch and lose a substantial, uncertain fraction of its envelope on the way The mass it retains sets where it lands on the branch; the mass it started with sets its age This study computes how uncertainty in the integrated mass loss, parametrised by the Reimers efficiency across its calibrated range, maps into an apparent age when br

papers.t: Subgiant-Branch Luminosity as a Lower-Systematics Age Indicator: An Error Budget Comparison
papers.r: The classic turnoff age is read partly from colour, and colour is where stellar models are least trustworthy — it depends on atmosphere models, convection near the surface, and reddening The subgiant branch offers a different observable: the luminosity of stars just leaving the main sequence, which changes rapidly with age while depending far less on surface physics This study assembles an explicit error budget for t

papers.t: The Age Spread of Galactic Globular Clusters as a Measure of the Halo Formation Duration
papers.r: If globular clusters had all formed in a single burst, their ages would scatter only by measurement error They do not This study deconvolves published errors from the observed age dispersions of three metallicity groups and measures how long cluster formation actually lasted.

papers.t: The Blue Straggler Dynamical Clock: Segregation Radii Converted to Dynamical Ages
papers.r: Two clusters can share a chronological age and differ utterly in dynamical age: one may have lived through dozens of relaxation times, reshuffling its stars completely, while another has barely begun Blue straggler stars — heavier than the turnoff population and therefore dragged toward the centre by dynamical friction — record that difference This study converts published segregation measures and relaxation times fo

papers.t: The CNO Sum and Turnoff Ages in Clusters With Anomalous Light-Element Mixtures
papers.r: In most clusters the light elements trade against each other — carbon down, nitrogen up — while their sum stays nearly constant, and stellar evolution, which cares chiefly about the sum through the CNO cycle, is unmoved A few clusters break that rule: sub-populations exist whose total carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen is genuinely higher This study computes the age consequence.

papers.t: The Horizontal-Branch Second Parameter Problem Recast as a Quantitative Age Test
papers.r: Metallicity is the first parameter of horizontal-branch morphology, but clusters of nearly identical composition can show strikingly different branches — one red and stubby, the other extended and blue This study asks, in numbers, how much of that difference age alone could supply For three classic matched pairs it divides the age difference that horizontal-branch models require by the observed morphology difference,

papers.t: The Polluter Mass Budget: How Much First-Generation Mass Multiple Populations Require
papers.r: Clusters today are dominated by stars whose composition was processed inside an earlier generation of the same cluster Making that much processed material from the stars available to make it is an accounting problem, and the accounts do not balance at the present cluster mass This study recomputes the budget for five clusters from published enriched fractions and standard polluter yields.

papers.t: White-Dwarf Cooling Ages Inside Globular Clusters Compared With Turnoff Ages of the Same Systems
papers.r: A globular cluster contains two independent clocks The turnoff clock reads the nuclear lifetime of stars now leaving the main sequence; the white-dwarf clock reads how long the cluster's dead stars have been cooling This study compares published values of both clocks in 4 clusters where deep Hubble photometry reaches the end of the cooling sequence.

classes.title: Gamma-Ray Astronomy: The Diffuse Background, Line Searches and Source Populations Against Density and Energy Bounds

papers.t: A Lifetime Bound for Decaying Dark Matter from the Isotropic Background, and Why It Is Conservative
papers.r: Decaying dark matter would contribute a smooth, nearly isotropic gamma-ray component whose intensity is set by the particle's mass and lifetime. Inverting the published isotropic background intensity in a transparent, calibrated form, this paper derives a lower bound on the lifetime as a function of mass from ten GeV to ten TeV. It finds bound at 100GeV s = 1.000e+28; bound at 1TeV s = 3.981e+27.

papers.t: An Annihilation Bound from the Isotropic Background: Turning a Measured of Everything into a Limit on One Thing
papers.r: If dark matter annihilates into ordinary particles, the summed annihilation light of all halos must appear in the isotropic diffuse gamma-ray background, which therefore limits the annihilation cross section.

papers.t: Cascades from Absorbed TeV Light: How Much of the GeV Background Is Reprocessed Blazar Emission?
papers.r: Some of the gamma rays absorbed on the extragalactic background light do not disappear: the pairs they produce re-radiate at lower energies, returning part of the absorbed power to the GeV background as cascade emission.

papers.t: Clusters and Structure Shocks in the Background: An Upper Bound from Non-Detection
papers.r: Galaxy clusters should glow in gamma rays if cosmic rays fill their intracluster media, and the Fermi Large Area Telescope's non-detection of nearby clusters limits how bright that glow can be. Scaling that limit to the full cluster population, this paper places an upper bound on the cluster and structure-shock fraction of the isotropic background from 0.3 to 30 GeV.

papers.t: Foreground Subtraction as the Limiting Error: How Galactic Model Spread Propagates into the Isotropic Residual
papers.r: The isotropic background is a residual, and residuals inherit the errors of everything subtracted to obtain them. This paper propagates the published spread among Galactic diffuse foreground models through the subtraction at 1, 10 and 100 GeV, using the Galactic-to-isotropic intensity ratio at each energy, and computes both the induced fractional uncertainty on the isotropic intensity and the largest additional compo

papers.t: How Much of the Background Would a Deeper Survey Resolve? Source Counts Below the Fermi Catalogue Threshold
papers.r: The division between resolved sources and diffuse background is an instrument property, not a property of the sky. Using a broken power-law source-count distribution anchored at the Fermi Large Area Telescope catalogue threshold, this paper computes the fraction of the blazar flux that remains unresolved as the detection threshold is lowered by factors of two, five and ten.

papers.t: Line Flux Limits from Counting Statistics: What a Gamma-Ray Line Search Can and Cannot See at Each Energy
papers.r: A gamma-ray spectral line would be a striking signal, and published Fermi Large Area Telescope searches report flux limits at each trial energy. This paper derives those limits from counting statistics alone, using the measured continuum level, a ten percent energy resolution, a stated effective area and exposure, and a two-sigma excess criterion in an energy window centred on the line.

papers.t: Millisecond Pulsars and the Isotropic Residual: A Leakage Estimate for a Galactic Population That Points Everywhere
papers.r: Millisecond pulsars are a Galactic population with a wide latitude distribution, which makes them a candidate contaminant of an isotropic residual derived by foreground subtraction. This paper estimates the population's total gamma-ray luminosity, its characteristic disk intensity scale, and the intensity that a spherical foreground template could misassign to the isotropic component, for a population of forty thousa

papers.t: Radio Galaxies in the Background Budget: The Misaligned Majority and Its Spectral Signature
papers.r: For every blazar pointed at the Earth there are many more active galactic nuclei pointed elsewhere, and those misaligned objects, seen as radio galaxies, also emit gamma rays. Anchoring their component at the published fraction of the isotropic background at 1 GeV and carrying its reported spectral shape across the band, this paper computes the radio-galaxy fraction from 0.3 to 100 GeV.

papers.t: Reading the Point-Source Fraction from the Background's Angular Power: A Poisson Inversion
papers.r: The isotropic background is not perfectly smooth: its small-scale angular fluctuations carry the Poisson signature of the unresolved point sources within it. This paper inverts the published Fermi Large Area Telescope angular power measurement into the point-source fraction it implies, as a function of the effective surface density of those sources.

papers.t: Separating Background-Light Models with Blazar Spectra: The Flux Precision the Discrimination Actually Requires
papers.r: Published models of the extragalactic background light differ in the optical depth they predict for distant blazars, and gamma-ray spectra can in principle choose among them. This paper converts representative model differences at 200 GeV, for sources at redshifts 0.3, 0.5 and 1.0, into ratios of predicted attenuated flux and into the flux precision a measurement would need to separate the models at three sigma.

papers.t: Star-Forming Galaxies in the Diffuse Background: Why a Steep Spectrum Confines Them to Low Energies
papers.r: Star-forming galaxies emit gamma rays from cosmic-ray interactions in their interstellar media, and the Fermi Large Area Telescope collaboration has estimated their collective contribution to the isotropic background.

papers.t: The Blazar Share of the Diffuse Background as a Function of Energy: A Two-Spectrum Consistency Test
papers.r: Blazars are the largest identified contributor to the isotropic diffuse gamma-ray background, and their share is strongly energy dependent. Fixing the blazar component to supply the published fraction above 10 GeV and giving it the harder spectrum reported for the unresolved blazar population, this paper computes the blazar fraction at energies from 0.1 to 300 GeV and the fraction integrated over the full band.

papers.t: The Energy Budget of the Isotropic Diffuse Gamma-Ray Background: How Much Light the Unresolved Sky Contains
papers.r: Integrating the published Fermi Large Area Telescope spectrum of the isotropic diffuse gamma-ray background over 0.1 to 820 GeV gives a self-contained energy budget for the unresolved sky. The calculation finds normalisation I0 ph cm2 s sr GeV = 9.517e-05; photon flux above 100MeV = 7.200e-06; energy flux erg cm2 s sr = 4.264e-09; energy density eV cm3 = 1.116e-06.

papers.t: The Gamma-Ray Horizon: Attenuation on the Extragalactic Background Light as a Function of Energy and Redshift
papers.r: Gamma rays above tens of GeV are absorbed by pair production on the extragalactic background light, so the observable universe shrinks with increasing photon energy. Using a compact representation of the published background-light models as constrained by Fermi Large Area Telescope blazar spectra, this paper computes the optical depth, the attenuation factor and the horizon redshift at which the optical depth reaches

papers.t: The Look-Elsewhere Cost of a Line Search: Local and Global Significance Across Energies and Regions
papers.r: A line search examines many energies in several sky regions, so a fluctuation that looks notable at one energy is less notable once the number of opportunities is counted. This paper computes that correction directly: the number of independent energy trials implied by a ten percent resolution over 5 to 300 GeV, multiplied by three regions of interest, converts local significances into global ones by a Bonferroni step

papers.t: The Running Spectral Index of the Isotropic Background: Where the Spectrum Steepens and What That Excludes
papers.r: A single power-law index is a poor description of a spectrum with a high-energy cutoff, and the difference matters when components are added or excluded. This paper computes the local, energy-dependent spectral index of the published Fermi Large Area Telescope background spectrum by finite differences, together with the energy-weighted intensity that locates the spectrum's peak contribution.

classes.title: Strong-Lensing Time-Delay Cosmography and Lens Substructure as Tests of the Frame

papers.t: A Bound on Uniform Distance Rescaling from Time Delays: What Lensing Can and Cannot Say about a Bounced Early Universe
papers.r: In a cosmology where collapse halts at the Aldred density for neutron matter, 9.72e+54 g per cubic centimetre, the early universe bounces rather than beginning at a singularity. If that epoch left a uniform rescaling of all comoving distances, by a factor one plus epsilon, time delays alone could not detect it, because delay distances and Fermat delays rescale together.

papers.t: Breaking the Mass Sheet with Stellar Kinematics: The Velocity-Dispersion Precision the Degeneracy Demands
papers.r: The mass-sheet degeneracy is broken, in practice, by the stellar velocity dispersion of the lens galaxy, because the dispersion scales with the square root of the sheet parameter. This paper inverts that scaling into a requirements table. A velocity dispersion measured to five per cent constrains the sheet parameter, and hence the Hubble constant from that lens, to 10 per cent.

papers.t: Cluster-Scale Time Delays: Why Many Image Pairs Do Not Average Like Independent Measurements
papers.r: Galaxy-cluster lenses offer many time-delayed image pairs at once, most famously the reappearing supernova Refsdal, and it is tempting to divide a per-pair uncertainty by the square root of the pair count. That division is wrong when the pairs share one cluster mass model, because their errors correlate.

papers.t: Doubles versus Quads: The Cosmographic Information Content of Two-Image and Four-Image Lenses
papers.r: Two-image lenses are more common and cheaper to monitor than four-image lenses, but each carries less cosmographic information. Costing both at their characteristic per-lens precisions (three per cent for a quad, five per cent for a double, reflecting the number of independent delays and the Fermat constraints available), seven quads combine to 1.13 per cent while seven doubles reach only 1.89 per cent.

papers.t: Flux-Ratio Anomalies as a Substructure Census: The Mass Fraction Seven Quad Lenses Jointly Imply
papers.r: Flux-ratio anomalies in seven classic quadruply imaged quasars are converted, through a stated calibration between anomaly amplitude and perturbing surface density, into implied substructure mass fractions. The median implied fraction is 0.0062 of the lens surface density at the image positions, with the seven systems spanning 0.0022 to 0.0134.

papers.t: How Well Must a Time Delay Be Measured? Inverting the Budget for Monitoring Campaigns
papers.r: Given a per-lens Fermat and modelling floor of 2.5 per cent, the delay precision a monitoring campaign must deliver for total per-lens budgets of four, five and seven per cent is computed. A four per cent total allows a delay fraction of 0.0312, which is 0.62 days on a twenty-day delay and 3.12 days on a hundred-day delay; a seven per cent total relaxes the allowance to 0.0654.

papers.t: Lenses Live in Crowded Places: The Sample-Level Hubble Bias from Overdense Lens Environments
papers.r: Lens galaxies are massive ellipticals, and massive ellipticals live in overdense environments. If external-convergence corrections are calibrated on random fields rather than on lens-like fields, the sample mean convergence is underestimated, and the inferred Hubble constant is biased high by the same fraction.

papers.t: Microlensing as a Delay Contaminant: Which Systems Have Their Cosmography Taxed by Stars
papers.r: Stars in the lens galaxy microlens the quasar's accretion disc, and because the disc is not a point, microlensing shifts the measured time delay of each image by an amount that varies with the microlensing configuration. Adopting perturbation amplitudes of half a day to two days, representative of published calculations, the added fractional delay error is tabulated across delay lengths.

papers.t: Pricing the Mass Sheet: External Convergence and the Size of the Correction the Hubble Constant Cannot Avoid
papers.r: An unmodelled external convergence biases the Hubble constant inferred from time delays by the factor implied by the mass-sheet transformation. Using published per-system convergence estimates for the six H0LiCOW fields, with a sample mean of 0.0295 and root-mean-square 0.03, ignoring the correction entirely would bias the combined Hubble constant high by 2.16 km/s/Mpc.

papers.t: Recombining Six Lensed Quasars: Where the Time-Delay Hubble Constant Error Budget Actually Sits
papers.r: The six lensed quasars of the H0LiCOW sample are recombined from their published individual Hubble constant inferences, and the combined error budget is decomposed into statistical and systematic parts. Inverse-variance weighting of the six published values gives H0 = 73.42 km/s/Mpc with a purely statistical uncertainty of 1.69 km/s/Mpc.

papers.t: Redshift Leverage in Time-Delay Distances: What the Lens and Source Redshifts Buy and What They Cost
papers.r: Time-delay distances are computed across a grid of lens and source redshifts in a flat reference cosmology, and the sensitivity of each configuration to the matter density is tabulated as the hidden cost of the leverage.

papers.t: The Double Source Plane as a Hubble-Free Cosmometer: Precision Requirements for the Distance Ratio Test
papers.r: A galaxy lensing two sources at different redshifts measures a ratio of distance combinations, the beta factor, in which the Hubble constant cancels exactly. For the configuration of the known double source plane system SDSSJ0946+1006, the fiducial beta is 0.7113, moving to 0.712 and 0.7103 as the matter density runs from 0.25 to 0.35, and to 0.7087 and 0.7138 as the dark-energy equation of state runs from minus 0.9

papers.t: The Fermat-Potential Precision Floor: How Well Must Image Geometry Be Modelled for a One Per Cent Hubble Constant?
papers.r: For each of the six H0LiCOW systems, the dimensionless Fermat-potential difference implied by the published time-delay distance and a representative measured delay is computed, and the absolute precision to which that difference must be modelled for one and two per cent distance precision is tabulated. The Fermat differences span a dynamic range of 9.69 across the sample, with a median of 1.601e-11.

papers.t: The Floor, Not the Count: A Forecast of What Sample Size Can and Cannot Buy for a One Per Cent Hubble Constant
papers.r: Forecasts for time-delay cosmography usually quote a number of lenses. This paper quotes the condition instead. With per-lens precision of five per cent and no shared floor, one per cent needs 25 lenses in the pure counting limit; with a shared floor of two per cent the target is unreachable at any sample size, and with a floor of half a per cent it needs 34 lenses.

papers.t: The Slope Tax: How Lens Mass-Profile Slope Uncertainty Propagates into the Hubble Constant
papers.r: Lens models commonly describe the deflector as a power-law ellipsoid whose logarithmic slope is near isothermal. The inferred Hubble constant responds to that slope with a coupling of approximately minus 0.9 in logarithmic terms, so a slope uncertainty of 0.05 becomes a 0.045 fractional Hubble uncertainty per lens.

papers.t: The Smallest Perturber: Minimum Subhalo Mass Detectable through Flux-Ratio Perturbations at a Given Magnification
papers.r: A subhalo near a lensed image perturbs its flux measurably only if it is massive enough for its magnification disturbance to clear the smooth-model residual floor. Under an adopted point-perturber scaling in which the fractional flux perturbation grows as the square root of perturber mass and of image magnification, the minimum detectable mass falls from the value at magnification five to a quarter of it at magnifica

papers.t: Whose Substructure Is It? Separating Line-of-Sight Haloes from Bound Subhaloes in Flux-Ratio Anomalies
papers.r: Flux-ratio anomalies are usually read as evidence about subhaloes bound to the lens galaxy, but haloes along the entire line of sight perturb magnifications as well. Using an adopted variance-share model calibrated so the two contributions are comparable at source redshift two, the line-of-sight share of anomaly variance reaches equality with the bound-subhalo share at source redshift 1.11, and ignoring it at source
