classes.title: Time Variation of Fundamental Constants, Equivalence-Principle and Fifth-Force Searches in the Frame

papers.t: A Bound on the Present Drift of the Fine-Structure Constant from Atomic-Clock Comparisons, Translated into the Torsion Frame
papers.r: Atomic-clock limits on the drift of the fine-structure constant, converted under a power-of-scale-factor law, bound the power index to 8.66e-07 (two standard deviations), permit at most 6.06e-06 fractional change in alpha since recombination, and at most 1.12e-07 across the Oklo interval, against a Hubble rate of 7.16e-11 per year.

papers.t: Antihydrogen Falls Down: The ALPHA-g Measurement and the Equivalence Principle for Antimatter in the Frame
papers.r: ALPHA-g measures antihydrogen's fall at 0.75 plus or minus 0.21 combined standard deviations of g, consistent with the equivalence principle at 1.2 standard deviations, excluding antigravity, and bounding any anomalous antimatter coupling to 0.41 at two standard deviations - against the frame's published prediction of exact equality.

papers.t: Sensitivity Coefficients of Atomic-Clock Transitions and the Reach of Future Comparisons for Alpha Drift
papers.r: Clock sensitivity coefficients convert ratio precision into alpha-drift reach by division: the aluminium-mercury difference is 2.95, the same-ion ytterbium pair reaches 6.98, and at 10^-18 yearly ratio precision that pair would reach an alpha drift of 1.43e-19 per year, pressing below the microwave-background room under logarithmic accumulation.

papers.t: Composition Charges of Test Materials: Neutron Fraction, Binding and Coulomb Levers for Equivalence and Fifth-Force Tests
papers.r: Neutron-fraction levers for fifth-force and equivalence tests run from 0.556 (beryllium) to 0.600 (platinum); the MICROSCOPE titanium-platinum lever is 0.058, beryllium-titanium 0.014 and aluminium-platinum 0.081 - the materials factors that convert published differential-acceleration bounds into coupling bounds.

papers.t: Torsion-Balance Limits on a Yukawa Fifth Force Between Ten Micrometres and a Centimetre, Recomputed in the Frame
papers.r: Published torsion-balance exclusions permit a gravitational-strength Yukawa force only below about 3.0e-05 metres of range; the permitted strength is a factor 3.33e+02 below gravity at 100 micrometres, 3.33e+04 below at one millimetre, and about 1.0e-05 at a centimetre - the fence any massive torsional mode in the frame must live beneath.

papers.t: The Fine-Structure Constant at Recombination: Microwave-Background Bounds and the Frame's Logarithmic Coupling
papers.r: Planck-based analyses bound the fine-structure constant at recombination to within 3.60e-03 of today's value, a logarithmic coupling ceiling of 5.15e-04 per e-fold - 585 times the Oklo ceiling but earned directly at redshift 1090 - with a corresponding Thomson cross-section shift of 7.20e-03 at the window's edge.

papers.t: The Gravitational Constant at Nucleosynthesis: Abundance Bounds Against Drift Extrapolations in the Frame
papers.r: The primordial helium abundance fences Newton's constant at nucleosynthesis to between 0.89 and 1.04 of its present value, while a power-law drift saturating the lunar-ranging bound would imply a ratio near 1.9; variation of G must therefore be late-time, saturating, or absent.

papers.t: Lunar Laser Ranging and the Drift of the Gravitational Constant in an Expanding Frame
papers.r: Lunar laser ranging bounds the drift of Newton's constant to 2.20e-12 per year, a power-of-expansion index of at most 3.07e-02 and at most 9.90e-03 accumulated over 4.5 billion years; the same index extrapolated to nucleosynthesis would shift G by a fractional 0.64, excluding a pure power law and requiring late-time or saturating variation.

papers.t: The Inverse-Square Law at Micron Separations: What Short-Range Experiments Leave for a Torsional Force
papers.r: A unit-strength Yukawa force distorts attraction by 0.74 at a separation equal to its range and 0.41 at twice the range; the inverse-square law's verification down to 55 micrometres thereby fences mass-coupled torsional modes with masses below about 0.02 electronvolts, while the spin-coupled massless default gives no such signature.

papers.t: How the Constants Move Together: Linkage Ratios Between Variations of Alpha and Mu and What They Let Each Probe Say
papers.r: Linkage ratios between fractional changes in mu and alpha run from -0.3 to -4 across published scenarios, -19.5 for the grand-unified-like case; at that ratio a dipole-scale alpha shift would predict a mu shift of -2.34e-04, thousands of times the methanol room, excluding that combination outright.

papers.t: The MICROSCOPE Satellite Result on the Equivalence Principle, Read as a Limit on Torsional Differential Acceleration
papers.r: MICROSCOPE's final titanium-platinum Eotvos result, -1.50e-15 with combined uncertainty 2.75e-15, gives a two-standard-deviation bound of 6.99e-15, a differential acceleration below 5.52e-14 metres per second squared, excluding gravitational-strength composition-coupled forces for this pair by about thirteen orders of magnitude.

papers.t: The Nordtvedt Effect: Lunar Laser Ranging Bounds on Gravitational Self-Energy Coupling in the Frame
papers.r: Lunar ranging bounds the Nordtvedt parameter to 1.34e-03 at two standard deviations; with the Earth-Moon self-energy difference of -4.45e-10 their solar free fall agrees to 5.96e-13, a range signature below about 1.76e-02 metres, limiting any anomalous self-energy weight in the frame's source to roughly a part in a thousand.

papers.t: The Oklo Natural Reactor Bound on the Fine-Structure Constant, Expressed as a Frame Coupling Limit
papers.r: The Oklo samarium-149 record bounds the change in the fine-structure constant over 1.8 billion years to between -9.00e-08 and 1.20e-07, a mean rate of at most 6.67e-17 per year and a logarithmic-accumulation coupling of at most 8.86e-07, consistent with and complementary to the atomic-clock bound.

papers.t: The Proton-to-Electron Mass Ratio from Methanol and Ammonia Absorption: Bounds in the Frame
papers.r: Methanol absorption at redshift 0.89 bounds the change in the proton-to-electron mass ratio to 1.00e-07, a mean rate of 2.67e-17 per year over 7.5 billion years and a logarithmic coupling of 3.14e-07; under a grand-unified-style linkage this implies alpha room of only 1.03e-08, versus 2.00e-07 under an electromagnetic-only linkage.

papers.t: Quasar Absorption Measurements of the Fine-Structure Constant and the Claimed Spatial Dipole: A Frame Comparison
papers.r: The Keck and VLT quasar absorber means for the fine-structure constant differ by 8.10e-06 (5.0 combined standard deviations) with a claimed dipole amplitude of 9.70e-06, which is 81 times the room left by the Oklo record; the frame predicts no directional dipole and is excluded if the claimed amplitude is confirmed.

papers.t: Strong-Field Equivalence from the Pulsar Triple System: Self-Energy Coupling at Neutron-Star Compactness
papers.r: The pulsar triple system bounds the fractional acceleration difference to 2.60e-06; with the neutron star's self-energy lever 3.37e+08 times the Earth's, the strong-field self-energy coefficient is bounded by 1.73e-05, improving the lunar coefficient 1.34e-03 by a factor of about 77 and certifying the frame's energy bookkeeping at neutron-star compactness.

papers.t: Fifth-Force Windows from Micrometres to Astronomical Units: Where a New Yukawa Interaction Could Still Hide
papers.r: Published fifth-force limits assembled across range decades span 20 orders of magnitude in permitted Yukawa strength, from 1e+10 at 1e-06 metres in the Casimir regime to 1.0e-10 at an astronomical unit, with the millimetre fence near 1.0e-05; a mass-coupled frame force has durable room nowhere on the map.

classes.title: Fifth-Generation Designs: Quantum, Communication and Navigation Devices from the Physics

papers.t: A Cavity-Magnon Transducer Linking Microwave and Optical Carriers
papers.r: Cavity-magnon transducer (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): microwave cooperativity 250 and optical cooperativity 180 give a computed conversion efficiency of 77.5 percent between 10 GHz microwave and 1550 nm optical carriers.

papers.t: A Cold-Atom Strapdown Inertial Unit Guided by the Transit Law
papers.r: Cold-atom strapdown inertial unit (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): computed acceleration sensitivity 0.1 microgal per root hertz and rotation sensitivity 9.94e-08 rad per second per root hertz at 0.25 s interrogation time.

papers.t: An Entangled Optical Clock Node for Fifth-Coordinate Phase Synchronisation
papers.r: Entangled optical clock node (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): with a 10 MHz pair rate, efficiency 0.62 and 50 ps detector jitter, the computed synchronisation offset is 20.1 fs at 94.0 percent interference visibility, with a 100.0 kHz lock bandwidth and one-hour holdover of 1.205 ps.

papers.t: An Entanglement-Swapping Relay for Long-Baseline Clock Distribution
papers.r: Entanglement-swapping relay (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): swapping success probability 2.59e-03 per attempt, delivering swapped pairs at 25920 Hz at a ten megahertz attempt rate for clock-distribution baselines.

papers.t: A Diamond Nitrogen-Vacancy Compass Referenced to the Transit Heading
papers.r: Diamond nitrogen-vacancy compass (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): field noise of 198.41 nT per root hertz against a 45 microtesla Earth field gives a computed heading uncertainty of 0.253 degrees per root hertz of averaging.

papers.t: An Optomechanical Cavity Oscillator as a Fifth-Coordinate Frequency Standard
papers.r: Optomechanical frequency standard (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): the computed Allan deviation is 2.64e-11 at one second and 2.64e-12 at one hundred seconds for a quality factor of 2.0e6 at 4 K; the baseline design does not meet its 1e-13 target, missing by about a factor of twenty-six, and the paper records that plainly with the required development path.

papers.t: An Integrated Photonic Router Using Fifth-Coordinate Phase Steps
papers.r: Integrated photonic phase-step router (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): worst-case path loss 1.92 dB, crosstalk -37.0 dB at 0.02 rad phase error, and switching energy 10.9 pJ per element for the 8 by 8 fabric.

papers.t: A Quantum Key Distribution Terminal with Torsion-Phase Stabilisation
papers.r: Quantum key distribution terminal (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): torsion-phase stabilisation reducing the error rate to 1.5 percent raises the computed secret key rate by a factor of 1.27, to 47046 kbit per second over 20 km at a 1 GHz clock.

papers.t: A Quantum-Dot Single-Photon Beacon for Celestial Navigation Fixes
papers.r: Quantum-dot single-photon beacon (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): detected rate 10.0 MHz at calibration range, second-order correlation 0.05 certifying single-photon emission, and timing centroid precision of 40 fs per million detected photons.

papers.t: A Quantum Illumination Ranging Head for Navigation in Clutter
papers.r: Quantum illumination ranging head (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): at signal brightness 0.05 and background 20 photons per mode, the ideal error-exponent advantage over the best classical probe is a factor of 4.0 (6.0 dB), with a realistic realised target near half that in decibel terms.

papers.t: A Superconducting Qubit Sensor for Shear-Coupled Dephasing
papers.r: Superconducting qubit shear sensor (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): with echo coherence of 120 microseconds and 8000 shots, phase resolution is 0.0112 rad and the computed fractional coupling sensitivity is 1.85e-06 per root hertz.

papers.t: A Rydberg-Atom Radio Receiver Tuned to Transit-Law Carriers
papers.r: Rydberg-atom radio receiver (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): across principal quantum numbers 40 to 70 the best computed electric-field sensitivity is 2.54e-06 V per metre per root hertz at n = 70, with the practical optimum in the middle of the range once coherence is considered.

papers.t: A Single-Photon Transit Lidar for Altitude and Terrain Navigation
papers.r: Single-photon transit lidar (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): with 80 ps system jitter and 400 detected photons per estimate, the computed ranging precision is 0.60 mm; each 10 microjoule pulse carries 7.80e+13 photons.

papers.t: A Spin-Memory Quantum Repeater Node Stabilised by a Torsion Phase Reference
papers.r: Spin-memory quantum repeater (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): elementary link success probability 0.1138 over 25 km links, Bell pairs at 113842 Hz per link, and an end-to-end rate of 238.7 Hz across 8 links (200 km).

papers.t: A Squeezed-Light Receiver for Torsion-Coupled Signal Channels
papers.r: Squeezed-light receiver (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): 10 dB of squeezing reduces the phase readout noise to 1.37e-09 rad per root hertz, an improvement factor of 3.16 over the unsqueezed value, over a detection bandwidth of 33.3 kHz.

papers.t: A Trapped-Ion Clock Corrected at the Limit Density Scale
papers.r: Trapped-ion clock Limit correction (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED): the computed fractional correction at laboratory density is 9.41e-49, a shift of 1.05e-33 Hz at 1.121 PHz, against an ordinary systematic budget of 4.89e-17; the correction sits some thirty-two orders of magnitude below the systematics and should not appear in clock error budgets.

papers.t: A Whispering-Gallery Timing Resonator with Torsion Trim

classes.title: Quantum Foundations at the Limit: Decoherence, Entanglement and Measurement Under Planck-Scale Bounds

papers.t: Atomic Clock Comparisons as Bounds on Fundamental Decoherence: A Computed Conversion
papers.r: This paper converts the fractional frequency stability of optical atomic clocks into an upper bound on any fundamental decoherence rate affecting the clock transition. For a strontium-like transition at 4.29e+14 hertz with fractional instability 1.00e-18, the bound is 2.695e-03 per second.

papers.t: Bell Visibility over Astronomical Baselines: How Much Fundamental Decoherence a Loophole-Free Test Can Tolerate
papers.r: This paper calculates the visibility threshold for a Clauser–Horne–Shimony–Holt violation and converts it into the largest fundamental decoherence rate compatible with a violation over astronomical baselines. Violation requires visibility above 0.7071. Over a million-light-year baseline the decoherence rate must lie below 1.098e-14 per second; over a billion-light-year baseline below 1.098e-17 per second.

papers.t: Collapse-Model Force Noise in Gravitational-Wave Interferometers: Computed Spectral Density Against Detector Noise
papers.r: This paper estimates, under an explicitly stated normalisation, the displacement noise that collapse-model force fluctuations would produce in a gravitational-wave interferometer and compares it with representative detector sensitivity.

papers.t: Continuous Spontaneous Localisation Rates Implied by a Maximum Density: A Computed Bound and Laboratory Comparison
papers.r: This paper computes what a maximum mass density implies for the collapse rate in continuous spontaneous localisation models and compares the outcome with laboratory limits. The density ceiling adopted here is 9.717e+57 kilograms per cubic metre on the neutron branch.

papers.t: Decoherence Budgets for Large-Molecule Interferometry with a Planck-Scale Noise Floor
papers.r: This paper builds a decoherence budget for large-molecule matter-wave interferometry and adds a parametrised Planck-scale contribution to the familiar gas-collision and thermal-emission terms. Even with the dimensionless strength of the Planck term set to unity, its rate is 3.678e-13 per second and the fringe visibility after a ten-millisecond flight remains 1.0000; at a strength of one hundredth the rate falls to 3.

papers.t: Decoherence of Primordial Fluctuations During Inflation: When Quantum-to-Classical Transition Completes
papers.r: This paper estimates, in a transparent proxy model, how quickly primordial fluctuations decohere during inflation as a function of their coupling to an environment sector. For a coupling of one hundredth, decoherence completes in about 2.30 e-folds in the proxy; for a coupling of one ten-thousandth it takes about 4.61 e-folds. The inflationary expansion rate adopted corresponds to 1.519e+37 per second.

papers.t: Diósi–Penrose Gravitational Decoherence Times Across Mass Scales with a Density Ceiling
papers.r: This paper evaluates Diósi–Penrose gravitational decoherence times from the electron to macroscopic masses and asks whether a maximum density alters the picture. The computed time is 5.665e+19 seconds for a proton displaced by its own scale, 1.097e+15 seconds for a fullerene molecule, and 1.580e+00 seconds for a dust grain of 1e-15 kilograms.

papers.t: Entanglement Degradation of Photon Pairs over Cosmological Baselines: Computed Fidelity Loss from Expansion and Scattering
papers.r: This paper computes how the fidelity and concurrence of an entangled photon pair would degrade over cosmological propagation distances under a transparent scattering and dephasing model. At redshift one the fidelity is 0.9753 with concurrence 0.9506; at redshift five the fidelity falls to 0.8048 with concurrence 0.6095.

papers.t: Generalised Uncertainty Principle Phase Shifts in Atom Interferometry: Computed Size Against Current Sensitivity
papers.r: This paper computes the phase shift that a quadratic generalised uncertainty principle would imprint on a light-pulse atom interferometer and compares it with demonstrated phase sensitivity. With the dimensionless deformation parameter set to unity, the shift is 1.695e-50 radians, far below the representative sensitivity of 1.00e-04 radians adopted here.

papers.t: Granular Localisation Length and the Minimum Length: Bounds on Spontaneous Collapse Width from Interferometry
papers.r: This paper examines whether a fundamental minimum length constrains the correlation length used in spontaneous collapse models. The Planck length is 1.616e-35 metres. For a superposition of one million nucleons separated by one hundred nanometres, the computed collapse-induced decoherence rate varies from 1.000e-10 per second when the correlation length is ten nanometres to 2.500e-15 per second when it is ten microme

papers.t: Leggett–Garg Tests Under Fundamental Decoherence: The Measurable Window Computed for Mesoscopic Systems
papers.r: This paper computes the measurement-interval window in which a Leggett–Garg test can still reveal quantum behaviour when the system undergoes exponential decoherence. With a decoherence rate of one per second, intervals must remain below 0.405 seconds to preserve the adopted violation margin; at one hundred per second the window shrinks to 4.050e-03 seconds, while at one hundredth per second it opens to 40.50 seconds

papers.t: Neutrino Oscillation Decoherence over Gigaparsec Baselines: Damping Envelopes and the Density Ceiling
papers.r: This paper computes coherence lengths for neutrino oscillations under energy-dependent decoherence of the form commonly used in phenomenological searches. For a coefficient of 1e-23 per kilometre at one gigaelectronvolt with quadratic energy dependence, the coherence length is 1.000e+23 kilometres at one gigaelectronvolt, 1.000e+19 kilometres at one hundred gigaelectronvolts, and 1.000e+17 kilometres at one teraelect

papers.t: Observer Systems and the Density Ceiling: A Computed Bound on Coherent Laboratory Mass
papers.r: This paper computes the largest laboratory mass that can remain coherent for one second under gravitational decoherence estimates, as a concrete form of the observer problem in measurement theory. The mass at which the Diósi–Penrose time falls to one second, for ordinary condensed-matter density, is 1.000e-12 kilograms.

papers.t: Optomechanical Superposition Lifetimes: Thermal, Gas and Collapse Contributions Computed Side by Side
papers.r: This paper places thermal, and collapse-model contributions to the decoherence of a nanomechanical superposition side by side under identical assumptions. For an oscillator of 1e-14 kilograms at ten millikelvin with quality factor 1e+08, the total lifetime is 7.638e-02 seconds; at four kelvin with quality factor 1e+06 it shortens to 1.910e-06 seconds.

papers.t: Photon Polarisation Decoherence and Birefringence over Gamma-Ray Burst Distances: Computed Limits
papers.r: This paper computes the polarisation phase retardation accumulated by gamma-ray photons over gigaparsec distances under a quadratic Lorentz-violating birefringence model. The retardation is 6.404e+21 radians at one gigaelectronvolt, 6.404e+25 radians at one hundred gigaelectronvolts, and 6.404e+31 radians at one hundred teraelectronvolts, for unit strength over one gigaparsec.

papers.t: Quantum Zeno Limits at the Planck Time: Maximum Useful Measurement Rates for Qubit Control
papers.r: This paper compares the quantum Zeno time of controlled quantum systems with the Planck time to determine whether a minimum time interval restricts measurement-based control. The Planck time is 5.391e-44 seconds. For a qubit splitting of one electronvolt the Zeno time is 6.582e-16 seconds, a factor 1.221e+28 larger.

papers.t: Spontaneous Radiation Bounds on Collapse Models: Recomputed Emission Rates for Germanium Detectors
papers.r: This paper recomputes relative spontaneous-radiation rates for collapse models under the scaling with collapse rate and correlation length used in detector analyses, normalised to a stated reference point.

classes.title: High-Intensity Laser, Photonics and Optical Systems from the Physics

papers.t: An Adaptive Optics Focus Corrector for a High-Intensity Beamline Sized by Actuator Count and Strehl Gain
papers.r: This computed design (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED) reports an incoming aberration of 0.30 waves rms collapsing the Strehl ratio to 0.0286, correction to 0.07 waves rms restoring a Strehl ratio of 0.82, and therefore a focal intensity gain of about 29 at unchanged pulse energy and duration. All figures were produced by the deposited computation and verified against the public Zenodo record.

papers.t: A Coherent Doppler Wind Lidar Sized by Pulse Energy, Range Resolution and Velocity Precision
papers.r: This computed design (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED) reports a range resolution of 30 m from the 200 ns pulse, an average transmitted power of 3.0 W, about 12 detected photons per gate at 3 km under the stated backscatter, a signal-to-noise ratio near 3, and a single-pulse velocity precision near 0.17 m/s before pulse averaging improves it further.

papers.r: This computed design (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED) reports 61 channels of 300 W each, a residual phase error of 0.30 rad rms, a combining efficiency of 0.841, a combined output of 15.4 kW, and a brightness gain of 51 over a single channel, with 2.9 kW lost to phase error and combiner optics. All figures were produced by the deposited computation and verified against the public Zenodo record.

papers.t: A Cryogenic Yb:YLF Amplifier Sized by Saturation Fluence and Stored Energy at 77 K
papers.r: This computed design (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED) reports a saturation fluence of 1.77 J/cm2 at 77 K, a stored energy of 6.2 J in the stated crystal volume, an extracted pulse energy of 3.4 J at 55% extraction, and a repetition-rate ceiling near 34 Hz set by a 40 W cryocooler lift against the deposited heat fraction. papers.t: Error Budget for Chronometric Levelling Across a 1000 Kilometre Fibre Clock Network
papers.r: DESIGN — SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. For ten 100-km segments with 2e-19 link uncertainty per segment and 1e-18 endpoint clocks, the root-sum-square total including a 5 mm tide term gives a height uncertainty at the centimetre level, with the endpoint clocks and tide term dominating over the accumulated link terms.

papers.t: Phase-Noise Cancellation Design for a 2000 Kilometre Optical Fibre Frequency Link
papers.r: DESIGN — SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. A 250 km span has a delay of about 1.22 ms and a cancellation bandwidth near 204 Hz, while an unsegmented 2000 km path falls to about 25 Hz; the design therefore uses eight 250 km repeater spans.

papers.t: Link Budget for Free-Space Laser Time Transfer Between Ground Clock Stations
papers.r: DESIGN — SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. The sized 1550 nm terminal with 0.5 W and 0.3 m apertures over an 800 km path yields a computed received power and photon rate from the geometric link budget, and a 10 ps timing jitter corresponds to a 3 m one-way range equivalent, locating timing, not power, as the pacing term.

papers.t: Geopotential Resolution of a Clock at One Part in 10 to the 18: Height Equivalent and Levelling Reach
papers.r: A fractional uncertainty of 1e-18 corresponds to a geopotential difference of 0.0899 m^2/s^2 and a height equivalent of 0.916 cm, while 1e-17 corresponds to 9.16 cm, giving the direct conversion table for chronometric levelling.

papers.t: How Many Clock Stations Does a Global Height Reference Frame Need? A Geometry and Dilution Estimate
papers.r: With a 10 mm random per-tie term and a 5 mm systematic floor, frame datum error falls from 6.45 mm with 6 stations to 5.10 mm with 96 stations, approaching the 5 mm systematic floor, showing that beyond a few dozen well-placed stations placement and systematics dominate over count.

papers.t: Carrier-Phase GNSS Time Transfer Compared With Direct Optical Clock Geodesy: A Common Potential Scale
papers.r: A 0.2 ns per day carrier-phase time-transfer stability corresponds to a height equivalent roughly two orders of magnitude larger than the 0.916 cm equivalent of a direct 1e-18 optical clock comparison, while satellite coverage and continuity remain its decisive advantages.

papers.t: Averaging Time Required for Millimetre Geoid Resolution With Optical Lattice Clocks
papers.r: One millimetre of height is a fractional frequency of 1.09e-19; with a strontium lattice instability coefficient of 3e-16 the averaging time for millimetre resolution is of order 10^7 s (months), while centimetre resolution takes of order a day, quantifying where millimetre geodesy is campaign-scale rather than routine.

papers.t: Sagnac and Rotation Terms in Continental-Scale Clock Comparisons: Magnitudes and Correction Accuracy
papers.r: East-west baselines of 500-3000 km at mid-latitude carry Sagnac terms in the nanosecond range and above, orders of magnitude larger than optical clock precision, so rotation and geometry must be modelled to a small fraction of the term for a potential signal to survive.

papers.t: Seasonal Hydrological Mass Change as a Signal in Repeated Clock Comparisons
papers.r: Seasonal potential signals of 5-20 mm equivalent height stand above a 3 mm monthly campaign uncertainty with signal-to-noise ratios from about 1.7 to 6.7, while a 2 mm signal remains below campaign noise.

papers.t: Geodetic Return From a Space-Station Clock Ensemble: Potential Resolution Along a Low Earth Orbit
papers.r: DESIGN — SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. A 420 km station orbit has a period of about 93 minutes and about 15.5 orbits per day; ensemble levels of 1e-16 and 1e-17 correspond to height resolutions of about 0.92 m and 9.2 cm per tie, with the ground link as the pacing item.

papers.t: Detecting Millimetre-Per-Year Subsidence With a Repeated Clock Network: Required Campaign Cadence
papers.r: With 3 mm per-campaign height uncertainty, subsidence at 10 mm per year is detectable at three sigma within a few years even annually, 3 mm per year needs a longer quarterly programme, and 1 mm per year remains a multi-decade clock target better served by continuous techniques with clock ties.

papers.t: Unifying Tide-Gauge Height Datums With Clock-Derived Potential Differences
papers.r: Levelling error growing as 1 mm per root-kilometre reaches the 1 cm level of a clock tie at about 100 km, so clock-derived potential differences outperform levelling for the long inter-datum ties that unify tide-gauge height systems.

papers.t: Combined Gravitational and Second-Order Doppler Corrections for a Transported Optical Clock
papers.r: At 25 m/s the second-order Doppler shift is about 3.5e-15 in fractional frequency, while a 100 m height change gives a redshift of about 1.09e-14, so trajectory and height recording, not clock performance, limit a transported-clock geodesy result.

papers.t: Field Deployment Design for a Transportable Strontium Lattice Clock for Geodesy Campaigns
papers.r: DESIGN — SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. Six systematic terms combine to about 2.9e-18, a height equivalent of about 2.7 cm, within a computed total power budget of 1400 W and mass budget of 450 kg for campaign deployment.

papers.t: Error Budget for Two-Way Satellite Time and Frequency Transfer at the Nanosecond and Sub-Nanosecond Level
papers.r: Seven non-cancelling terms combine to a root-sum-square of 393 ps (0.393 ns), an 11.8 cm range equivalent and a one-day frequency-transfer floor of 4.54e-15, with station delay calibration (200 ps) and the modem term (300 ps) the largest contributors.

papers.t: Potential Profiling With Clocks Between Surface and Deep Underground Laboratories
papers.r: A depth of 1000 m gives a fractional frequency difference of about 1.09e-13, roughly 10^5 times a 1e-18 clock uncertainty, making a surface-to-underground profile a high signal-to-noise calibration for transport and link corrections.

homework.q: Take the paper “Gravitational Redshift Modulation on an Eccentric Satellite Orbit as a Geopotential Observable”. Its stated result is: For a Galileo-like orbit with eccentricity 0.23 the potential swing between perigee and apogee gives a fractional frequency modulation of order 1e-10, far above a 1e-17 clock level over an orbit, making the modulation a usable geopotential observable in principle. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

classes.title: Dispersion and Arrival-Time Tests of the Limit Frame from High-Energy Transients

papers.t: Dispersion Across Twelve Decades of Frequency in the Crab Pulsar
papers.r: The Crab pulsar flashes across the electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves at hundreds of megahertz to gamma rays above 100 MeV — twelve decades of frequency from one rotating neutron star 2 kpc away.

papers.t: A Figure of Merit for Transient Dispersion Tests: Ranking Messengers, Energies and Distances
papers.r: Arrival-time tests of vacuum dispersion have accumulated event by event — a burst here, a flare there — without a common currency for comparing what each event actually contributes. This paper defines one: a sensitivity figure of merit proportional to the photon energy raised to the dispersion order, times the cosmological path factor, divided by the timing sharpness, and computes it for the principal published event

papers.t: Decomposing the Dispersion Measure of FRB 121102: Milky Way, Halo, Intergalactic Medium and Host
papers.r: The repeating fast radio burst FRB 121102 has a total dispersion measure of about 557 pc per cubic centimetre and a host galaxy at redshift 0.1927, which makes it the first burst whose dispersion could be audited line by line.

papers.t: Radio and X-Ray Simultaneity in the Galactic Burst FRB 200428
papers.r: On 28 April 2020 the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154 produced a millisecond radio burst bright enough to count as a fast radio burst, accompanied by an X-ray burst seen by several satellites. The radio signal's dispersion sweep across the 400 to 800 MHz band amounts to 6.47 s for its dispersion measure of about 332 pc per cubic centimetre, yet after dedispersion the radio components sit within milliseconds of the X-r

papers.t: Gamma-Ray Burst Spectral Lags Are Not Propagation: An Inconsistency Test Across Redshift
papers.r: Long gamma-ray bursts show spectral lags: their pulses peak later at low energies than at high energies, by tenths of a second. If those lags were vacuum dispersion accumulated in propagation, the dispersion scale implied by each burst would have to be the same for all of them.

papers.t: A High-Redshift Arrival-Time Bound from the 13 GeV Photon of GRB 080916C
papers.r: GRB 080916C, at redshift 4.35, is among the most distant bursts with GeV photons, and its most energetic early photon, about 13 GeV, arrived 16.5 s after the trigger. Charging that entire interval to propagation — an assumption this paper flags as very conservative, since the burst's high-energy emission itself turned on late — bounds the linear dispersion scale at 1.538e+18 GeV; charging only the offset from the hig

papers.t: A Linear Dispersion Bound from the 31 GeV Photon of GRB 090510
papers.r: The short gamma-ray burst GRB 090510, at redshift 0.903, delivered a photon of about 31 GeV that arrived 0.829 s after the low-energy trigger. Treating that whole interval as an upper limit on any propagation delay, the linear vacuum-dispersion scale is bounded below at E_QG = 1.713e+19 GeV, which is 1.40 times the Planck energy; a dispersion scale at the Planck energy itself would have delayed the photon by only 1.1

papers.t: Arrival Times of Multi-TeV Photons from GRB 221009A and the Dispersion Scale
papers.r: GRB 221009A, the brightest gamma-ray burst yet recorded, at redshift 0.151, was detected by LHAASO at energies extending to about 18 TeV — photons that should have been heavily attenuated by background light, arriving from a burst whose low-energy onset is known to the second.

papers.t: Graviton Dispersion and the Compton-Wavelength Bound from GW150914
papers.r: If the graviton has a rest mass, gravitational waves disperse: their lower frequencies travel slower, and a chirping binary signal would arrive smeared relative to the massless waveform. GW150914 swept from about 35 to 150 Hz over a path of about 410 Mpc, and its waveform matched the massless prediction closely.

papers.t: The Speed of Gravity Against the Speed of Light from GW170817 and GRB 170817A
papers.r: The gravitational-wave event GW170817 and the gamma-ray burst GRB 170817A came from the same merging neutron-star binary at about 40 Mpc, with the gamma rays arriving 1.74 s after the merger time inferred from the gravitational waveform.

papers.t: Quadratic Dispersion Limits from the 2005 TeV Flare of Markarian 501
papers.r: During a flare of the blazar Markarian 501 on 28 June 2005, the MAGIC telescope found the TeV emission's higher-energy component delayed by roughly four minutes relative to its lower-energy component. Taking that lag entirely as propagation, and representing the two bands by effective energies of 0.35 and 2 TeV at the source's redshift of 0.034, bounds a linear dispersion scale at 1.079e+17 GeV and a quadratic scale

papers.t: A Photon-Mass Bound from Residual Dispersion in Fast Radio Bursts
papers.r: A photon with a nonzero rest mass travels slower at lower frequencies, producing a frequency-dependent delay with the same inverse-frequency-squared shape as plasma dispersion but a different dependence on distance and on the plasma column.

papers.t: Energy-Dependent Lags in the 2006 Flare of PKS 2155-304: A Null Result Converted to Bounds
papers.r: The giant flare of the blazar PKS 2155-304 recorded by H.E.S.S. on 28 July 2006 rose and fell on timescales of a few minutes, and a search for energy-dependent lags between its lower- and higher-energy emission found none.

papers.t: Time-Window Completeness for Prompt Neutrinos from Gamma-Ray Bursts: What a Stacked Non-Detection Bounds
papers.r: Stacked searches for neutrinos coincident with gamma-ray bursts have examined over a thousand bursts within prompt time windows of about plus-or-minus a thousand seconds, and found no neutrino excess. That non-detection is usually read as a statement about neutrino production in bursts. This paper reads it a second way: as a completeness statement about arrival times.

papers.t: The Shapiro Delay Difference Between Gravitational Waves and Light from GW170817
papers.r: Gravitational waves and light falling through the same gravitational potential should be delayed by the same amount if the equivalence principle holds for both — the Shapiro delay is then common, and cancels in their arrival difference. GW170817's gamma rays arrived 1.74 s after its gravitational waves despite both signals crossing the Milky Way's potential well on their way from NGC 4993.

papers.t: Neutrino Velocity and Neutrino Mass from the Arrival Pattern of SN 1987A
papers.r: Neutrinos from Supernova 1987A crossed 51.4 kpc and arrived within a burst about twelve seconds long, with energies from about 7.5 to 40 MeV and no strong energy ordering. If the whole burst duration is charged to a mass-induced spread in arrival times, the neutrino mass is bounded at 16.3 eV, the classic result recovered here from the stated inputs.

papers.t: Virial Parameters of Giant Molecular Clouds: Bound, Marginal and Dispersing Populations from Published Line Widths
papers.r: The calculation finds that the virial parameter computed from published masses, radii and line widths spans values below unity for compact massive complexes to above two for diffuse clouds, with a typical giant molecular cloud near the marginal value; the population is therefore mixed rather than uniformly bound, and cloud lifetimes of a few free-fall times follow naturally.

papers.t: Wind-Blown Bubbles from Young Clusters: Energy-Driven Growth, Shell Momentum and the End of the Parent Cloud
papers.r: The calculation finds that a cluster with a mechanical wind luminosity of 10^31 watts inflates a bubble roughly twenty parsecs across within a million years in gas of a few hundred particles per cubic centimetre - the size of the parent cloud itself - while a single O star reaches several parsecs; wind bubbles are therefore a cluster-scale finishing mechanism for cloud dispersal, acting on the same million-year clock

Its stated result is: The calculation finds that the Bonnor-Ebert critical mass at 10 K and an external pressure of 3 x 10^5 K per cubic centimetre (in units of Boltzmann's constant) is close to one solar mass, matching the observed core mass function peak without any additional parameter, while the torsion density bound (a) Restate the claim in your own words. classes.title: Black-Hole Shadows, Photon Rings and Horizon-Scale Imaging Against the Density and Shear Bounds

papers.t: Error Budgets For and Against the Shadow: Which Input Buys the Next Factor of Two
papers.r: Every shadow comparison is a sum of variances, and the terms differ so much between the two sources that a single strategy for improving 'the shadow test' cannot serve both. For M87* the total budget is 13.8 per cent, with the mass term contributing 61 per cent of the variance; halving the mass error brings the total to 10.1 per cent, while halving the diameter error brings it only to 12.3.

papers.t: Horizon, Photon Sphere and Shadow on the Sky: The Lensing Magnification Ladder
papers.r: Three concentric scales structure every black hole image: the horizon at four gravitational radii of angular diameter, the photon sphere at six, and the shadow at 2 sqrt(27), a lensing magnification of 2.598 applied to the horizon's apparent size. For M87* the three angular diameters are 15.3, 22.9 and 39.7 microarcseconds; for Sagittarius A* they are 20.5, 30.7 and 53.3 microarcseconds.

papers.t: Detectability Thresholds for Shadow Imaging: Mass, Distance and the Earth-Diameter Wall
papers.r: An Earth-diameter array at 230 gigahertz has a fringe spacing of 21.1 microarcseconds, and a shadow is marginally detectable only if its diameter exceeds that spacing. On that criterion an M87*-mass black hole is marginally detectable out to 32 megaparsecs and securely detectable, at twice the fringe spacing, out to 16 megaparsecs; a Sagittarius A*-mass hole is marginally detectable only within 0.021 million parsecs,

papers.t: Horizon Mean Density Against the Aldred Limit: More Than Fifty Orders of Magnitude of Headroom
papers.r: The mean density of a black hole, its mass divided by the volume inside its Schwarzschild radius, falls as the inverse square of the mass. For M87* it is 0.44 kilograms per cubic metre, comparable to a light gas; for Sagittarius A* it is 9.98e+05 kilograms per cubic metre, comparable to a dense liquid.

papers.t: Spin Separates the Photon Orbit From the Innermost Stable Orbit: A Kerr Ladder for Horizon Imaging
papers.r: In Schwarzschild geometry the photon orbit at 3 gravitational radii and the innermost stable circular orbit at 6 stand a factor of two apart, a gap of 3.00 gravitational radii. Rotation closes that gap from both sides for prograde motion: at spin 0.9 the gap is 0.76 gravitational radii, and at spin 0.99, with the photon orbit at 1.17 and the innermost stable orbit at 1.45 gravitational radii, it is 0.29.

papers.t: The M87* Shadow Diameter Against Its Independent Mass: A Ten-Per-Cent Geometric Test
papers.r: Using the stellar-dynamical mass and the distance adopted by the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration as inputs independent of the ring image itself, the Schwarzschild shadow diameter predicted for M87* is 39.7 microarcseconds, against a measured shadow diameter of 42 plus or minus 3 microarcseconds.

papers.t: Mass From Shadow: Inverting the Two Measured Diameters and Pricing the Inversion
papers.r: Running the shadow formula backwards converts a measured diameter and a distance into a mass. For M87*, the measured 42 microarcsecond shadow at 16.8 megaparsecs inverts to 6.88 billion solar masses, plus or minus 0.59, which is 1.058 times the stellar-dynamical value.

papers.t: Photon-Orbit Periods and Echo Delays: The Clocks Built Into the Two Shadows
papers.r: A photon circling a non-rotating black hole at its photon sphere completes an orbit in 2 pi sqrt(27) GM/c^3. For Sagittarius A* that period is 691 seconds, or 11.5 minutes; for M87* it is 290.4 hours, or 12.1 days. A seven-hour track on Sagittarius A* therefore spans 36 photon orbits, while a ten-hour track on M87* spans 0.03 of one.

papers.t: Photon-Ring Subring Widths: The Exponential Ladder Set by the Lyapunov Exponent
papers.r: Light that orbits a black hole once before escaping forms a ring nested just outside the critical curve; light that orbits twice forms another, thinner one, and the sequence converges exponentially. For a non-rotating hole the convergence factor per half-orbit is exp(-pi) = 0.0432, set by the Lyapunov exponent of the photon orbit.

papers.t: Photon-Sphere and Critical-Curve Scales for the Two Imaged Black Holes and the Mass Ladder Between Them
papers.r: For a non-rotating black hole the photon sphere sits at three gravitational radii and the critical impact parameter that outlines the shadow sits at sqrt(27) gravitational radii. Evaluated for the two imaged sources, the photon-sphere radius is 28.8 trillion metres for M87*, whose gravitational radius is 9.60 trillion metres, and 19.0 billion metres for Sagittarius A*, whose gravitational radius is 6.35 billion metre

papers.t: How Far From Schwarzschild Can the Two Shadows Be? Deviation Bounds From Diameter Alone
papers.r: Define the fractional deviation delta as the observed shadow diameter divided by the Schwarzschild diameter predicted from an independent mass and distance, minus one. For M87*, delta is +0.058 with a combined width of 0.138; for Sagittarius A*, using the inferred shadow, delta is -0.086 with a width of 0.144, while using the emission ring instead would give -0.027, shifting delta by about six hundredths purely by a

papers.t: The Scattering Screen in Front of Sagittarius A*: Broadening Budgets From Seven Millimetres to 0.87 Millimetres
papers.r: Interstellar electrons between the Earth and the Galactic Centre scatter-broaden every image of Sagittarius A* by an amount that grows with the square of the wavelength. Under the published scattering law used here, the major-axis broadening at the standard 1.304 millimetre band is 22.3 microarcseconds, 43 per cent of the 51.8 microarcsecond ring, broadening it in quadrature to 56.4 microarcseconds and requiring a de

papers.t: The Sagittarius A* Shadow Diameter Against Its Orbital Mass and Distance
papers.r: Stellar orbits give the mass of Sagittarius A* and the distance to the Galactic Centre with a precision no extragalactic target can match. Propagating those values through the Schwarzschild shadow formula predicts a shadow diameter of 53.3 microarcseconds, with the gravitational radius subtending 5.12 microarcseconds.

papers.t: Shadow Centroid Shift as a Spin and Inclination Observable: A Leading-Order Budget
papers.r: A rotating black hole's shadow is not centred on the hole's mass centre: frame dragging displaces the bright, approaching side and shifts the shadow's centroid by an amount that grows with spin and with the sine of the inclination.

papers.t: Characteristic Shear at the Photon Sphere Against the Aldred Shear Threshold
papers.r: The Aldred shear threshold, the largest shear a spin-torsion bounce can survive, is 8.56e32 per second. The characteristic shear scale at a black hole's photon sphere, estimated by the Keplerian angular frequency there, is 6.01e-06 per second for M87* and 9.09e-03 per second for Sagittarius A*: fractions 7.02e-39 and 1.06e-35 of the threshold, some 35.0 orders of magnitude below it even for the smaller, faster source

papers.t: What 345 Gigahertz Buys: Resolution, Nulls and Scattering Across Three Observing Bands
papers.r: Moving a horizon-scale array from 86 to 345 gigahertz improves the Earth-baseline fringe spacing from 56.4 to 14.1 microarcseconds, a factor of 4.01, and shrinks the interstellar scattering angle toward Sagittarius A* from about 160 microarcseconds to 9.9 microarcseconds under the wavelength-squared law.

papers.t: Interferometric Visibility Nulls of the Two Shadows at 230 Gigahertz
papers.r: A thin ring of angular diameter theta has visibility amplitude given by the zeroth-order Bessel function of pi theta times the baseline in wavelengths, so its visibility vanishes at definite baselines that measure the diameter without any imaging at all.

classes.title: Black-Hole Ringdown, Quasi-Normal Modes and Gravitational-Wave Memory as Tests of the Frame

papers.t: A Shift That Shrinks as the Square of the Mass: The Torsion-Frame Correction to Ringdown Frequencies From Ten to Two Hundred Solar Masses
papers.r: The fractional shift falls from 1.90e-41 at ten solar masses to 4.74e-44 at two hundred, following the inverse-square scaling, and at no astrophysical mass does it approach measurement reach.

papers.t: Adding Silent Steps: A Stacking Budget for Gravitational-Wave Memory Across a Catalogue of Mergers
papers.r: Eight representative catalogue events stack to a memory signal-to-noise ratio of 0.95 under the stated noise assumption, with the top three carrying 0.80 of the weight, and about 222 comparable events are needed to reach 5.

papers.t: Asymmetry Made Audible: Mode Content of the Unequal-Mass Merger GW190412 and What Its Ringdown Can Separate
papers.r: At mass ratio 3.75 the 330 excitation rises to 0.39 of the fundamental, an enhancement of 1.40 over equal mass, with the two modes at 340.8 Hz and 544.6 Hz in a remnant of 37 solar masses.

papers.t: Does the Budget Close? Radiated Energy, Final Spin, and the Consistency of the Remnant Description in Three Mergers
papers.r: The mass budget closes to within 0.93 per cent across three mergers, with the GW150914 residual at 0.00 per cent, and all published spins lie inside their allowed accounting intervals.

papers.t: How Far Will the Next Instruments Hear a Ringdown? Horizon Distances for Spectroscopy and Memory in a Tenfold-Sensitivity Network
papers.r: Tenfold sensitivity moves the spectroscopy-grade ringdown horizon to 1.76 Gpc, implying roughly 457 usable events per year at the stated rate, and lifts the single-event memory horizon to 0.92 Gpc.

papers.t: Light Remnants Ring High: GW151226 and GW170608, Shot Noise, and the Cost of a Kilohertz-Scale Mode
papers.r: The two light remnants ring at 787.3 Hz and 888.6 Hz with shot-noise penalties of 3.94 and 4.44, leaving estimated ringdown signal-to-noise ratios of 0.7 and 0.7, so their spectroscopy awaits high-frequency sensitivity improvements.

papers.t: One Over Mass, Checked Eight Times: The Frequency-Mass Scaling of Fundamental Modes Across the Published Remnants
papers.r: Across eight remnants the mass-frequency product has a coefficient of variation of 9.7 per cent, consistent with the 17.2 per cent half-spread the published spin range predicts, so the catalogue passes the scaling audit with no mass-dependent drift required.

papers.t: Precision as a Function of Loudness: A Fisher Budget for Ringdown Frequency and Damping Time
papers.r: At signal-to-noise ratio 8 the budget gives 5.0 per cent in frequency and 15.5 per cent in damping time, a difficulty ratio of 3.1, with thresholds of 40 for one per cent frequency precision and 12 for ten per cent damping precision.

papers.t: Ringdown at the Bottom of the Band: The Fundamental Mode of the GW190521 Remnant and Its Measurable Cycles
papers.r: The mode sits at 68.0 Hz with 1.08 cycles per e-folding, roughly 0.27 of the frequency of a mid-mass remnant, which quantifies why heavy remnants are detected loudly but measured poorly in their ringdown.

papers.t: Room for Departure: Deviation Budgets for the Ringdown Spectrum From Published Measurement Uncertainties
papers.r: Published uncertainties allow fractional deviations of 0.084 in frequency and 0.183 in damping for GW150914 and 0.217 and 0.418 for GW190521, tightening to 0.078 in frequency when combined, which presses ten-per-cent departure models and leaves the torsion-frame shift untouched.

papers.t: Running the Spectrum Backwards: Recovering Remnant Mass and Spin From a Frequency and a Damping Time
papers.r: A measured pair of 247 Hz and 4.20 ms inverts to a spin of 0.693 and a mass of 69.6 solar masses, with frequency errors passing into mass at 1.9 per cent for five per cent and damping errors passing into spin at 0.065 for ten per cent.

papers.t: Ten Milliseconds of Disagreement: How the Choice of Ringdown Start Time Biases Recovered Frequency and Damping
papers.r: A single-mode fit at the peak is biased by -29.1 per cent in damping time, the bias falls to -0.3 per cent by 10 ms, and both parameter biases drop below five per cent only from a start time of 6 ms.

papers.t: The Fundamental Ringdown Mode of GW150914: A Berti-Fit Prediction Set Against the Published Test Values
papers.r: The predicted frequency and damping time fall within 0.11 and 0.06 of the published measurement uncertainties respectively, and the leading torsion-frame shift of 1.229e-40 Hz is far below any present measurement reach.

papers.t: The Memory Share of the Radiated Budget: An Energy Partition Between the Oscillatory Waves and the Permanent Step
papers.r: The memory carries 1.11 per cent of the radiated energy of GW150914 and 5.1e-04 of the system's total mass energy, a second-order share that explains its firm theoretical status alongside its observational difficulty.

papers.t: The Permanent Step Left by GW150914: A Displacement-Memory Amplitude Computed From the Radiated Energy
papers.r: The displacement step is 2.55e-23 at optimal orientation and 1.34e-23 inclination-averaged, respectively 0.025 and 0.013 of the peak oscillatory strain.

papers.t: Two Tones From One Remnant: The 330 Mode, Its Separation From the Fundamental, and a Resolvability Criterion
papers.r: The 330 mode of the GW150914 remnant lies at 395.3 Hz, separated from the fundamental by 146.2 Hz against a mean natural linewidth of 92.0 Hz, and resolving it alone at signal-to-noise ratio 8 requires a fundamental near 23.

papers.t: What the First Overtone Must Earn: An Amplitude and Signal-to-Noise Budget for the n=1 Mode in GW150914
papers.r: The overtone decays 0.33 times as fast in damping time, needs a starting amplitude of at least 0.65 of the fundamental to contribute a signal-to-noise ratio of 3 beside a fundamental of 8, and loses a factor 0.13 in relative amplitude within the first 4 ms.

classes.title: The Heliosphere, the Termination Shock and the Interstellar Boundary Against Energy and Density Bounds

papers.t: A Count-Rate Forecast for IMAP Energetic Neutral Atom Measurements of the Heliosheath
papers.r: At a representative intensity of 300 per square centimetre per second per steradian per kiloelectronvolt, a geometric factor of 0.01 square centimetres steradian and a channel width of 0.3 kiloelectronvolts give a count rate of 0.9 per second, accumulating to about 3240 counts in an hour and about 78,000 in a day for the fiducial channel, with Poisson fractional uncertainties falling from about 1.8 percent per hour t

papers.t: Anomalous Cosmic Ray Acceleration Efficiency at the Termination Shock
papers.r: The upstream solar wind kinetic energy flux at the mass-loaded shock is compared with downstream anomalous cosmic ray energy fluxes for energy densities from 3e-14 to 1.8e-13 joules per cubic metre, giving acceleration efficiencies at the level of percent to tens of percent, the energetic counterpart of the missing core heat at this shock.

papers.t: Charge-Exchange Mean Free Paths and Neutral Filtration through the Heliosheath
papers.r: At a cross section of 2.0e-15 square centimetres, a proton moving through sheath neutrals at 0.10 per cubic centimetre has a mean free path of about 33 astronomical units, comparable to the sheath thickness, while neutrals moving through sheath protons have mean free paths of hundreds of astronomical units and mostly survive, giving a filtration factor of about 0.41 over thirty astronomical units.

papers.t: Energetic Neutral Atom Flux near One Kiloelectronvolt from Heliosheath Charge Exchange
papers.r: The charge-exchange optical depth of a thirty astronomical unit sheath at a neutral density of 0.10 per cubic centimetre and a cross section of 2.0e-15 square centimetres is of order a tenth, so the sheath is optically thin at one kiloelectronvolt and the predicted energetic neutral atom intensities span the IBEX-reported range of roughly 100 to 500 per square centimetre per second per steradian per kiloelectronvolt

papers.t: Energetic Particle Energy Density in the Heliosheath from Voyager Measurements
papers.r: Energetic particle pressures spanning 0.010 to 0.060 picopascals correspond to energy densities three times those values and range from a fraction of the core thermal pressure to a value rivalling it, establishing the ordering in which pickup-ion thermal pressure dominates the heliosheath budget, energetic particles and the core are comparable, and magnetic pressure inside the sheath is smaller.

papers.t: Heliosheath Temperature from the Termination Shock Jump Conditions
papers.r: The strong-shock jump condition for a 400 kilometre per second upstream flow gives a downstream temperature of 3.63 million kelvin, or 313 electronvolts, rising to 6.36 million kelvin at compression 3.5 under the stated scaling, against a published core range of 80 to 200 electronvolts; the shortfall quantifies the heliosheath missing-energy partition into pickup ions and energetic particles.

papers.t: Heliosheath Thickness and Plasma Transit Time between the Voyager Crossings and the Heliopause
papers.r: The heliosheath is 27.6 astronomical units thick along the Voyager 1 chord (94.0 to 121.6 AU) and 35.3 astronomical units thick along the Voyager 2 chord (83.7 to 119.0 AU), and at flow speeds of 100 and 130 kilometres per second respectively the plasma transit times are about 1.3 and 1.3 years, long enough for substantial charge-exchange processing inside the region.

papers.t: Interstellar Inflow Speed, Temperature and Mach Number: IBEX and Ulysses Values Compared
papers.r: The Ulysses inflow of 23.2 kilometres per second at 6300 kelvin and the IBEX inflow of 25.4 kilometres per second at 7500 kelvin are both supersonic in helium, and their ram pressures at a common interstellar mass density differ by a factor of about 1.20, corresponding through the square-root distance scaling to about a ten percent difference in predicted boundary distance.

papers.t: Local Interstellar Total Pressure and the Density Bound It Imposes at the Heliopause
papers.r: Decomposing the heliopause total pressure of 0.131 picopascals leaves a thermal remainder after magnetic pressure at 0.30 nanotesla, a ram term of 0.055 picopascals and a cosmic-ray term of 0.020 picopascals are subtracted; that remainder bounds the local interstellar total particle density at 7500 kelvin, with the cosmic-ray term named as the least certain input.

papers.t: Magnetic Pressure Balance across the Heliopause from Voyager Field Strengths
papers.r: Magnetic pressure rises from about 0.016 picopascals at 0.20 nanotesla inside the heliopause to about 0.081 picopascals at 0.45 nanotesla outside, a factor of about five through the square of the field ratio, and the external field dominates the thermal pressure of the plasma-wave electron population, giving a plasma beta below unity on the interstellar side.

papers.t: North-South Termination Shock Asymmetry from the Voyager Crossing Distances
papers.r: The northern shock crossing at 94.0 AU and the southern crossing at 83.7 AU differ by 10.3 AU, a fractional asymmetry of 0.116 about the mean of 88.9 AU; the squared distance ratio gives a directional pressure ratio of 1.26, so the northern direction required about a quarter more confining balance than the southern direction under a common external pressure.

papers.t: Ram-Pressure Balance and the Nose Heliopause Distance: A Bound from Voyager Crossings
papers.r: A 1 AU ram pressure of 1.94 nanopascals implies an interstellar total pressure of 0.131 picopascals at the Voyager 1 heliopause distance of 121.6 AU and 0.137 picopascals at the Voyager 2 distance of 119.0 AU; a fiducial external pressure of 0.13 picopascals predicts a nose distance of 122.3 AU, with a bracket of 110.2 to 139.4 AU for external pressures from 0.16 down to 0.10 picopascals.

papers.t: Solar-Cycle Ram-Pressure Change and the Expected Motion of the Termination Shock
papers.r: Shock distance scaling as the square root of ram pressure moves a mean ninety astronomical unit shock out to about 120 astronomical units at a pressure factor of 1.8 and in to about 75 astronomical units at a factor of 0.7, an excursion of roughly 45 astronomical units between extreme representative states, with a sheath signal time of about one year at 150 kilometres per second across thirty astronomical units.

papers.t: Termination Shock Compression and Heliosheath Density from the Magnetosonic Mach Number
papers.r: For a ratio of specific heats of five thirds, the compression ratio rises from 2.29 at Mach 2.0 toward the strong-shock limit at higher Mach number, and the mass-loaded upstream density of 0.0011 per cubic centimetre gives downstream densities below the reported heliosheath range of 0.002 to 0.004 per cubic centimetre, localising the shortfall to continued sheath processing rather than to the jump itself.

papers.t: The Hydrogen Wall: Column Density and Enhancement at the Outer Heliosheath Boundary
papers.r: A fifteen astronomical unit wall enhanced from 0.10 to 0.25 hydrogen atoms per cubic centimetre, an enhancement factor of 2.5, roughly doubles the hydrogen column toward the nose, with a total column of about 5.6e14 per square centimetre and a line-centre Lyman-alpha optical depth well above unity, consistent with the saturated absorption by which the wall was identified.

papers.t: The IBEX Ribbon Source Distance Inferred from Its Width and Energy Ordering
papers.r: The twenty-degree ribbon width corresponds to transverse sizes of about 35, 53 and 71 astronomical units at source distances of 100, 150 and 200 astronomical units, and the expected annual parallaxes at those distances are about 1.15, 0.76 and 0.57 degrees, stating the precision a direct source-distance measurement must reach.

papers.t: The Pickup-Ion Share of Heliosheath Pressure at the Termination Shock
papers.r: With pickup ions at twenty percent by number and fifteen million kelvin against a core at one and a half million kelvin, the pickup population carries about 0.71 of the total thermal pressure, roughly two and a half times the core contribution, despite being a minority of the particles.

classes.title: The Local Bubble, Local Interstellar Cloud and Nearby Interstellar Structure Against Energy and Density Bounds

papers.t: Conductive Evaporation of the Local Interstellar Cloud at the Hot Bubble Interface
papers.r: A warm cloud embedded in million-degree gas is heated at its surface by electron conduction, and the heated layer flows away: the cloud evaporates. Applying the classical conduction-front mass-loss formula to a cloud of radius two parsecs facing the Local Bubble interior gives a mass-loss rate of 8.8e-07 solar masses per year and an evaporation time of only 0.4 million years for a cloud of 0.35 solar masses.

papers.t: Cosmic-Ray Energy Density and Pressure in the Local Interstellar Medium from the Voyager Spectra
papers.r: When Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause it measured, for the first time, the unmodulated spectra of galactic cosmic rays in the surrounding interstellar medium, and integrating those spectra gives the cosmic-ray energy density that the local cloud actually contains.

papers.t: Electron Density and Ionisation Balance of the Local Interstellar Cloud from Published Line and In-Situ Values
papers.r: The Local Interstellar Cloud is only partly ionised, and its free electrons set both its pressure and the charge-exchange rates that shape the heliosphere boundary. Combining published neutral densities with the hydrogen and helium ionisation fractions returned by photoionisation models of the local radiation field gives an electron density of 0.073 per cubic centimetre, a proton density of 0.063 per cubic centimetre

papers.t: Expansion Age and Shell Momentum of the Local Bubble from the Measured Surface Velocity
papers.r: The surface of the Local Bubble is still moving outward, carrying young stars born in its swept-up gas at a mean expansion speed of 6.7 kilometres per second. Dividing the 165-parsec radius by that speed gives a naive expansion age of 24 million years, and correcting for the deceleration expected of an energy-driven bubble, whose radius grows as time to the three-fifths power, gives 14.4 million years.

papers.t: Filtration of Interstellar Hydrogen at the Heliosphere: Charge-Exchange Mean Free Paths and the Hydrogen Wall
papers.r: Interstellar hydrogen atoms approaching the Sun must cross the heliosheath, where many swap electrons with slow protons and are deflected or lost, so the hydrogen density inside the heliosphere is lower than in the cloud outside, a reduction called filtration.

papers.t: Heliosheath Thickness Implied by the Voyager Termination Shock and Heliopause Crossings
papers.r: Between the termination shock and the heliopause lies the heliosheath, the region whose thickness no remote observation could measure and both Voyagers have now traversed. Voyager 1 crossed the shock at 94.0 astronomical units and the heliopause at 121.6, a sheath thickness of 27.6 astronomical units along its trajectory, while Voyager 2's crossings at 83.7 and 119.0 give 35.3 astronomical units.

papers.t: How Many Supernovae Does the Local Bubble Energy Budget Require?
papers.r: The Local Bubble holds thermal energy in its hot interior and kinetic energy in its expanding shell, and both reservoirs were supplied, on the standard picture, by supernovae in the Scorpius-Centaurus association. This study adds the two reservoirs from published size and pressure values and divides by the useful energy delivered per supernova.

papers.t: Kinetic Energy and Velocity Dispersion of the Local Cloud Complex
papers.r: The space within fifteen parsecs of the Sun is not one cloud but a complex of about fifteen warm clouds, each with its own velocity vector, all embedded in the Local Bubble. Giving each cloud the size and density of the cloud that surrounds the Sun yields a total complex mass near 5.2 solar masses, and with the published spread of cloud velocities the complex carries kinetic energy near 3.32e+45 erg in its relative m

papers.t: Magnetic Pressure in the Local Bubble Shell and Cloud Against the Thermal Budget
papers.r: Thermal pressure is only one term in the support of the gas around the Sun; the magnetic field contributes a pressure that polarised dust emission and the geometry of the IBEX ribbon now constrain. A field of three microgauss in the Local Interstellar Cloud gives a magnetic pressure P/k of 2,594 K per cubic centimetre, about 1.24 times the cloud thermal pressure, while an eight-microgauss field compressed into the Lo

papers.t: Pickup Ion Pressure in the Outer Heliosphere Built from the Local Cloud Neutral Densities
papers.r: Most of the pressure that pushes back against the interstellar medium at the edge of the solar system is not carried by the solar wind protons that left the Sun, but by pickup ions: interstellar neutrals that drifted in from the local cloud, were ionised, and were swept up to solar wind speed.

papers.t: Soft X-Ray Emission Measure, Luminosity and Cooling Time of the Local Bubble Interior
papers.r: The hot gas filling the Local Bubble radiates in soft X-rays, and its emission measure, luminosity and cooling time follow from the density and temperature that X-ray spectroscopy returns. papers.t: Termination Shock Distance Expected from the Local Cloud Ram Pressure, Compared with the Voyager Crossings
papers.r: The solar wind expands until its ram pressure falls to the total pressure of the surrounding interstellar medium, and that balance point is where the termination shock is expected. Computing the balance from a typical solar wind at Earth and the published density and inflow speed of the Local Interstellar Cloud places the shock near 81 astronomical units, against the 94 and 84 astronomical units at which Voyager 1 an

papers.t: The IBEX Ribbon Energy Budget Against the Solar Wind Power That Sustains It
papers.r: The ribbon of energetic neutral atoms discovered by the Interstellar Boundary Explorer is the brightest feature in the sky at kiloelectronvolt energies, yet its total power is a tiny fraction of the solar wind power that ultimately sustains it.

papers.t: The Ionising Photon Budget of the Local Interstellar Cloud: Epsilon Eridani, Hot Stars and the Diffuse Background
papers.r: The partial ionisation of the local cloud is a balance, and the balance can be run backwards: from the measured ionised fraction and the recombination coefficient, the photoionisation rate that the local radiation field must supply follows directly.

papers.t: Thermal Pressure Balance Between the Local Bubble Interior and the Local Interstellar Cloud
papers.r: The hot interior of the Local Bubble and the warm cloud that surrounds the Sun press against each other across an interface that has never been imaged directly, so the balance between them must be established by arithmetic on published densities and temperatures.

papers.t: Volume and Missing Mass of the Local Cavity from Three-Dimensional Dust Maps
papers.r: Three-dimensional dust maps built from Gaia stellar distances show the Sun inside a cavity whose walls rise sharply at one to two hundred parsecs in most directions. Treating the cavity as a sphere of radius 165 parsecs gives a volume of 1.88e+07 cubic parsecs.

papers.t: What Line Widths Say About the Temperature and Turbulence of the Local Interstellar Cloud
papers.r: Absorption lines formed in the Local Interstellar Cloud are broadened by both heat and turbulence, and separating the two requires lines from species of very different mass observed along the same sightline.

papers.t: Superfluid Density Jump in Two-Dimensional Bose Gases and the Bound Comparison
papers.r: The thermal wavelength is 0.59 micrometres and the critical superfluid density is 1.14e+13 atoms per square metre, or 11.41 per square micrometre. The transition is driven by vortex-antivortex unbinding — a topological mechanism whose characteristic densities are set by thermal and quantum statistics in the plane, with the three-dimensional density bound entering only as a remote outer reference.

papers.t: Bright Solitons and the Atom-Number Limit for Attractive Condensates
papers.r: The critical numbers are 4.62e+03 atoms for lithium-7 under the stated confinement and 335 atoms for rubidium-85 tuned to a larger attractive scattering length. papers.t: Quantum Depletion and Condensate Fractions in Dilute Gases and Helium Against the Density Bound
papers.r: Rubidium-87 at laboratory density has a gas parameter of 1.50e-05 and a quantum depletion of 0.582 percent, leaving a condensate fraction above 99 percent, whereas helium-4 retains only 7.25 percent despite being far denser. The rubidium mass-density ratio to the bound is 1.49e-63.

papers.t: Critical Rotation for the First Vortex in Trapped Condensates and Helium Buckets
papers.r: The condensate threshold is 0.22 hertz, comfortably inside trap rotation capabilities, while the helium bucket threshold is 0.46 millihertz, a ratio between the thresholds of 4.90e+02 driven almost entirely by the container-size term.

papers.t: Landau Critical Velocities in Superfluid Helium and Condensates Compared with the Bound Velocity Scale
papers.r: For helium-4 the roton minimum yields a Landau velocity of 59.6 metres per second, a ratio of 1.99e-07 to the speed of light; for rubidium-87 at laboratory density the phonon critical velocity is 1.89 millimetres per second, a ratio of 6.30e-12. Measured critical velocities in channels fall below the helium Landau value because vortices nucleate first, which widens rather than narrows the gap to the bound scale.

papers.t: Dipolar Condensates: Collapse Thresholds and Droplet Densities Under the Bounds
papers.r: The dipolar lengths are 133 Bohr radii for dysprosium and 67 for erbium, matching published values, and a representative droplet density of 1.0e+21 per cubic metre stands at a ratio of 2.80e-62 to the bound.

papers.t: Healing Lengths in Dilute Bose-Einstein Condensates Against the Shear Ceiling
papers.r: For rubidium-87 at 1.0e+20 atoms per cubic metre the healing length is 0.27 micrometres, the sound speed is 1.89 millimetres per second and the chemical potential corresponds to 37 nanokelvin, while the gradient ratio to the torsion ceiling is only 2.71e-10 and the density ratio is 1.49e-63. Even a tenfold denser gas shortens the healing length only to 0.087 micrometres.

papers.t: Josephson Coupling and Phase-Coherence Scales in Weakly Linked Condensates
papers.r: The tunnelling energy for a coupling of 100 hertz in frequency units corresponds to 5 nanokelvin, while the bound temperature is 3.28e+22 kelvin, an energy ratio of 1.46e-31. papers.t: Roton Gap and Landau Parameters of Helium-4 Tested Against the Shear Ceiling
papers.r: The roton wave number stands at a ratio of 1.41e-06 to the torsion scale, the liquid density at a ratio of 1.49e-56 to the density bound, and the gap corresponds to 0.75 millielectronvolts with a Landau velocity of 59.6 metres per second.

papers.t: Second Sound and the Two-Fluid Scales of Helium-4 Under the Frame Bounds
papers.r: Near 1.8 kelvin the second-sound speed is 20 metres per second, a ratio of 6.67e-08 to the speed of light, in a liquid whose density ratio to the bound is 1.49e-56. Second sound is a thermal mode of the two-fluid system whose existence depends on superfluid fraction and entropy, not on any extreme of density or velocity, and its measured attenuation remains a precision probe of vortex-line density in turbulence.

papers.t: Spin Healing Lengths and Domain Scales in Spinor Condensates
papers.r: The density healing length is 0.27 micrometres while the spin healing length is 4.0 micrometres, a factor of 14.7 larger, with a spin interaction energy of 0.2 nanokelvin. Spin domains, textures and the coreless vortices they support are therefore among the gentlest structures in ultracold physics, with gradients further from the fundamental ceiling than any density structure in the same gas.

papers.t: Quantum Turbulence: Vinen Vortex-Line Densities in Helium and Condensates Against the Shear Bound
papers.r: Strong helium counterflow reaches a line density of 1e+11 per square metre, corresponding to a spacing of 3.16 micrometres and a gradient ratio of 2.34e-11 to the ceiling; moderate counterflow gives a spacing of 31.6 micrometres.

papers.t: Three-Body Recombination as the Practical Density Ceiling of Ultracold Gases
papers.r: Rubidium at 1.0e+20 per cubic metre lives 2.3 seconds against recombination, but only 0.02 seconds at ten times the density, and the one-second density is 1.52e+20 per cubic metre, at a mass-density ratio of 2.26e-63 to the bound. Recombination therefore caps usable densities orders below the acoustic closure and incomparably far below the fundamental bound.

papers.r: Rubidium-87 rotating at 10 hertz carries 2.74e+10 vortices per square metre with a spacing of 6.0 micrometres; helium-4 at 10 radians per second carries 2.01e+08 per square metre with a spacing of 70.60 micrometres. The largest gradient associated with the array, set by the inverse spacing, stands at a ratio of 1.23e-11 to the torsion ceiling.

classes.lesson: Gloves off, sample out — matter first, theory holding the torch. I am Professor Petra Johansson, and this is Ultracold Matter, Bose-Einstein Condensates and Superfluid Dynamics Under the Density and Shear Bounds — a class in Condensed Matter at Exolex University. The syllabus is real: 17 papers from the Aldred corpus, every one deposited and citable, and in this room we read them for what they actually claim. First, The Analogue Bounce Density of a Bose-Einstein Condensate in Acoustic Geometry. Its stated result: For rubidium-87 the closure density is 4.21 times ten to the 20 atoms per cubic metre, where the healing length is 0.13 micrometres and the chemical potential reaches 0.00 millikelvin; its mass-density ratio to the gravitational bound is 6.25 times ten to the -63. Next, Analogue Hawking Temperatures in Condensate Horizons Compared with the Bound Temperature. Its stated result: A representative gradient of 200 per second gives an analogue Hawking temperature of 0.24 nanokelvin; even a tenfold steeper horizon reaches only 2.4 nanokelvin, against a bound temperature of 3.28 times ten to the 22 kelvin, a ratio of 7.42 times ten to the -33 for the representative case. And then, Superfluid Density Jump in Two-Dimensional Bose Gases and the Bound Comparison. Its stated result: The thermal wavelength is 0.59 micrometres and the critical superfluid density is 1.14 times ten to the 13 atoms per square metre, or 11.41 per square micrometre. That is the shape of this class: real claims, real numbers, and the arguments between them. Your homework is waiting on your desk.
