papers.t: Designing a Fog Collector Instead of Copying One: Droplet-Capture Physics, Shade-Coefficient Optimisation and an Honest Seasonal Yield for an Arid Coastal Climate
papers.r: Computing droplet capture from the Stokes number across a stated fog spectrum selects a 0.3 mm fibre at shade coefficient 0.50 (total collection efficiency 0.3213), and a 40 m² panel of that design yields 111,041 L per season in the central arid-coastal fog class — 21.77 times the 5,100 L per year of a 40 m² rain roof at the same site.

papers.t: Forward Osmosis Priced Honestly: A Regeneration Bound That Closes the Seawater Claim, and the Fertilizer-Draw Irrigation Design That Survives It
papers.r: Regenerating any forward-osmosis draw costs more minimum work than desalinating the feed directly (bound 1.53 vs 1.06 kWh/m³ for seawater at 0.50 recovery; a stated NaCl draw totals 6.09 vs 3.04 kWh/m³ for RO at equal efficiency, and a thermolytic draw flips only if 56.49 kWh/m³ of heat at 60 °C is free), while a fertilizer-draw unit that skips regeneration entirely — 1,484 m² of membrane delivering 50 m³/day from 2.

papers.t: Freeze Desalination Priced Honestly: Full Accounting of Washing, Brine Entrainment and Refrigeration for Natural and Refrigerated Freezing of Seawater
papers.r: With brine entrainment and washing charged, refrigerated freeze desalination of seawater costs 53.2 kWh/m3 at COP 2.5 (17.7 times reverse osmosis at 3.0 kWh/m3), while natural tray freezing at −10 °C in light wind yields a net 13.25 L/m2/day — 75.5 m2 per m3/day — so the latent-heat advantage survives only where the cold is free.

papers.t: Intermittent Water Supply: The Intrusion Volume per Outage Computed from First Principles, and a Household Break-Tank Design That Defeats It
papers.r: For the stated 10 km reference network, each supply outage draws 1.49 m³ of soil water in through the network's own leaks (2.98 m³/day, 0.30% of daily supply), and a nominal 75 L household break tank with a 40 mm air-gap inlet bridges the two-window supply pattern at 50 L/day essential demand with a chlorine re-dose interval of 6.0 days at 20 °C falling to 2.0 days at 35 °C.

papers.t: Locating Distribution Leaks by Pressure-Transient Timing on a Network of Low-Cost Loggers: A Method for Plastic-Pipe Networks Where Acoustic Correlation Fails
papers.r: Timing low-frequency pressure transients between $30-class loggers at 250 m spacing and 10 Hz sampling locates leaks in polyethylene pipe to a standard error of 6.7 m — 4.07 times tighter than in ductile iron, because the plastic wave is slower — with a detection floor of a 3.08 mm equivalent hole at 250 m, covering a 5,000-person town's 50 km of mains with 201 loggers for $6,030 in hardware.

papers.t: Rainwater Tank Sizing by Stochastic Reliability Simulation: Storage–Reliability Design Curves for a Semi-Arid and a Monsoon Climate
papers.r: Storage–reliability curves from a Markov-generator daily balance (249 simulated years per configuration) give explicit tank sizes for 90% and 98% reliability in semi-arid (520.7 mm/yr) and monsoon (1511.5 mm/yr) climates; the semi-arid 40 m² / 50 L/day case is supply-limited (ratio 0.91) so no tank reaches 98%, the one-month rule delivers only 50.1–84.8%, and the largest dry-spell rule delivers 87.7–100.0% at up to f

papers.t: The Electrodialysis–Reverse Osmosis Crossover for Brackish Groundwater: A First-Principles Energy Derivation and a Sized Village Electrodialysis Unit
papers.r: Derived from stated first principles under one accounting rule, electrodialysis and reverse osmosis specific energies for brackish desalination to 0.5 g/L cross at a feed salinity of 6.90 g/L — ED lower below, RO lower above, and no crossover up to 20 g/L if RO brine energy recovery is removed — and a village ED unit for a 2.5 g/L borehole producing 5 m³/day needs 26 cell pairs at 10.50 A and 7.49 V, uses 1.82 kWh/da

papers.t: The Reservoir Is the Sand: Extractable-Storage Accounting, Evaporation Suppression and Worked Sizing for a Sand Dam on a Seasonal River
papers.r: Priced as a porous reservoir, a sand dam for 400 people at 20 L/day through a 180-day dry season needs 1,440 m³ of extractable water in a corrected sand body 147.4 m × 20 m × 2.0 m (5,895.8 m³ at specific yield 0.25), and storing in sand saves 2,873.6 m³ of evaporation against an open reservoir of the same plan area (34.0 m³ lost through a 0.30 m dry crust against 2,907.5 m³ open), equivalent to 359.2 days of village

papers.t: The Virus-Removal Ceiling of Gravity Ceramic and "Nano" Point-of-Use Filters: A Sieving and Adsorption Accounting
papers.r: At their stated pore ratings of 0.2–0.9 µm, gravity ceramic and "nano" point-of-use filters have a sieving ceiling of at most 0.66 log10 virus removal (0.000 log10 for 20–30 nm viruses), so marketed 4–6 log virus claims understate viral passage by factors of 2,163 to 216,290, while the same model confirms cyst removal at the 12-log cap and strong bacterial removal at finer ratings.

homework.q: Take the paper “A Batch Reverse-Osmosis Cycle Whose Pressure Follows the Osmotic Curve: First-Principles Energy Accounting and a Sized Village Unit”. Its stated result is: A batch seawater reverse-osmosis cycle whose feed pressure ramps to follow the osmotic curve of the concentrating charge uses 1.814 kWh per cubic metre of permeate at 35 g/L and 50% recovery — 21.7% less than a conventional continuous plant with isobaric energy recovery computed the same way (2.318 (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

professor.name: Professor Shota Ito
professor.personality: A sunny and hands-on teacher of Designs & Engineering who writes the units on the board before opinions, every time. Examinations in his room are open-book, because he is testing thinking, not storage.
professor.greeting: In, in. Designs & Engineering waits for no one, and neither do we.

classes.title: Food

papers.t: A Combined Solar Tunnel Dryer and Desiccant-Bead Store for Village Seed Saving: Design, Budgets, and Failure Floor
papers.r: A 24 m² solar tunnel dryer held at or below 40 °C plus 198.6 kg of regenerable desiccant beads per tonne dries seed from 20 % to 9 % moisture in 1.56 days of dry-season sun, but the station fails below an insolation floor of 3.74 kWh m⁻² day⁻¹.

papers.t: A No-Electronics Witness Label for Sealed Grain Stores: Integrating Moisture Exposure and Seal Failure on One Passive Card
papers.r: A passive two-channel label costing US $0.057 per store at a volume of 100,000 reaches red in 0.76 days on a failed seal and in 0.66 days on grain sealed wet — the two cases each single channel alone misses in one direction or the other — while staying green through 90 days in an intact store, and it is honest only between 15 °C and 35 °C.

papers.t: A Phase-Change Cold Box for the Last Mile Without a Grid: Computed Sizing, Hold Times, and Recharge for the +4 °C Cargo Class
papers.r: A 100 mm EPS box with 14 kg of sealed paraffin panels melting at 5.0 °C holds a 15.0 kg payload for 50.9 hours at 35 °C ambient in the model and recharges overnight in a freezer, while plain ice in the same box holds longer per kilogram but at 0 °C, below the safe cargo band.

papers.t: A Pond-and-Field Nutrient Loop, Closed by Arithmetic or Not at All: A Full Nitrogen and Phosphorus Budget for a 0.2 ha Fish Pond Serving 0.5 ha of Crops
papers.r: The pond loop supplies 57.7% of the crops' phosphorus demand but only 19.2% of their nitrogen, so the farm still buys $69.56 of fertiliser a year, and the loop turns polluting at 1,700 kg of feed a year.

papers.t: A Solar-Regenerated Desiccant Dryer for One Tonne of Smallholder Grain: Water Budget, Sizing and Failure Limits
papers.r: A solar-regenerated silica-gel dryer can dry one tonne of maize from 25% to 13% moisture in 3.0 days with 191.6 kg of gel and 24.0 m² of collector at 5.0 kWh/m²/day insolation, and it fails below 3.15 kWh/m²/day.

papers.t: A Village Solar Dehydrator for a 50 kg Mango Batch: Water Budget, Collector and Airflow Sizing, Drying Time and the Humid-Season Failure Line
papers.r: A solar dehydrator with an 8.0 m² collector and a 110 m³/h fan dries a 50 kg mango batch in 1.96 days for a net advantage of $66.89 per batch, but in the humid season above 81.7% relative humidity it stretches past the three-day mould window and fails.

papers.t: A Village Struvite Reactor Turning Source-Separated Urine into Fertiliser: Design and Phosphorus Budget for a 100-Person Community
papers.r: A 200 L batch reactor for 100 people is calculated to recover 87.8% of urine phosphorus as 2.31 kg of struvite per person per year, and it stops paying on fertiliser value alone when magnesium oxide exceeds $1.23 per kg.

papers.t: An Evaporative Cooling Store for a Village Produce Market: Design, Simulated Performance Across Climates, and the Humidity Failure Line
papers.r: A 3.0 cubic metre brick-and-charcoal evaporative store holds 24.6 degrees Celsius in 40 degree arid heat and extends modelled tomato life from 2.5 to 9.6 days for 6.7 litres of water per day, but it stops being useful above 61.5 percent ambient relative humidity at 35 degrees Celsius.

papers.t: Capturing the Nitrogen That Escapes from Stored Manure: An Acid-Scrubbed Vent for a Covered Store, Its Nitrogen Budget and Its Break-Even Herd Size
papers.r: An acid-scrubbed vent on a covered store for an 800-cow dairy herd captures 6,919 of 7,358 kg of emitted nitrogen per year at $1.55 per kg N, and capture stops paying below 720 cows, below a mean slurry temperature of 11.3 °C, and above a vent rate of 0.76 air changes per hour.

papers.t: Edge-of-Field Runoff Capture Sized from First Principles: A Woodchip Denitrification Bioreactor for 20 Hectares of Drained Cropland
papers.r: A 612.0 m³ woodchip bioreactor on 0.255% of a 20 ha field removes a simulated 26.3% of the seasonal nitrate load and bypasses in rainfall events above about 26.5 mm in 24 h.

papers.t: Farm-Scale Electrochemical Ammonia: A Costed Design and Its Failure at Small Scale
papers.r: Even with free electricity the designed farm-scale unit makes nitrogen at $16.30 per kg N, 8.8 times the delivered remote fertiliser price, so electrochemical ammonia does not pencil out at farm scale.

papers.t: Gravity-Fed Drip Irrigation from a Raised Tank Without a Pump: A Low-Head Design for a 0.1 Hectare Plot, Its Water Budget and Its Uniformity Limits
papers.r: A raised tank with no pump can drip-irrigate a 0.1 hectare tomato plot evenly (98.84% emission uniformity) on flat ground, delivering 6,644 L/day in four zones, provided uphill laterals stay at or below a 2.4% slope and 100 m in length.

papers.t: Non-Thermal Plasma Nitrogen Fixation at Village Scale: A Computed Design Budget for a Solar-Powered Gliding-Arc Unit, Compared with a Dielectric Barrier Discharge and with Delivered Synthetic Fertiliser
papers.r: A solar gliding-arc unit captures 0.433 kg of nitrogen per day at USD 13.00 per kg — beating a dielectric barrier discharge by a factor of 17.8 in energy, but still costing 6.3 times more per kg of nitrogen than urea delivered to a remote region.

papers.t: Oxygen-Scavenger Sachet Sizing for Hermetic Grain Storage: A First-Principles Oxygen Budget and Design Rule
papers.r: At 25 °C a hermetic grain store needs 1,087 grams of iron-based oxygen scavenger per tonne upfront plus 14.2 grams per tonne for each month of storage to keep oxygen below the level that kills stored-grain insects for the whole storage period.

papers.t: Rainwater Tank Sizing for Dry-Season Irrigation as a Computed Bound: Storage Is Set by Dry-Season Demand, Reliability Is Bought with Catchment Area
papers.r: For a 100 m² dry-season vegetable field needing 78.2 m³ in an 800 mm rainfall climate, a four-in-five reliable tank holds about 76 m³ but only works if the catchment is at least about 1.5 times the field area, and the system stops closing at any tank size once rainfall variability exceeds CV ≈ 0.33 at that ratio.

papers.t: Recovering Heat from Compost to Warm a Small Greenhouse: System Design, Heat Production Curve, and the Pile Mass Below Which the Plumbing Is Not Worth Installing
papers.r: An 8,000 kg compost pile with a water loop covers 46.0% of a 48 m² propagation greenhouse's 90-night heating demand (2,727 kWh delivered), and below a pile mass of 6,500 kg the plumbing is not worth installing.

papers.t: Soil Water Amendments Priced by Water Held per Dollar: A Common Yardstick, a Ranking Across Soil Textures, and the Break-Even Rainfall Deficit
papers.r: On sand, bentonite and low-temperature wood biochar deliver the most plant-available water per dollar and are the only options that ever pay for a maize crop on water alone, while synthetic hydrogel at field rates holds only 0.10 mm of water and returns 222 times less water per dollar than the best option.

homework.q: Take the paper “A Combined Solar Tunnel Dryer and Desiccant-Bead Store for Village Seed Saving: Design, Budgets, and Failure Floor”. Its stated result is: A 24 m² solar tunnel dryer held at or below 40 °C plus 198.6 kg of regenerable desiccant beads per tonne dries seed from 20 % to 9 % moisture in 1.56 days of dry-season sun, but the station fails below an insolation floor of 3.74 kWh m⁻² day⁻¹. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

professor.name: Professor Camila López
professor.personality: A quiet and relentless teacher of Designs & Engineering who tells the field story first and the theory immediately after. She believes the worked example is a moral act: nobody should have to guess what good looks like.
professor.greeting: Welcome to designs & Engineering. We start where the subject starts: at the beginning.

classes.title: Energy access

papers.t: A Solar Cooker That Can Cook the Evening Meal: A Panel Cooker with an Oil Thermal Store and a Retained-Heat Basket, Sized for a Family of Five
papers.r: A 1.6 m² panel cooker charging 22 kg of palm oil to 180 °C can deliver 1.93 MJ in the evening against a 1.62 MJ meal need for a family of five, serving food at about 92 °C, but it delivers nothing on a heavily overcast day and it cannot fry.

papers.t: A Village Microgrid Architecture Designed to Survive Its Own Failure Modes
papers.r: In an hourly simulation of a low-sun week, a 60-household village microgrid built as four independent clusters with a direct-current path for critical loads served 72.3% of demand through a dead inverter where a conventional single-inverter design of the same capacity served 0.0%, at a premium of $321.66 per household (14.19%).

papers.t: A Village-Fabricable Chimney Rocket Stove for Clean Cooking: Design, Thermal Performance, Draft, and Indoor Exposure Estimates
papers.r: The modelled stove cooks a stated day's food on 1.202 kg of wood instead of 3.505 kg and brings carbon monoxide below the guideline level used, but its fine-particle average remains 6.68 times the WHO 24-hour guideline.

papers.t: An Iron-Air Battery from Abundant Materials for Household and Village Electricity Storage: A First-Principles Design and Cost Test
papers.r: An iron-air battery loses to lithium iron phosphate for daily cycling at 10-hour duration because its round-trip efficiency is only 58.6 percent, but at 48-hour duration it delivers energy at $0.104 per kWh — about a quarter of the lithium cost — and it beats lead-acid at every duty tested.

papers.t: Battery-Free Solar Refrigeration for Off-Grid Clinics and Homes: A Direct-Drive Design with Ice-Bank Thermal Storage
papers.r: A 600 Wp direct-drive solar refrigerator with a 55.2 kg ice bank holds a 200-litre cabinet at 5 °C in a 32 °C ambient through three sunless days and costs USD 4,830 less over ten years than the battery-based equivalent.

papers.t: Building-Scale Gravity Energy Storage for Off-Grid Homes: A First-Principles Design and Cost Test
papers.r: Gravity storage fails at household scale — 235.8 tonnes at 10 metres delivers only 5 kWh overnight at about $1.96 per kWh versus $0.11 for lithium — and beats lead-acid only as a shared village hillside system of about 25 kWh per night or more.

papers.t: Counter-Rotating Vertical-Axis Wind Turbine Arrays: Designing Against the Spacing Tax from the Other Side
papers.r: A specified array of small counter-rotating vertical-axis rotors (771.6 per hectare) produces a mean of 6.351–8.861 W per square metre of its own hectare across the full range of assumed neighbour-interaction factors — above the 0.5–1.0 W/m² horizontal-axis landscape baseline even when neighbours are assumed to hurt rather than help — but that advantage is borrowed from surrounding air and falls back to the same 0.5–

papers.t: Flywheel Energy Storage at Household and Village Scale: A Reference Design, Its Self-Discharge, and the Duties It Can and Cannot Serve
papers.r: A 71.7 kg carbon-fibre flywheel can deliver a household's 2.00 kWh overnight load, but its 42 W standing loss drains 1.41% of its stored energy per hour — empty in about 71 hours — so at one cycle per day it costs $1.084 per delivered kWh against $0.376 for lithium iron phosphate, and it wins only at 10 or more cycles per day, in short power smoothing, and in minutes-long bridging.

papers.t: Household Biogas from the Waste a Family Actually Has: An Honest Energy Budget and a Digester Design for a Six-Person Household with Three Cattle
papers.r: A digester sized from a family's real waste — 18 kg of collectable dung and 1.5 kg of kitchen waste a day — covers 53% of that family's cooking energy over a year, falling to 38% in a cold spell.

papers.t: Pico-Hydro Power Without a Dam: A Run-of-Stream Design for a 45-Household Hill Village, Sized to Its Dry Season
papers.r: Sized to its dry season, a dam-free pico-hydro plant on the reference stream delivers 12.35 kW continuous in its driest month — 1.73 times the village's daily energy demand — at $0.060 per kWh served, against $0.42 for solar plus battery delivering the same continuous service.

papers.t: Sand-Battery Thermal Storage for Home Heating: A First-Principles Residential Design for Three Sunless Days in a Cold Climate
papers.r: A 4.51-tonne sand store in 2.82 cubic metres holds enough heat for three sunless days in the stated cold-climate house, beats direct electric heating when charged with surplus solar and used often, but usually loses to a heat pump and cannot be filled from winter rooftop solar in the stated case.

papers.t: Small-Scale Compressed-Air Energy Storage for a Village or Workshop: A First-Principles Design, Efficiency and Cost Test
papers.r: For evening light and phone charging for 50 households, village compressed-air storage returns only 15.9% of its charging electricity without heat storage (28.3% with it) and costs $1.545 per delivered kWh against $0.324 for lithium iron phosphate — and even with a free vessel the machinery alone costs more than a complete battery system — so it wins only where a tested vessel already exists, the charging power is tr

papers.t: Solar Water Pumping That Stores Water, Not Electricity: A Battery-Free Design for Drinking Water and Small-Plot Irrigation
papers.r: A 340 Wp direct-drive array with a 6.67 m³ elevated tank delivers 3.265 m³ per day in the worst month for the stated 3,000 litre daily demand and costs $5,756.54 over 20 years in present value ($0.263 per m³), saving $1,050.39 against a lithium battery-buffered equivalent.

papers.t: Thermochemical Heat Storage for Homes: A Strontium Bromide Seasonal Store Designed From First Principles
papers.r: A strontium bromide store holding 3,500 kg of salt stores 795.0 kWh usable in 8.16 m³, retains 0.996 of its charge over four months, and delivers 779.8 kWh, but at $4.93 per delivered kWh in seasonal use it loses decisively to a heat pump at $0.166 per kWh and to a seasonal water tank at $0.92 per kWh.

papers.t: Wake-Steering Fleet Control for a Wind Farm: Designing Against the Spacing and Wake Tax
papers.r: For a 20-turbine, 60 MW reference farm spaced 6 by 4 rotor diameters, an optimised wake-steering yaw schedule recovers +0.68% of fleet power in the dominant sector and +389 MWh a year (+0.25%, +64.3 W per hectare) in neutral air — rising to +4.37% in stable air, vanishing in turbulent air, and turning negative under fixed scheduling or direction spread, for a net of +$7,109 a year after added yaw maintenance.

papers.t: Waste-Heat Recovery for a Small Intermittent Brick Kiln: Air Preheat and Brick Drying, with Costs, Failure Modes and the Cases Where It Is Not Worth Building
papers.r: A bypassed steel-tube recuperator plus a brick-drying shed recovers 11.21 GJ per batch from a 10,000-brick intermittent kiln, saving 747 kg of firewood per batch (19.7%) and paying back in 2.12 years at 70 batches per year and 75 dollars per tonne of wood, while neither an electric tail nor a low-duty or cheap-fuel case survives the arithmetic.

papers.t: Water as a Seasonal Heat Store: A First-Principles Design for Half of a Cold-Climate Winter, Its Six-Month Loss, and the Scale at Which the Loss Becomes Acceptable
papers.r: A buried 202.3 cubic metre water tank can deliver half of the stated cold-climate house's yearly heat, but it loses 35.7 percent of the stored heat over six months and delivers heat at $1.167 per kilowatt-hour against $0.148 for a heat pump, and the loss fraction only falls to 15 percent or below when about twenty houses share one store.

homework.q: Take the paper “A Solar Cooker That Can Cook the Evening Meal: A Panel Cooker with an Oil Thermal Store and a Retained-Heat Basket, Sized for a Family of Five”. Its stated result is: A 1.6 m² panel cooker charging 22 kg of palm oil to 180 °C can deliver 1.93 MJ in the evening against a 1.62 MJ meal need for a family of five, serving food at about 92 °C, but it delivers nothing on a heavily overcast day and it cannot fry. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

professor.name: Professor Min-Ji Kim
professor.personality: A gentle and rigorous teacher of Designs & Engineering who slows down exactly where the textbooks speed up. Once a term, she teaches a whole session from the class's own questions and nothing else.
professor.greeting: Come in. Designs & Engineering is a craft here, and crafts are learned by hand.

classes.title: Health

papers.t: A Hand-Powered Centrifuge for Blood Separation Where There Is No Power: A Design Envelope Specified from Rotor Physics
papers.r: A 100:1 hand-crank design sustaining 6,797 g separates hematocrit samples in a specified 9 minutes and malaria concentration samples in 11 minutes at 48 patients per hour for USD 38.00 in parts, while platelet-poor plasma and quantitative buffy-coat work remain outside the hand-drive envelope.

papers.t: A Low-Cost Pulse Oximeter with an Honest Accuracy Budget: Design, Error Propagation, and the Accuracy Floor for Triage
papers.r: A US $17.50 discrete-part oximeter design computes to A_rms 1.52 points at perfusion index 3% at rest, 3.37 points in dark pigmentation with a broad emitter, and 2.41 points at the dark low-perfusion corner with narrowband emitters and melanin-stratified calibration — and must blank, not display, readings below perfusion index 1% or above A_rms 3.0 points.

papers.t: A Low-Dose Chest Radiography Protocol for Tuberculosis Screening Derived from the Dose-Resolution Trade
papers.r: A quantum-noise model gives a proposed TB screening protocol of 0.0069 mGy per film, 43.48 times below standard practice, preserving cavities, infiltrates and nodules of 5 mm or larger but not miliary nodules.

papers.t: A Passive Phase-Change Vaccine Carrier Sized for 72 Hours at 43 °C: Design and Thermal Model
papers.r: With 8.0 kg of 5 °C phase-change material behind a 20 mm vacuum-panel plus 30 mm foam wall, the model holds a 6 kg vaccine payload within 2–8 °C for 88.4 hours at a constant 43 °C ambient, never below 4.23 °C, at an estimated parts cost of US $254.53 (simulated, not measured).

papers.t: A Phase-Change Neonatal Warmer for Births Where No Incubator Exists: Design and Lumped Thermal Model
papers.r: A 2.5 kg phase-change mattress in an insulated wrap holds modelled skin temperature at or above 36.5 °C for at least 6.2 hours for every birth-weight class from 1.0 to 3.5 kg at ambient temperatures of 15 °C and above after one hot-water recharge, and its boiling-water recharge is bounded at a 40 °C pack maximum by a guard phase-change tray.

papers.t: A Water Witness for Clinics: Design and Accuracy Budget of a Low-Cost Photometer for Free Chlorine and Turbidity at the Point of Care
papers.r: A $37.90 dual-channel photometer design is computed to detect free chlorine to 0.063 mg/L with about 0.020 mg/L standard uncertainty across the WHO 0.2–0.5 mg/L band and turbidity to 0.159 NTU, sufficient to flag a lost chlorine residual and adjudicate the 5 NTU limit but not to certify samples within about 0.04 mg/L of either chlorine band edge.

papers.t: Airborne-Infection Control in a Low-Resource Clinic Waiting Room, Priced per Dollar: A Model-Derived Ranked Protocol
papers.r: Wind cross-ventilation buys the most tuberculosis risk reduction per dollar (24.22 percentage points per $100), and pairing its openings with a $180 exhaust fan holds infection probability at 0.0173 even with no wind.

papers.t: An Ultrasound-First Diagnostic Pathway for Suspected Appendicitis Where No CT Scanner Exists: A Proposed Decision Protocol with a Cohort Model
papers.r: In a 1,000-case cohort model, the ultrasound-first protocol settles 52.3% of suspected appendicitis cases by ultrasound alone, avoids 79.57% of transfers and 716.09 mSv of collective dose per 100 patients versus transfer-all-for-CT, at $158.63 per patient, with 5.90 missed cases per 1,000 under the discharge rules and a 17.64% negative-appendectomy implication among settled-positive patients.

papers.t: Gravity-Fed Intravenous Infusion Without Pumps, Made Accurate: An Error Budget for the Standard Drip Set and a Constant-Head Mariotte Insert Design
papers.r: A standard gravity drip set modelled over 1,000 mL at 125 mL/h finishes 20.8% slow and 12.1% late (22.7% combined error budget), while a US$2.30 Mariotte constant-head insert removes the head-decay term (residual 0.84%) and reaches 9.5% total error only when the clamp is set at the patient after fitting.

papers.t: Hearing Screening with a Smartphone: An Error Budget and the Protocol It Permits
papers.r: With model-specific calibration the phone screen supports a binary referral decision at 35 dB HL in a quiet room (PTA error 4.126 dB) but not exact WHO grade assignment, and in a typical room the masking floor removes the normal-to-mild distinction entirely.

papers.t: Household Smoke from Solid-Fuel Cooking: A Low-Cost Chimney Hood Priced by Draft Physics
papers.r: Sized by draft physics (3.5 m, 200 mm flue; 12.02 Pa, 0.0689 m3/s), the chimney hood gives the largest modelled exposure reduction (66.3%) but ranks last per dollar (1.053 %/USD) behind a solar fan (1.411) and an improved stove (1.182), and it fails against adverse wind above about 5.39 m/s.

papers.t: Oxygen for Childhood Pneumonia Where Cylinders Run Out: A Solar Oxygen Concentrator Sized and Priced from Physics
papers.r: For a 10-child ward at a mean 1.25 L/min per child, a 4.5 kWp solar array with a 33 kWh battery and three 10 L/min concentrator modules supplies 18.0 m³ of oxygen per day at $0.91 per patient-day, against $18.61 per patient-day for delivered cylinders.

papers.t: Passive Cooling for Medicine Storage in a Hot Clinic Without Reliable Power: A Radiative, Evaporative and Thermal-Mass Cabinet Design and Its Computed Climate Envelope
papers.r: In the model the cabinet holds at or below 25 °C through a 40 °C peak day in dry air (maximum 24.95 °C on radiative cooling alone, 23.84 °C with the evaporative stage), holds in 26 of 48 swept climate combinations, and fails in humid heat and at every 45 °C combination.

papers.t: Solar Water Disinfection Made Quantitative: A UV-A Dose Model for a PET Bottle and a Fixed-Geometry Reflector Backing
papers.r: A foil V-trough reflector backing (gain 1.72 clear-sky, $0.96 in materials) cuts time to 3-log E. coli from 1.97 h to 1.23 h on a clear mid-latitude summer day, but a single overcast day remains insufficient for viruses and Giardia cysts with or without it.

papers.t: Steam Sterilization of Instruments with a Household Pressure Cooker, Priced from Physics — and an Honest Verdict on Solar Sterilization Claims
papers.r: A validated 121 °C pressure-cooker cycle for 2.0 kg of instruments needs 1.547 MJ and costs $0.061–$0.091 in fuel with 5 cycles per day, while a flat-plate solar collector cannot hold 121 °C at 500 W/m² and is not reliable as a sole-source sterilizer, though evacuated or concentrating collectors of 1–2 m² can complete a cycle in about 1–1.5 sun-hours on a clear day.

papers.t: Ultraviolet Disinfection for Low-Resource Clinics with Honest Dose Budgets: A Priced Specification for Upper-Room Air Treatment and Surface Terminal Disinfection
papers.r: Upper-room 254 nm air treatment delivers 12.1 equivalent air changes per hour for tuberculosis at $0.88 per room per day, while occupied far-UVC is capped by exposure limits and surface disinfection cannot reach shadowed sites at any exposure time.

papers.t: Vision Screening with a Smartphone, Bounded by Optics: A Protocol Derived from Display, Camera and Pinhole Limits
papers.r: Bounded by its own optics, a smartphone supports a 2 m distance-acuity screen at the 6/12 boundary plus a pinhole step that identifies a refractive cause from 1.19 dioptres, while its built-in photorefraction geometry is blind below 3.33 dioptres and fine acuity grades, dioptre values and astigmatism axis are not supported.

homework.q: Take the paper “A Hand-Powered Centrifuge for Blood Separation Where There Is No Power: A Design Envelope Specified from Rotor Physics”. Its stated result is: A 100:1 hand-crank design sustaining 6,797 g separates hematocrit samples in a specified 9 minutes and malaria concentration samples in 11 minutes at 48 patients per hour for USD 38.00 in parts, while platelet-poor plasma and quantitative buffy-coat work remain outside the hand-drive envelope. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

professor.name: Professor Giovanni Almeida
professor.personality: A measured and methodical teacher of Designs & Engineering who learns every student's name by the second meeting, and uses them. Once a term, he teaches a whole session from the class's own questions and nothing else.
professor.greeting: In, in. Designs & Engineering waits for no one, and neither do we.

classes.title: Shelter & infrastructure

papers.t: A 20% Rice-Husk Ash, 6% Alkali Formulation for Fly-Ash Geopolymer Wall Blocks: A Formulation Search Priced in Strength, Cost and Carbon per Square Metre of Wall
papers.r: A fly-ash block with 20% rice-husk ash and a 6% alkali dose, cured at 60 °C for 24 hours, reaches a simulated 8.02 MPa at US$17.30 and 24.28 kg CO2e per square metre of wall, but the activator carries 76.7% of the carbon and any dose above 8% is ruled out by the alkali handling limit.

papers.t: A Confined-Masonry Wall System for One-Storey Stabilised-Earth Housing: Tie-Column and Ring-Beam Layout with a Computed Seismic Shear and Stability Budget
papers.r: For a 7.2 m by 4.8 m one-storey house in 140 mm stabilised-earth block with tie-columns at no more than 2.4 m spacing and a continuous ring beam, the computed design envelope ends at 0.291 g, set by in-plane shear of the short walls, with drift at that point of 0.0419% against a stated 0.40% limit.

papers.t: A Continuous Load-Path Strap-and-Anchor Roof Tie-Down Assembly for Low-Cost Housing: A Computed Uplift Budget and Its Limit Wind Speed
papers.r: The computed zoned strap-and-grouted-anchor assembly reaches its design limit at a wind speed of 41.3 m/s (149 km/h), governed by grout-to-masonry anchor bond at 3.67 kN design per unit, against 30.1 m/s for uniform 0.9 m spacing, at USD 264.00 per house.

papers.t: A Flood-Resilient Amphibious Foundation for a Small House: Buoyancy, Guide-Post Loads and Failure Limits
papers.r: A 38,000 kg house on a 10.0 m by 8.0 m buoyant base lifts off at 0.50 m of flood water, floats with 0.925 m of freeboard, and carries the design 3.0 m flood at 2.0 m/s with a guide-post bending margin of 1.85, while a guide jammed after 1.00 m of rise fails at a margin of 0.13.

papers.t: A Household Greywater Treatment and Reuse Bed for Water-Short Settlements: A Sizing Rule and Computed Treatment Budget for a Gravel-and-Reed Subsurface-Flow Design
papers.r: For five people producing 250 litres of greywater per day, organic loading governs the size at a design area of 6.5 m² (1.30 m² per person), the computed effluent BOD falls from 150 mg/L to 17.0 mg/L at 20 °C, clogging arrives after 3.52 years without a pre-filter and 7.05 years with one, and the treated water may be used only for below-ground irrigation — never for drinking or household contact.

papers.t: A Lashed-Plus-Bolted Bamboo–Timber Joint for Low-Rise Housing: Connector Design and a Computed Shear, Pull-Out and Slip Budget Across Culm Diameter and Moisture
papers.r: A single M12 bolt with washer plates plus six turns of rope lashing gives a 120 mm bamboo culm a design shear capacity of 8.29 kN and a pull-out capacity of 7.93 kN at US$4.63 per joint, with every diameter and moisture combination tested in simulation passing.

papers.t: A Low-Cost Bridge-Scour Witness Instrument: A Tilt-Node Chain Design and Its Computed Detection Budget
papers.r: A chain of 16 tilt nodes spaced 0.20 m apart is computed to witness pier scour to within 0.20 m over a 3.2 m range, detect a new exposure with probability 0.892 within one hour at a model false-alarm rate of 0.0110 per chain per year, run a computed 9.32 years on one battery pack (service capped at 5.0 years), and cost $191.40 in parts.

papers.t: A Passive Radiative-Cooling Roof Assembly for Heat-Wave Housing: Computed Cooling Budget and Price per Degree of Indoor Temperature Reduction
papers.r: The computed assembly lowers the daily-mean indoor temperature of a vulnerable 16 m² room by 3.61–3.75 K versus a dark roof at USD 76.75–79.80 per degree, but in humid heat its sub-ambient cooling at peak sun falls to effectively zero (4.8 W/m², 0.4 K), leaving solar rejection as the only supported benefit.

papers.t: A Passive Solar Heating Wall for Cold-Climate Low-Income Housing: A Computed Sizing Rule, Temperature-Lift Budget, and Cost per Degree
papers.r: An 8.0 m² glazed thermal-mass wall 0.25 m thick lifts a poorly insulated room by 3.45 K at 45° N under a partly cloudy January sky (7.95 K at 35° N clear, 0.64 K at 55° N overcast), delivers 3.368 kWh per night at the central case, is sized by area at 0.37 K per m² with mass thickness held to 0.15–0.25 m, costs $734.49 per degree of lift at the central case, and needs 0.10 m² of vent area to hold an autumn peak of 31

papers.t: A Porous Ceramic Evaporator Wall for a Single Room in Arid Housing: Computed Indoor Temperature Reduction, Water Use per Degree, and the Humidity Ceiling
papers.r: At 40 degrees Celsius and 20 percent relative humidity outside, the wall holds the room at 29.00 degrees Celsius, a reduction of 11.00 degrees, for 47.21 litres of evaporated water per 12-hour day (4.29 litres per day per degree), and it stops working above 62.7 percent outdoor relative humidity at 40 degrees Celsius.

papers.t: A Rainwater-First Roof and Storage System for a Water-Short Household: Integrated Sizing of Roof, First-Flush Diverter and Tank Against a 450 mm Rainfall Regime
papers.r: A 120.0 m² roof, a 120.0 litre first-flush diverter and a 20,000 litre tank supply a five-person household's 100.0 litres per day on 352.23 days per year (96.50% reliability) in a 450 mm rainfall regime, but reliability falls to 57.12% in drought at 60% rainfall.

papers.t: A Sacrificial Crack-and-Strain Witness Strip for Small Bridges and Culverts: Design and Computed Threshold Budget
papers.r: Eight graded sacrificial ligaments on a passive 100 mm strip are computed to record peak crack opening from 0.20 mm to 1.25 mm in 0.15 mm steps with a worst-case temperature effect of 0.0235 mm against the 0.20 mm first threshold, a governing computed service life of 8.63 years (replacement capped at 5.0 years), and a parts cost of $9.45 per crossing point.

papers.t: A Sewerless Thermal Sanitation Unit for a Household: Computed Pathogen Lethality, Energy per Use, and Safe-Handling Intervals for a 2-Litre Batch Design
papers.r: A 2.0 kg household batch held at 65 °C for 25 min gives a computed 7.41-log reduction of Ascaris suum eggs (the limiting organism; 6-log needs 20.24 min) using 0.1188 kWh per use, with safe handling after 11.06 h sealed or 1.11 h vented to 40 °C, in a unit costing US$118.00 in parts (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED).

papers.t: A Slope-Failure Witness Network for Informal Hillside Settlements: Node Design and a Computed Warning Budget
papers.r: A tilt and soil-moisture witness network is computed to give a hillside settlement 8.14 hours (watch) and 3.90 hours (warning) of lead before a rainfall-driven slope failure in the reference storm (20 mm/h, 1.2 m slip plane), at a nuisance warning rate of 0.192 per slope per year and a parts cost of $22.38 per household.

papers.t: A Solar Desiccation Sanitation Chamber for Households Without Sewers: Computed Moisture-Removal, Pathogen Die-Off, and Safe-Storage Budgets Across Humidity and Season
papers.r: A solar drying chamber can dry a household's weekly faecal batch in about a week of ordinary sun, but the dried material still needs about five months of sealed storage before it reaches the stated safe-handling threshold.

papers.t: A Straw and Rice-Husk Fibre Insulation Panel: Specification and Computed Thermal, Moisture, Cost and Fire-Behaviour Envelope
papers.r: A 100 mm straw/rice-husk panel gives 2.041 m²K/W dry and 1.624 at 80% relative humidity at US$8.42/m², with a 16% moisture design limit, and is combustible with computed ignition in about one second above the critical flux so it may be used only as protected infill behind a non-combustible lining.

papers.t: A Universal 6% Equal-Split Lime-Cement Formulation for Stabilised-Earth Wall Blocks: A Mix-Selection Computation Balancing Strength, Wet Durability, Embodied Energy and Cost
papers.r: One recipe — 94% local soil with 3% cement and 3% lime — works in simulation across soils from 15% to 40% clay and cuts the wall's embodied energy by 23.8% compared with an 8% cement-only block.

homework.q: Take the paper “A 20% Rice-Husk Ash, 6% Alkali Formulation for Fly-Ash Geopolymer Wall Blocks: A Formulation Search Priced in Strength, Cost and Carbon per Square Metre of Wall”. Its stated result is: A fly-ash block with 20% rice-husk ash and a 6% alkali dose, cured at 60 °C for 24 hours, reaches a simulated 8.02 MPa at US$17.30 and 24.28 kg CO2e per square metre of wall, but the activator carries 76.7% of the carbon and any dose above 8% is ruled out by the alkali handling limit. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

professor.name: Professor Rachel Phillips
professor.personality: A wry and well-read teacher of Designs & Engineering who makes the class derive it once before anyone is allowed to quote it. She has one unbreakable rule: nobody apologises for a question.
professor.greeting: In, in. Designs & Engineering waits for no one, and neither do we.

classes.title: Fishing and Small Boats (Wave 6)

papers.t: An Anchor Sizing and Scope Rule for Small Fishing Boats: Holding in Sand and Mud at 20 and 30 Knots of Wind
papers.r: At a scope of 7:1 the anchor weight required is 2.68 kg in sand and 6.69 kg in mud at 20 knots, rising to 4.53 kg in sand and 11.32 kg in mud at 30 knots. Scope is worth more than weight in this model: at 30 knots in sand, shortening the scope from 7:1 to 3:1 raises the required weight from 4.53 kg to 11.32 kg, exactly the weight that soft mud demands at full scope, while in mud at 3:1 the requirement reaches 28.30 k

papers.t: A Safe-Load Rule for Dugout Canoes: Freeboard, Metacentric Height and the Cost of Standing Up
papers.r: For the reference canoe of 5.0 m length, 0.85 m beam and 0.45 m depth, the safe payload with everyone seated is 300 kg, while the freeboard alone would allow 588 kg; loading to the freeboard figure would leave the metacentric height negative in the standing case and at the stated minimum in the seated case.

papers.t: Sizing the Walls of a Low-Cost Insulated Fish Box: Expanded Polystyrene versus a Sawdust-Filled Double Wooden Wall
papers.r: Two low-cost constructions are sized. Expanded polystyrene sheet (thermal conductivity 0.035 W/(m·K)) requires a wall 69.5 mm thick, which in practice means building to 70 mm; it leaves an internal volume of 182.9 litres, 50.8 percent of the 360-litre gross volume.

papers.t: A Waiting Rule for Newly Anchored Fish Aggregating Devices: How Long a New Device Must Stand Before Fishing It, with a Mooring Scope and Anchor Table
papers.r: A new device reaches 50 percent of its settled catch rate after 4.85 days, 80 percent after 11.27 days, 90 percent after 16.12 days, and 95 percent after 20.97 days. The recommended rule is therefore to let a new device stand for about 16 days before fishing it in earnest if 90 percent of the settled rate is wanted, or about 21 days for 95 percent.

papers.t: A Minimum-Freeboard Bound for Small Open Boats: Wave Height, Bow Immersion and a Hand-Span Rule
papers.r: For a 5.0 m boat of standard bow shape, a loaded freeboard of 0.30 m is exceeded at a wave height of 0.439 m; a freeboard of 0.20 m is exceeded at 0.293 m, and one of 0.40 m at 0.585 m. In units a fisherman can measure on his or her own hand, taking a stretched hand span as 0.20 m, the rule for the 5.0 m boat is that the largest wave that can be met without boarding is about 1.46 times the loaded freeboard, so one an

papers.t: A Degradable Escape Panel Specification for Fish Traps: A Cotton-Twine Fastener That Ends Ghost Fishing Within Thirty Days
papers.r: The study then originates a specification for a degradable escape panel intended to stop a lost trap within a chosen deadline of 30 days: a buoyant 200 mm by 200 mm panel held shut by four ties of untreated cotton twine, sized so that seawater decay brings the twine's strength down to the panel's steady opening load at the right time, neither during normal service nor long after the deadline.

papers.t: Hanging Ratio Moves a Gillnet's Catch Band but Cannot Narrow It: A Geometric Selection Rule
papers.r: Both edges of the caught-length band turn out to be proportional to the same quantity, so their ratio is fixed at 1.4238 for every hanging ratio from 0.30 to 0.70: hanging ratio moves the band and stretches it, but cannot change its relative width. The result is then worked in the form a fisherman actually needs.

papers.t: An Ice-Planning Rule for Small Fishing Trips: Ice Needed to Chill the Catch and to Offset Heat Leak, and the Trip Length at Which a 1:2 Ice-to-Fish Ratio Runs Out
papers.r: The rule is R = 0.01078 × T + 0.00706 × T × t, where R is kilograms of ice per kilogram of fish, T is ambient temperature in °C and t is trip length in days. Chilling alone consumes 0.216 kg of ice per kilogram of fish at 20 °C and 0.377 kg/kg at 35 °C. Heat leak melts a further 14.12 kg of ice per day per 100 kg of fish at 20 °C, rising to 24.72 kg per day at 35 °C.

papers.t: Choose the Line by Its Knotted Strength, Not the Number on the Spool: A Weakest-Link Table for Handline and Longline Gear
papers.r: On a line whose spool figure is 20 kgf, the knotted strength is 18.6 kgf with a Palomar knot, holding a fish of 6.2 kg under the load model, but only 15.0 kgf with an improved clinch knot (a fish of 5.0 kg) and only 10.0 kgf with an overhand knot (a fish of 3.33 kg).

papers.t: The Escape Length of a Stretched Mesh: An Inscribed-Circle Rule Linking Mesh Size, Opening Shape, and Fish Girth
papers.r: For a 100 mm stretched mesh the rule gives an escape length of 335.1 mm for a square opening and 288.3 mm for a diamond opening, a ratio of 0.86, so opening shape alone changes the escaping size by about one seventh at fixed mesh size. Across stretched mesh sizes from 25 mm to 150 mm the escape length rises from 73.3 mm to 509.6 mm for square openings and from 61.6 mm to 439.5 mm for diamond openings.

papers.t: A No-Ice Working Clock for Landed Fish: Hours to the Quality Limit across Temperatures, and the Extension from Wet Sacking in Shade
papers.r: Taking a reference shelf life on ice of 12 days (288 hours) at 0 °C to the limit of acceptable quality, and a Q10 of 2.5 for the temperature dependence of spoilage, the remaining saleable time is 182.1 hours at 5 °C, 115.2 hours at 10 °C, 72.9 hours at 15 °C, 46.1 hours at 20 °C, 29.1 hours at 25 °C, 18.4 hours at 30 °C and 11.7 hours at 35 °C.

papers.t: Sizing the Outrigger Float of a Single-Outrigger Canoe: Ama Volume, Crossbeam Length and Heel Limits
papers.r: For a two-crew canoe of 260 kg total mass facing a heeling moment of 715 N m, the rule requires an ama of 48.6 litres at a centreline distance of 3.0 m, of diameter 0.153 m over a length of 3.3 m; the corresponding volumes are 58.3 litres at 2.5 m and 41.6 litres at 3.5 m. The one-crew case requires 24.3 litres and the three-crew case 80.4 litres at the same 3.0 m distance.

papers.t: A Salt-Penetration Rule for Whole and Split Fish: Salting Times by Thickness, the Spoilage Thickness Limit, and Dry Salting Compared with Brining
papers.r: Salting time grows with the square of the half-thickness, so splitting a fish open, which halves its thickness, cuts the curing time by a factor of 4.0 exactly in this model. Against a stated spoilage clock of 36 hours for an unsalted centre at 25 degrees C, a whole fish thicker than 2.30 cm dry salted, or 1.69 cm brined, has a centre that spoils before the salt arrives; splitting raises those limits to 4.60 cm and 3

papers.t: A Closing Bound for Beach Seining: The Largest Seine a Standard Hauling Team Can Close, and the Haul Rate Longer Seines Require
papers.r: Against a stated design bound of one fish in five escaping (a fraction of 0.20), the largest seine a standard team of two haulers per end, pulling 400 N per end, can close in time is 25 m: at 25 m the model's escape fraction is 0.1677, and at 30 m it has already risen to 0.2471. For longer seines the paper inverts the calculation and gives the minimum haul rate.

papers.t: A Sizing Rule for Fish Trap Funnel Throats: Throat Diameter and Cone Angle Against Entry and Escape
papers.r: A throat equal to the body depth admits only half the target fish (entry probability 0.50), so the throat must exceed the depth: the recommended window runs from 1.18 to 1.40 times the body depth for every target size computed.

papers.t: The Soak-Time Peak: Why a Longer Soak Does Not Always Catch More in a Baited Fish Trap
papers.r: Under the baseline assumptions the catch rises to a peak of 19.43 fish at 18.04 hours and then falls: a trap hauled at 48 hours holds 12.86 fish, which is 31.9 percent fewer than it held at 24 hours and fewer than the 18.49 fish it already held at 12 hours. Halving the peak soak time costs 12.8 percent of the peak catch; doubling it costs 17.2 percent.

papers.t: A Trip Fuel-Planning Rule for a Small Outboard Fishing Boat: Speed, Load, and Why a Larger Engine Does Not Burn Proportionally More
papers.r: For the headline case — a total trip distance of 20 nautical miles at 7 knots with a medium load — the 15 hp engine burns 4.434 litres for the trip, and the planning rule proposed here, fuel to carry equals computed trip burn multiplied by a reserve factor of 1.50, gives 6.651 litres to carry. Speed is expensive in this model: the same 20 nautical mile trip burns 3.110 litres at 5 knots and 5.421 litres at 9 knots.

homework.q: Take the paper “An Anchor Sizing and Scope Rule for Small Fishing Boats: Holding in Sand and Mud at 20 and 30 Knots of Wind”. Its stated result is: At a scope of 7:1 the anchor weight required is 2.68 kg in sand and 6.69 kg in mud at 20 knots, rising to 4.53 kg in sand and 11.32 kg in mud at 30 knots. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

professor.name: Professor Ji-Yeon Kim
professor.personality: A unhurried and exact teacher of Designs & Engineering who asks the room to predict first, and only then shows the answer. She believes the worked example is a moral act: nobody should have to guess what good looks like.
professor.greeting: Welcome to designs & Engineering. We start where the subject starts: at the beginning.

classes.title: Bees, Honey and Wax (Wave 6)

papers.t: A Winter Stores Bound for the Honey Bee Hive: Insulation, Heat Loss, and the Honey a Colony Must Spend
papers.r: Under a held-cavity upper-bound model over a 150-day cold continental winter (mean −6.83 °C), the stores bound falls from 73.16 kg for bare 19 mm pine to 22.17 kg with 50 mm EPS insulation, a 69.7% reduction, while roof-only insulation barely helps (64.25 kg). The sizing rule originated: whole-hive conductance, floor included, at or below 1.013 W/K holds the cold-winter bound within 20 kg of stores.

papers.t: Condensation Arithmetic in the Winter Hive: Water Production, Wall Temperature, and Where the Moisture Falls
papers.r: Honey metabolism yields 0.48 kg of water per kilogram of honey consumed (48.0 g/day at 100 g/day). At −10 °C outside, a bare pine inner wall sits at 1.78 °C, 4.93 °C below the 6.71 °C dew point of cavity air, condensing an estimated 618.1 g/m²/day, while a 50 mm EPS wall holds 8.52 °C and condenses nothing.

papers.t: Summer Heat Load in the Honey Bee Hive: Fanning Bees, Water Demand, and a Roof and Shade Sizing Rule
papers.r: At 43 °C a dark uninsulated hive needs 273.7 g of water per hour and 336 fanning bees (1,642.0 g over 6 hours) against 85.3 g/hour and 105 bees in full shade. Fanning never exceeds 3.4% of a 10,000-bee forager force — water, not bee numbers, is the binding cost — and an 80 g/hour water target at 43 °C is infeasible for any roof colour. The rule originated: light finish first, roof insulation second, shade third.

papers.t: The Cost of Wrong Frame Spacing: A Season Budget Model and a Millimetre Tolerance for Ten-Frame Boxes
papers.r: Costs are zero while gaps stay inside the 6.0–9.0 mm bee-space range, then grow linearly; against season budgets of 0.50 kg honey equivalent and 30 extra minutes, the spacing tolerance is −1.7 mm to +1.6 mm (usable shop rule ±1.5 mm).

papers.t: Population Arithmetic and the Supering Rule: When Storage Binds and What a Week of Delay Costs
papers.r: The cohort model peaks at 71,400 adults on day 122. At the stated nectar flow the brood box's 26,500 free cells bind in 4.77 days, giving the rule: super at 10 days of storage cover (55,556 free cells). Supering one week late costs 16.84 kg of honey — 5.57 kg never stored plus 11.26 kg forgone because backfilled brood cells remove 22,525 adults — and two weeks late costs 34.34 kg.

papers.t: What Drawn Comb Costs: The Honey Price of a Box of Comb and a Bound on Annual Comb Renewal
papers.r: At the stated 7.0 kg of honey per kilogram of wax, a box of comb costs 8.4 kg of honey foundationless against 2.8 kg on foundation and nothing for drawn comb — first-season penalties of 21.0% versus 7.0% of a 40 kg crop.

papers.t: The Economic Forage Radius of a Honey Bee Colony: A Flight-Energy Bound on Net Gain per Trip
papers.r: At 12.0 J/km flight cost and a 40 mg nectar load, the break-even radius is 4.94 km at 20% sugar, 7.72 km at 30%, 10.51 km at 40% and 13.29 km at 50%; the half-maximum working radius is 3.86 km at 30% sugar.

papers.t: How Many Colonies a Landscape Carries: A Stocking-Rate Bound from Seasonal Sugar Production and Colony Demand
papers.r: With 20% of produced sugar harvestable and 60 kg of seasonal demand per colony, per-colony surplus halves at 35.3 colonies/km² on oilseed rape, 18.8 on clover and 7.1 on wildflower meadow; energetic break-even is 50.0, 26.7 and 10.0 colonies/km² respectively. These are energetic ceilings for pure stands, stated as bounds rather than recommended stocking rates.

papers.t: A Scored Hive Placement Rule from Morning Sun, Wind Exposure and Distance to Water
papers.r: An east-facing entrance gains 128.6 extra foraging minutes on the stated spring morning (first flight 07:26 against 09:34 shaded); exposed wind costs 25.4% of a 3.0 km trip's net gain and delays first flight by 64.3 minutes. On a 35 °C day with 1.0 L of water demand and 200 water carriers, the maximum tolerable water distance is 368 m — water at 1.0 km delivers only 0.55 L.

papers.t: Swarm Timing and the Price of a Swarm: A Congestion Crossing, an Inspection-Interval Bound, and a Honey Cost in Kilograms
papers.r: Under stated spring growth assumptions the bees-per-litre congestion threshold is crossed 36.48 days after 1 March, with cell occupancy following at 38.89 days; the derived inspection-interval bound is 7 days, from queen-cell sealing at day 8 less a one-day margin.

papers.t: A Bait Hive Sized by Arithmetic: A Capture-Odds Model and the Cheapest Specification That Reaches a Stated Probability
papers.r: In a multiplicative capture-odds model over 240 specifications, only 8 reach the target probability of 0.4 against a reference box at 0.5, because compromises multiply. The cheapest compliant specification is 30 L volume, 12.5 cm² entrance, mounted at 3 m, with old comb: relative odds 0.693, probability 0.409, cost $73.0 against $94.0 for the reference box.

papers.t: Smoker Fuel and the Inspection Clock: A Fuel Sizing Rule in Grams per Hive and the Pace at Which Smoke Demand Outruns the Chamber
papers.r: The fuel sizing rule runs from 15.6 g per hive for wood pellets to 33.6 g per hive for dried grass, with pine needles at 28.8 g. Chamber endurance is density-driven: 35.77 hives per load for pellets against 2.81 for pine needles, stretching a 24-hive round from 4.8 to 5.4 hours through refills alone. Smoke demand outruns the chamber within the hour above 12.5 hives/hour on burlap and 6.25 hives/hour on cardboard.

papers.t: Wax Rendering, Weighed Honestly: Mass Balance, Method Losses, and a Solar Melter Sizing Rule
papers.r: Old brood comb yields 0.2132 kg of wax per kilogram in a water bath (0.1725 kg solar, 0.2484 kg with a second pressing) against 0.8565 kg for cappings; the belief that old comb renders about half wax does not survive, since its wax fraction is only 0.32 to begin with.

papers.t: The Moisture Bound and the Fermentation Clock: Water Activity, Yeast Growth, and a Ripening Rule for Honey
papers.r: The moisture ceiling for 365-day storage with a safety factor of 2 at 25 °C is 19.0% (water activity 0.601); past it the clock runs fast, with detectable fermentation in 55.3 days at 20% moisture and 29.3 days at 21% at 25 °C (122.3 and 65.1 days at 15 °C), so the slogan that honey never spoils does not survive for high-moisture honey.

papers.t: Crystallisation and the Storage Temperature Rule: Glucose Supersaturation, Temperature-Dependent Rates, and the Cost of Warming Honey Back
papers.r: Cellar-cool storage near 14 °C is the fastest-crystallising condition: clover honey at a glucose-to-water ratio of 1.85 shows crystals in 29.6 days at 14 °C against 80.5 days at 25 °C, 2.72 times longer, so liquid honey should be stored warm and out of the low teens.

papers.t: The Varroa Arithmetic That Treatment-Free Claims Must Answer: Per-Cycle Growth, Threshold Crossing Dates, and the Removal Fraction Required to Hold a Colony Flat
papers.r: Per-cycle mite multipliers are 1.5729 in the worker-brood season and 1.7181 in the drone-brood season, requiring 36.4% and 41.8% removal per cycle to hold the load flat; annual growth is 104.86× untreated, 49.42× with one brood break and 18.26× with drone removal and a break combined, while drone removal alone delivers only 26.7% in-season.

papers.t: Top-Bar Versus Frame Hive Economics Over a Working Life: Cost per Kilogram, Labour Valuation, and the Break-Even Bounds Between the Two Systems
papers.r: The top-bar hive wins at unpaid labour (1.87 against 4.16 $/kg over 5 years; 1.13 against 2.88 $/kg over 10 years) and the frame hive wins at $20/hr (8.96 against 9.20 $/kg over 5 years; 7.68 against 8.47 $/kg over 10 years).

homework.q: Take the paper “A Winter Stores Bound for the Honey Bee Hive: Insulation, Heat Loss, and the Honey a Colony Must Spend”. Its stated result is: Under a held-cavity upper-bound model over a 150-day cold continental winter (mean −6.83 °C), the stores bound falls from 73.16 kg for bare 19 mm pine to 22.17 kg with 50 mm EPS insulation, a 69.7% reduction, while roof-only insulation barely helps (64.25 kg). (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
