professor.name: Professor Magnus Laine
professor.personality: A sunny and hands-on teacher of Designs & Engineering who slows down exactly where the textbooks speed up. He favourite sentence is: show me.
professor.greeting: Mind the threshold. Designs & Engineering is bigger inside than it looks.

classes.title: Wells, Hand Pumps and Rope (Wave 6)

papers.t: Bad Air at the Bottom: A Ventilation Bound and a Test Rule for Hand-Dug Wells
papers.r: Without ventilation, the stated 0.5% concentration level is reached in 0.34 hours at 5 m, 0.68 hours at 10 m, 1.02 hours at 15 m, and 1.35 hours at 20 m; the stated 4.0% immediately-dangerous level is reached in 2.93 hours, 5.85 hours, 8.78 hours, and 11.70 hours at the same depths.

papers.t: Holding a Load with Two Fingers: The Capstan Rule for Well Work, and Where Wet Rope Breaks It
papers.r: Two wraps multiply a holding force by 43.38 in the dry-on-wood state, but by only 6.59 when the same rope is wet, by 12.35 on steel, and by 3.51 on wet steel. At the stated maximum one-person holding force of 150 N, two wraps therefore restrain at most 663.2 kg dry on wood, but only 100.7 kg wet on wood, 188.8 kg on steel, and 53.7 kg on wet steel.

papers.t: Chain or Rope: A Weight, Stretch, and Strength Accounting for Raising Water and Loads
papers.r: Chain weighs 18.33 times as much per metre as the polyester rope and 7.1 times as much as the manila rope. At a depth of 5 m the chain alone already weighs 11.0 kg, exactly the payload, and the total suspended mass is 22.0 kg; at 50 m the chain system totals 121.0 kg against 26.5 kg for manila and 17.0 kg for polyester, and the energy required for the lift is 32373.0 J for chain against 9196.9 J for manila and 6867.0

papers.t: The Counterweight Well: Sizing the Stone That Reduces the Work of Raising Water
papers.r: For the main case, an empty bucket of 3.0 kg carrying 15 kg of water raised through 10 m, the counterweight that minimises the peak force in the cycle is 10.5 kg, which equalises the two strokes at a peak force of 73.6 N, well below the unaided peak of 176.6 N.

papers.t: Sizing the Cylinder to the Well: A Force-Balance Rule for Hand-Pump Bore Diameter Against Depth
papers.r: Under the central assumptions — a sustainable handle force of 150 N, a lever ratio of 4, seal friction of 45 N, and a steel pump rod of 12 mm diameter weighing 8.709 N per metre — the maximum bore is 77.9 mm at a depth of 10 m, 49.7 mm at 20 m, 35.6 mm at 30 m, and 25.9 mm at 40 m.

papers.t: How Long to Reach Water: Excavated Volume, Hoisting Work, and Digging Time by Depth and Soil
papers.r: For the nominal shaft the excavated volume to a depth of 20 m is 22.62 m³, corresponding to spoil masses of 38.45 t in loose sand and gravel, 40.72 t in medium clay, 42.98 t in stiff clay, and 47.50 t in weathered rock and hardpan, moved in 1,301, 1,414, 1,470, and 1,583 bucket lifts respectively.

papers.t: What One Person Can Actually Pump: Sustained Power and the Litres-per-Hour Bound by Depth
papers.r: On those assumptions the hydraulic power available is 30.0 W, and the sustainable delivery is 1101 litres per hour against a depth of 10 m, 550 litres per hour at 20 m, 367 litres per hour at 30 m, 275 litres per hour at 40 m, and 183 litres per hour at 60 m. Over a 6-hour pumping day those rates give total volumes of 6606 litres from 10 m, 3303 litres from 20 m, 2202 litres from 30 m, and 1651 litres from 40 m.

papers.t: What a Knot Costs: Residual Strength of the Knots People Actually Tie
papers.r: Midpoint efficiencies range from 0.775 for the figure-eight loop, a loss of 22.5%, down to 0.475 for the overhand knot, a loss of 52.5% — a spread of 30.0 percentage points and a best-to-worst ratio of 1.632.

papers.t: The Leaking Pump Delivers Nothing: A Leak-Area Bound for Loss of Delivery in a Piston Hand Pump
papers.r: At the baseline condition of a lift of 10 m and a stroking rate of 40 strokes per minute, net delivery reaches zero when the total leak area reaches 113.2 mm^2, which is 2.56 percent of the piston area of 4417.9 mm^2 and corresponds to an equivalent annular gap of 0.481 mm around the piston.

papers.t: What the Earth Asks of a Well Lining: Lateral Pressure, Ring Load, and a Thickness Rule
papers.r: At a depth of 30 m the computed total lateral pressure is 383.1 kPa in loose sand and gravel, 417.8 kPa in medium clay, 468.5 kPa in stiff clay, and 385.4 kPa in weathered rock and hardpan, producing hoop forces of 229.9 kN/m, 250.7 kN/m, 281.1 kN/m, and 231.3 kN/m respectively in a shaft of 1.2 m diameter.

papers.t: Mechanical Advantage After Friction: The Pulley Count at Which Another Wheel Stops Helping
papers.r: Under this model the double tackle, conventionally quoted at an ideal advantage of 5, delivers a real advantage of 4.524 with bushed sheaves, a shortfall of 9.51 percent, and 4.804 with bearing sheaves, a shortfall of 3.92 percent. The luff tackle falls from an ideal 4 to 3.71 bushed and 3.882 bearing.

papers.t: The Found-Rope Problem: A Derating Schedule for the Safe Working Load of Used Rope
papers.r: With a design factor of 5 applied after derating, a pristine 12 mm nylon rope with a new breaking strength of 27.0 kN has a safe working load of 5.4 kN, or 550.5 kg, whereas the same rope in a heavily degraded found condition — product factor 0.0862 — has a derated breaking strength of only 2.327 kN and a safe working load of 0.465 kN, or 47.4 kg.

papers.t: The Rope Pump Depth Bound: Slip, Washer Spacing, and the Depth at Which Output Falls Away
papers.r: Delivered flow is 2.924 m^3/h at a lift of 1 m, defined here as the surface output, and 2.625 m^3/h at a lift of 5 m, after which the power limit governs: delivered flow falls to 1.908 m^3/h at a lift of 10 m, 1.272 m^3/h at a lift of 15 m, and 0.954 m^3/h at a lift of 20 m.

papers.t: Seven Metres, Not Ten: The Working Depth Limit of a Suction Pump Once Losses Are Counted
papers.r: At sea level with water at a temperature of 20 °C, the gross head remaining after vapour pressure alone is 10.09 m, the pipe losses at the resulting lift are 0.166 m, and the corrected working limit is 7.23 m — a total deduction of 3.1 m from the textbook figure, of which the surviving limit is a fraction 0.7. Rounded down to the nearest half metre for practical use, the working limit at that condition is 7.0 m.

papers.t: Two Legs Against the Head: Discharge Bounds for the Treadle Pump by Depth
papers.r: Delivered discharge holds at the displacement cap of 4.283 m^3/h from a head of 1 m through a head of 3 m, passes a crossover head of 3.98 m at which power and displacement limits coincide, and then declines with head to 3.413 m^3/h at a head of 5 m and 2.438 m^3/h at a head of 7 m, equivalent to 40.63 L/min at the deeper head.

papers.t: Three Legs and a Load: Buckling, Splay Angle, and the Safe Load of a Well-Digging Tripod
papers.r: Across the grid the safe load runs from 152 kg to 8,904 kg, but the useful lesson sits at the working end: length costs capacity much faster than splay does, and one ordinary-looking arrangement — 60 mm poles, 5 m long, at 30 degrees — cannot carry the 200 kg design working load adopted here, failing the buckling criterion with a utilisation of 1.271, and carries even the 140 kg pump-cylinder case only at a utilisati

papers.t: The Windlass Wind-Up: Drum Diameter, Rope Layers, and the True Effort of Raising a Bucket
papers.r: For the main case, a drum of 0.15 m diameter raising 15 litres of water from a depth of 15 m, the lift begins within a single layer and finishes on a second layer, the effective radius grows by 14.8 percent, and the crank force rises from 37.8 N at the start to 40.5 N at the end, through 28.77 drum rotations.

homework.q: Take the paper “Bad Air at the Bottom: A Ventilation Bound and a Test Rule for Hand-Dug Wells”. Its stated result is: Without ventilation, the stated 0.5% concentration level is reached in 0.34 hours at 5 m, 0.68 hours at 10 m, 1.02 hours at 15 m, and 1.35 hours at 20 m; the stated 4.0% immediately-dangerous level is reached in 2.93 hours, 5.85 hours, 8.78 hours, and 11.70 hours at the same depths. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

professor.name: Professor Amanda Johnson
professor.personality: A wry and well-read teacher of Designs & Engineering who writes the units on the board before opinions, every time. She keeps the last word of every lesson for what the subject is for — not just how it works.
professor.greeting: Come in and take a seat — designs & Engineering first, opinions after.

classes.title: The Market Stall (Wave 6)

papers.t: Spoilage Against Selling Time: A Temperature-Dependent Decay Model for Leafy Greens and a Break-Even Rule for How Much to Bring to Market
papers.r: First, saleable fraction by temperature and age, with a half-life of 23.10 hours at 20 °C, falling to 9.24 hours at 30 °C and 5.85 hours at 35 °C. Second, a costing of unsold stock: at 30 °C, bringing 100 bunches against demand of 85 sells 80.23, loses 19.77 to spoilage, and carries an unsold cost of $23.73.

papers.t: End-of-Day Discounting for a Decaying Perishable: A Triggered Single-Markdown Schedule That Maximises Computed Revenue
papers.r: The originated result is a triggered, single-markdown schedule. At the midpoint, count the stock remaining. If it exceeds 39.6 bunches — 1.2 times the 33 bunches expected to sell at full price in the remaining three hours — apply one markdown of 20 percent for the rest of the day. Otherwise hold full price.

papers.t: Harvest Timing Against Market Timing: Quality-Loss Bounds for Morning-of and Evening-Before Harvest of Leafy Greens, and a Rule for When Each Wins
papers.r: At opening, morning-of retains 0.9576, 0.9339, 0.8974, and 0.8428 across those days — a loss of 4.2 to 15.7 percent. Evening-before at ambient retains only 0.7707, 0.6624, 0.5214, and 0.3571 — a loss of 22.9 to 64.3 percent. The cool box retains 0.8608 on every day, because its temperature does not depend on the weather. Two thresholds are originated.

papers.t: Stall Shading and Wilting: How Much Selling Time Shade Buys for Leafy Produce, and When It Pays
papers.r: On a typical day defined here as 30°C air temperature and 45% relative humidity, the modelled time to wilting is 2.756 hours in open sun, 3.287 hours under cloth transmitting 0.7 of the sun, 3.727 hours under cloth transmitting 0.5, and 4.259 hours under cloth transmitting 0.3. Medium shade, at transmission 0.5, therefore buys 0.971 hours, a gain of 35.2%.

papers.t: Display Height and Reach: The Reachable Fraction of a Market Stall and a Stepped Display Rule
papers.r: On a flat table 120 cm deep, only 0.3333 of the stock, uniformly distributed by depth, lies within customer comfortable reach, and only 0.5000 lies within customer maximum reach. The middle 30 cm is beyond comfortable reach from either side, although it can be reached at full stretch by someone. On a table 150 cm deep a dead zone appears: 20 cm in the middle is beyond maximum reach from either side.

papers.t: Stacking Depth and Crushing: Maximum Safe Depth for Ripe Tomatoes and the Cost of Exceeding It
papers.r: Under these assumptions each additional layer adds 1.65 N to the bottom fruit. Damage in the model begins well before the threshold is formally crossed: the bottom layer damage fraction is 0.0000 at six layers, 0.1378 at seven layers, and 0.2904 at eight layers, where the force is 11.54 N and the pressure is 65.3 kPa. At nine layers, a depth of 53.6 cm, the force reaches 13.18 N and exceeds the threshold.

papers.t: Transport Damage by Vehicle and Road: A Viability Distance for Fragile Produce
papers.r: The new result is a viability distance for each combination: the distance at which damage reaches 15%, taken here as the point at which the load stops being worth transporting in that way. On paved road the viability distances are 20.31 km on foot, 13.54 km by pickup, 10.83 km by bicycle, 6.50 km by motorcycle, and 4.64 km by cart.

papers.t: How Far a Load Can Survive: A Combined Bound from Jolting, Time, and Temperature Rise
papers.r: Solved numerically, the maximum viable distances on paved road are 10.67 km walking, 11.90 km cycling, and 4.40 km by cart. On gravel they are 8.33 km walking, 7.29 km cycling, and 2.86 km by cart. On rough earth they are 5.96 km walking, 4.33 km cycling, and 1.77 km by cart.

papers.t: Packaging That Pays for Itself: A Break-Even Rule for Cushioning a Market Load
papers.r: On a bicycle journey over gravel, newspaper wrap breaks even at 2.07 km, banana-leaf cushioning at 2.22 km, straw or shredded paper bedding at 2.61 km, foam net sleeves at 6.51 km, and moulded pulp trays at 6.97 km. By cart over gravel, every option breaks even within 2.99 km. By pickup on paved road, foam nets do not break even until 14.65 km and pulp trays not until 15.69 km.

papers.t: Packaging That Does Not Pay: Sealed Film, Respiration Heat, and the Shortened Saleable Life of Market Produce
papers.r: In shade at an ambient temperature of 22 °C, the computed temperature rise from sealing is 0.655 K for tomatoes, 1.761 K for lettuce, and 0.407 K for carrots, with corresponding reductions in saleable life of 5.3%, 13.6%, and 3.3%.

papers.t: Weighing Accuracy and Short Weight: What a Small Systematic Error Transfers Over a Market Season
papers.r: A systematic short weight of 1% transfers $960 from buyers to the vendor over the season, 2% transfers $1,920, and 5% transfers $4,800. Per transaction the same errors are only 17.9 g, 35.7 g, and 89.3 g on an average purchase of 1.786 kg, worth 7.1, 14.3, and 35.7 cents respectively, which explains why no individual buyer is likely to notice or contest them.

papers.t: Checking a Spring Scale With What Is at Hand: A Water-Litre Calibration Method and Its Certified Bound
papers.r: Reading resolution contributes 2.5% at a 1 kg load on a typical 5 kg scale with 50 g graduations, tilting the scale or its load by 10 degrees makes it read 1.519% low, and a 20 K temperature shift changes the indication by 0.5%. Adding the controlled error components for the prescribed procedure gives a worst-case bound of 6.23% at a 1 kg load, and a root-sum-square figure of 3.39%.

papers.t: Pricing by the Piece against Pricing by Weight: Buyer Selection, Fairness, and a Two-Size Grading Rule for Apples
papers.r: When fruit is allocated at random, the methods return almost the same revenue. When buyers choose the largest fruit, piece pricing transfers a substantial sum from vendor to buyer: the vendor receives $109.50 for fruit that would return $124.49 by weight in a day, a loss of $14.99, or 9.99 cents per apple sold. The same piece price charges different buyers between $3.07 and $5.74 per kilogram.

papers.t: Queues at a Single-Vendor Stall: Waiting through the Morning Peak, the Point at Which Customers Leave Faster than They Are Served, and a Rule for a Second Pair of Hands
papers.r: At 20 arrivals per hour the mean wait before service is 4.0 minutes. At 28 per hour it is 28.0 minutes, with a mean of 13.07 customers waiting. In the peak hour, at 35 arrivals per hour against service of 30 per hour, no steady state exists and the queue grows while that rate lasts.

papers.t: Rounding and Change: What Coin Denominations Cost a Produce Vendor over a Day and a Season, and the Arithmetic of Giving Produce Instead of Small Change
papers.r: Rounding each cash total to the nearest 5 cents is fair on average: mean gain in simulation is $0.006 per day and $0.60 per season, with a daily standard deviation of $0.148 and an approximate 95 percent season range from −$27.29 to $28.50. Rounding systematically one way is different. Always rounding down costs an average of 2 cents per cash transaction, $2.24 per day, and $215.04 per season.

papers.t: A Cold Box Sized for One Day of Trading: An Ice Sizing Rule per Kilogram of Produce per Trading Hour
papers.r: For an 8-hour day it gives 10.417 kg of ice at 20 °C ambient, 15.47 kg at 30 °C and 20.524 kg at 40 °C. At 30 °C that is 0.7735 kg per kilogram of produce, or 0.09669 kg per kilogram per hour. The ice at 30 °C costs $6.19 and, under the stated spoilage model, prevents $13.91 of value loss, for a net benefit of $7.72 on a $60.00 lot, or $2.25 saved per dollar spent on ice. At 20 °C the net benefit is only $0.98.

papers.t: More Ice Is Not Always Better: Chilling Injury and Falling Saleable Value in Over-Iced Tropical Produce
papers.r: Banana reaches its best net value of $20.51 at r = 0.21, enters chilling conditions at r = 0.322, and at r = 1.0 retains only $1.73, a fall of 91.6% from its grid optimum. Mango peaks at $54.49 at r = 0.35 and falls to $25.00 at r = 1.0. Lettuce, with no chilling threshold above 0 °C in the model, loses only 8.6% between its grid optimum and r = 1.0, mainly through ice cost.

homework.q: Take the paper “Spoilage Against Selling Time: A Temperature-Dependent Decay Model for Leafy Greens and a Break-Even Rule for How Much to Bring to Market”. Its stated result is: First, saleable fraction by temperature and age, with a half-life of 23.10 hours at 20 °C, falling to 9.24 hours at 30 °C and 5.85 hours at 35 °C. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

professor.name: Professor Lorenzo Ribeiro
professor.personality: A sunny and hands-on teacher of Designs & Engineering who refuses to move on while a single honest question is still standing. Once a term, he teaches a whole session from the class's own questions and nothing else.
professor.greeting: Welcome to designs & Engineering. We start where the subject starts: at the beginning.

classes.title: Household Manufactures (Wave 6)

papers.t: A strength test for wood-ash lye without instruments
papers.r: The central egg, at 1.060 g/mL, reaches neutral buoyancy at 65.2 g/L of alkali as potassium carbonate, but eggs spanning 1.030 to 1.090 g/mL indicate anywhere from 32.6 to 97.8 g/L at the same visual point, a range 65.2 g/L wide against a target band only 40.0 g/L wide. An egg floating with 5% exposed corresponds to 125.9 g/L, near the top of the target band of 90.0 to 130.0 g/L.

papers.t: One recipe does not fit every fat
papers.r: A fixed recipe of 140.0 g of sodium hydroxide per kilogram requires, in fact, 99.1 g for lard and 182.5 g for coconut oil, a range whose maximum is 1.84 times its minimum. On tallow the fixed recipe leaves 39.5 g of surplus alkali per kilogram, a free alkali content of 3.06% in the cured bar, 30.6 times a 0.1% reference limit. On coconut oil it falls short by 42.5 g and leaves 23.3% of the fat unsaponified.

papers.t: The curing bound: when is a bar of soap actually ready?
papers.r: For a stated 120.0 g bar measuring 80 by 55 by 25 mm, starting at 28.0% water and curing at 20 °C and 50% relative humidity, water falls to 20.2% at day 7, 15.6% at day 14 and 11.3% at day 28. Free alkali in a zero-superfat batch falls from 2.40% at demoulding to 0.43% at day 7 and reaches 0.1% only at day 22.9.

papers.t: Sizing a solar salt pan
papers.r: For seawater at a mass fraction of 0.035, the rule gives 5.059 m2 of pan per kilogram of salt per day in an arid coastal climate with net evaporation of 5.45 mm per day, and 19.694 m2 per kilogram per day in a humid coastal climate with net evaporation of 1.4 mm per day.

papers.t: The break-even salinity for boiling brine
papers.r: Boiling seawater at a salt mass fraction of 0.035 requires 70.586 MJ of heat and 31.371 kg of wood for each kilogram of salt. At a mass fraction of 0.2 the cost falls to 10.491 MJ and 4.662 kg of wood, and at 0.26, near saturation, to 7.549 MJ and 3.355 kg of wood.

papers.t: Evaporate to dryness is worse salt
papers.r: Stopping at 7.0 g of water remaining recovers 24.48 g of NaCl, a recovery of 90.7 percent, at a dry-crystal purity of 0.9532, or 0.9163 after allowing for retained mother liquor. Evaporating to complete dryness recovers the full 27.0 g of NaCl but delivers 35.0 g of mixed salts at a purity of 0.7714.

papers.t: Can a small cane operation fuel itself?
papers.r: A single-roller press recovering 54.0% of the soluble solids extracts 464.7 kg of juice and leaves 535.3 kg of bagasse at 60.1% moisture; it delivers 944.9 MJ of useful heat against 897.9 MJ needed to make 127.1 kg of syrup at 68% solids, a ratio of 1.052 — self-sufficient, but only just. A three-roller press without imbibition water, recovering 68.0% of the solids, also passes narrowly, at a ratio of 1.044.

papers.t: Knowing the endpoint without a thermometer
papers.r: The thread test, the cold-water test, and the sheet test each centre between 70% and 72% solids with an error of ±3.0 percentage points of moisture. A litre measure weighed on a kitchen scale does better, at ±1.0 percentage points.

papers.t: Why household crystallisation yields cap where they do
papers.r: From a stated massecuite of 100 kg at 93% solids and 85% purity — 79.05 kg of sucrose and 13.95 kg of non-sucrose solids — the theoretical first-strike crystal yield, with the mother liquor exhausted to 40% purity, is 69.75 kg of sucrose, which is 88.2% of the sucrose present and 69.8% of the massecuite mass.

papers.t: A wick selection rule for tallow and beeswax candles
papers.r: The energy needed to melt a kilogram of wax, at 20 °C ambient, is 234.0 kJ/kg for tallow and 280.0 kJ/kg for beeswax, a ratio of 1.197. At the same wick class, W3 at 7.0 g/h, the predicted pool is 36.9 mm in tallow and 29.8 mm in beeswax, a reduction of 19.2%.

papers.t: Light per kilogram: candles against oil lamps
papers.r: The results are 1500.0 lumen-hours per kilogram for the tallow candle, 2000.0 lumen-hours per kilogram for the beeswax candle, and 3333.3 lumen-hours per kilogram for the oil lamp. For a stated evening of light, defined as 100 lumens of source flux for 4 hours, or 400.0 lumen-hours, the fuel required is 266.7 g of tallow candle, 200.0 g of beeswax candle, or 120.0 g of vegetable oil.

papers.t: The burn-time law for candles
papers.r: In the model, burn rate grows as diameter to the power 1.5, so burn time at fixed height grows only as the square root of diameter: doubling diameter multiplies burn time by 1.414, not by 2. For beeswax at 100 mm height, burn times are 18.8 hours at 25 mm diameter, 26.5 hours at 50 mm, and 37.5 hours at 100 mm.

papers.t: The strength ceiling of household vinegar
papers.r: At a combined retention of 0.8035, a 5% cider yields a practical vinegar of 4.13% acetic acid by weight per volume, and a 12% wine yields 9.92%, against a theoretical 12.34% for the wine. A starting liquid of at least 6.05% alcohol is required for a practical 5.00% vinegar.

papers.t: Starch recovery, stage by stage
papers.r: Fresh cassava containing 25.0 kg of starch yields 18.44 kg of dry starch, or 20.95 kg of finished starch at 12% moisture, an overall recovery of 0.7375 of the starch present. Maize grain containing 62.0 kg of starch yields 46.09 kg dry, or 52.37 kg finished, a recovery of 0.7434. The largest single loss for cassava is washing and extraction, 2.88 kg; for maize it is steeping and washing, 9.02 kg.

papers.t: More dye does not mean proportionally deeper colour
papers.r: Uptake rises from 28.94 g/kg at a dose of 50 g/kg to 48.37 g/kg at 100 g/kg, 67.41 g/kg at 200 g/kg, and only 79.05 g/kg at 400 g/kg. Doubling the dose from 200 g/kg to 400 g/kg buys a depth gain of 17.3%; doubling from 400 g/kg to 800 g/kg buys 7.2%, while bath exhaustion falls to 10.6%. A linear prediction calibrated at 50 g/kg overstates uptake at 800 g/kg by a factor of 5.46.

papers.t: The fuel bound of a small lime kiln, and a weighing test for completeness
papers.r: Pure calcium carbonate requires 1.78 MJ per kilogram of stone, or 3.178 MJ per kilogram of quicklime. With air-dry wood at 15.0 MJ/kg and stated efficiencies of 0.15 for a clamp or pit kiln and 0.30 for a small shaft kiln, the fuel bound is 1.412 kg of wood per kilogram of quicklime in the clamp and 0.706 kg in the shaft kiln.

papers.t: What a household charcoal filter can and cannot do
papers.r: For granular activated carbon at a stated capacity of 50 mg/g, usable volume before breakthrough at a utilisation factor of 0.50 is 5000.0 litres per kilogram; for plain wood charcoal at 10 mg/g it is 1000.0 litres per kilogram.

homework.q: Take the paper “A strength test for wood-ash lye without instruments”. Its stated result is: The central egg, at 1.060 g/mL, reaches neutral buoyancy at 65.2 g/L of alkali as potassium carbonate, but eggs spanning 1.030 to 1.090 g/mL indicate anywhere from 32.6 to 97.8 g/L at the same visual point, a range 65.2 g/L wide against a target band only 40.0 g/L wide. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

professor.name: Professor Richard Martin
professor.personality: A plainspoken and immovable teacher of Designs & Engineering who refuses to move on while a single honest question is still standing. Students leave his room able to explain the idea to a stranger, which he counts as the only real grade.

classes.title: Building with Local Materials (Wave 6)

papers.t: Lime and Ash: What a Wood-Ash Pozzolan Mortar Can and Cannot Do
papers.r: Per 100 kg, wood ash carries only 3.0 kg of reactive silica against rice husk ash's 77.44 kg. Wood ash with water alone forms at most 8.73 kg of gel per 100 kg (0.78 MPa dry, 0.08 MPa wet), and wood ash with clay at 50:50 gives 0.49 MPa dry and 0.02 MPa wet, so neither belief survives the arithmetic.

papers.t: How Far Can a Bamboo Culm Span? Bending Strength and Deflection Bounds for Single and Bundled Culms
papers.r: Deflection at span/240 governs every case computed; bending strength never does. A single 100 mm culm under 250 N/m spans 3.96 m by deflection against 7.89 m by strength; bundling two culms reaches 4.89 m and three reach 5.48 m at the same load, and a 1,000 N midspan point load bounds the single 100 mm culm to 3.23 m.

papers.t: The Bamboo Column Bound: Safe Axial Load by Culm Diameter, Wall Thickness, and Node Spacing
papers.r: Safe axial load is the smaller of factored Euler buckling and crushing, with diameter and wall taken at mid-height: a 100 mm culm with a 10 mm wall carries 62.2 kN at 1.0 m unsupported length, 38.6 kN at 2.0 m, and 17.2 kN at 3.0 m.

papers.t: A Bolt Through a Bamboo Culm Does Not Use the Culm's Strength: Splitting and Bearing Bounds at Pinned Joints, and a Lashing Rule That Does
papers.r: A 12 mm through-bolt in a 100 mm culm with a 10 mm wall reaches an ultimate bearing load of 8.4 kN, which is 5.4% of the culm's crushing strength, and a safe transfer of only 2.8 kN. The selection rule that follows: a single lashing to 3.75 kN, a double lashing to 6.75 kN, a plugged bolt to 12.0 kN, and beyond that multiple joints rather than a stronger fastener.

papers.t: The Dry-Stone Retaining Wall Bound: Batter, Base Thickness, and the Height a Vertical Face Cannot Reach
papers.r: A vertical dry-stone face needs a base of 0.58 times the retained height; a 1-in-6 batter needs 0.538 times the height with about a fifth less stone. At equal stone volume and 3.0 m retained height, the battered wall's overturning factor is 3.857 against the vertical wall's 3.010, a 28.1% gain; under a 1.50 m base cap the battered face reaches 2.75 m, a height the vertical face cannot reach.

papers.t: Foundation Width from the Ground Up: A Bearing Rule for Stone Strip Footings
papers.r: Wall, roof, and floor loads are accumulated openly — 35.16 kN/m for a cottage, 71.82 kN/m for a two-storey stone house — and the footing width is the larger of the bearing width and wall thickness plus 0.30 m.

papers.t: The Honest Load of a Green-Timber Lintel: Strength Loss and Creep in Unseasoned Wood
papers.r: Strength alone requires giving up 30.0–40.0% by species class when timber goes in green, but with green stiffness loss and drying-under-load creep the honest give-up for ordinary openings is 51.2–59.5%: a pine 100×200 mm lintel over 1.8 m carries 9.36 kN/m green against 21.95 kN/m seasoned, and green sag grows to 3.0 times its initial value over the years against 1.6 times seasoned.

papers.t: Lashed, Pegged, or Notched: Computed Strengths for Timber Joints Without Metal, and a Selection Rule
papers.r: A 10-turn lashing on a 100 mm member resists 2.1 kN in slip and 4.2 kN in tension; a single 25 mm peg carries 4.42 kN in single shear and 8.84 kN in double shear, governed by peg shear rather than bearing; a quarter-depth notch retains 56.2% of bending capacity.

papers.t: The Round-Log Beam Rule: Span from Diameter for Roof and Floor Loads
papers.r: Sag governs in all 54 combinations of diameter, species class, and load case computed; strength-only sizing overspans by roughly a factor of two. A 200 mm pine-class log has a 9.23 m strength span but governs at 4.64 m on a floor and 5.02 m on a roof, and the oak class at the same diameter governs at 4.95 m — only 1.18 times the light-softwood span, because stiffness, not strength, binds.

papers.t: Mud Brick and Stabilised Earth: Strength by Mix, and the Least Cement or Lime That Does the Work
papers.r: Wet strength, not dry strength, sets almost every least stabiliser dose: unstabilised mixes reach 0.96–1.92 MPa dry but only 0.10–0.19 MPa wet. One storey needs 1.5–3.5% cement or lime in every soil; two storeys need 3.0% cement in loam against 5.5% lime, and expansive heavy clay fails the two-storey threshold at the 8.0% cap under either stabiliser, though it passes one storey at 3.5%.

papers.t: Scaffolds and Formwork from Poles: Safe Loads, Bracing, and the Bay Size That Holds
papers.r: A braced 90 mm upright at a 2.0 m lift carries 23.84 kN, falling to 15.26 kN at 2.5 m and to 5.96 kN unbraced, so bracing on both faces is a structural necessity. Ledger bending governs the bay: 1.52 m, 1.35 m, and 1.13 m for light, medium, and heavy load classes with a 90 mm ledger. A 90 mm formwork prop at a 2.0 m lift may carry at most 3.51 m² of a 0.20 m wet slab.

papers.t: Roof Trusses from Poles: Geometry and Member Sizes for Spans from Four to Eight Metres
papers.r: For a king-post pole truss with two struts, solved exactly by joint equilibrium and sized against buckling, combined compression and bending, and joint capacities, the rafters govern: 90 mm under thatch at 4 m span to 165 mm under tile at 8 m, while the tie needs 60–90 mm and the king post passes at the 60 mm floor throughout.

papers.t: Rammed Earth by Layers: Lift Thickness, Compaction Energy, and the Slenderness Bound
papers.r: At 350 kJ/m³ of compaction energy, strength falls from 2.12 MPa at 100 mm lifts to 1.58 MPa at 200 mm lifts, with a moisture optimum of 10.0%. The originated rule is lifts of 100–120 mm, a 0.60 m pour height, and an 8–12% moisture window. Slenderness, not crushing, governs height: maximum unsupported height is 3.6 m at 300 mm thickness, 5.4 m at 450 mm, and 7.2 m at 600 mm.

papers.t: How Long Does Timber Take to Dry? A Diffusion Bound Tested Against the One-Month-Per-Inch Rule
papers.r: Drying time scales with the square of thickness, so both linear rules of thumb fail: one month per inch understates thick refractory stock (a 150 mm board to a 15% core target has a 27.77-month bound against the rule's 5.91 months) and overstates thin permeable stock, while one year per inch exceeds the bound everywhere.

papers.t: How Thick Must a Rubble Stone Wall Be? A Stability Bound by Height and Mortar
papers.r: The middle-third resultant check, not overturning or sliding, sizes a rubble stone wall: a free-standing dry wall needs 0.40 m at 1.0 m height, 0.64 m at 3.0 m, and 0.905 m at 6.0 m, against 0.30 m, 0.41 m, and 0.58 m mortared. Unmortared rubble stops working at 5.95 m under a 0.90 m practical thickness cap, and at 2.65 m at the common 0.60 m thickness.

papers.t: Termites and Damp: The Detailing Limits That Decide How Long a Timber Building Stands
papers.r: Modelled time to structural loss of a 150 mm post runs from 4.3 years for the least durable class in the ground in a wet climate to beyond the 50-year design life on a ventilated, shielded 450 mm plinth. The charcoal and ash belief does not survive: a 75 mm layer is crossed by a mud tube in 3.0 days at the stated build rate, and even a perfectly intact layer extends a ground post's life only from 12.5 to 14.5 years.

papers.t: Thatch Against Rain and Rot: Pitch, Thickness, and Service Life by Material and Climate
papers.r: Most dry and temperate combinations are governed by a shedding floor — 45° for long straw, 40° for reed, 35° for palm — but rain penetration governs thin wet-tropical coats: 200 mm palm needs 57.2°, and 150 mm long straw and 150 mm palm in a wet tropical climate fail at any pitch up to 60°.

homework.q: Take the paper “Lime and Ash: What a Wood-Ash Pozzolan Mortar Can and Cannot Do”. Its stated result is: Per 100 kg, wood ash carries only 3.0 kg of reactive silica against rice husk ash's 77.44 kg. Wood ash with water alone forms at most 8.73 kg of gel per 100 kg (0.78 MPa dry, 0.08 MPa wet), and wood ash with clay at 50:50 gives 0.49 MPa dry and 0.02 MPa wet, so neither belief survives the arithmetic (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

classes.title: Rain, Roofs and Stormwater (Wave 7)

papers.t: Dose Past the Demand, Then Mind the Calendar: Chlorine, Contact Time, and Re-Dosing for Stored Roof Water
papers.r: A 1.0 mg/L chlorine dose in water with a demand of 1.5 mg/L leaves no free residual and disinfects nothing at any waiting time; the typical case (demand 0.8 mg/L, dose 2.0 mg/L, residual 1.2 mg/L, 40 mL of 5 percent bleach per 1,000 L) reaches the bacterial CT target of 15 mg·min/L in 12.5 minutes, and its protection lasts 35.8 days in a cool dark covered tank but only 4.5 days in a warm light-admitting one, so re-do

papers.t: Clean by the Mound, Not by the Calendar: A Sediment Accumulation Rule for Rainwater Cisterns
papers.r: Sediment concentrates near the inlet, so the typical tank (60 g/m²/yr, no first-flush diverter) builds local depth at 3.57 mm per year and reaches a 50 mm cleaning trigger in 14.0 years rather than the 70 years a whole-floor average suggests; intervals across load classes run from 4.2 years (ageing shingles, no diverter) to 117.6 years (clean metal roof, diverter fitted), a 28-fold spread, and a maintained diverter m

papers.t: A Barrier Is a Pump Specification: Hydrostatic Load, Sandbag Count, and Leakage at a Household Flood Door
papers.r: Floodwater 0.6 m deep exerts 1,589 N across a 0.90 m doorway — four times the 397 N at 0.3 m, because load grows with the square of depth — a sandbag wall for that duty takes about 93 bags per metre (roughly 139 for a doorway with returns), and even a well-compressed seal passes 11.1 L/min across the door at 0.6 m depth, so a barrier specification is incomplete without a leakage class and a matched pump.

papers.t: Counted, Not Placed for Symmetry: How Many Downpipes a Roof Actually Needs
papers.r: Counting downpipes from rational-method design flow rather than elevation symmetry: a 200 m2 roof at 150 mm/h produces 8.33 L/s and needs three 82 mm or two 110 mm downpipes, so the customary pair of 82 mm pipes is undersized, and every roof needs at least two outlets for blockage redundancy.

papers.t: The Drip Lands Further Out Than the Trench: Width, Wind, and Impact Energy at an Unguttered Eave
papers.r: Water leaving a 3.5 m eave lands 0.253 m from the wall in still air, so a trench must be 0.45 m wide once splash is allowed for, and the conventional 300 mm trench misses the drip line even with no wind; a 2 m/s wind raises the required width to 0.70 m, a 600 mm trench tolerates only about 1.55 m/s of wind at that height, and impact energy rises from 34.4 J per litre at 3.5 m to 68.7 J per litre at 7.0 m.

papers.t: One Millimetre for Every Roof? First-Flush Diversion Depth Set by Wash-Off Behaviour
papers.r: Against the exponential wash-off model, the popular fixed 1 mm first-flush rule captures only 19.7 percent of the load on a typical suburban roof; 90 percent capture needs 10.47 mm there and 19.19 mm under trees, while the extra diversion costs only a few percent of the annual harvest.

papers.t: Depth Is a Load Before It Is a Sponge: Substrate Depth, Retention, and the Structural Cap on Green Roofs
papers.r: Substrate depth buys annual runoff retention with diminishing returns — 72.8 percent at 40 mm, 86.9 percent at 100 mm, 92.4 percent at 200 mm — while saturated load rises linearly, so a stated spare allowance of 1.5 kN/m2 caps a retrofit roof at 122 mm of substrate: set depth from the structure first, then take the retention the permitted depth provides.

papers.t: The Level Gutter Is a Sediment Trap: Minimum Fall for Self-Cleansing in a 125 mm Half-Round Gutter
papers.r: For a 125 mm half-round gutter flowing half full, a level installation gives zero sediment transport: reaching the 0.6 m/s self-cleansing velocity requires a fall of 0.443 percent and moving 2 mm grit requires 0.528 percent, so gutters should be installed at about 0.6 percent and checked over the full run.

papers.t: Blamed on the Arc: Sheet Flow Cannot Jump a Gutter, but Rivulets Can
papers.r: Trajectory calculations acquit uniform sheet flow of gutter overshoot — its throw at 300 mm/h is 0.085 m against a standard lip offset of about 0.125 m — and convict concentrated rivulet flow, which occupying a tenth of the slope width throws 0.181 m at the same intensity: overshoot is a concentration problem, remedied by breaking up threads and valley discharges or placing the gutter for the concentrated throw.

papers.t: Maintenance-Free for How Long? Debris Matting and Bypass Growth on Guarded Gutters
papers.r: Modelling debris matting on a guarded gutter, bypass of a 2.0 L/s design inflow first exceeds ten percent at month 4 under trees and month 9 on an open roof, reaching 62.0 percent under trees by month 12 — so the product relocates maintenance rather than abolishing it, with service intervals of about a season under trees and about a year on an open roof.

papers.t: An Expiry Date for Permeable Paving: Sediment Loading, Infiltration Decay, and the Sweeping Interval
papers.r: With sediment-driven clogging, a permeable driveway laid at 250 mm/h falls to its 40 mm/h design floor in 3.7 years at street-side loading and 7.4 years sheltered; vacuum sweeping restores a threshold surface to 176 mm/h against 92 mm/h for ordinary sweeping, giving maintenance intervals of roughly three and six years.

papers.t: Three Hundred Millimetres of What? Ponding Depth Set by Soil Drawdown, Not by the Standard Detail
papers.r: Drawdown arithmetic displaces the standard 300 mm ponding detail: at stated soil infiltration rates a 300 mm pond clears in 50 hours on loam and 120 hours on clay loam against a 48-hour limit, so ponding depth must be set at no more than forty-eight times the measured infiltration rate — 288 mm on loam, 120 mm on clay loam — with slow soils answered by area or an underdrain, not depth.

papers.t: A Square Metre of Roof Is Not a Square Metre of Water: Annual Harvest by Covering
papers.r: On the same 100 m2 roof under 800 mm of rain, annual harvest after system losses ranges from 69,920 litres for standing-seam metal to 25,760 litres for an extensive green roof — a factor of 2.71 set by the covering alone — so yield calculators, tank sizes, and payback claims that ask only for area and rainfall inherit that error whole.

papers.t: Two Gates for a Soakaway: Storage Scanned Over Storm Durations, and a Recovery Test That Size Cannot Pass
papers.r: Sizing a soakaway for a 120 m2 catchment by maximising storage over eight storm durations gives 3.48 cubic metres on sandy loam (critical duration 6 hours, half-emptying 9.7 hours) and 6.17 cubic metres on clay loam, whose half-emptying time of 171.4 hours fails the 24-hour recovery gate at any size and disqualifies infiltration on that soil.

papers.t: Drawn to Fit the Site, Sized by the Flow: The Length a Grass Swale Needs to Treat Runoff
papers.r: At a stated first-order removal rate, eighty percent suspended-solids removal needs 14.6 minutes of residence time, which for a standard trapezoidal swale at 0.15 m treatment depth means 55.7 m of length at 10 L/s and 111.5 m at 20 L/s — swales must be sized by the flow they treat, not drawn to fit the site.

papers.t: Buy the Knee, Not the Tank: A Daily Water Balance Locates Where Rainwater Storage Stops Paying
papers.r: A twenty-year daily water balance for a 110 m2 roof and a demand averaging about 130 L/day shows reliability rising from 87.4 percent at 1,000 litres to 99.5 percent at 3,000 litres and reaching 100 percent at 5,000 litres, while overflow stays near 27,000 litres a year at every large size — so buyers should purchase the knee of the curve, around 3,000 to 5,000 litres, not the largest tank on offer.

papers.t: The Screen Sizes the Overflow: Mosquito Mesh, Surcharge Head, and Vent Area on a Covered Rainwater Tank
papers.r: A 1.2 mm mosquito screen leaves an overflow only 46.8 percent of its bare capacity, so a 100 square metre roof delivering 4.17 L/s needs a 136 mm screened overflow (select 150 mm) where bare-pipe arithmetic suggests 93 mm, a screened 75 mm overflow passes only 1.27 L/s, and a pumped draw-off of 30 L/min needs a screened vent of just 10.4 mm — making vent blockage, not vent size, the real hazard.

homework.q: Take the paper “Dose Past the Demand, Then Mind the Calendar: Chlorine, Contact Time, and Re-Dosing for Stored Roof Water”. Its stated result is: A 1.0 mg/L chlorine dose in water with a demand of 1.5 mg/L leaves no free residual and disinfects nothing at any waiting time; the typical case (demand 0.8 mg/L, dose 2.0 mg/L, residual 1.2 mg/L, 40 mL of 5 percent bleach per 1,000 L) reaches the bacterial CT target of 15 mg·min/L in 12.5 minutes, (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

classes.title: Clay, Pottery and Kilns (Wave 7)

papers.t: Chimney Height for a Downdraft Pottery Kiln: The Draft Pressure Needed and the Height Beyond Which Fuel Use Barely Falls
papers.r: A 3 m chimney gives the lowest fuel use in the sweep at 427.2 kg per firing (draft 22.3 Pa), 5.7 percent below a 2 m chimney (453.0 kg), while a 10 m chimney wastes fuel on excess draft at 514.6 kg per firing.

papers.t: Covered Drying for Green Bricks: How Much Roof per Thousand Bricks Keeps Rain Losses Below Fuel Savings
papers.r: Covering 60 percent of the drying yard minimises cost per batch of 10,000 bricks at USD 152.5, cutting rain losses from 2,200 bricks uncovered to 628, against USD 198.0 uncovered and USD 178.0 for full cover.

papers.t: Ceramic Water Filter Wall Thickness: The Flow and Pathogen-Removal Trade-Off and a Thickness That Meets Both Targets
papers.r: A 12 mm filter wall is the thinnest section meeting both stated targets at once, flowing 1.67 litres per hour with a log removal value of 3.36; a 6 mm wall flows 3.33 litres per hour but removes only 1.68 log, and an 18 mm wall reaches 5.04 log at 1.11 litres per hour.

papers.t: Wet Fuelwood and Kiln Fuel Bills: The True Fuel Mass Multiplier at Common Moisture Contents, Against the Claim That Wet Wood Burns Almost as Well
papers.r: The claim that wet wood burns almost as well as dry wood is disproved by evaporation arithmetic: effective heat falls from 15.94 MJ per kg at 10 percent moisture to 5.64 MJ per kg at 60 percent, so fuel mass must rise by a factor of 2.07 at 50 percent moisture and 1.35 at 30 percent to deliver the same heat.

papers.t: A Crazing-Free Window for Low-Cost Glazes: The Thermal Expansion Mismatch a Fired Glaze Can Tolerate on a Porous Earthenware Body
papers.r: The crazing threshold for the stated glaze is an expansion mismatch of 0.75 parts per million per degree C: at a mismatch of +1.0 the glaze stress reaches 46.7 MPa, above the 35 MPa tensile strength, while +0.5 gives 23.3 MPa and is the largest safe positive mismatch in the sweep.

papers.t: Rice Husk in Fired Bricks: Why More Husk Is Not Always Better, and the Blend That Best Balances Strength, Weight and Cost
papers.r: The claim that more rice husk always improves a brick does not survive the arithmetic: the scored optimum is a 0.10 husk fraction (strength 11.1 MPa), while at 0.30 the strength falls to 5.2 MPa, below the 7 MPa loadbearing threshold, even though density falls to 1152 kg per cubic metre.

papers.t: Flywheel Sizing for a Human-Powered Potter's Kick Wheel: The Rim Mass That Holds Speed Within a Usable Band While Centring Clay
papers.r: A 35 kg flywheel rim is the lightest that holds speed droop to 21.3 percent during a centring episode, against 49.7 percent at 15 kg; a 100 kg rim stores 809 J against 283 J at 35 kg, with correspondingly heavier starting effort.

papers.t: How Much Insulation Pays in a Small Brick Kiln: A Thickness Rule Balancing Fuel Saved Against Blanket Cost
papers.r: Under the stated assumptions, 38 mm of ceramic fibre blanket on a 12 m2 kiln wall minimises total annual cost at USD 916.0, saving USD 466.4 per year against the uninsulated kiln (USD 1382.4) and cutting fuel per firing from 432.0 kg to 181.8 kg of wood.

papers.t: Sizing a Settling Tank for Washed Clay: The Residence Time That Drops Sand While Keeping Fine Clay in Suspension
papers.r: A settling residence time of 2 hours minimises combined loss: sand remaining falls to 0.0045 of its initial fraction (against 0.2592 at half an hour), while extending settling to 8 hours loses 0.086 of the fine clay fraction for little further gain.

papers.t: Cooking Pot Wall Thickness and Thermal Shock: A Lower Bound on Survival Over an Open Flame and an Upper Bound Set by Heating Time
papers.r: Cooking pot walls have a survival window of 4 to 6 mm under the stated assumptions: at 3 mm the mechanical factor of safety is only 1.01, at 10 mm the thermal factor of safety falls to 0.89, and heating time at the top of the window is 24.6 minutes.

papers.t: Washing Clay to Prevent Efflorescence: The Number of Wash Cycles That Brings Soluble Salt Below a Visible-Bloom Threshold
papers.r: Three wash cycles first bring residual soluble salt below the stated 0.08 percent visible-bloom threshold, from an initial 0.85 percent (0.104 percent after two cycles), using 1200 litres of water per tonne of clay.

papers.t: Sand Temper and Drying Cracks: The Temper Fraction That Minimises Combined Crack and Strength Losses in Hand-Formed Ware
papers.r: A sand temper fraction of 0.25 by volume minimises combined drying-crack and strength losses at USD 117.9 per 1,000 pieces, against USD 372.0 untempered, with a crack loss of 0.077 and fired strength of 11.4 MPa at the optimum.

papers.t: Soak Time at Peak Temperature: The Hold Duration That Minimises the Combined Cost of Fuel and Underfired Rejects
papers.r: A 3 hour soak at peak temperature minimises combined cost at USD 35.0 per firing, against USD 270.0 with no soak; the reject fraction falls from 0.300 with no soak to 0.024 at the optimum, and a 4 hour soak already costs more (USD 36.5).

papers.t: How Tightly a Kiln Can Be Stacked: A Load Density Limit Set by Temperature Spread Across the Setting
papers.r: Profit is maximised at a stacking density of 0.55 of kiln volume (USD 305.3 per firing, 937 good pieces, temperature spread 152.7 degrees C); packing to 0.75 widens the spread to 263.0 degrees C and lowers profit to USD 219.7 despite loading more ware.

papers.t: Sun Pre-Drying Bricks Before Firing: The Moisture Content at Which Further Drying Stops Paying in Saved Kiln Fuel
papers.r: Drying ware to 6 percent moisture before firing minimises total cost at USD 53.5 per firing, against USD 86.1 at 18 percent moisture (of which USD 23.8 is fuel alone) and USD 54.2 at 4 percent, where extra yard days outweigh the remaining fuel saving.

papers.t: Setter Spacing for Flat Roof Tiles: The Support Interval That Keeps Firing Warpage Within a Stated Tolerance
papers.r: Setter supports may be spaced up to 300 mm apart while keeping retained firing bow within the 3 mm tolerance; at 400 mm the bow reaches 5.45 mm, against 0.34 mm at 200 mm spacing.

papers.t: A Span Limit for Self-Supporting Brick Kiln Vaults: The Width a Catenary Arch of Fired Brick Can Cover Without Steel
papers.r: A standard 0.46 m two-brick abutment wall supports a catenary brick vault up to a 4.0 m span (required abutment 0.441 m, thrust 4.67 kN per metre); at 5.0 m the required abutment rises to 0.551 m and exceeds what the standard wall provides.

papers.r: In the computed results, the bound tension cn is 85; the bound breaks is 0.2; the bound pct strength is 28.3; the next step breaks is 2.1; the high tension breaks is 487.7. The study is simulated, not measured, and rests on stated assumptions that readers may replace and re-run.

papers.t: Sorting the Fleece by Fibre Diameter: The Value Gained, the Labour Charged, and the Wage at Which Sorting Stops Paying
papers.r: In the computed results, the fine pct is 22.1; the medium pct is 42.9; the coarse pct is 35; the sorted revenue per clean kg is 8.88; the unsorted revenue per clean kg is 7.8. The study is simulated, not measured, and rests on stated assumptions that readers may replace and re-run.

papers.t: Weaving a Water Filter Cloth to a Stated Pore Size: The Ends per Inch That Deliver It, and What the Flow Costs
papers.r: In the computed results, the chosen epi is 92; the chosen pore um is 56.1; the chosen capture pct is 74.8; the chosen flow index is 0.3; the coarse epi is 45. The study is simulated, not measured, and rests on stated assumptions that readers may replace and re-run.

papers.t: A Twist Optimum for Handspun Warp Yarn: Where Added Twist Stops Buying Strength and Starts Buying Breaks
papers.r: In the computed results, the best multiplier is 3.5; the best tenacity is 18.34; the best breaks is 16.2; the best value index is 12.68; the strongest multiplier is 4.5. The study is simulated, not measured, and rests on stated assumptions that readers may replace and re-run.

homework.q: Take the paper “How Many Cleaning Passes Does Seed Cotton Profit From? The Pass at Which Lint Value Stops Rising”. Its stated result is: In the computed results, the best passes is 3; the best value usd is 609.81; the best trash pct is 1.46; the best lint kg is 343; the zero pass value usd is 556.11. The study is simulated, not measured, and rests on stated assumptions that readers may replace and re-run. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

professor.name: Professor Shanice Owens
professor.personality: A quiet and relentless teacher of Designs & Engineering who keeps a notebook of the class's mistakes and teaches from it the following week. Students leave her room able to explain the idea to a stranger, which she counts as the only real grade.
professor.greeting: Sit down, open your notebook — designs & Engineering rewards the prepared.

classes.title: Sleep, Bedding and the Night Room (Wave 7)

papers.t: Bed Height for Older Sleepers: The Seat-Height Rule That Minimises Sit-to-Stand Effort, and the Fall Energy Cost of Exceeding It
papers.r: For a popliteal height of 42 cm, standing from a 45 cm bed top requires an effort index of 103.7, against 100.0 at the recommended height and 57.1 from a fashionable 65 cm top — the effort curve is steep below knee height and flat above it. Raising the top to 75 cm raises the energy of a roll-out fall for a 70 kg sleeper from 316 J at the recommended height to 515 J.

papers.t: Blackout Is a Gap Problem: Light at the Eye from Blind Edge Leakage as a Function of Gap Width, and the Overlap That Replaces Expensive Fabric
papers.r: With the gaps sealed, blackout fabric holds the eye to 0.15 lux; a gap of only 2.0 mm around the perimeter breaches a stated 1 lux design criterion, and a 10 mm gap admits 4.6 lux — more than an ordinary curtain with sealed edges delivers through its fabric at 7.5 lux. A simple overlap strip that forces gap light through two reflections cuts the 10 mm case to 0.32 lux.

papers.t: How Much Blanket Is Enough: A Tog Sizing Rule from Sleeping Heat Production, Room Temperature, and the Insulation Already Supplied by the Mattress
papers.r: The requirement falls from 15.5 tog at 10 degrees to 8.0 tog at 19 degrees and 5.5 tog at 22 degrees. A 13.5 tog duvet in a 19 degree room therefore carries 5.5 tog of surplus insulation, which in the model would drive mean skin temperature to 40.1 degrees if the sleeper did not respond by throwing it off.

papers.t: Dawn Simulation, Priced in Lux-Minutes: The Ramp Duration and Peak Illuminance a Wake-Up Light Needs at Realistic Pillow Distances
papers.r: At the bedside the peak is 300.0 lux and a 30-minute ramp delivers 4500 lux-minutes; across the room at 1.8 metres the peak collapses to 23.1 lux and the same ramp delivers 347 lux-minutes, far below a stated effective band of 2500 to 7500. Reaching the band's middle from across the room would need a ramp of 432.0 minutes.

papers.t: Heat the Bed or Heat the Room: The Energy Arithmetic of an Electric Blanket Against Night-Time Space Heating
papers.r: Faced with a cold bedroom, a household can heat the room or heat the bed, and the two strategies differ in energy use by a large factor. This paper computes both sides from stated assumptions: an electric blanket at 60 watts with a stated duty cycle of 0.55 uses 0.26 kilowatt-hours over an eight-hour night, while holding the bedroom three degrees warmer against a stated room heat-loss coefficient of 55 watts per kelv

papers.t: Soft Infant Sleep Surfaces and Exhaled-Air Pooling: A Rebreathing Model That Converts Surface Firmness into a Carbon Dioxide Fraction at the Face
papers.r: With stated pocket volumes of 120 millilitres on a soft surface against 25 on a firm one, the steady inspired carbon dioxide fraction reaches 4.4 percent on the soft surface, against 0.04 percent — effectively fresh air — on the firm surface, while inspired oxygen falls to 16.6 percent. Firmness, converted into pocket geometry, becomes a number a parent can reason with.

papers.t: Mattress Firmness as a Pressure Problem: Peak Interface Pressure Across Body Masses, and the Mass Above Which No Uniform Surface Stays Below the Capillary Threshold
papers.r: Peak pressure rises steadily with stiffness — at 75 kg, from 3.97 kPa on the softest layer to 6.38 kPa on the firmest — while sink depth falls. Scoring both failures against a capillary threshold of 4.27 kPa and a 110 mm support limit, a stiffness window exists for the 55 kg sleeper (40, 60, 80, 100 kPa per metre) and a narrow one for the 75 kg sleeper (40), but none at all for the 95 kg sleeper, whose best achievabl

papers.t: When Is a Mattress Finished: A Sag-Growth Model and a Measurable Replacement Rule Based on the Depth That Matters to the Spine
papers.r: Foam reaches the stated 25 mm sag criterion at 6.6 years and the 2.5 degree misalignment criterion at 18.4 years; innerspring reaches the sag criterion at 16.4 years and does not reach the alignment criterion within the thirty-year horizon modelled, standing at 1.21 degrees at year ten. At ten years the two constructions carry 29.8 mm and 19.3 mm of sag respectively.

papers.t: How Far a Toss Travels: Motion Transfer Across a Shared Mattress as a Function of Distance, and the Separation at Which a Partner's Turn Falls Below Perception
papers.r: Against a stated perception threshold of 0.8 mm, the disturbance stays perceptible for 1.39 m across a coil mattress, 0.71 m across pocket springs, and 0.4 m across foam. At the 0.85 m centre separation of a queen bed, the coil mattress still delivers 2.13 mm to the partner while foam delivers 0.05 mm.

papers.t: The Mosquito Net Trade-Off: Mesh Aperture Against Air Movement, and the Hole Size at Which a Net Stops Cooling the Sleeper It Protects
papers.r: At the 1.2 mm aperture that excludes the malaria mosquito, the open fraction is 0.685 and the air speed under the net falls to 0.567 of the unnetted value, with relative cooling at 0.711. The 0.6 mm mesh needed against sandflies cuts air speed to 0.352 and cooling to 0.534.

papers.t: The Closed Bedroom Door: Overnight Carbon Dioxide Accumulation for One and Two Sleepers, and the Door Gap or Vent Area That Holds It Below 1000 ppm
papers.r: Two sleepers behind a closed door end the night at 4777 ppm, heading for a steady state of 8332 ppm, and spend 7.2 hours above 1000 ppm; one sleeper ends at 2598 ppm. Holding two sleepers at or below 1000 ppm requires 1.36 air changes per hour — a flow of 13.8 litres per second.

papers.t: Bedroom Humidity Against Dust Mites: The Ventilation and Temperature Conditions That Hold a Bedroom Below the Mite Breeding Threshold Through a Winter Night
papers.r: At the closed-door infiltration rate of 0.1 air changes per hour the room settles at 100.0 percent, deep inside breeding territory; holding it at or below a stated 55 percent target requires 0.27 air changes per hour. The same calculation exposes a winter constraint in the other direction: single glazing condenses once room humidity passes 61.3 percent.

papers.t: The Bathroom Trip at 3 a.m.: How Bright, and in What Colour, a Night Light Can Be Before Its Melanopic Dose Rivals the Evening Screen
papers.r: A low amber fitting delivers 2.2 melanopic lux-minutes, 0.09 percent of the evening's dose; a bright daylight-white fitting delivers 114.0, 4.8 percent of the evening dose in four minutes. Inverting the calculation gives a design bound: to keep a single trip under two percent of the evening dose, light at the eye must stay below 12.0 melanopic lux — 66.7 photopic lux if amber, but only 12.6 lux if daylight-white.

papers.t: Sizing Earplug Attenuation for Street-Facing Bedrooms: The Reduction Actually Required to Bring Passing-Traffic Peaks Below the Sleep-Disturbance Criterion
papers.r: A foam plug labelled 32 dB delivers 17.6 dB in the model, which is ample for the arterial case, leaving peaks of 40.4 dBA, but on an urban main road the requirement is 23.0 dB and the same plug leaves 50.4 dBA — above criterion. The practical output is a three-line sizing table, and a clear statement of the exposure level at which plugs alone stop being the answer and the window or the room must change instead.

papers.t: A Pillow-Loft Rule from Neck Geometry: Compressed Loft as a Function of Shoulder Width, Head Mass, and Fill Stiffness for Side and Back Sleeping
papers.r: A standard 15 cm down pillow leaves that sleeper's neck tilted 28.0 degrees from neutral. The deliverable is a two-measurement rule — shoulder breadth and fill compression — that replaces firmness adjectives with arithmetic.

papers.t: What a Sleeping Bag Rating Actually Buys: Insulation Thickness Required per Degree Below Freezing, and the Cost of the Mattress Pad the Rating Assumes
papers.r: The loft needed over the body is 7.4 cm at 10 degrees, 10.8 cm at freezing, 14.1 cm at minus 10, and 17.4 cm at minus 20 — about 1.7 cm of additional loft for every five degrees. Beneath the body the bag's loft compresses nearly flat, and the paper computes the pad resistance that must replace it: at minus 10 degrees the pad must supply at least 1.04 square-metre kelvin per watt, without which the underside alone wou

papers.t: The Weighted Blanket Claim, Weighed: Interface Pressure from a 10 Percent Body-Weight Blanket Against the Pressures Its Marketing Invokes
papers.r: A blanket of 7.0 kg for a 70 kg sleeper, resting on a stated 0.85 square metres of body surface, produces a mean interface pressure of 0.08 kPa and a modelled peak of 0.18 kPa over bony areas — 2 percent of the 4.27 kPa capillary threshold, and far below the pressures of the hugs and compression garments the advertising evokes.

professor.name: Professor Stefano Oliveira
professor.personality: A plainspoken and immovable teacher of Designs & Engineering who sets problems that look small and open like trapdoors. Once a term, he teaches a whole session from the class's own questions and nothing else.
professor.greeting: Welcome to designs & Engineering. We start where the subject starts: at the beginning.

classes.title: Eyes, Vision and Low-Cost Spectacles (Wave 7)

papers.t: Reading Additions Derived, Not Guessed: An Age-and-Distance Table from Hofstetter's Amplitude with Half Held in Reserve
papers.r: Ready-made reading spectacles are sold by age-banded guesses, and the guesses are rarely shown. This paper derives the banding from a published empirical relation - Hofstetter's average amplitude of accommodation, 18.5 minus 0.30 times age, in dioptres - combined with the stated working rule that half the amplitude is held in reserve, and computes the reading addition for ages 40 to 65 at three working distances.

papers.t: Span Before Polish: The Dioptric Range a Variable-Focus Spectacle Must Cover, and Why Its Resolution Is Not the Problem
papers.r: Variable-focus spectacles, in which the wearer dials a power rather than wearing a fixed lens, are repeatedly proposed for settings without refractionists. Their feasibility turns on a number rarely stated: the span of powers one mechanism must cover.

papers.t: The Axis Budget: How Many Degrees of Cylinder Misalignment Each Cylinder Power Can Afford
papers.r: When a cylindrical lens is rotated away from its prescribed axis, it does not simply weaken: it leaves a new, oblique astigmatism whose size is twice the cylinder power times the sine of the axis error. This paper turns that standard vector result into a fitting tolerance table for workshops without lensmeter verification at every step.

papers.t: Ninety-Five Percent of Six Percent: A Spectral Test of the Claim That Blue-Blocking Lenses Remove the Burden of Screen Light
papers.r: Lenses marketed as blocking 95 percent of blue light are sold with the implication that they remove most of the light burden from screens. The implication does not survive band arithmetic. Under stated photopic weights for a daylight-like spectrum, the 400-450 nm band that such lenses target carries only 6.0 percent of the light the visual system actually uses; removing 95 percent of it reduces total photopic light b

papers.t: The Small-Room Correction: What Testing at Three Metres Does to a Six-Metre Chart, and the Arithmetic That Repairs It
papers.r: Schools and clinics with small rooms routinely test acuity at three or four metres with charts designed for six, often without adjusting the result. This paper computes what that shortcut costs and the two corrections it requires.

papers.t: Outgrown Before Worn Out: How Long a Child's Frame Truly Fits, and the Adjustable Range That Multiplies It
papers.r: Children's spectacles are usually replaced because the prescription changed, but a quieter expiry runs underneath: the child's face grows, the pupils separate, and a frame centred for last year's face progressively decentres its lenses. This paper computes fit life from a stated pupillary-distance growth model and the decentration tolerance used in dispensing.

papers.t: How Large Is Large Print? A Fluent-Reading Specification Labelled by the Acuity It Serves
papers.r: 'Large print' is sold as a point size with no stated reader in mind, and much of it is not large enough for the readers it names. This paper derives the print specification from letter geometry and the established finding that fluent reading requires print about three times the reader's acuity threshold - the critical print size.

papers.t: Diameter Is the Free Lever: How Frame Size Sets the Weight and Edge of a Minus Lens
papers.r: Minus lenses get heavy at their edges, and the edge is bought by diameter. This paper computes sagitta, edge thickness, and mass for minus lenses of -2, -4, and -6 D cut to diameters from 50 to 70 mm, from stated surface geometry for a refractive index of 1.50 and a 1.0 mm centre.

papers.t: The Keyhole Limit: Magnifier Power, the Shrinking Window, and the Strongest Lens That Still Lets a Sentence Be Read
papers.r: A hand magnifier trades the two things a reader wants against each other: stronger lenses enlarge print more but show less of the page at once. This paper computes that trade-off for a stated geometric model of a 50 mm diameter simple magnifier and a stated word footprint of 12 mm, and finds where fluency breaks.

papers.t: A Millimetre Is Not a Formality: Pupillary-Distance Tolerance by Lens Power, from Prentice's Rule
papers.r: Pupillary distance is the cheapest measurement in dispensing and one of the most consequential, because a lens centred away from the pupil acts as a prism. By Prentice's rule, prism equals decentration in centimetres times lens power, and this paper converts that rule into a tolerance table for low-cost dispensing, where pupillary distance is often estimated or taken from a ready-made pair's fixed geometry.

papers.t: Millimetres, Not 'Medium': Letter Heights and Pixel Counts a Phone Must Reach for Each Level of Acuity
papers.r: Phone text settings are offered as small, medium, and large, which tells a low-vision user nothing. This paper computes the actual letter heights, in millimetres and in pixels, that each level of acuity requires at ordinary holding distances, from the stated geometry that a threshold letter subtends five times the minimum angle of resolution.

papers.t: The Pinhole Aperture That Minimises Blur: An Optimum Diameter, Its Acuity Ceiling, and a Test of the Claim That Smaller Is Sharper
papers.r: Pinhole spectacles are sold in fixed apertures, often with the suggestion that a smaller hole gives sharper sight. That suggestion does not survive a standard blur calculation. For an eye with defocus, geometric blur grows in proportion to aperture while diffraction blur grows as aperture shrinks; combining the two at 550 nm gives, for 2 D of defocus, a minimum total blur of 7.96 minutes of arc at an aperture of 0.82

papers.t: Prescribe Light and Print Together: The Illuminance Each Age Needs for Each Print Size, and the Point Where Light Stops Working
papers.r: A brighter lamp is the cheapest vision aid in the world, but advice about reading light is usually given in watts and adjectives. This paper replaces both with a stated model relating the eye acuity threshold to illuminance for three ages, and computes the light each age needs for fluent reading of four print sizes.

papers.t: Four Centuries, One Constant: The Resolution Bound of the Scheiner-Disc Self-Refractor
papers.r: The Scheiner disc - two pinholes before the eye, through which a point of light appears double whenever focus is imperfect - is the oldest self-refraction principle in optics, described in 1619, and periodically reinvented as a low-cost refractor.

papers.t: The Step Is the Accuracy: How Trial-Lens Step Size Caps Self-Selected Correction, and a Two-Stage Kit That Beats It
papers.r: Where no refractionist is available, wearers can be offered trial lenses and asked which is clearer - but the fineness of the set decides in advance how good the result can be. This paper computes the ceiling that the step size imposes.

papers.t: Drawing the Shelf from the Distribution: The Smallest Stock-Lens Inventory That Serves a Stated Share of Wearers Within a Quarter Dioptre
papers.r: Ready-made and stock-lens services fail quietly at the ordering stage: the powers on the shelf decide in advance which fraction of a population can be served. This paper computes that fraction for a stated population model - spherical equivalent normally distributed with mean -0.50 D and standard deviation 2.00 D - and finds the smallest inventories that serve stated shares of wearers within 0.25 D of their true powe

papers.t: The Prescription Is a Place: How Vertex Distance Rewrites Strong Lenses, and the Power at Which It Starts to Matter
papers.r: A lens's power is not a property of the lens alone: it is the power at a stated distance from the eye, and moving the lens changes what the eye receives. This paper computes the effective power change when spectacles sit at a different vertex distance from the one used at refraction, for powers from 4 to 14 D in both signs, using the standard vertex formula.

Its stated result is: Ready-made reading spectacles are sold by age-banded guesses, and the guesses are rarely shown. This paper derives the banding from a published empirical relation - Hofstetter's average amplitude of accommodation, 18.5 minus 0.30 times age, in dioptres - combined with the stated working rule that ha (a) Restate the claim in your own words. professor.name: Professor Preston Hughes
professor.personality: A crisp and formal teacher of Designs & Engineering who builds every lesson around one real example before any definition is allowed. He office door carries a hand-written sign: stuck is a place, not a person.

classes.title: Teeth, Oral Care and Low-Resource Dentistry (Wave 7)

papers.t: Hand-Mixed or Capsule: Glass Ionomer Waste and Restorations per Kit in Atraumatic Restorative Treatment
papers.r: Atraumatic restorative treatment depends on glass ionomer, bought either as powder and liquid for hand mixing or as pre-dosed capsules. This study compares the two routes at stated values: a restoration needs 0.20 g of mixed material; hand mixing prepares 0.35 g per attempt with 12 percent of mixes discarded for ratio failure; a capsule delivers 0.40 g with 2 percent failure.

papers.t: When a Toothbrush Stops Cleaning: A Splay-Based Replacement Rule and Its Cost per Effective Brush
papers.r: Toothbrush replacement is usually governed by habit or by a calendar printed on packaging, not by how well the brush still cleans. This study models plaque-removal efficacy as falling linearly by 0.045 per week of twice-daily use from an initial index of 1.00, and computes end-of-life and mean efficacy, brushes per year, and annual cost at a bulk price of USD 0.60 for replacement intervals from 2 to 16 weeks.

papers.t: Brushing with a Cup Instead of a Running Tap: Water Saved per Person and the Rinse Volume That Still Clears Paste
papers.r: Toothbrushing advice assumes a running tap and never prices the water. This study compares a running-tap routine (6 litres per minute for 45 seconds, 4.5 litres per brushing) with a single 200 mL cup, and checks the cup against a stated dilution model of paste clearance in which the residual fraction after rinsing with volume V is exp(-V/60).

papers.t: Charcoal Toothpaste and the Whitening Claim: Abrasive Wear per Shade Gained and the Fluoride the Claim Leaves Out
papers.r: Charcoal toothpastes are sold on a whitening claim. This study tests the claim against a stated saturating model of stain removal, in which any paste above an abrasivity index of 60 reaches the same shade gain of 1.90 shades at four weeks, and a stated wear model in which annual abrasive wear is proportional to the abrasivity index.

papers.t: A Smear, a Pea, or a Ribbon: Fluoride Dose per Brushing for Young Children and the Dispensing Rule That Keeps It in Range
papers.r: Advice on how much toothpaste a young child should use is given in pictures, a smear or a pea, without stating the dose those pictures deliver. This study computes fluoride applied and swallowed for three dispensing amounts (smear 0.10 g, pea 0.25 g, full ribbon 0.60 g), two paste strengths (1000 and 1450 ppm), and two age bands, with stated swallowed fractions and a stated upper intake criterion of 0.10 mg per kg pe

papers.t: Half a Tablet Cleans as the Label Fears It Might Not: Concentration, Soak Time, and Cost in Denture Cleansing
papers.r: Denture cleansing tablets are used one per soak by label instruction, and halving them is a common household economy of unknown effect. This study evaluates dose and soak time together under a stated concentration-time criterion of 3.0 normalised units, where a whole tablet in 150 mL defines a concentration of 1.00 and a half tablet 0.50.

papers.t: How Much Floss Is Enough: The Handling Length That Cleans Every Contact and the Waste in the Standard Instruction
papers.r: The standard floss instruction, to take about 45 cm, is tested against the geometry of the task it describes. Cleaning 26 interdental contacts with a fresh 2.5 cm segment for each, plus 8 cm for each of two hand wraps, requires 81.0 cm of floss.

papers.t: Light for Looking in Mouths: Illuminance at Working Distance, Battery Life, and the Cheapest Headlamp Class That Meets an Examination Threshold
papers.r: Examiners working without a dental operating light rely on headlamps sold by lumen ratings that do not state the illuminance at the mouth. This study converts three lamp classes (100, 200, and 400 lumens, priced at USD 6, 12, and 25 as stated values) into illuminance at a 0.35 m working distance, assuming the output is focused into a 0.20 m spot with a stated optical efficiency of 0.70, and compares the result with a

papers.t: Sizing Interdental Brushes by Passage Diameter: A Selection Rule That Covers the Spaces a Single Size Misses
papers.r: Interdental brushes are commonly supplied in a single size, as if all interdental spaces were alike. This study models 26 spaces with stated passage diameters (eight at 0.6 mm, eight at 0.8 mm, six at 1.0 mm, four at 1.3 mm) and a stated fit rule under which a brush cleans a space when its diameter is at least the passage diameter and at most 0.4 mm larger.

papers.t: Miswak or Manufactured Brush: Cost per Year of Effective Cleaning Where Brushes and Paste Are Hard to Afford
papers.r: Miswak, the chewing stick of Salvadora persica, is widely described as the economical alternative to a manufactured brush and paste. This study tests that description at stated prices: a stick at USD 0.15 replaced weekly, against a brush at USD 0.60 replaced every eight weeks plus toothpaste at USD 0.80 per 100 g tube consumed in 100 days.

papers.t: A Day at the Mobile Dental Clinic: Appointment Length, Turnaround, and the Schedule That Treats the Most Patients Without Rushing Treatment
papers.r: A mobile dental clinic's scarce asset is chair time in a community it may not revisit for months. This study builds the clinic day from stated values: 420 minutes of chair time, treatment times of 20, 30, and 25 minutes for examination with cleaning, filling, and extraction, a case mix of 50, 30, and 20 percent giving a weighted treatment time of 24.0 minutes, and turnaround of 5 minutes with parallel instrument proc

papers.t: The 20 Millilitre Habit: Dispensing Volume for Antiseptic Mouth Rinse and the Cost of the Oversized Cup
papers.r: Antiseptic mouth rinse is prescribed at a label dose of 10 mL but commonly dispensed in brim-filled cups of 20 or 30 mL. This study costs a stated course of twice-daily rinsing for 14 days (28 doses) from a 300 mL bottle priced at USD 4.50, at dispensing volumes of 10, 15, 20, and 30 mL.

papers.t: A Level Teaspoon in a Cup of Water: The Actual Salt Concentration of the Standard Aftercare Rinse and a More Repeatable Recipe
papers.r: Patients recovering from a tooth extraction are told to rinse with a teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water, an instruction whose terms are undefined. This study computes the concentration of six common versions using stated spoon masses (half teaspoon 3.0 g, level teaspoon 6.0 g, heaped teaspoon 9.0 g) and vessel volumes of 200, 250, and 350 mL, against the isotonic reference of 0.9 percent and a stated tolerable b

papers.t: Drying Matters More Than Disinfectant: Spacing and Airflow Rules for Storing Forty Toothbrushes in a Classroom
papers.r: School toothbrushing programmes store dozens of brushes between sessions, and guidance often reaches for disinfectant soaking where the underlying problem is that brushes stay wet and touching. This study models drying under stated assumptions: a shaken brush head carries 2.0 mL of water, evaporation proceeds at 0.020 mL per minute with heads separated and at half that rate with heads touching, and the dry target is

papers.t: Steam Sterilisation for a Small Dental Clinic: Cycle Capacity, Daily Throughput, and the Instrument Sets That Remove the Bottleneck
papers.r: In a small dental clinic the steriliser, not the clinician, can set the pace of the day. This study models a benchtop steam steriliser holding six instrument sets per 45-minute cycle across an eight-hour day, and derives both daily capacity and the stock of sets a clinic must own to keep chairs working. Capacity is ten cycles and 60 sets per day, which meets demand at four, six, and eight patients per hour.

papers.t: What Stays in the Tube: Residual Toothpaste by Tube Type and the Annual Loss for a Family of Five
papers.r: Every toothpaste tube is discarded with paste still inside. This study quantifies the residue for a family of five using 5.0 g per day, at stated residuals of 8 g for a standard crimped tube emptied by hand, 3 g with a rolling key, and 2 g for a stand-up pump, from a nominal 100 g tube priced at USD 0.80.

papers.t: One Varnish Vial, How Many Children: The Dose per Child That Covers the Teeth Without Emptying the Vial Early
papers.r: Fluoride varnish in school programmes is usually dispensed as one unit-dose vial per child, so the package sets the dose. This study models a 0.40 mL vial of 5 percent sodium fluoride varnish (22.6 mg fluoride per mL), a stated coating need of 0.20 mL for a full primary dentition, and 15 percent applicator waste, and computes fluoride applied and children served per ten vials at doses of 0.20 to 0.40 mL.

Its stated result is: Atraumatic restorative treatment depends on glass ionomer, bought either as powder and liquid for hand mixing or as pre-dosed capsules. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

professor.name: Professor George Clark
professor.personality: A unhurried and exact teacher of Designs & Engineering who slows down exactly where the textbooks speed up. Colleagues send him their hardest teaching problems, because his explanations have a reputation for landing.
