classes.title: Household Pests and Stored-Goods Protection (Wave 8)

papers.t: Bait Stations Along an Ant Trail: The Spacing at Which Discovery Time, Not Dose, Becomes the Limit
papers.r: Place liquid bait stations about 2 m apart along the active trail (nine stations for an 18 m trail, about USD 9.90 in hardware), refill weekly, do not spray the trail during baiting, and allow ten days before judging the attempt; on the stated assumptions the colony dose is complete in about 2.8 days at this spacing, and wider spacings fail mainly by delaying discovery.

papers.t: The Thick Mattress Problem: Heat-Soak Time Scales With the Square of Thickness in Bed Bug Room Treatments
papers.r: Plan the hold from the thickest item: at 60 C air, allow at least 4 hours for 10 cm of foam, 16 hours for 20 cm, and treat 30 cm items (36 hours) as impractical to clear in place — split, open or remove thick items so no conduction path exceeds about 10 cm, and verify with a probe in the core of the thickest remaining item.

papers.t: One Trap or Two? Detection Probability for a Light Clothes Moth Infestation in a Wool Store
papers.r: Hang two pheromone traps per small textile store room, at low level and at opposite ends, replace them every eight weeks (USD 12 per round), and treat any catch as a trigger to inspect and treat the textiles themselves; a third trap in the same room adds cost without detection.

papers.t: Gel Dots on a Grid: The Widest Spacing That Still Collapses a German Cockroach Population in a Kitchen
papers.r: Apply gel dots of about 0.1 g at no more than 1.1 m spacing along every harbourage line, counting each cabinet level separately (19 dots for 20 m of line, under USD 1 of gel), and re-apply at the same spacing after about three weeks; spacings of 3 m or more should be expected to fail outright, however much gel each dot contains.

papers.t: Warm Washes and Dust Mites: The Temperature Below Which No Practical Cycle Reaches a Three-Log Reduction
papers.r: Wash bedding intended as a mite control measure at 60 C with a normal-length cycle (about 24 minutes of allowance covers the 3-log target at the load's coldest point); treat 40 C washing as allergen-removal cleaning only, and use hot tumble drying, freezing or encasements for items that cannot be washed at 60 C.

papers.t: Vacuuming Against the Flea Life Cycle: The Interval Below Which a Carpet Reservoir Collapses Without Insecticide
papers.r: Vacuum the pet's resting and sleeping areas daily for the first 14 days of a flea infestation and every second day for the following 14, alongside effective treatment of the pet; weekly vacuuming should be expected to leave a breeding reservoir in place indefinitely.

papers.t: Sieving Infested Flour: The Aperture That Removes the Adults and Leaves the Eggs, and the Finer Mesh That Still Leaves Most of Them
papers.r: Never treat sieving as a cure for infested flour: use a sieve of about 0.45 mm to inspect and to prepare flour for a freezing or heating step, expect it to leave roughly four eggs in five behind, and discard flour whose visible catch suggests contamination near 100 individuals per kilogram.

papers.t: One Vinegar Trap Does Not Clear a Fruit Fly Outbreak: A Growth-and-Capture Disproof for Kitchens
papers.r: Do not rely on a vinegar trap to clear an outbreak while any breeding site remains; clean or remove the site first (drains, fruit, bins, spills), then run one or two traps for a fortnight as mop-up and as indicators of a missed site.

papers.t: Cooling Grain With Night Air: Why Bin Diameter Drops Out of the Aeration Time and Airflow Rate Does Not
papers.r: Budget about 29 nights of eight cool, dry hours to bring a wheat bulk from 28 C to a 15 C mean at 5 m3/h per tonne, whatever the bin diameter; halve the airflow rate only if twice as many nights are available, and double it if only a fortnight of suitable nights remains.

papers.t: How Long Until a Sealed Grain Bag Runs Low on Oxygen? Infestation Density Sets the Clock in Hermetic Storage
papers.r: Keep a hermetic bag sealed for at least five weeks when the grain went in with a light infestation (around 2 adult-equivalents per kg), at least a fortnight at moderate density, and treat any opening as resetting the protection clock to zero; hold grain for weekly use in a separate small bag.

papers.t: Wet Combing for Head Lice: Four Passes, Four Sessions — A Schedule Set by the Egg, Not the Adult
papers.r: Wet-comb with a 0.22 mm comb in four full passes per session on days 1, 5, 9 and 13 (about 25 minutes per session), checking close contacts on the same days; do not judge the treatment by the first session, and protect the day-9 session above all others.

papers.t: How Far Apart Can Snap Traps Sit? A Wall-Coverage Rule for the House Mouse in Kitchens and Store Rooms
papers.r: Space snap traps no more than 12 m apart along a confirmed mouse run, concentrate them at wall junctions, corners and the gaps behind appliances, and check and reset them every night; on the stated assumptions this gives a 0.995 capture probability within 48 hours for a single mouse, and extra traps should be justified as redundancy, not coverage.

papers.t: Forty-Eight Hours in the Freezer: Where the Pantry Moth Rule Holds for Single Bags and Fails for Stacked Flour
papers.r: Freeze flour and grain in single bags or a single layer for 48 hours at minus 22 C; never rely on 48 hours for a tight stack — allow about 4.5 days for a 40 cm stack or restack it halfway through so that every bag spends time on the outside of the pile.

papers.t: Twelve-Millimetre Mesh Does Not Exclude Mice: A Passage-Probability Bound for Household Exclusion Work
papers.r: Proof against mice with mesh or grille apertures of at most 6 mm (about 4 to 5 mm for a strict below-1-percent bound), treat every clear gap over 6 mm as an entry regardless of material around it, and never rely on expanding foam as the barrier layer.

papers.t: Drying a Store Room Below the Silverfish Threshold: Dehumidifier Capacity From a Moisture Balance
papers.r: For a roughly 48 m3 basement store room in a humid summer climate, buy a dehumidifier rated at 12 L per day or more, plumb it for continuous drainage, seal the room's air leaks first, and verify with a hygrometer that the room holds at or below 60 percent relative humidity.

papers.t: Beans in the Sun: Bag Mass, Projected Area, and the Hours Needed to Reach 50 Degrees in a Black Enclosure
papers.r: Solar-treat beans in a single layer in bags of at most 25 kg where possible (about 4.7 hours including a one-hour hold in strong sun), split 50 kg sacks first, turn bags at the midpoint, and verify 50 C at the core of the largest bag before storing.

papers.t: Stations Around a House Perimeter: Termite Interception Probability as a Function of Spacing
papers.r: Space subterranean termite bait stations about 3 m apart around the perimeter (15 stations for a 44 m house), inspect them quarterly, and reject layouts wider than 4 m as materially weaker; beyond 6 m the interception probability falls below three chances in four per season.

homework.q: Take the paper “Bait Stations Along an Ant Trail: The Spacing at Which Discovery Time, Not Dose, Becomes the Limit”. Its stated result is: Place liquid bait stations about 2 m apart along the active trail (nine stations for an 18 m trail, about USD 9.90 in hardware), refill weekly, do not spray the trail during baiting, and allow ten days before judging the attempt; on the stated assumptions the colony dose is complete in about 2.8 day (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

professor.name: Professor Fitri Le
professor.personality: A wry and well-read teacher of Designs & Engineering who reads the primary source aloud before trusting any summary of it. Examinations in her room are open-book, because she is testing thinking, not storage.
professor.greeting: Come in and take a seat — designs & Engineering first, opinions after.

classes.title: Paper, Ink, Books and Printing (Wave 8)

papers.t: A Box That Buys Decades: Alkaline Reserve, Acid Migration and the Service Life of a Low-Cost Storage Box for Books and Papers
papers.r: A storage box board with a 3 percent alkaline reserve protects its contents for 12.0 years at 20 degrees Celsius and a high-buffer 8 percent board for 32.0 years, but the high-buffer board's life falls to 16.0 years in a 30-degree store, so reserve and cool storage together, not either alone, deliver decades of protection.

papers.t: Thick Book, Heavy Bill: Paper Bulk, Grammage and the Postage Cost of a Three-Hundred-Page Book
papers.r: For a 300-page A5 book, a 70 gsm bulky paper gives a 446 g book with a 16.8 mm spine, against 493 g and 14.4 mm for 80 gsm standard paper; against a 90 gsm standard paper the bulky choice also saves USD 0.80 per posted copy by staying in the lower postal band while looking thicker, not thinner.

papers.t: Four Pages at a Time: An Imposition Bound for A5 Booklets on A4 and A3 Sheets That Minimises Trim and Signature Waste
papers.r: An A5 booklet must contain a multiple of four pages: a 50-page text becomes a 52-page booklet with 2 blank pages (3.8 percent waste), a 32-page booklet needs exactly 8 A3 sheets, and at the stated sheet prices paper cost per booklet is identical on A3 and A4 stock, so the stock choice should be made on equipment and labour, not paper price.

papers.t: Carbon Ink That Stays in the Bottle and on the Page: Pigment Loading, Opacity and Settling Time for a Low-Cost Writing and Printing Ink
papers.r: For a carbon ink whose opacity saturates with pigment loading, 6 grams per litre is the lowest loading meeting the stated document optical density of 1.2, with a settling life of 113 days and a pen-safe viscosity, whereas 20 grams per litre raises density only to 1.83 while cutting settling life to 28 days.

papers.t: When Duplex Printing Saves Nothing: Reprint Losses, Jam Rates and the Net Paper Saving From Printing on Both Sides
papers.r: Duplex printing saves 49.8 percent of sheets with no user errors, 47.3 percent at a 5 percent reprint rate and 39.8 percent even at 20 percent errors; the saving is not exhausted until the reprint error fraction reaches 0.998, so duplex should be mandated for standard long documents and management effort spent on templates rather than on policing short jobs.

papers.t: Envelopes From the Offcut: Blank Sizes, Sheet Nesting and the Envelope Format That a Small Cutter Should Standardise On
papers.r: Nesting rectangular envelope blanks on a 650x900 mm sheet gives 6 DL blanks per sheet at 24.5 percent waste, 4 C5 blanks at 36.0 percent waste, and 9 C6 blanks at 13.8 percent waste, so C6 is the format a small cutter should standardise on for this sheet size, with the other formats quoted at their true waste penalty.

papers.t: Cutting the Ream Without Waste: A Guillotine Layout for Exercise Books That Recovers the Trim Strip as Usable Product
papers.r: On a 700x900 mm parent sheet, the stated 300x420 mm exercise-book blank fits 4 per sheet in portrait orientation with 20.0 percent trim, against 3 per sheet rotated; the leftover arrives as a single 100 mm side strip wide enough to cut into secondary products such as bookmarks and labels instead of being discarded.

papers.t: Drying Without Warping: Airflow, Sheet Thickness and Time to Safe Moisture for Handmade Paper Dried on Racks
papers.r: A 2 mm handmade sheet dries to safe moisture in 15.6 hours in still air at 60 percent relative humidity, in 5.9 hours under a 1.0 m/s fan, and in 31.2 hours if formed 4 mm thick in still air; at 80 percent humidity the same 2 mm sheet needs 18.0 hours against 6.0 hours at 40 percent, so airflow and humidity each matter as much as thickness.

papers.t: A Safe Humidity Band for Stored Paper: Curl, Jam Risk and the Cost of Running a Copier Outside It
papers.r: Jam rate stays at its baseline inside a 45–55 percent relative humidity band and rises to 4.7 jams per thousand sheets at both 30 and 70 percent humidity; at 20,000 sheets a month that raises monthly jam cost from USD 36.00 in band to USD 84.60, an extra USD 48.60 that placement and sealed wrappers, rather than room plant, can recover.

papers.t: Ink by the Square Metre: A Coverage Rule That Predicts Ink Use per Thousand A4 Pages Within a Stated Dot-Gain Allowance
papers.r: At 20 percent nominal coverage on A4, ink use is 0.017 kg per thousand pages costing USD 0.30 at the stated ink price, rising to 0.076 kg and USD 1.37 per thousand at full coverage; one kilogram of ink therefore covers about 58,824 pages at text-like coverage, and including dot gain in the conversion is what makes the prediction usable for pricing.

papers.t: Make-Ready Is a Fixed Tax: Combining Small Jobs on One Sheet and the Saving From Gang Printing Common Sizes
papers.r: Combining three representative short jobs (200, 300 and 500 sheets) into one gang run cuts their total cost from USD 49.62 to USD 40.54 at the stated rates, saving USD 9.08 (18.3 percent) and 36 make-ready sheets, because the duplicated setup and spoilage charges simply cease to exist.

papers.t: Washing Recycled Pulp Until It Stops Paying: Deinking Yield, Brightness and the Optimum Number of Wash Cycles for Small-Scale Production
papers.r: For a 100 kg batch of recovered newsprint under the stated rates, two wash cycles are optimal: brightness reaches 58.0 points, yield is 95.6 kg, and net value is USD 38.43, compared with USD 21.00 unwashed and USD 25.93 after eight washes, because further washing spends fibre faster than it buys brightness.

papers.t: Staples That Hold and Staples That Tear: Wire Length and Leg Formation for Saddle-Stitched Booklets by Page Count
papers.r: For the stated book paper, a 32-page booklet needs only a 6 mm staple leg, a 64-page booklet needs 8 mm, and 6 mm legs suffice up to 48 pages; longer legs loaded by default on thin booklets fold badly in the clinch and tear centre pages, so leg length should change at the tabulated page counts.

papers.t: Choosing a Screen Mesh for Poster Printing: Ink Deposit, Edge Definition and Cost per Hundred Posters
papers.r: Ink cost per hundred posters at the stated size and coverage falls from USD 7.32 on a 43 threads-per-centimetre mesh to USD 3.08 on a 90 mesh, a saving of USD 4.24 per hundred, while the coarsest mesh that still holds a 0.30 mm line is 77 threads per centimetre — so mesh should be chosen by the finest detail in the job.

papers.t: How Much Glue Is Enough: Spine Adhesive Thickness, Pull Strength and Cost for Paperback Books Bound in Small Workshops
papers.r: Page-pull strength saturates with adhesive thickness: the thinnest application clearing the stated 60 N school threshold is 0.3 mm, giving 70.7 N for USD 0.016 of adhesive, while a habitual 1.0 mm application gives 94.0 N for USD 0.053 — more than three times the adhesive cost for a third more strength.

papers.t: The Run Length at Which a Stencil Duplicator Stops Beating a Photocopier: A Cost Crossover for Schools and Churches
papers.r: At the stated prices — a USD 0.35 master, USD 0.30 of setup labour, USD 0.008 per duplicator copy and USD 0.035 per photocopy — a stencil duplicator becomes cheaper than a photocopier at 25 copies; at 100 copies it costs USD 1.47 against USD 3.50, and at 300 copies it saves USD 7.40.

papers.t: Refill Twice, Then Replace: Cartridge Yield Decay, Print Quality and the Economic Life of a Remanufactured Toner Cartridge
papers.r: Refilling a toner cartridge costs USD 0.63 per hundred good pages on the first refill against USD 2.14 for a new cartridge, rising to USD 0.92 at the third refill and USD 1.50 at the fifth, by which point spoilage has reached 31.9 percent of pages — so cartridges should be tallied at each refill and retired on spoilage in their middle cycles.

Its stated result is: A storage box board with a 3 percent alkaline reserve protects its contents for 12.0 years at 20 degrees Celsius and a high-buffer 8 percent board for 32.0 years, but the high-buffer board's life falls to 16.0 years in a 30-degree store, so reserve and cool storage together, not either alone, delive (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

professor.name: Professor Jennifer Hall
professor.personality: A energetic and exacting teacher of Designs & Engineering who brings one object from the real world to every single class. She favourite sentence is: show me.

classes.title: Soap, Bathing and Hygiene (Wave 8)

papers.t: The Longest-Lived Bar: Soap Bar Dimensions That Maximise Washes per Gram at Fixed Mass
papers.r: At 100 g the best grippable block found, 5.6 x 5.0 x 3.4 cm, lasted 916 washes, while the thinnest admissible slab lasted 417 washes and a typical oval approximated as a 22 mm thick tablet lasted 584 washes. The best block therefore delivers 56.8% more washes than the typical tablet from the same mass of soap, at a modelled cost of 0.1 US cents per wash against 0.15 cents.

papers.t: Buckets to a Safe Bath: A Mixing Ratio for Bath Water Without a Thermometer
papers.r: At a cold supply of 15 C, the exact ratio is 4.9 buckets of hot per 10 buckets of mixed water, and whole-bucket filling gives a bath at 36.5 C, inside the band. At 8 C the hot share rises to 5.6 buckets in 10 and at 22 C it falls to 3.9 in 10. Hot-supply drift of plus or minus 3 C moves the finished bath by plus or minus 1.3 C at the middle ratio.

papers.t: Keeping Shared Water Honest: The Exchange Rate a Communal Bath Needs to Hold a Stated Load Limit
papers.r: At six bathers per hour the exchange flow needed to hold the stated limit was 24 litres per hour, or 0.6% of the bath volume per hour. Stepped simulation reached a peak of 30000 units per litre, at the limit as designed. Session operation with a full change every 3 hours spent 74 minutes above the limit per session and used 8000 litres per operating day against 288 litres for continuous exchange.

papers.t: Warm Water Is Not the Active Ingredient: Energy Saved by Cold-Water Handwashing at Equal Modelled Removal
papers.r: Modelled removal at twenty seconds was 79.6% at 15 C and 87.5% at 40 C, a difference of 7.9 percentage points across the whole practical range, and 83.7% at 25 C. Heating the wash water to 35 C cost 71.9 kWh and USD 10.79 per household per year at the stated use, for that difference.

papers.t: Hard Water Eats Detergent: A Dosing Rule for Washing Cloth Nappies by Water Hardness Band
papers.r: The hardness tax alone was 14.8 g in soft water and 74.2 g in hard water, a difference of 59.4 g before any cleaning began. Total recommended doses were 42.8 g (soft), 72.5 g (moderate), 102.2 g (hard) and 136.9 g (very hard).

papers.t: Soap That the Garden Can Forgive: A Sodium Budget for Reusing Bath Water on Plants
papers.r: The baseline household applied 98.6 g of sodium per square metre per year before leaching, or 69.0 g net, against the stated ceiling of 12 g, an exceedance of 5.8 times. Halving bathing soap events reduced the net load to 34.5 g, still above the ceiling.

papers.t: A School Day Without an Empty Tap: Sizing a Gravity Handwashing Station and Its Refill Schedule
papers.r: Daily demand was 259.0 litres, and with the reserve the required capacity was 297.8 litres, so the 25 litre container was selected and the 20 litre container rejected as 277.8 litres short. The 4 mm outlet delivered the target wash in 20 seconds at the stated head.

papers.t: A Superfat Margin That Cannot Go Negative: Weighing Tolerances and Saponification Uncertainty in Home Soap Making
papers.r: The computed lye requirement for the recipe is 150.8 grams before any discount. Saponification uncertainty alone can raise the true requirement by 3.0 percent, and adverse weighing errors add a further 1.27 percent, giving a worst-case guarantee threshold of 4.27 percent superfat. The traditional 5 percent discount therefore meets the guarantee, with little to spare for this recipe and equipment.

papers.t: Changing by the Clock Instead of by Failure: An Absorbency-Based Interval for Menstrual Pads
papers.r: Computed waking intervals were 2.0 hours on day 1, 1.5 hours on day 2, 3.5 hours on day 3, 7.5 hours on day 4 and 8 hours on day 5, giving 19 pads across the waking hours of the five days against 20 for a flat four-hourly habit, which nevertheless modelled a leak on day 2 when peak flow filled the pad in 1.3 hours.

papers.t: One Full Push Is Too Much: The Smallest Pump Dose That Still Covers Both Hands
papers.r: The ideal film volume before losses is 1.36 mL, and 1.36 mL must actually reach the skin after the modelled losses. A dose of 2.0 mL per push was the smallest tabulated dose reaching at least 95.4% coverage, while the common 3.0 mL push reached 99.0% coverage and used 50.0% more soap than the recommended dose for a gain of only a few percentage points of coverage.

papers.t: Foam Without Waste: A Dilution Ratio for Shampoo in a Foaming Dispenser That Preserves Cleaning Power
papers.r: Neat use applied surfactant at 15% at the point of contact but averaged 4.1% over the head after spreading losses. Dilution to the threshold occurred at a ratio of 1:11.5, and the recommended working ratio of 1:4 delivered 3.0% at the hair, a margin of 150% above threshold.

papers.t: Is the Shared Bar a Hazard? A Transfer Bound for Bar Soap Under Rinsing and Drying Conditions
papers.r: Under the full chain, a bar used again after 3 hours of draining delivered at most 5 organisms to the next user's hands before their wash, and at most 0.1 remained after the wash itself, against a typical pre-existing hand load in the model of 1000000. Removing the pre-rinse raised the bound tenfold to 50, and keeping the bar standing in water, so that no drying occurred, raised it to 500.

papers.t: Slower Is Not Always Drier: The Shower Flow Rate That Minimises Total Water for a Complete Rinse
papers.r: Under the stated kinetics the volume-minimising flow was 4 litres per minute, using 1.8 litres to complete the rinse in 27 seconds. At 4 litres per minute the rinse took 27 seconds and used 1.8 litres, which is 0.0% more water than the optimum despite the lower flow. At 14 litres per minute the rinse used 2.6 litres.

papers.t: A Full Wash on Two Litres: Sequencing a Sponge Bath to Minimise Water at a Stated Cleanliness Standard
papers.r: The optimised sequence used 2.6 litres in total, including cloth rinses, and met every zone standard. Top-to-bottom habit used 4.1 litres and generous basin changing by appearance used 5.5 litres, while an attempt to use a single basin throughout failed the standard for 3 zones.

papers.t: The Ribbon Is an Advertisement: Tube Life and Fluoride Dose at Pea-Sized Dispensing
papers.r: A 100 g tube lasted 22.7 days at the ribbon dose and 100 days at the adult pea dose, a 4.4 fold difference. Annual cost per adult was USD 56.28 against USD 12.78, and for a household of two adults and two children the combined saving was USD 38.4 per year.

papers.t: When Does a Towel Stop Drying and Start Seeding? A Reuse Interval from Drying and Growth Curves
papers.r: In the ventilated case the towel fell below the growth threshold in 5 hours and could serve 6 daily uses before crossing the ceiling, corresponding to a 6 day interval. In the still humid bathroom it needed 13 hours to leave the growth zone and crossed the ceiling after 3 uses, a 3 day interval at daily use. Twice-daily use shortened the humid interval to 2 days while barely changing the ventilated one.

papers.t: How Long Is Long Enough? A Contact-Time Rule for Soap Handwashing Derived from a Removal Model
papers.r: With soap, 90 percent removal required 27 seconds, 99 percent required 136 seconds and 99.9 percent required 251 seconds. With water alone the same targets required 54, 271 and 502 seconds respectively. The modelled load remaining after 20 seconds of soap washing was 13.52 percent of the starting load, and after 40 seconds 6.88 percent, so the second twenty seconds removed less than a fifth as much as the first.

homework.q: Take the paper “The Longest-Lived Bar: Soap Bar Dimensions That Maximise Washes per Gram at Fixed Mass”. Its stated result is: At 100 g the best grippable block found, 5.6 x 5.0 x 3.4 cm, lasted 916 washes, while the thinnest admissible slab lasted 417 washes and a typical oval approximated as a 22 mm thick tablet lasted 584 washes. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

professor.name: Professor Fitri Wijaya
professor.personality: A deliberate and kind teacher of Designs & Engineering who writes the units on the board before opinions, every time. Students leave her room able to explain the idea to a stranger, which she counts as the only real grade.
professor.greeting: Come in. Designs & Engineering is a craft here, and crafts are learned by hand.

classes.title: Household Money, Savings and Bookkeeping (Wave 8)

papers.t: Which Categories Belong in Cash? A Selection Rule for Envelope Categories Based on Overspend and Transaction Counts
papers.r: Pricing stated card-overspend factors against cash's hassle and forgone cashback, cash envelopes pay for online impulse purchases (net USD 563.33 a year), dining (USD 711.75) and entertainment (USD 277.20), but lose money on transport extras (USD -32.67); the selected set is worth USD 2093.68 a year.

papers.t: Cashback Against Interest: The Payoff Fraction Below Which a Rewards Card Costs More Than It Returns
papers.r: Simulating USD 1,400 a month on a 1.5% cashback card at 24.9% APR, the break-even payoff fraction is 59%: at 90% payoff the household carries a steady USD 159.15 balance and loses money net, and one month's spending carried for three months costs USD 88.97 of interest, erasing 4.2 months of cashback.

papers.t: The Coin Jar Examined: What a Year of Hoarded Change Costs Against Even a Modest Deposit Rate
papers.r: A USD 1.85-a-day change stream kept in a jar at home holds USD 5376.49 after ten years against USD 8291.54 if swept monthly into a 4.0% account — a gap of USD 2915.05, or 43.1% of contributions, with the three-year gap at USD 364.34 confirmed by stochastic simulation (median USD 500.92).

papers.t: How Many Months Is Enough? Emergency Fund Size Against the Duration of Income Interruptions
papers.r: Against a stated interruption process (4% monthly onset, 30% income continuation, essential spending USD 2600), a three-month emergency fund is exhausted in 21.8% of interruptions; 7 months brings exhaustion under 5% and 7 months under 1%, with a 99.2% chance of at least one interruption per decade.

papers.t: Setting the Cash Envelope: A Quantile Rule for Weekly Discretionary Caps That Bounds Overspend Without Starving Ordinary Weeks
papers.r: Setting a weekly discretionary envelope at the 90th percentile of desired spending (USD 250.99 for a distribution with mean USD 180 and standard deviation USD 55) limits breaches to about one week in ten, with a mean excess of USD 32.31 at the nearest tabulated cap and monthly exhaustion of a USD 150 buffer in 1.2% of months, whereas a cap at the mean is exceeded in 50.4% of weeks.

papers.t: Subscription Creep Priced: How Much a Statement Audit Recovers, and How Often It Must Run to Be Worth Its Time
papers.r: Simulating an eleven-subscription household with a 3.5% monthly forgetting rate at USD 13.40 a forgotten subscription, never auditing costs USD 10069.21 a year in payments for unused services; a statement audit every six months gives the best total — USD 299.24 residual waste plus USD 24.00 of time, USD 323.24 in all.

papers.t: Sizing the Irregular-Bills Fund: A Percentile Rule for Monthly Set-Asides Against Lumpy Annual Costs
papers.r: Simulating nine irregular bills a year (mean annual total USD 3228.30), the usual mean-divided-by-twelve set-aside (USD 269.03) still leaves 80.8% of years with a shortfall month; setting aside the 90th percentile instead (USD 378.96) cuts that to 55.0%, and a one-time USD 500 float at the mean-based amount cuts it to 52.4%.

papers.t: A Set-Aside Percentage for Irregular Income: Keeping the Quarterly Tax Bill From Becoming a Debt
papers.r: Simulating irregular freelance income (median USD 4,100 a month) with a mean effective tax rate of 18.8%, setting aside 20% of each receipt still leaves an unpayable tax quarter in 61.1% of years; a 28% set-aside cuts that to 12.4% with mean shortfall depth USD 447.48.

papers.t: How Often Should a Household Reconcile Its Books? Error Accumulation and the Optimal Interval Between Checks
papers.r: Simulating a ledger with 1.14 recording errors a month and harm accruing the longer an error survives, total annual cost (harm plus checking time at USD 7.50 a session) is minimised by monthly reconciliation at USD 101.47, against USD 52.17 quarterly and USD 68.00 for checking once a year.

papers.t: Paying the Minimum, Priced: Clearing Time and Total Interest on a Card Balance Paid at the Minimum Versus a Fixed Sum
papers.r: A USD 3200 balance at 24.9% APR paid at the minimum (interest plus 1% of balance) takes 192 months and USD 5507.32 of interest to clear; fixing the payment at the first month's minimum of USD 98.40 clears it in 55 months, and a fixed USD 150 a month in 29 months at USD 1070.04 interest.

papers.t: Living One Month Ahead: The Overdraft Protection Purchased by Holding Last Month's Income as This Month's Budget
papers.r: For a household earning USD 3,900 and spending USD 3,780 a month with early-month bill clustering, no buffer means 0.33 overdraft events and USD 10.12 of fees a year; living one month ahead cuts that to 0.00 events and USD 0.00, and the buffer takes 12 months to build at 8% of income.

papers.t: Splitting the Paycheck on Arrival: Transfer Fractions That Keep the Bills Account Solvent Between Paydays
papers.r: For a household paid USD 2150 fortnightly with USD 1890 monthly bills, a single account fails a payment in 5.5% of years despite sound totals; splitting at least the exact required 40.6% of each paycheck to a bills account — 50% in the tested grid — cuts failure years to 100.0%, while 44% still fails in 100.0% of years.

papers.t: How Many Days Early Is Early Enough? Payment Lead Time, Processing Delay, and the Expected Cost of Late Fees
papers.r: Simulating processing delays (electronic mean 1.2 days, paper cheque mean 4.5 days), a cheque posted on its due date arrives late 98.8% of the time and costs an expected USD 2445.84 a year in fees at six bills a month; 10 days of lead (against 4 electronically) brings lateness under 1%.

papers.t: What Round-Up Saving Actually Accumulates: A Bound on Spare-Change Programmes Under Stated Card Spending
papers.r: Under stated spending (68 purchases a month, median purchase USD 24), round-up saving yields a median USD 33.86 a month at the one-dollar setting and USD 169.27 at five dollars — reaching USD 1,000 only after 30 or 6 months respectively, an implied saving rate of 1.40% of card spending.

papers.t: Funding the December Spike: The Latest Start Month and Monthly Amount That Cover Seasonal Costs Without Borrowing
papers.r: Simulating December (median USD 1150) and late-summer (median USD 420) cost clusters, saving USD 200 a month from November still fails in 100.0% of years and USD 150 from September in 100.0%; the cheapest schedule covering both clusters in 95% of years starts in month 2 at USD 290 a month.

papers.t: The Arithmetic of the Small Daily Leak: What a Five-Dollar Habit Costs at Ten, Twenty and Thirty Years
papers.r: A five-dollar daily leak is 3.5% of a USD 52,000 income and compounds at 5.0% to USD 23632.02 in ten years and USD 126659.36 in thirty (USD 125108.37 for ten dollars a day over twenty years), reaching USD 10,000 in 4.9 years invested against 5.5 years uninvested.

papers.t: Budget Billing for Utilities: What the Levelled Payment Buys, and What It Costs, Against Smoothing the Bills Yourself
papers.r: Simulating seasonal utility bills (mean USD 118.02, standard deviation USD 47.96), a household smoothing pot levels outlay completely and holds its own float (mean USD -32.18, negative in 58.5% of months), while utility budget billing levels outlay nearly as well (SD USD 4.37) but holds the float itself and, at a USD 2 monthly fee, costs USD 600 over twenty-five years.

Its stated result is: Pricing stated card-overspend factors against cash's hassle and forgone cashback, cash envelopes pay for online impulse purchases (net USD 563.33 a year), dining (USD 711.75) and entertainment (USD 277.20), but lose money on transport extras (USD -32.67); the selected set is worth USD 2093.68 a year (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.

classes.title: Locks, Fences, Gates and Security (Wave 8)

papers.t: Euro Cylinder Protrusion: Testing the Three-Millimetre Rule Against a Wrench Torque Model
papers.r: Euro-profile cylinders that stand proud of the door furniture can be gripped and snapped, and fitting guidance commonly allows at most 3 mm of protrusion. This study tests that rule against a stated torque model in which a wrench attack develops T = 18 + 2.6 p newton-metres at protrusion p millimetres, a standard cylinder bridge fails at 28 Nm, and a reinforced cylinder with a sacrificial cut fails at 55 Nm.

papers.t: Deadbolt Throw Length: How Much Engagement Depth a Longer Bolt Actually Buys Against Frame Splitting
papers.r: A deadbolt is sold by its throw, the distance the bolt travels into the frame, yet what a household needs is resistance to the frame splitting around the strike. This study models that resistance from stated assumptions: a steel bolt of 11 mm by 20 mm section has a shear capacity near 61,600 N and never governs, while the timber frame around the strike pocket is modelled as failing at F = 700 + 330 e^0.8 newtons, whe

papers.t: The Door Chain Claim Examined: Why a Chain Assembly Cannot Hold What Its Packaging Suggests
papers.r: Door chains are sometimes sold with language suggesting they withstand hundreds of kilograms of force. This study examines a claim of 750 kg, about 7,350 N, by computing the strength of each element of a typical chain assembly from stated assumptions: the chain itself fails in tension at 4,200 N, its keep plate bends at 1,800 N, and the anchor plate's four small screws, embedded 16 mm into the edge grain of a timber

papers.t: Boundary Fence Height: Climb Delay, Cost per Metre, and the Height at Which Extra Panels Stop Paying
papers.r: A boundary fence delays rather than stops, and the useful question is how much delay each additional increment of height buys for its cost. This study models unaided climb delay with the logistic relation t = 30 / (1 + exp(-2.6 (h - 1.75))) seconds for height h in metres, and fence cost as USD 34 + 52 (h - 1.2)^1.25 per metre run, both stated relations.

papers.t: Fence Post Spacing Under Wind Load: The Widest Bay a Timber Post Can Carry Before Bending Governs
papers.r: A solid garden fence is a sail, and its posts are the masts. This study computes post bending stress under a stated gust pressure of 0.55 kN per square metre on a 1.8 m solid fence, with each interior post carrying one bay and acting as a 125 mm square timber section of stated allowable bending stress 8 MPa.

papers.t: Timber Gate Sag: Diagonal Brace Angle and the Widest Gate That Still Latches After Five Summers
papers.r: A timber garden gate that sags drops at its latch edge until the latch misses its keep, at which point the gate stops performing any security function at all. This study models sag from stated assumptions: an unbraced ledged gate drops 4.5 W^3 millimetres at width W metres after five seasons, a correctly fitted diagonal brace removes a fraction of that drop peaking at a brace angle of 45 degrees, and a latch tolerate

papers.t: How Many Different Keys a Five-Pin Lock Really Has: Counting Usable Bitting Combinations Under an Adjacent-Cut Rule
papers.r: A five-pin cylinder with six depth steps per pin is often described as offering 7,776 different keys, the value of six to the fifth power. That figure counts combinations a manufacturer cannot actually cut, because a working key must satisfy the maximum adjacent cut rule: neighbouring depths that differ too steeply produce a ramp the key cannot slide past the pins.

papers.t: Worn Keypad Digits: How Visible Wear on a Code Lock Collapses Its Search Space
papers.r: A keypad lock's code is only as secret as its buttons are unworn. When daily pressing polishes or fades a subset of digits, an observer learns which digits the code contains, and the search space collapses. This study counts the collapse exactly, by enumerating all 10,000 four-digit codes and retaining those built only from the worn digits.

papers.t: Letterbox Reach: The Minimum Distance Between a Mail Slot and the Inside Latch That Defeats a Hooked Tool
papers.r: A mail slot through a front door is also a hole through which a hooked wire can be worked toward the inside latch, and on many doors the latch sits within easy reach of the slot. This study models the geometry from stated assumptions: a 700 mm hooked tool, after losses at the flap, the door thickness and its own bends, commands an effective radius of 520 mm from the slot centre, while an internal cover box behind the

papers.t: Motion-Activated Lighting: The Mounting Height That Covers a Driveway Without Leaving a Dark Path Beneath the Sensor
papers.r: A motion-activated light protects only the ground its sensor actually sees, and mounting height moves two boundaries at once: the far edge of detection, set by the sensor's 12 m slant range, and the dead zone beneath the fitting, which grows with height.

papers.t: Padlock Shackle Diameter: The Thickness at Which Hand Bolt Cutters Run Out of Jaw Force
papers.r: A padlock is usually attacked through its shackle with bolt cutters, and whether the attack succeeds is a contest between the force the jaws can develop and the force the shackle's cross-section demands.

papers.t: Pool Gate Latch Height: The Placement at Which a Latch Leaves a Young Child's Reach Without Leaving an Adult's
papers.r: A gate between a garden and a swimming pool must be operable by every adult and by almost no young child, and the dimension that decides the matter is latch height. This study models a child's chance of reaching and operating a latch as a logistic function of height, with a midpoint of 1.38 m for five-year-olds and 1.43 m for six-year-olds, both stated values, and asks where the chance falls below one percent.

papers.t: Sliding Door Security Bars: The Dowel Diameter at Which a Timber Bar Stops Buckling Under a Forcing Load
papers.r: A length of timber dropped into the track of a sliding patio door is among the cheapest security devices sold, and among the least specified: dowels are bought by eye, in diameters that vary by a factor of two.

papers.t: The Hidden Spare Key: How Much of a Burglar's Search the Common Hiding Places Already Cover
papers.r: A spare key hidden outside the house is a second front door whose lock is the obscurity of its hiding place, and obscurity can be priced. This study uses a stated distribution of hiding places among households that hide a key, from 22 percent under a mat down to single-figure novelties, and models an intruder who searches places in order of popularity at 40 seconds per place.

papers.t: Strike Plate Screws: The Length at Which a Door Strike Stops Being the Weakest Part of the Lock
papers.r: Many deadbolts are defeated not at the bolt but at the strike plate, whose short screws bite only into the thin frame facing rather than the structural timber behind it. This study computes strike resistance from stated assumptions: a 4 mm screw embedded in softwood resists pull-out at 35.2 N per millimetre of embedment, four screws share load with a factor of 0.7, and the frame itself splits at 5,400 N, capping the

papers.t: Thorn Hedge Planting Spacing: Closing the Gaps in a Living Barrier Before Its Second Winter
papers.r: A thorn hedge is a fence that grows, and its weak years are its first ones, when the whips stand in a row of separate bushes with walk-through gaps between them. This study models shrub spread as r(t) = 0.18 + 0.22 t metres from stated values, and computes when neighbouring canopies meet at each planting spacing: at 0.9 m spacing the hedge closes in 1.23 years, at 1.5 m spacing it takes 2.59 years, a full extra growi

papers.t: Window Sash Lock Spacing: How Many Locks a Wide Window Needs Before Prying Flexes the Rail Open
papers.r: A wide sliding or casement window fitted with a single central lock can be opened by prying at a corner, flexing the meeting rail until the latch clears its keeper, without breaking anything. This study models the rail as a beam from stated values: a 700 N pry, an aluminium rail of elastic modulus 69 GPa and second moment of area 7.5e-9 m^4, and a 6 mm flex at which the latch disengages.

classes.title: Postal Services, Addresses and Deliveries (Wave 8)

papers.t: How Often Must an Address List Be Re-Canvassed? Household Churn and the Cost of Stale Addresses
papers.r: An address list begins rotting the day it is finished: households move, buildings appear and vanish, names change. This paper prices that decay against the cost of repairing it. With a stated household churn of 3 percent per month, the stale fraction of a list reaches 30.6 percent after a year untouched.

papers.t: A Post Counter Inside a Village Shop: The Daily Transaction Count That Covers an Agency's Costs
papers.r: Where a staffed post office cannot pay, a counter inside an existing shop — an agency — is the standard alternative, but agencies are opened on enthusiasm and closed on arithmetic. This paper states the arithmetic. The agency's fixed monthly costs to the operator are USD 99.0 (retainer USD 45, equipment and training USD 22, cash float USD 14, audit visits USD 18), and each transaction earns a stated net USD 0.31.

papers.t: Bicycle or Motorbike for the Rural Round? The Daily Distance at Which the Faster Machine Starts Paying
papers.r: Whether a rural postman should ride a bicycle or a motorbike is usually argued from purchase price, but the honest comparison is annual: the motorbike carries a fixed annual penalty of USD 370.0 in depreciation, maintenance and insurance, and repays it only through the rider's time, valued here at USD 1.50 per hour, saved by travelling at 28 rather than 12 km/h.

papers.t: Spacing Communal Letter Boxes Along a Road: The Interval That Balances Walking Against Collection Cost
papers.r: Where door-to-door delivery is unaffordable, households collect mail from communal box clusters along the road, and someone must choose how far apart the clusters stand. This paper balances the two costs that spacing controls: each cluster carries a stated annual cost of USD 180 (bank, shelter and collection stop), while households walk an average of a quarter of the spacing and value that walking at USD 6 per househ

papers.t: Collect the Roadside Box on a Schedule or When It Is Full? A Fill-Trigger Rule and Its Overflow Risk
papers.r: Posting boxes are emptied on timetables written for the average box, though boxes fill at wildly different rates. This paper compares a fixed collection schedule with a fill trigger — empty the box when it holds a stated number of items, reported by sensor or by the deliverer's count.

papers.t: How Short Can a Location Code Be? Cell Size, Search Distance, and the Code Length a Settlement Actually Needs
papers.r: Many settlements have no street names, so a delivery address must be built from a grid code spoken, written on an envelope, or sent by phone. This paper computes how long such a code needs to be. A square settlement 4 km on a side is divided by a 20-symbol grid alphabet; each additional pair of characters divides the cell side by 20.

papers.t: When to Reorder Mailbags and Forms: An Order Quantity and Reorder Point a Small Branch Can Actually Run
papers.r: A branch office does not run out of forms because it uses them; it runs out because nobody computed when to reorder. This paper applies the standard inventory results with stated local numbers. For printed forms used at 42.0 a day with a 12.0-day supplier lead time, the economic order quantity is 1256 units (12.2 orders a year, 29.9 days of cover each), and the reorder point is 565 units — 504 to cover the lead time

papers.t: One Clerk or Two at the Counter? The Arrival Rate at Which a Second Server Pays for Itself in Waiting Time
papers.r: A small post office counter is staffed by habit until the queue becomes a local scandal. This paper computes the staffing threshold from queueing theory: customers arrive at random, service averages four minutes, and the service standard is a mean queue wait of at most ten minutes.

papers.t: Relay Posts for Foot Couriers: How Long a Stage Can Be When the Courier Must Also Walk Home
papers.r: Where no vehicle goes, mail still moves by relay: couriers walk stages between posts, handing the bag onward like a baton. This paper sizes the stage from the courier's day. A courier walks loaded at a stated 3.6 km/h and returns unladen at 4.4 km/h; if the same courier must walk out and back within a seven-hour working day, the longest stage is 13.8 km.

papers.t: Daily or Alternate-Day Delivery? The Letter Volume at Which Running the Round Every Day Stops Paying
papers.r: Halving delivery frequency is the first economy every struggling postal operator considers, and it is usually debated as ideology — service versus savings. This paper prices it. A round costs a stated USD 64 each day it runs; a letter-day of delay is priced at USD 0.05.

papers.t: Drone or Porter on a Hill Path? A Distance Crossover for Light, Urgent Postal Loads
papers.r: For light urgent loads — medicines, documents, blood samples, a single critical parcel — hill settlements are served either by a porter on a path or, increasingly, by a small drone. This paper compares the two on stated costs: a porter paid USD 1.20 per hour walking at 3 km/h loaded and 4 km/h returning, against a drone cruising at 40 km/h whose capital, battery and maintenance costs are spread over eight trips a day

papers.t: Mail by Boat: The Dispatch Interval That Balances Waiting Letters Against the Cost of the Trip
papers.r: For a settlement reached by boat, every dispatch decision trades a trip's cost against a pile of waiting letters. This paper prices both sides: a mail trip costs a stated USD 38, and a letter held one day carries a stated delay cost of USD 0.04.

papers.t: Sizing a Village Parcel Locker Bank: How Many Compartments Keep Turned-Away Parcels Under Two Percent
papers.r: A parcel locker bank fails quietly: it does not queue, it turns parcels away when every compartment is occupied. This paper sizes the bank as an Erlang loss system. Parcels arrive at 15 per day and stay a mean of 2.0 days awaiting collection, an offered load of 30.0 compartment-days per day.

papers.t: How Long Should an Uncollected Parcel Wait? A Holding-Period Rule from the Decay of Collection
papers.r: Every parcel office holds a shelf of the uncollected, and every office has a rule — a week, a fortnight, a month — for when a parcel goes back to its sender. The rule is rarely derived. This paper derives it from the shape of collection itself: recipients collect with a probability that decays over days (modelled as a Weibull curve with a stated scale of 4.2 days), a stated 6.0 percent never collect at all, a shelf d

papers.t: How Many Digits Does a Local Postal Code Need? Capacity, Growth Headroom, and a Check Character That Catches Copying Errors
papers.r: A local postal code introduced for one settlement must do three jobs: name every household, leave room to grow, and betray its own copying errors. This paper sizes the code for a settlement of 8500 households with a stated growth factor of 1.8 over the planning horizon and a quarter of the code space held in reserve: 20400 codes are required, so 5 digits — capacity 100000, a headroom of 4.9 times — plus one check cha

papers.t: How Many Stops Fit in a Delivery Round? A Time Bound for a Single Rural Postman
papers.r: A delivery round is planned by drawing a boundary on a map, but what actually limits it is time. This paper bounds the number of stops a round can contain: from a 360-minute working round, fixed overhead takes 75 minutes, each stop takes 1.6 minutes of service, and travel between stops in a 6.0 km2 area follows the Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley square-root estimate at bicycle speed.

papers.t: Sizing a Hand-Sorting Frame: When One Pass Stops Reaching, and What a Second Pass Costs in Errors
papers.r: Hand sorting looks like a furniture problem — how big a frame of pigeonholes to build — and is actually a decision about passes, reach and errors. A sorter can work comfortably with at most a stated 48 compartments within reach.

papers.t: Albedo Modification to Amplify the Yarkovsky Effect on a 50-Metre Asteroid Over Twenty Years
papers.r: This paper computes the deflection obtained by changing the surface albedo of a 50 m asteroid of mass 111,264,740 kg so as to amplify its natural thermal recoil acceleration from 6.72e-13 to 3.02e-12 m per second squared, an enhancement factor of 4.5, using 1,200 kg of coating applied over 62 percent of the surface.

papers.t: An Anchored Chemical Propulsion Tug: A Short, High-Thrust Push on a 75-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes an anchored chemical tug that pushes a 75 m asteroid of mass 618,501,054 kg using propellant carried from Earth. At a specific impulse of 322 s the rocket equation requires 5,320.0 kg of propellant, which is 0.00086 percent of the body's mass, to deliver the required 27.2 mm per second for a 6,000 km displacement with five years of warning. At 1,450 N the burn lasts 0.134 days.

papers.t: An Anchored Electric Propulsion Tug: Five Years of Low Thrust on a 210-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes an anchored electric tug delivering 2.2 N at a specific impulse of 3,400 s to a 210 m asteroid of mass 11,152,811,000 kg, supplied with 45 kW of electrical power. The acceleration of 1.97e-10 m per second squared, sustained for 5.5 years, delivers 34.2 mm per second against a requirement of 22.6 mm per second for a 10,000 km displacement with ten years of warning, a margin ratio of 1.51, a compute

papers.t: An Anchored Electromagnetic Mass Driver Throwing Regolith from a 260-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes an anchored mass driver that excavates regolith from a 260 m asteroid of mass 18,405,544,160 kg and accelerates it away at 420 m per second. At a mass flow of 0.011 kg per second the driver produces 4.62 N and an acceleration of 2.51e-10 m per second squared, drawing 1,347.5 W.

papers.t: An Attached Solar Sail Using Radiation Pressure to Deflect a 60-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes a solar sail of 9,000 m2, a square 94.9 m on a side at an areal density of 7.5 g per square metre, attached to a 60 m asteroid of mass 282,743,339 kg. Solar radiation pressure of 9.08e-06 N per square metre gives a force of 0.0817 N and an acceleration of 2.89e-10 m per second squared.

papers.t: A Centrifugal Regolith Sling on a 290-Metre Asteroid: Rotational Ejection as a Deflection Engine
papers.r: This paper computes a surface installation that excavates regolith from a 290 m asteroid of mass 26,178,603,603 kg and releases it tangentially from a rotor of radius 46 m turning at 1.15 radians per second, giving a tip and ejection speed of 52.9 m per second. At a mass flow of 0.09 kg per second the sling produces 4.76 N and an acceleration of 1.82e-10 m per second squared, drawing 157.4 W.

papers.t: An Electrostatic Tractor: Coulomb Attraction Between a Charged Spacecraft and a 130-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes an electrostatic tractor in which a spacecraft held at 60,000 V and a 130 m asteroid of mass 2,300,693,020 kg charged to 45,000 V of opposite sign attract one another across a centre separation of 80 m.

papers.t: A Heavy Gravity Tractor: Eight Years of Gravitational Towing for a 180-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes the performance of a gravity tractor of 40,000 kg hovering 40 m above the surface of a 180 m asteroid of mass 6,412,618,925 kg, so that its centre is 130.0 m from the body's centre. Mutual gravitation supplies a towing force of 1.01 N and an acceleration of 1.58e-10 m per second squared.

papers.t: An Ion-Beam Shepherd for a 140-Metre Asteroid: Beam Momentum Transfer Without Contact
papers.r: This paper computes an ion-beam shepherd that directs a 1.1 N ion plume at a 140 m asteroid of mass 3,735,563,105 kg from a hovering spacecraft. Beam divergence and imperfect interception reduce the transferred force to 0.792 N, an acceleration of 2.12e-10 m per second squared.

papers.t: A Kinetic Impactor Fleet Sized by Momentum Enhancement: Computed Deflection of a 320-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper sizes a fleet of kinetic impactors against a 320 m asteroid of density 1,900 kg per cubic metre and mass 32,598,840,890 kg, discovered nine years before a predicted encounter. Each impactor of 1,200 kg strikes at 14,500 m per second and, with a momentum enhancement factor of 3.2 from excavated ejecta, delivers 9.25 mm per second of velocity change at an impact energy of 683.3 GJ.

papers.t: A Laser Ablation Shepherd: Surface Vaporisation Thrust on a 110-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes a laser ablation shepherd that delivers 12,000 W of optical power onto a 110 m asteroid of mass 1,672,583,929 kg. With an ablation energy of 8,000,000 J per kilogram and an ejecta speed of 1,100 m per second, the vaporised mass flow of 0.000825 kg per second produces 0.908 N of recoil thrust and an acceleration of 5.43e-10 m per second squared.

papers.t: A Magnetic Tractor for an Iron-Rich Asteroid: Field-Gradient Coupling to a 95-Metre Metallic Body
papers.r: This paper computes a magnetic tractor for an iron-rich 95 m asteroid of density 5,200 kg per cubic metre, iron fraction 68 percent and mass 2,334,386,601 kg. A superconducting coil on a spacecraft 85 m away produces a field of 0.018 T at the body, and the field gradient exerts 0.42 N, an acceleration of 1.8e-10 m per second squared, drawing 64 kW.

papers.t: A Microwave Thermal Shepherd: Volumetric Heating and Outgassing Thrust on an 85-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes a microwave shepherd that radiates 6,000 W toward an 85 m asteroid of mass 610,954,686 kg, of which a fraction 0.48 is absorbed within a penetration depth of 0.35 m. Heating drives off 0.000384 kg per second of volatile material, producing 0.315 N of recoil and an acceleration of 5.15e-10 m per second squared.

papers.t: A Plasma-Beam Shepherd: Neutralised Particle-Beam Momentum Transfer to a 170-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes a plasma-beam shepherd that directs 260,000 W of beam power at 48,000 m per second toward a 170 m asteroid of mass 6,173,857,883 kg. papers.t: A Plume-Impingement Shepherd: Rocket Exhaust Pressure on the Surface of a 90-Metre Asteroid
papers.r: This paper computes a shepherd that hovers 60 m above a 90 m asteroid of mass 725,236,664 kg and directs the exhaust of a 200 N engine at the surface. A plume transfer fraction of 0.31 gives an effective force of 62 N on the body and an acceleration of 8.55e-08 m per second squared.

papers.t: A Solar Concentrator for Asteroid Deflection: Passive Collection and Surface Sublimation on a 90-Metre Body
papers.r: This paper computes a deflection system that collects sunlight with a 12 m2 mirror of diameter 3.91 m and focuses 10,126 W onto the surface of a 90 m asteroid of mass 839,747,716 kg. The resulting mass flow of 0.000563 kg per second yields 0.534 N of sublimation recoil and an acceleration of 6.36e-10 m per second squared.

papers.r: This paper computes a deflection system that deposits 52,000 kg of volatile material on the sun-facing surface of a 100 m asteroid of mass 837,758,041 kg and lets sunlight sublime it, the escaping gas leaving at 610 m per second with an alignment efficiency of 0.58.

classes.title: Space-Based Solar Power and Wireless Power Beaming Systems Derived from the Physics

papers.t: Compact Geostationary Microwave Power for an Island Direct-Current Microgrid
papers.r: Operating principle: A right-sized geostationary photovoltaic station transmits at 5.8 gigahertz to a single rectenna that feeds an island direct-current microgrid directly, matching the rectenna's native direct-current output to distribution without an inversion stage for local loads.

papers.t: Direct Solar-Pumped Laser Station Beaming to a Ground Receiver
papers.r: Operating principle: Sunlight collected by a large primary mirror pumps a laser medium directly, with no photovoltaic or electrical stage in space; the resulting beam near 1.06 micrometres is received on the ground by wavelength-matched photovoltaic converters.

papers.t: Geostationary Laser Power Beaming to a Dedicated Photovoltaic Receiver Farm
papers.r: Operating principle: A geostationary photovoltaic array drives solid-state lasers near 1.07 micrometres, and the narrow optical beam is received by photovoltaic cells tuned to that single wavelength rather than by a radio-frequency rectenna.

papers.t: Geostationary Microwave Phased-Array Solar Power for Continuous Baseload Delivery
papers.r: Operating principle: A geostationary photovoltaic array converts sunlight to direct current, feeds a 2.45 gigahertz phased-array transmitter, and beams microwaves to a large ground rectenna that converts the radio-frequency power back to direct current for the grid.

papers.t: Highly Elliptical Orbit Microwave Solar Power for High-Latitude Winter Supply
papers.r: Operating principle: Stations in highly elliptical Molniya-type orbits, dwelling for hours over the northern hemisphere near apogee, transmit at 2.45 gigahertz to a subarctic rectenna that receives little useful sunlight of its own in winter.

papers.t: Inflatable Concentrator Photovoltaic Station with Microwave Downlink
papers.r: Operating principle: Inflatable reflective troughs concentrate sunlight by a factor of about one hundred onto narrow strips of high-efficiency cells, shrinking the expensive semiconductor area by two orders of magnitude while a 5.8 gigahertz transmitter beams the power to a medium rectenna.

papers.t: Low-Earth-Orbit Microwave Power Demonstrator Smoothed by Ground Storage
papers.r: Operating principle: A low-Earth-orbit photovoltaic demonstrator transmits at 5.8 gigahertz during short passes over a test rectenna, and ground battery storage smooths the pulsed delivery into a steady small output for a research facility.

papers.t: Lunar Orbiter Microwave Power for Surface Installations Through the Lunar Night
papers.r: Operating principle: A photovoltaic station in lunar polar orbit transmits at 5.8 gigahertz to a rectenna at a polar surface installation, delivering power through the long lunar night from orbiters that pass regularly into sunlight.

papers.t: Lunar Polar Illumination Relay from Sunlit Rim to Shadowed Crater Floor
papers.r: Operating principle: Photovoltaic arrays on a sunlit crater rim, where sunlight is available for most of the lunar cycle, transmit power by microwave across a few kilometres of airless terrain to a rectenna on the permanently shadowed crater floor where water ice is mined.

papers.t: Mars Orbiter Laser Power Delivery to a Surface Habitat
papers.r: Operating principle: A photovoltaic orbiter at Mars delivers power by laser near 1.07 micrometres to wavelength-matched converters at a surface habitat, working with the weaker Martian sunlight and a thin, dusty atmosphere.

papers.t: Medium-Earth-Orbit Microwave Solar Power Constellation with Receiver Handover
papers.r: Operating principle: A constellation of medium-Earth-orbit photovoltaic stations, each transmitting at 5.8 gigahertz, hands a ground rectenna from one station to the next so that a mid-latitude receiver is served through most of the day without a geostationary path length.

papers.t: Millimetre-Wave 35 Gigahertz Solar Power Beaming with Compact Apertures
papers.r: Operating principle: A geostationary photovoltaic station transmits at 35 gigahertz, where the short wavelength lets a space aperture of a few hundred metres and a compact city-edge rectenna replace the kilometre-class apertures of lower-frequency systems, at the cost of serious rain attenuation.

papers.t: Orbital Laser Power Support for Long-Endurance Electric Aircraft
papers.r: Operating principle: A low-orbit photovoltaic constellation delivers laser power near 1.55 micrometres to converter panels on a long-endurance electric aircraft, supplementing its batteries during the night portion of multi-day flights.

papers.t: Orbital Reflector Illumination of Ground Photovoltaic Farms at Dawn and Dusk
papers.r: Operating principle: Large thin orbital reflectors redirect sunlight directly onto existing ground photovoltaic farms near dawn and dusk, with no electrical conversion in space at all: the space segment is a mirror, and conversion happens in panels that already exist on the ground.

papers.t: Retrodirective Pilot-Signal Phased Array for Self-Steering Solar Power Delivery
papers.r: Operating principle: The ground rectenna radiates a low-power pilot tone, and each element of the space phased array conjugates the phase it receives, so the power beam forms and steers itself toward the pilot source without any open-loop pointing model of the array geometry.

papers.t: Solar Thermal Dynamic Brayton Station with Microwave Transmission
papers.r: Operating principle: Concentrating mirrors heat a closed Brayton-cycle working fluid that drives an alternator, replacing photovoltaic conversion in space entirely; the electricity so generated feeds a conventional 2.45 gigahertz microwave transmitter and ground rectenna.

papers.t: Space-to-Space Laser Power Transfer for Satellite Servicing and Life Extension
papers.r: Operating principle: A photovoltaic power tanker in geostationary orbit delivers electricity to client satellites by laser near 1.07 micrometres, received by converter cells on the client, with no atmosphere anywhere in the path and ranges of tens to hundreds of kilometres.

homework.q: Take the paper “Compact Geostationary Microwave Power for an Island Direct-Current Microgrid”. Its stated result is: Operating principle: A right-sized geostationary photovoltaic station transmits at 5.8 gigahertz to a single rectenna that feeds an island direct-current microgrid directly, matching the rectenna's native direct-current output to distribution without an inversion stage for local loads. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

homework.q: Take the paper “Attenuator Chain Wave Power: Segment Flexure, Joint Power and Length-to-Wavelength Budgets”. papers.t: Breastshot Waterwheel Driving a Generator at a Heritage Mill: Cell Filling, Rim Speed and Torque Budgets for a 14 Kilowatt Plant
papers.r: Headline result: The wheel of 4.2 metres turns at a rim speed of 1.98 metres per second, its shaft carries 17.5 kilonewton metres, and the generator delivers 14.4 kilowatts net, about 0.076 gigawatt-hours a year.

papers.t: Bulb Tubular Turbine for a Wide Low-Head River: Submergence, Annulus Velocity and Axial Runner Budgets for a 1.3 Megawatt Plant
papers.r: Headline result: The annulus passes 30 cubic metres per second at 4.01 metres per second, the runner sits 4.0 metres below tailwater, and the plant delivers 1,303 kilowatts net, about 6.8 gigawatt-hours a year.

papers.t: Crossflow Banki Turbine for a Village Micro-Hydro Scheme: Two-Stage Admission, Runner Length and Torque Budgets for a 74 Kilowatt Plant
papers.r: Headline result: The runner is 0.62 metres long and 0.30 metres in diameter; roughly 70% of the energy is taken on the first pass through the blades, and the plant delivers 73 kilowatts net, about 0.37 gigawatt-hours a year.

papers.t: Deriaz Diagonal-Flow Turbine for a Variable-Head Storage Plant: Blade Geometry, Runner and Reversibility Budgets for a 2.8 Megawatt Plant
papers.r: Headline result: The diagonal runner of 1.11 metres delivers 2,660 kilowatts net at a net head of 52.2 metres, with a cavitation margin of 2.1 between the plant number 0.151 and the critical value 0.073.

papers.t: Francis Plant on a Long Pressurised Conduit with a Surge Tank: Water Hammer, Thoma Area and Oscillation Budgets for a 7.8 Megawatt Plant
papers.r: Headline result: Instant closure would raise pressure by 236 metres, some 2.1 times the net head; the tank of 55 square metres, against a stability minimum of 14, caps the rise at 9.0 metres with an oscillation period of 389 seconds.

papers.t: Hydrokinetic River Turbine on a Moored Pontoon: Stream Power, Rotor Loading and Mooring Budgets for a 16 Kilowatt Plant

papers.t: Kaplan Axial-Flow Turbine for a Low-Head River Reach: Blade Regulation, Flow Coefficient and Submergence Budgets for a 2.7 Megawatt Plant

papers.r: Headline result: With seawater at 1025 kilograms per cubic metre, the clifftop basin stores 135 megawatt-hours, discharge runs about 4.8 hours at 27,901 kilowatts, and the round trip returns 76%. papers.r: Headline result: A speed range of plus or minus 10% lifts round-trip efficiency to 80%, the reservoirs store 180 megawatt-hours for about 7.7 hours at 23,347 kilowatts, and the unit can move its output materially within 8 seconds.

classes.title: Earth Ocean Observation Systems Derived from the Physics

papers.t: Benthic Crawler Rover for Seafloor Transects: Traction, Power and Imaging Budgets for a 4,000 Metre Bottom Rover
papers.r: Headline result: At a survey pace of 0.28 metres per second the battery carries 19.7 hours of combined drive and imaging load, enough for its 9 kilometre transect plan with reserve; ground pressure under the tracks is a computed 4.7 kilopascals on the adopted sediment bearing figure, and the acoustic link to the ship holds 46 decibels of margin for supervision and data summaries.

papers.t: Benthic Lander with Pop-Up Data Capsules: Ballast, Ascent and Endurance Budgets for a 6,000 Metre Seafloor Observatory
papers.r: Headline result: The capsule ascent from 6000 metres takes about 2.0 hours at the adopted rise rate; the acoustic command link holds a margin of 43 decibels at slant range, and the battery carries the 0.85 watt average seafloor load for the full 540 day deployment with the capsule releases charged separately.

papers.t: Buoyancy Glider with Sawtooth Flight for Ocean Sections: Glide, Hull and Endurance Budgets for a 1,000 Metre Vehicle
papers.r: Headline result: Each dive to 950 metres advances the vehicle about 4.9 kilometres at the adopted glide ratio; the 5.2 kilowatt-hour battery supports roughly 255 dives, near 1262 kilometres of section, before the hotel and buoyancy loads exhaust it.

papers.t: Buoyancy-Engine Profiling Float for the Open Ocean: Displacement, Hull and Drift Budgets for a 2,000 Metre Profiling Cycle
papers.r: Headline result: At its 2000 metre rating the hull sees 20.2 megapascals and needs 9.9 millimetres of wall; a swept volume of 0.85 litres spans the density range of a full profile, and the energy budget supports 153 ten-day cycles, about 4.2 years of profiling.

papers.t: Cabled Seafloor Observatory Node: Pressure Housing, Power and Telemetry Budgets for a 2,500 Metre Shore-Connected Station
papers.r: Headline result: Shore power removes the endurance ceiling: the node distributes 3000 watts delivered over 82 kilometres of backbone, the titanium instrument housings at 2500 metres need 17.1 millimetres of wall, and the five-year drift account, not energy, becomes the limit that schedules servicing.

papers.t: Deep Hovering Vehicle for Midwater Sampling: Station-Keeping Thrust, Hull and Energy Budgets for a 4,000 Metre Hovering Platform
papers.r: Headline result: Holding station against a 0.50 metre per second current costs a computed 0.25 kilowatts of thruster power; with the 320 watt sampling hotel load the battery gives 34.7 hours on station, and the titanium sphere-and-cylinder hull at 4000 metres carries 31.9 millimetres of wall.

papers.t: Drifting Hydrophone Recorder for Passive Acoustic Monitoring: Wire, Buoyancy and Recording Budgets for a Deep Listening Station
papers.r: Headline result: At the adopted 25% recording duty cycle and 96 kilohertz sampling, the recorder fills its 4 terabyte store in about 643 days while the daily detection summaries ride the satellite link; the hydrophone housing at 1000 metres needs 4.2 millimetres of titanium wall, and wire drag at the adopted drift current sets the hang angle at 9 degrees.

papers.t: Expendable Bathythermograph-Style Sensor Line for Rapid Surveys: Fall-Rate, Depth-Accuracy and Cost Budgets for Underway Temperature Sections
papers.r: Headline result: The fall-rate equation places the probe at 760 metres after 118 seconds, with a depth uncertainty of about 17 metres from the adopted fall-rate tolerance; a 48 probe line at 12 knots spaces profiles 17 kilometres apart and consumes its whole instrument budget in a single transit, by design.

papers.t: Ice-Tethered Profiler for Polar Oceans: Winch, Buoy and Cold-Energy Budgets for a Sea-Ice Drifting Observatory
papers.r: Headline result: Each winch cycle to 760 metres costs a computed 7.4 watt-hours at the adopted winch load; after the cold derating of the battery the system supports about 1230 profiles, near 1.7 years at two profiles a day, with the wire and ice-hole budget, not the sensors, setting the practical limit.

papers.t: Lagrangian Drifter Cluster with Satellite Relay: Drogue Drag, Buoyancy and Telemetry Budgets for a 24-Unit Surface Dispersion Study
papers.r: Headline result: The drag-area ratio of drogue to buoy is 40 to one, which holds wind slip to a computed 3.7 percent of wind speed at the adopted 8 metre per second wind; the 0.80 kilowatt-hour battery supports 545 days of hourly satellite positions, and the cluster of 24 units resolves pair dispersion from metres to tens of kilometres.

papers.t: Moored Water-Column Profiler with Inductive Telemetry: Winch Energy, Mooring and Data Budgets for a 500 Metre Mooring
papers.r: Headline result: A profile cycle over 480 metres costs 8.3 watt-hours; at four profiles a day the battery supports 452 days, and each profile's data crosses the mooring inductively in about 5.3 minutes at the adopted coupling rate, well inside the interval before the next profile.

papers.t: Propeller-Driven Autonomous Underwater Vehicle for Seafloor Survey: Thrust, Hull and Energy Budgets for a 3,000 Metre Vehicle
papers.r: Headline result: At a cruise speed of 1.6 metres per second the drag budget draws 0.62 kilowatts of propulsion; with hotel load the 18 kilowatt-hour battery gives 20.2 hours and about 117 kilometres of survey line per dive, while the titanium hull at 3000 metres needs 28.6 millimetres of wall.

papers.t: Sail-Assisted Surface Data Vehicle: Sail Thrust, Solar and Hull Budgets for Long-Endurance Ocean Monitoring
papers.r: Headline result: At the adopted 7 metre per second wind the wing sail delivers about 299 newtons against 51 newtons of hull and keel drag at cruise; solar harvest of 620 watts peak covers the 28 watt payload and steering load, and the battery bridges 154 hours of calm overcast running on thruster alone at reduced speed.

papers.t: Solar Surface Catamaran with Profiling Winch: Solar, Winch and Station Budgets for Autonomous Water-Column Sampling
papers.r: Headline result: A winch cycle to 180 metres costs 12.2 watt-hours; six profiles a day plus hotel and telemetry loads total a computed 649 watt-hours against a solar harvest of about 4536 watt-hours at the adopted capacity factor, leaving the battery as a weather buffer of 8.9 days rather than a primary source.

papers.t: Subsurface Drifting Float with Acoustic Positioning: Sound-Source Ranging, Buoyancy and Endurance Budgets for Deep Lagrangian Trajectories
papers.r: Headline result: At a source range of 800 kilometres the low-frequency acoustic budget still holds a margin of 10 decibels, because absorption at 0.26 kilohertz is a small fraction of a decibel per kilometre; clock drift over the 730 day mission maps to a ranging error of about 4.7 kilometres, which the trajectory reconstruction must absorb.

papers.t: Towed Undulating Vehicle Behind a Research Vessel: Cable, Flight and Sampling Budgets for High-Resolution Ocean Sections
papers.r: Headline result: At a tow speed of 4 metres per second the vehicle completes a full undulation over 470 metres of depth every 17.4 minutes, spacing its profiles about 4.2 kilometres apart along track; cable tension at cruise is computed at 4.8 kilonewtons, inside the stated cable working load with margin.

papers.t: Wave-Propelled Surface Vehicle with Subsea Tow Body: Wave Thrust, Tether and Endurance Budgets for Persistent Coastal Observation
papers.r: Headline result: At the adopted sea state the foil system delivers about 95 newtons against 91 newtons of combined float and tow-body drag, a slim positive margin that sets the vehicle's weather limits; solar input covers the 11 watt payload with the battery bridging 115 hours of calm darkness.
