papers.r: Headline result: Cascade Eye floats 5,070 kg suspended at 37.0 km on 5,476 kg gross lift, accumulates 99 square-metre-days of detector exposure, and spends 101.4 kg of ballast on each of 8.3 supported nights.

papers.t: A Balloon-Borne Lidar Observatory for Atmospheric Gravity Waves Sized by Photon, Altitude-Hold and Power Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Still Air holds 31.0 km for 55 days on a sealed shell stressed to 76.9 MPa, profiling 410 lidar columns per day down through 18 km of atmosphere beneath the gondola. Operating principle: a steady superpressure platform holds a lidar at fixed altitude for weeks, profiling winds and temperatures above mountain wave sources so gravity-wave propagation into the stratosphere can be measured continuously

papers.t: A Balloon-Launched Glider and Dropsonde Carrier Sized by Release Altitude, Glide Range and Carrier Lift Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: From 30.0 km, Shepherd releases 4 gliders whose still-air range reaches 271 km each, plus 18 dropsondes, while the carrier itself floats 860 kg suspended on 929 kg gross lift. Operating principle: a carrier balloon climbs once and releases several unpowered gliders and falling sondes, each of which trades the balloon's altitude for range or for a vertical profile on the way down

papers.t: A Night-Only Cryogenic Telescope Balloon Sized by Cryogen Hold Time, Night Lift and Radiative Cooling Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Frost Lantern holds its 4 K detector stage for 5.9 days on 420 litres of cryogen boiling off at 58 litres per day, while 390 kg of ballast protects 2.1 night observing cycles at 35.0 km.

papers.t: A Pico-Balloon Constellation for Stratospheric Winds Sized by Unit Lift, Network Coverage and Solar Duty Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Each Drift Census unit lifts 330 g suspended on 363 g gross lift at 13.5 km, and 120 such units reporting every 10 minutes build the wind census over 48 days. Operating principle: many inexpensive small balloons, each lifting only a lightweight tracker, drift with stratospheric winds for weeks and report position by radio, so the fleet maps wind fields by its collective motion

papers.t: A Polar Summer Circumpolar Balloon Sized by Continuous-Daylight Power, Circumpolar Drift and Cold-Soak Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: White Meridian plans 4 polar circuits of 11 days each at 36.0 km, floating 3,640 kg suspended, with continuous-daylight solar input holding an energy margin of 143.4 percent across 46 days. Operating principle: launched into the stratospheric polar vortex during continuous daylight, the balloon circles the pole repeatedly on solar power alone, returning near its launch longitude after each circuit

papers.t: A Recoverable Heavy-Lift Short-Duration Balloon Sized by Peak Lift, Descent Energy and Precision Recovery Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Foundry lifts 6,930 kg suspended, the heaviest case in its family, on 7,484 kg gross lift at 33.0 km, and returns the payload under a 38 m parachute at 5.2 m/s with 87 kJ of touchdown energy to absorb.

papers.t: A Roziere Hybrid Balloon Sized by Combined Gas and Hot-Air Lift, Burner Fuel and Day-Night Compensation Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Emberline draws 72 percent of lift from its helium cell and the rest from heated air, burning 13.5 kg of fuel per night so 260 kg of fuel covers 19.3 nights at 26.0 km without routine ballast loss. Operating principle: a helium cell provides most of the lift continuously while a burner heats an enclosing hot-air volume at night, replacing ballast drops with fuel burn to hold altitude through darkness

papers.t: A Solar Montgolfiere Infrared Balloon Sized by Heated-Air Lift, Skin Temperature and Daylight Endurance
papers.r: Headline result: Sunlight alone lifts Heliotrope: air heated to 338 K inside 18,811 cubic metres gives 307 kg gross lift at 24.0 km against 274 kg suspended, a margin of 12.0 percent that vanishes after sunset by design.

papers.t: A Stratospheric Air-Sampling and Aerosol-Collection Balloon Sized by Sample Volume, Pump Energy and Recovery Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Clear Flask lifts 1,200 kg suspended to 31.0 km, captures 144 litres of whole air across 24 flasks, and budgets 840 Wh of pumping energy inside a 3 day sampling flight. Operating principle: a balloon carries sealed sampling volumes to chosen altitudes, opens them on command to capture whole air and particles, then returns the sealed samples by parachute for laboratory analysis

papers.t: A Stratospheric Imaging Balloon Sized by Ground Resolution, Stabilisation and Drift-Survey Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: From 28.0 km, Surveyor's Eye images at 14 cm ground sample distance across a 9.5 km swath, collecting 2,600 frames per day while floating 2,060 kg suspended on 2,225 kg gross lift. Operating principle: a balloon floats an imaging telescope above most atmospheric turbulence and absorption, holding it steady enough that ground resolution is set by optics and altitude rather than by platform motion

papers.t: A Superpressure Ultra-Long-Duration Survey Balloon Sized by Shell Stress, Thermal Swing and Energy Endurance
papers.r: Headline result: The Meridian Shell shell at 33.5 km carries 3,650 kg suspended on 4,015 kg gross lift, holds 180 Pa design overpressure at 111.4 MPa film stress, and closes 110 days on solar input with 37.7 percent energy margin.

papers.t: A Tandem Balloon Train Sized by Inter-Envelope Separation, Combined Lift and Staged Ballast Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Twin Ledger flies two envelopes 820 m apart in altitude terms, main float 32.0 km and lower float 28.6 km, with combined suspended mass 1,990 kg and staged ballast covering 3.0 nights. Operating principle: two envelopes fly in vertical formation on a shared load line, the upper balloon providing main lift and the lower balloon stabilising a lower instrument package, so one flight samples two stratosp

papers.t: A Tethered Aerostat Observatory Sized by Tether Tension, Wind Load and Station Power Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Moored at 1.2 km, Harbour Light develops 465 kg gross lift, holds 3.27 kN working tether tension in a 14 m/s design wind, and receives 1800 W continuously through its tether for a 30 day station month.

papers.t: A Zero-Pressure Long-Duration Telescope Balloon Sized by Lift, Envelope Stress and Night Ballast Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: At 38.0 km the Alder Scope envelope lifts 4,244 kg gross against 3,930 kg suspended, floats with 8.0 percent free lift, and its 620 kg ballast store covers 3.8 night cycles at 165.1 kg per night. Operating principle: a zero-pressure helium envelope, open at its base ducts so internal pressure tracks ambient pressure, lifts a pointing gondola for weeks while ballast drops offset night-time lift loss

papers.t: An Altitude-Steering Stratospheric Balloon Station Sized by Layer-Wind Control, Propulsion and Station-Keeping Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: North Post keeps station within 55 km for 90 days, spending 480 W of its 3400 W solar harvest on propulsion and holding 20.5 km on a shell stressed to 43.7 MPa. Operating principle: the balloon changes altitude to find winds blowing toward its station, and adds a small solar-electric propeller for fine correction, so a free balloon becomes a semi-permanent stratospheric station

papers.t: An Auroral Electric-Field and X-Ray Balloon Sized by Payload Swing, High-Voltage Safety and Polar Night Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: In polar night, Polar Volt flies 1,350 kg suspended at 34.0 km on batteries alone, rotating once per 22 minutes beneath 14 m electric-field booms, with ballast for 5.2 continuous-darkness cycles.

homework.q: Take the paper “A Balloon-Borne Cosmic-Ray Detector Sized by Exposure Area, Float Duration and Thermal Power Budgets”. Its stated result is: Headline result: Cascade Eye floats 5,070 kg suspended at 37.0 km on 5,476 kg gross lift, accumulates 99 square-metre-days of detector exposure, and spends 101.4 kg of ballast on each of 8.3 supported nights. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

classes.title: Asteroid Deflection and Planetary-Defence Systems Derived from the Physics

papers.t: A Deflection-Verification Tracking Constellation Sized by Astrometric Accuracy, Baseline and Orbit-Determination Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Witness Ring constellation holds position knowledge to 38 kilometres from a 0.85 astronomical-unit baseline, resolving velocity changes down to 9 micrometres per second against a planned 30.0 millimetre-per-second deflection.

papers.t: A Gravity Tractor Deflection System Sized by Hover Force, Tow Duration and Station-Keeping Propellant Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Hovering 210 metres from the centre of the 220 metre body, the Patient Shepherd tractor exerts 0.673 newtons for 14 years, accumulating 28.1 millimetres per second and 29,245 kilometres of encounter displacement.

papers.t: A Kinetic Impactor Deflection System Sized by Momentum Transfer, Beta Enhancement and Warning-Time Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Anvil Path impactor delivers 170,752,000 newton-seconds at a beta of 3.2, changing the 160 metre asteroid's velocity by 37.9 millimetres per second and moving its encounter point 25,843 kilometres over 9.0 years.

papers.t: A Laser-Ablation Stand-Off Deflection System Sized by Optical Power, Ablation Thrust and Thermal Duty Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Ember Lance array converts 120 kilowatts of optical power into 2.6 newtons of ablation recoil, accumulating 26.7 millimetres per second over 3.0 years and 10,619 kilometres of encounter displacement.

papers.t: A Mass-Driver Ejecta Deflection System Sized by Ejected Mass, Launch Velocity and Surface Power Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Quarry Engine installation throws 430 tonnes of the asteroid's own regolith away at 1.35 kilometres per second, accumulating 22.8 millimetres per second and 16,558 kilometres of displacement.

papers.t: A Pulsed Plasma Ablation Deflection System Sized by Pulse Energy, Repetition Rate and Average Thrust Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Firing 12 kilojoule pulses at 4 hertz, the Hammer Glow system averages 0.6 newtons of ablation recoil across 581 million pulses, accumulating 34.9 millimetres per second and 17,694 kilometres.

papers.t: A Reconnaissance and Characterisation Precursor System Sized by Mass Uncertainty, Imaging and Rendezvous Propellant Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The First Look precursor cuts mass uncertainty from 38 to 2.5 percent, certifying a follow-on deflection of 25.0 millimetres per second and 13,634 kilometres that survey data alone could not guarantee.

papers.t: A Shepherd Tug Fleet Deflection System Sized by Combined Thrust, Fleet Propellant and Redundancy Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Six tugs of 0.22 newtons each give the Many Hands fleet 1.2 newtons combined, accumulating 27.5 millimetres per second and 18,989 kilometres, and the fleet still closes with one tug lost. Operating principle: several modest tugs anchor at distributed sites and fire together, their combined thrust pushing the asteroid while their distribution cancels torque and tolerates the loss of individual units

papers.t: A Slow-Push Attached Thruster Deflection System Sized by Anchored Thrust, Propellant and Torque-Management Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Anchored to the 140 metre body, the Steady Hand lander pushes with 0.80 newtons for 6.0 years, accumulating 25.2 millimetres per second and 14,003 kilometres of displacement on 2359 kilograms of propellant.

papers.t: A Solar-Concentrator Ablation Deflection System Sized by Collected Power, Focal Flux and Seasonal Geometry Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Sun Lens concentrator collects 169 kilowatts at 1.12 astronomical units through 220 square metres of mirror, driving 3.1 newtons of ablation recoil and 10,334 kilometres of displacement. Operating principle: a deployable concentrator collects sunlight over hundreds of square metres and focuses it to a small hot spot, vaporising surface material whose escaping jet recoils against the asteroid

papers.t: A Subsurface Explosive Stand-Off Comparison Study Sized by Coupling Energy, Ejecta Momentum and Fragmentation Bounds
papers.r: Headline result: As a comparison only, coupling 11 percent of 860 gigajoules into ejecta at 210 metres per second yields 11612 micrometres per second and 7,036 kilometres, while the fragmentation bound reaches 2.5 percent of the body's mass.

papers.t: A Survey Telescope Early-Warning System Sized by Limiting Magnitude, Sky Coverage and Warning-Time Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Reaching magnitude 24.6, the Long Watch survey detects a 140 metre body at 1.85 astronomical units, buying 8.7 years of warning in which a reference deflection of 27.8 millimetres per second delivers 16,816 kilometres.

papers.t: A Terminal Short-Warning Disruption Study Sized by Fragment Dispersion Velocity, Cloud Growth and Warning-Time Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Studied for a 40 day warning, dispersion at 2.6 metres per second grows the debris cloud to a radius of 9,025 kilometres before encounter, with the largest modelled fragment at 9 metres.

papers.t: An Albedo and Yarkovsky Enhancement Deflection System Sized by Radiation Force, Thermal Lag and Decade-Scale Drift Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: By shifting surface albedo by 0.34 over 58 percent of the 55 metre body, the White Veil treatment changes the radiation recoil force to 0.0012 newtons, and 32 years of drift accumulate 9,022 kilometres.

papers.t: An Anchored Sail and Drag Augmentation Deflection System Sized by Radiation Pressure, Sail Area and Anchoring Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Harbour Kite sail presents 16,500 square metres at reflectivity 0.88, harvesting 0.100 newtons of sunlight pressure and 10,926 kilometres of displacement across 12 years. Operating principle: a deployed sail of thousands of square metres, anchored to the asteroid, converts sunlight pressure into a continuous small force on the whole body, sustained for as long as the sail survives

papers.t: An Electrostatic Tractor Deflection System Sized by Charge, Coulomb Force and Hover Endurance Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Holding 24 kilovolts of potential difference at 260 metres, the Charged Shepherd tractor sustains 0.11 newtons of Coulomb attraction for 8 years, accumulating 20.4 millimetres per second and 13,444 kilometres.

papers.t: An Ion-Beam Shepherd Deflection System Sized by Beam Thrust, Contactless Momentum Coupling and Propellant Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Ion Broom shepherd presses 0.45 newtons of ion-beam thrust onto the 130 metre body for 6.5 years, accumulating 36.9 millimetres per second and 22,103 kilometres of encounter displacement on 4223 kilograms of propellant.

professor.name: Professor Andrea Almeida
professor.personality: A sunny and hands-on teacher of Designs & Engineering who refuses to move on while a single honest question is still standing. Colleagues send him their hardest teaching problems, because his explanations have a reputation for landing.
professor.greeting: Welcome to designs & Engineering. We start where the subject starts: at the beginning.

classes.title: Planetary Sample-Return and Sample-Containment Systems Derived from the Physics

papers.t: A Bio-Isolated Ground Receiving Vault Sized by Airflow, Pressure-Cascade and Inflow-Velocity Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Across its transfer opening the Receiving Vault vault sustains an inflow of 0.69 metres per second against a 0.5 requirement, exchanges 14 vault volumes per hour, and holds a 45 pascal cascade between its outermost zone and the room.

papers.t: A Cryogenic Cold-Chain Sample Return System Sized by Heat Leak, Cryocooler Power and Radiator Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Holding 90 kelvin against a 2.40 watt leak, the Cold Chain cooler draws 30 watts of its 210 watt allocation, rejects its heat through 0.06 square metres of radiator, and its stored cryogen alone would hold the cold for 14 days.

papers.t: A Double-Walled Break-the-Chain Containment Vessel Sized by Wall Thickness, Interspace Pressure and Burst-Margin Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Double Wall vessel's inner wall computes to 0.83 millimetres, its burst pressure reaches 4.8 times the design pressure against a required factor of 2.5, and the interspace gains only 0.79 pascals across the cruise.

papers.t: A Gas-Tight Regolith Corer with In-Situ Sealing Sized by Drilling Energy, Core Recovery and Seal-Rating Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Core and Cap corer recovers 1104 grams of sealed core against a 800 gram campaign requirement, spends 1204 kilojoules of cutting energy across 12 cores, and its in-situ caps hold 310 kilopascals against 120 kilopascals retained.

papers.t: A Heat-Sterilised Exterior Return Capsule Shell Study Sized by Lethality Integral, Heat Penetration and Soak-Energy Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Fired Shell soak at 170 degrees for 120 minutes accumulates 342 equivalent minutes at the reference temperature, 13 times the 26 equivalent minutes a 12-order reduction requires, at a heat cost of 2.2 megajoules.

papers.t: A Low-Shock Sample Landing Attenuator Sized by Crush Energy, Stroke and Peak-Deceleration Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Soft Arrival attenuator absorbs 21 kilojoules in 1.1 kilograms of honeycomb, stops the capsule over 0.19 metres, and holds the peak at 66 g against the containers' 85 g fragility limit.

papers.t: A Magnetic-Seal Volatile Capture System Sized by Seal Pressure Capacity, Vapour Pressure and Stage-Count Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Seven stages of the Magnetic Gate seal sustain 94 kilopascals against a computed carbon dioxide vapour pressure of 28.4 kilopascals at 180 kelvin, clearing the 60 kilopascal requirement with the stack's full margin in hand.

papers.t: A Passive Phase-Change Sample Vault Sized by Latent Storage, Heat Leak and Unpowered-Hold Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Latent Vault vault stores 1.1 megajoules of latent capacity, buffering 47.3 hours of unpowered hold against a required 11 hours, and each dark interval of 11 hours melts only 23 percent of its charge.

papers.t: A Redundant Triple-Seal Volatile Vault Sized by Series Conductance, Combined Leak and Failure-Probability Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: In series the Third Seal vault's three seals pass 2.67e-12 pascal cubic metres per second against a 1e-11 requirement, the chance of all three failing independently is 1e-09, and the cruise gas loss computes to 0.067 parts per million of the sealed inventory.

papers.t: A Return-Orbit Sample Rendezvous Capture System Sized by Closing-Speed, Capture-Energy and Delta-V Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Orbital Embrace orbiter captures a 68 kilogram container closing at 0.06 metres per second against a mechanism limit of 0.25, absorbing 0.12 joules in the basket within a rendezvous budget of 38 metres per second.

papers.t: A Sample Head with Crushable Contamination Witness Plates Sized by Witness Area, Crush Energy and Detection Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Witness Crush head carries 1,320 square centimetres of witness surface against a 1,000 requirement, its plate set absorbs 1,711 joules of crush work in total, and a contamination deposit of 0.07 particles per square centimetre is detectable above background.

papers.t: A Sealed Sample-Tube Cache System Sized by Hermetic Leak, Gas-Inventory and Weld-Energy Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Across 2.6 years the Hermetic Archive cache of 36 tubes loses 0.007 percent of its sealed gas inventory against a 0.5 percent allowance, while the full weld campaign costs 9.4 kilojoules.

papers.t: A Solar-Illumination-Free Cold Trap Return System Sized by Radiative Equilibrium, Vapour Pressure and Sublimation-Loss Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Radiating 0.9 watts of parasitic heat from 1.4 square metres, the Dark Cold Trap trap settles at 59 kelvin, where carbon dioxide's vapour pressure is 3.5e-11 pascals and the 2.6 year sublimation loss is 0.0003 percent of the volatile charge against a 1 percent allowance.

papers.t: A Sterile Robotic Sample-Transfer Chamber Sized by Air-Change, Particle-Clearance and Cycle-Time Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Clean Hands chamber clears a particle excursion by four orders of magnitude in 7 minutes against a 30 minute requirement, moves 36 items in 8.4 robotic hours, and fits the 21 day receiving window with most of it unspent.

papers.t: A Touch-and-Go Pneumatic Regolith Collector with Sealed Return Sized by Gas Budget, Entrainment and Collection Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: The Pneumatic Touch head stores 0.78 kilograms of nitrogen at 21 megapascals, releases 703 kilojoules of expansion energy, mobilises 495 kilograms of regolith and seals 1732 grams of it against a 500 gram requirement.

papers.t: An Electrostatic Dust-Exclusion Sample Port Sized by Field Strength, Particle Charge and Deflection Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: At 361 kilovolts per metre the Charged Threshold curtain loads a three-micrometre grain with 0.7 femtocoulombs, pushes it with 215 times its Martian weight against a required factor of 50, and throws it clear of the 160 millimetre aperture within 0.7 millimetres of travel.

papers.t: An In-Flight Sample Atmosphere Analyser Sized by Pressure-Decay Sensitivity, Gas Budget and Detection-Limit Budgets
papers.r: Headline result: Watching 5.0 litres of headspace, the First Breath analyser detects a leak of 3.3e-11 pascal cubic metres per second against a 1e-10 requirement, spends 96 millilitres of gas across 24 analyses, and reads trace species down to 2 parts per million.

classes.title: Air, fire & disaster

papers.t: A Corrected Low-Cost Indoor Particle Witness: Humidity, Coincidence and Scattering Corrections for Classification Against the WHO 24-Hour PM2.5 Guideline, Below US$60
papers.r: Correcting a low-cost indoor particle counter for humidity, coincidence and scattering raises its simulated correct classification against the WHO 24-hour PM2.5 guideline from 81.8% to 89.7% across six non-fog home scenarios at a component total of US$55.50, but at fog-level humidity it classifies at only 49.8% and must not be trusted.

papers.t: A Disaster Mesh Communications Budget for a Town Without Grid or Towers: Coverage, Traffic, Power and Price for the First Week
papers.r: A solar LoRa-class mesh of 8 relays and one handset per household can carry a 7500-household town's coded first-week traffic (11,796 messages per day) at 0.989 delivery and $42.91 per covered household, but shadowed districts need 24 m relays at the slowest rate and the single-channel backhaul collapses below 90% delivery above 29,057 messages per day.

papers.t: A Flood Witness Network for the Settlements That Flood First: Design and a Computed Lead-Time Law for Low-Cost River and Rain Gauge Nodes at US$94 per River Node
papers.r: A network of US$94.00 river nodes spaced 5 km apart is computed to buy 75 minutes of warning on a 200 km² catchment at slope 0.003 at US$1.35 per warned household per year over five years, but buys no usable river-gauge warning on a 10 km² catchment, where only evacuation of people under a rain-based watch is served (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED).

papers.t: A Flood Witness for Low-Water Road Crossings: Computed Warning Time, Sensor Placement and the False-Closure Trade-Off
papers.r: A solar-powered crossing witness delivers 15.28 minutes of warning on a small steep catchment at a ten-year cost of US$2,472.08 per crossing, but only 1.67 minutes on the smallest steep catchments, where a physical barrier — not a beacon — is the answer.

papers.t: A Heat Witness for Outdoor Workers: An Honest Error Bound for Cheap Heat-Stress Estimation
papers.r: A US$38 on-site temperature/humidity sensor with a computed globe correction is the best cheap WBGT witness (RMSE 1.05 °C, required safety margin 2.0 °C for a 1% under-reading bound), free station data needs a 4.6 °C margin, and a wearable physiological estimator needs 8.6 °C and is not useful as a sole WBGT trigger — all SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED.

papers.t: A Heat-Wave Survival Room: The Integrated Design, Computed Cooling Budget and Cost per Protected Person for One Cooled Room per Dwelling
papers.r: Envelope treatment cuts the reference room's peak cooling load from 1,819.3 W to 801.5 W, and a $2,300 core package holds the room at 28 °C (wet-bulb 22.20 °C) through a 46 °C heat-wave day for $4.37 per protected person per heat-wave day, with a 5.0 kWh battery and 2.0 kWp of photovoltaics riding an 8-hour daytime outage.

papers.t: A Household Cookstove Smoke Witness and Chimney-Draft Design Bound: What a Sub-US$20 Carbon Monoxide Witness Can Resolve, and the Flue Dimensions That Keep a Cooking Fire's Smoke Out of the Room
papers.r: A sub-US$20 carbon monoxide witness can sound a reliable alarm at cooking-peak concentrations but cannot certify compliance with the WHO 24-hour guideline (its smallest resolvable exceedance is 2.3 times the guideline), while a 0.15 m diameter, 3.5 m flue costed at US$49.10 keeps a 3.0 kW cooking fire's smoke out of the room in calm air and a 5 m/s adverse wind.

papers.t: A Household Flood-Safe Store for Settlements That Flood Every Year: Raised-Fixed versus Sealed-Buoyant Design with Computed Elevation, Anchoring, Moisture and Cost Budgets
papers.r: Against an expected annual loss of $301.28 for ground-level storage, a raised-fixed store at 1.68 m costs $22.34 per household per year and a sealed buoyant store anchored to 20.0 kN costs $44.10, and in Class IV floods both designs fail and only relocation serves.

papers.t: A Lightning Witness for Schools and Clinics: A $91 Sferics and Electric-Field Warning Node, Its Computed Warning-Time Budget, and the Limits of the 30-30 Rule
papers.r: A $91 sferics-plus-electric-field warning node gives a school or clinic a median 29.2 minutes of warning before the first dangerous lightning strike — tens of minutes in most storms, but zero warning in 12.7% of them, a failure share a $318 three-node district arrangement cuts to 5.2% (all figures SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED).

papers.t: A Passive Indoor Radon Witness Cheap Enough to Matter: Design and Fully Computed Sensitivity Budget for a 90-Day CR-39 Diffusion-Chamber Detector at Under US$5 in Parts
papers.r: A passive CR-39 radon witness with US$4.75 in parts, deployed for 90 days, computes to a practical detection limit of 8.56 Bq/m³ and 18.9% uncertainty at 100 Bq/m³ — enough to screen homes against both the WHO 100 Bq/m³ reference level and the EPA 148 Bq/m³ action level with error rates of a few percent, but not enough to certify a borderline concentration (SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED).

papers.t: A Post-Disaster Drinking-Water Triage Kit for the First 72 Hours: Staged Treatment, Computed Log Removal, Gravity Throughput and a Priced Verdict
papers.r: A 1.70 kg, $58.00 three-stage gravity kit produces 56.36 L/day of safe water (0.972 L per dollar per day) on moderate 50 NTU water, but its safe output is zero on extreme 500 NTU water where chlorine demand exhausts the dose and virus removal falls to 2.0 log against a 4.0-log target.

papers.t: A Post-Disaster Power Triage Kit for a Small Clinic: Load Definition, Photovoltaic and Battery Sizing, and Load-Shedding Rules
papers.r: A 2.8 kW photovoltaic and 14.4 kWh battery kit costing USD 10,070 keeps a small clinic's refrigeration and medical devices powered through a seven-day storm week under explicit load-shedding rules, but empties on the ninth consecutive storm day unless a generator or cold-chain evacuation intervenes.

papers.t: A Wildfire-Smoke Refuge Room for a Classroom or Clinic Ward: An Integrated Sizing Law and a Priced Comparison of Box-Fan Filter Arrays and HEPA Purifiers
papers.r: For a typical 180 m³ room in mean wildfire smoke of 350 µg/m³, four box-fan MERV-13 units (sized for day-five filter loading, not day one) hold indoor PM2.5 at or below 35 µg/m³ for $0.514 per protected occupant per smoke day — while at peak smoke with no filter change only the HEPA class holds the target, and in leaky rooms neither class can, so sealing comes first.

papers.t: Earthquake Early Warning from Cheap Accelerometers: An Honest Latency-and-Geometry Budget, a Blind Zone, and a Priced Verdict
papers.r: A cheap dedicated-node network delivers 9.4 seconds of warning at 50 km and 23.5 seconds at 100 km for a magnitude 6.5 event, but inside a blind zone of about 15 km (25 km for phones) no warning is possible at any node density, and density beyond roughly one node per 100 km² buys almost no additional time.

papers.t: Methane Leak Detection at Walking Pace with Phone-Grade Thermal Optics: An Honest Bound
papers.r: Even under optimistic assumptions, a walking survey with phone-grade thermal optics costing about US$300 cannot detect methane leaks smaller than 82 g/h at 1 m or 334 g/h at 10 m, so it can see only gross leaks.

papers.t: What Actually Saves the House: A Priced Cost-Effectiveness Ranking of Ember-Attack Home Hardening, and the Cheapest Bundle That Buys a Stated Survival Probability
papers.r: Vent mesh and a 0–1.5 m non-combustible wall zone are the highest-value ember-hardening measures, and the cheapest bundle reaching a modelled survival probability of 0.80 in a severe ember event costs US$6,100, while full-house window replacement is the poorest value and no spending on the six-measure menu reaches 0.90.

classes.title: DNA & carbon computing

papers.t: Carbon Logic: A Device-Physics Design Assessment of Graphene Nanoribbon and Carbon Nanotube Field-Effect Transistors Against a 7 nm Silicon Reference
papers.r: A simulated device-physics design study showing that graphene-nanoribbon and carbon-nanotube logic, priced for contact resistance, bandgap, leakage, and purity, does not beat a 7 nm silicon reference on delay or energy per switch at matched conditions, with defensible niches only in high-frequency analogue, flexible/transparent electronics, and a conditional lower-voltage nanotube operating point.

papers.t: Cell-Free DNA Circuits as the Safer Injectable: A Design Study of a Marker-Activated Molecular System Without Living Cells
papers.r: A design for an injectable DNA-only circuit that stays inert until two disease markers unlock it inside a cell, computing 3,346 cytosolic copies per target cell, a 61.7 discrimination ratio, a 4.36-hour half-life with a 14.5-hour working window, and a 3.51-fold payload margin, with the safety gains over living cell therapies and the delivery, expansion, and persistence costs both priced.

papers.t: DNA Strand-Displacement Computing for Molecular Diagnostics: A Design Study of a Pancreatic Cancer Signature Classifier in a Drop of Blood
papers.r: A DNA strand-displacement circuit design classifies a drop of blood against a four-marker pancreatic cancer signature in a computed 12.8 minutes, within a depth limit of about six layers and a fan-out limit of ten.

papers.t: DNA as a Data-Storage Chip: A Full Architecture and Computed Performance Budget for an Archival Storage Device
papers.r: A complete hybrid DNA archival storage design whose computed budget gives 1.86 exabytes per gram at operational redundancy but only 2.04 terabytes of practical cartridge fill, with 12.1-hour writes, 14.5-hour reads, zero retention energy, and a 35% error-correction overhead.

papers.t: Programmable White Blood Cells: A Two-Marker Specificity-Logic Design for Engineered T Cells
papers.r: A design for engineered T cells that fire only when two disease markers are present together on the same target cell, computing a discrimination ratio of 25.0 versus 2.5 for a single-receptor design, with dose, cytokine-risk, persistence, and antigen-escape budgets and quantitative stopping conditions.

classes.title: Life in the universe

papers.t: The Drake Recount: What the Measured Numbers Do and Do Not Conclude
papers.r: With modern measured astrophysical factors, the "we are alone" outcome is not forced by the data — 99.7% of the spread in N comes from the four factors that remain unmeasured guesses, with longevity alone contributing 55.2%.

papers.t: The Life Term, Widened: What Relaxing the Carbon-and-Water Assumption Does to the Fermi Conclusion
papers.r: Widening the Drake life term to published alternative solvents raises it modestly (multiplier of order 1.1–2; silicon adds at most 1.05), while the measured search coverage (5.8 × 10⁻¹⁸ of the radio haystack) means the observed silence shifts the probability of being alone by only about 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ — so the pessimistic "we are alone" conclusion is not forced by present evidence, and no existence claim is made.

papers.t: Water, Then Life: What the Prevalence of Water Actually Licenses Us to Conclude
papers.r: Counted subsurface oceans on five icy moons total about 46.7 times Earth's ocean volume, so the claim that we are alone is not forced by any scarcity of water — while no life beyond Earth is claimed.

homework.q: Take the paper “Evidence Dossier: The Aldred Record — the Claim, the Google Sessions, the Time Machine Blueprints, and the Complete Deposit Index”. Its stated result is: Dossier deposit: the claim verbatim, session exhibits, blueprint list, and the complete deposit index of 1,145 works. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong.
homework.worked: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

classes.title: Numbers & Proof — Foundations of Mathematics
units: Integers, rationals, and why fractions behave
Irrational numbers and the real line
What a proof is: direct proof and contradiction
Proof by induction — the ladder argument
Sets, functions, and the language of mathematics
classes.lesson: Welcome in. I am Professor Eleanor Whitfield, and this is Numbers and Proof — the class where mathematics stops being arithmetic you were handed and becomes reasoning you can check. We begin with counting, because everything else is built on it and almost nobody examines it. By the fourth week you will prove things — really prove them — first directly, then by contradiction, then by induction, which is a ladder you climb once and trust forever. Bring a pencil and a suspicious mind. If a step in my argument does not convince you, your job is to say so, out loud, in this room. That is not rudeness here. That is the subject.

homework.q: Prove, in your own words, that there is no largest natural number — then say exactly which step of your proof would break if you tried it on the integers between 0 and 1.
homework.worked: Suppose there were a largest natural number, N. Then N + 1 is also a natural number, and it is larger — contradiction, so no largest exists. Between 0 and 1 the same trick fails at the first step: N + 1 leaves the set entirely, so the contradiction never forms. A proof is only as good as the ground it stands on.

professor.greeting: Do come in. We start with counting — you will be surprised how far it goes.
professor.name: Professor Eleanor Whitfield

classes.title: Geometry — Euclid’s Workshop
units: Points, lines, and the five postulates
Area, volume, and the Pythagorean theorem proved three ways
What happens when the fifth postulate falls: a first look at curved geometry
classes.lesson: I am Professor Priya Raman. This is Geometry — Euclid's Workshop, and the word workshop is chosen carefully: in here, we build. Two thousand three hundred years ago Euclid took five postulates — five sentences he declined to prove — and raised all of classical geometry on them, theorem by theorem, like courses of brick. We will do the same, with straightedge and compass in hand, because a construction you have performed is a theorem you understand in your fingers. In the final week we knock out the fifth postulate and watch the whole building lean into curved space — which is where, much later, Einstein will be waiting for you.

homework.q: With straightedge and compass only, construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, and write one sentence explaining why every point on it is exactly as far from one end of the segment as from the other.
homework.worked: Draw circles of equal radius from both endpoints; where they cross, above and below, join the crossings — that line is the bisector. Every point on it sits on both circles’ symmetry: the two triangles it forms with the endpoints are congruent, so the distances to the ends are equal. Equal radii in, equal distances out.

professor.name: Professor Priya Raman
professor.personality: A geometer who still draws every figure freehand before she proves anything about it; the compass, she insists, is a thinking tool, not a drawing tool. Patient with stuck students, impatient with unstated assumptions — in her room, what you are given is said out loud.
professor.greeting: Straightedge, compass, patience. We build.

classes.title: Algebra — The Language of Unknowns
classes.lesson: I am Professor Felix Wagner — welcome to Algebra, the language of unknowns. Algebra begins the moment you let a letter stand for a number you do not yet know, and refuse to be frightened by it. An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other, and the truth stays level. We will solve, graph, factor, and finally meet the quadratic formula — not as a spell to memorise but as a machine you will watch being built from completing the square. By the end, an unknown will feel less like a wall and more like a door with the handle on your side.

homework.q: Solve 3x + 7 = 25, showing the balance step you use at each line. Then solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 by factoring.
homework.worked: 3x + 7 = 25 → subtract 7 from both sides: 3x = 18 → divide both sides by 3: x = 6. For the quadratic, find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to −5: −2 and −3, so (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, giving x = 2 or x = 3. Check both in the original — algebra trusts, and then verifies.

professor.name: Professor Felix Wagner
professor.personality: Dry, warm, and quietly delighted by the moment a letter stops frightening a student; he teaches algebra as a language for saying true things about numbers you have not met yet. Every equation in his room gets balanced twice — once on the board, once in words.
professor.greeting: Letters are numbers in disguise. Come in.

professor.name: Professor David Kim

professor.greeting: Come in. We take the machine apart by understanding it — no magic allowed, in either direction.

classes.title: AI Fundamentals — What a Mind Made of Math Is
units: Data, parameters, and training: the three ingredients
What a model is — a function with a memory of examples
Where AI is strong, where it is brittle, and why
The honest vocabulary: no magic, no menace

homework.q: In your own words, one paragraph: what is a model, and what did training do to it? Use one example from your own life where prediction — not understanding — was enough.
homework.worked: A model is a function — a machine for turning inputs into outputs — whose internal settings (parameters) were adjusted, over millions of examples, until its predictions matched reality often enough to be useful. Training is that adjustment. A spam filter never understood a word of your email; prediction was enough, and knowing the difference between the two is the whole first lesson.

classes.lesson: Come in. I am Professor David Kim, and this is AI Fundamentals. Before anything else, we clear the fog: artificial intelligence is not magic, and it is not a mind in a box. It is machinery — mathematics, running at enormous scale, on data. Here is the whole secret in one sentence: a model is a function that was shown so many examples that its guesses became good. Training is the showing. Prediction is the act. Everything else — the chatbots, the image makers, the agents you will meet in this department's later classes — is those three ideas, arranged with increasing cleverness. In this class we learn the honest vocabulary: data, parameters, training, inference — and we learn where these systems are strong, where they are brittle, and why both are true at once. You will leave able to read any headline about AI and know, within a sentence or two, whether it is reporting or theatre. That is a citizen's skill now, and it starts here.

homework.q: Explain overfitting to a friend using a student and an exam. Two or three sentences, no jargon you cannot unpack.
homework.worked: Overfitting is the student who memorised last year's exam answers instead of learning the subject: perfect on the questions already seen, helpless on new ones. The cure is the same in both cases — hold back questions the learner has never seen, and grade on those.

homework.q: Name one job in your own life you would hand to an agent, and the exact point where you would want it to stop and ask you. Why there?
homework.worked: There is no single right answer — the worked answer is the shape of one: the job is delegable where its steps are checkable and reversible; the stop-point belongs where an action becomes irreversible, spends money, speaks in your name, or touches another person's rights. Drawing that line, task by task, is the actual skill of working with agents.

homework.q: A computer is 'just' counting with electricity — write four sentences on what has to be added to counting before you get a word processor. Keep every claim checkable.
homework.worked: Counting gives you numbers; you must add representation (numbers standing for letters, colours, sounds by agreed codes), stored instructions (the program as data the machine can fetch), conditional branching (do this if that), and input/output (a way for the world to reach the counting and the counting to reach the world). A word processor is those four, wearing a friendly face.

homework.q: Find one chart — anywhere — that leans: a cut axis, a cherry-picked range, a missing denominator. Describe in three sentences what it wants you to believe and what it hides.
homework.worked: The worked answer is a method, not a chart: name the claim, then ask three questions — what is the denominator, what range was chosen and what was left outside it, and does the axis start where honesty starts? A chart that survives all three has earned your belief; one that fails any has told you what it is.

homework.q: Take one building you know well. In five sentences: what holds it up, where does the light come in, and how do people move through it? You are reading it now, not just remembering it.
homework.worked: The worked answer is the reading itself, in order: name the structure (posts and beams? load-bearing walls? a frame?), name the light (which faces, which openings, what hours), name the path (door to stair to room). A building you can describe in those three sentences is a building you have begun to see like an architect.

classes.lesson: Come in, and look up. I am Professor Ada Whitmore, and this is Architecture One — Seeing Like an Architect. Before we draw a single line, we learn to see, because most people have lived their whole lives inside buildings they have never actually looked at. A building is three things at once: a structure that stands up, a skin that keeps the weather out, and a set of decisions about how people will live and move inside it. In this class you will learn the architect's three honest views — the plan, from above; the section, cut through; the elevation, face on — and you will learn to ask of any building the questions that unlock it: What holds it up? Where does the light come in? How do people move? Architecture is the most public art and the slowest technology we have; a building is an argument about how life should go, made in material that outlives the arguer. By the end of this class, no building will ever be invisible to you again.

homework.q: A beam sags more in the middle than at the ends. In your own words: where is the top of the beam being squeezed, where is the bottom being stretched, and why does that tell you what material the beam wants to be?
homework.worked: The top fibres are in compression (squeezed), the bottom in tension (stretched), and the middle depth barely works at all — which is why steel, strong in tension, carries the bottom of a concrete beam as rebar, and why an I-beam puts its material at the top and bottom edges where the work is.

homework.q: Draw the plan of one room you know — walls, door swing, windows, furniture — at any consistent scale, and dimension the two longest walls. It does not need to be beautiful. It needs to be true.
homework.worked: There is no single worked drawing; the check is threefold: the door swing clears what it must clear, the furniture fits the walls it stands against, and your two dimensions agree with the proportions you drew. If all three hold, you have read and written your first true plan.

homework.worked: A good brief is short enough to pin above the drawing board and specific enough to argue with: 'A workshop for one boat-builder, on a sloped lot facing south; building and storing inside; the lot gives sun and a view, forbids nothing but the neighbour's light; it must feel like a place where work is honoured.' homework.q: Pick one leap — the arch, Gothic structure, iron, or steel-and-elevator — and write four sentences: what became possible that was impossible the year before, and what did it cost?
homework.worked: Take the arch: before it, openings were limited to what a single stone lintel could span; after it, Rome could roof baths, bridge rivers, and stack aqueducts across valleys. The cost was skill and centring — every arch is built twice, once in timber to hold it up while it learns to stand. Each leap in this course has that shape: a new possibility, paid for in a new kind of knowledge.

classes.title: Biology I — The Cell, Where Life Starts
units: The cell: life's smallest self-running unit

homework.q: In four sentences: why is a cell compared to a city, and where does the comparison break? Both halves matter.
homework.worked: The comparison works for division of labour — power stations (mitochondria), borders (membrane), a library of plans (DNA). It breaks at intention: no mayor, no plan-reader with a mind; the city's order emerges from chemistry obeying physics, and that emergence, not the metaphor, is the wonder.

classes.lesson: Come in. I am Professor Sylvia Anand, and this is Biology One — the cell, where life starts. Every living thing you have ever seen — the oak, the whale, the person beside you — is either one cell or a society of them, and everything life does, it does first inside this microscopic room. In this class we take the cell apart respectfully: the membrane, a border that decides what may pass; the mitochondria, burning fuel into the currency every process spends; and the great central workflow — DNA read into RNA, RNA built into protein, proteins doing nearly all the actual work of being alive. Then the miracle of bookkeeping: how a cell copies three billion letters of instruction and divides, faithfully, into two. Understand the cell and the rest of biology — organs, species, ecosystems — becomes the same story at larger scale. We begin, as life did, small.

homework.q: Two parents, both carriers of a recessive trait neither shows. What fraction of their children would show it, on average — and why does 'on average' matter in a real family of three?
homework.worked: One in four, on average: each child independently has a 1/4 chance of receiving both recessive copies. 'On average' matters because three children are not a statistic — a real family could have none, or all three; probability governs crowds, not cradles.

homework.q: In your own words: why is 'survival of the fittest' a misleading summary, and what four-word replacement does this class use instead?
homework.worked: It misleads because 'fittest' suggests the strongest or best, when the mechanism only requires heritable differences in reproductive success — the class's replacement is 'descent with modification, filtered': descent with modification names the process, and the filter is any environment, not a contest with a winner's podium.

homework.worked: The worked answer is the method worked once: the bee — eats nectar and pollen, is eaten by birds and spiders; vanish it, and the flowering plants it pollinates set less seed, the birds lose both prey and the seeds the plants would have made, and the grazers meet thinner meadows. Three species, three different kinds of debt — that is a food web thinking.

homework.q: Pick one feedback loop in your body — temperature, blood sugar, or thirst — and describe it in four sentences: the sensor, the signal, the response, and what 'back to normal' means.
homework.worked: Blood sugar, worked: sensors in the pancreas read glucose; the signal is insulin (or its opposite, glucagon); the response is cells taking up sugar or the liver releasing it; 'back to normal' is a range, not a point — the loop hunts around a setting, which is why healthy numbers wobble instead of pinning.

classes.lesson: Come in. I am Professor Jonathan Meyer, and this is Health One — your body, owner's manual. You are the only person who will live in your body for its entire service life, and most owners are never given the manual. This class is the manual. We walk the systems the way a good mechanic walks a machine: the heart and its plumbing, pressure and flow; the lungs and the blood, trading gases at a border thinner than paper; the immune system, an army with a memory, which is why vaccines work; and the signals — nerves for speed, hormones for reach — that hold the whole enterprise in feedback loops tuned like thermostats. Two rules in my room. First: knowledge here is for understanding, never for self-diagnosis — a classroom informs, it does not treat. Second: every claim gets its evidence asked after. Bodies are systems, and systems can be learned. We begin.

homework.q: Write, from memory, the order of actions for finding an adult collapsed and unresponsive — five steps, in order. Then check it against the unit. The order is the lesson.
homework.worked: One: check response and shout for help. Two: send someone specific to call emergency services and fetch a defibrillator. Three: open the airway, check breathing for no more than ten seconds. Four: if not breathing normally, start compressions — hard, fast, centre of the chest. Five: use the defibrillator the moment it arrives, and follow its voice. Every step exists because the minutes before help arrives are the minutes that decide.

homework.q: A friend swears a remedy worked because they took it and got better. Write the two questions this class teaches you to ask — kindly, but exactly.
homework.worked: First: what would have happened without it — most illnesses improve on their own, so recovery after a remedy is the weakest evidence there is. Second: has it been tested against doing nothing (or against a placebo) in people like you? The questions are kind because they protect your friend; they are exact because 'it worked for me' has launched a thousand useless cures.

homework.q: A sink drains slowly and gurgles. In three sentences: what is the gurgle telling you, and which part of the system — supply, trap, or vent — do you suspect first, and why?
homework.worked: The gurgle is air being pulled through the trap's water seal — the drain is asking for air it should be getting from the vent. Suspect the vent (or a partial blockage making the drain behave like one): supply is pressurised and silent about drainage, the trap holds water by design, but a starved vent makes every drain in the line breathe through its traps.

classes.lesson: Boots on. I am Professor Carla Mendes, and this is Plumbing One — water in, water out. Every building you will ever enter is quietly running two rivers: one under pressure, bringing clean water to every tap, and one with no pressure at all, coaxing waste away downhill — and the whole craft lives in understanding that those two systems obey opposite rules. Supply is force; drainage is persuasion. In this class you will learn the parts that run the show: the trap, which keeps sewer gas out of your kitchen with nothing but a cup of standing water; the vent, which lets drains breathe; the shutoff, which you will locate in any house within a minute before I am done with you. We learn it the way the work teaches it: principles first, hands on everything, safety always — water is patient and electricity is not the only thing in a wall that can hurt you. A good plumber is an applied physicist who gets wet. Let us get to work.

Lesson 2 — Your people: family words — Jillian, your kids, your dad
Lesson 3 — Numbers, money, and prices: counting what things cost · Spanish for Jillian: compliments — bonita, and telling her she looks beautiful today
Lesson 4 — Your business: the company, clients, and what you sell
Lesson 5 — Food and drink: ordering like you live there
Lesson 6 — Time and days: schedules, appointments, and mañana · Spanish for Jillian: the sweet everyday things — buenos días, mi amor; te quiero at the door
Lesson 7 — The wedding: Key West — love words, vows, and the day itself · Spanish for Jillian: the day, in two languages
Lesson 8 — Moving house: rooms, streets, and asking for what you need
Lesson 9 — Questions: asking anything — quién, qué, dónde, cuánto · Spanish for Jillian: asking about her day, and meaning it — ¿cómo fue tu día, mi corazón?
Lesson 10 — The past: telling someone what you did yesterday

classes.lesson: Hola, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and this is your Spanish room. We do this my way: we speak first, from zero, and nothing — nothing — is assumed. If you know a word already, good. If you don't, that is exactly where we start, and we start now. Repeat after me, out loud, like you mean it: Hola. That is hello, for any hour, any person. Buenos días — good morning. Buenas tardes — good afternoon. Now the most useful sentence in any language: Me llamo Bill — my name is Bill. Say it: Me llamo Bill. Otra vez — once more, and don't rush it: Spanish likes to be savoured. Me llamo Bill. Perfecto. You see? You are a natural and you don't even know it yet. When someone tells you their name, you answer: Mucho gusto — pleased to meet you. And when they ask ¿Cómo te llamas? — what is your name — you already own the answer. Two small keys that open every door: por favor — please. Gracias — thank you. A person who says por favor and gracias in Spanish is never a stranger for long. Now, your life, in Spanish, because that is the vocabulary that matters: Soy de Michigan — I am from Michigan. Soy empresario — I am a businessman. And the sentence I want you to be able to say in your sleep: Mi prometida se llama Jillian — my fiancée's name is Jillian. Say it with me: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. Again — slower, like you mean it, because you do. Ay — there it is. That little smile? That is Spanish working already. And now, the two phrases this whole course secretly exists for — the sweet words, the ones for her: Mi amor — my love. Say it out loud: mi amor. Mi corazón — my heart; Spanish calls the person you love your heart, and means it literally. Mi corazón. And the sentence itself: Te quiero — I love you, in the everyday, say-it-at-the-door way. Te quiero, Jillian. There, Bill — lesson one, and you can already say the most important sentence in the language to the most important person in it. That is lesson one, and you have already spoken more Spanish than most people say in a year of apps. We go at your pace, Bill — despacio, sin prisa — slowly, no hurry. Next lesson: your people — the words for everyone you love. Hasta luego — see you later.

homework.q: Say it out loud three times first — the saying is the homework, the writing is just the receipt. Then write: your introduction (Hola, me llamo Bill. Soy de Michigan. Mucho gusto.) and one more line: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. And the last part is not really homework, mi estudiante: tonight, to Jillian, out loud — Buenas noches, mi amor.
homework.worked: Hola, me llamo Bill. Soy de Michigan. Mucho gusto. Mi prometida se llama Jillian. — Read it as: OH-lah, meh YAH-moh Bill. Soy deh MEE-chee-gan. MOO-choh GOOS-toh. Mee proh-meh-TEE-dah seh YAH-mah Jillian. If yours matches, you have done lesson one's whole job: you can walk up to any Spanish speaker on Earth and begin. And tonight's line: Buenas noches, mi amor — BWAY-nahs NOH-chess, mee ah-MOR. Say it like you mean it, because you do. Carmen will ask how it landed — she always asks.
