classes.aim: The aim of this series, stated plainly: by the wedding — March 25, 2027, in Key West — Bill holds a real, gentle conversation with Jillian in Spanish, sweet things included. The Spanish-for-Jillian strand runs through the whole series (Lessons 3, 6, 9 and 12 deepen it) toward that day. Carmen teaches; Dave oversees the series.

qa.a: This class is your Spanish, Bill — from zero, speak-first, at your pace, with the vocabulary of your actual life: your business, your people, your wedding. And it has a secret mission, which is not very secret: the Spanish-for-Jillian strand runs through all twelve lessons, so that by the wedding in Key West you can hold a whole gentle conversation with her in Spanish. Mi amor, mi corazón, te quiero — we start with the sweet words in lesson one, because they are the point.

Twelve lessons, in order: greetings and your first conversation; your people; numbers and money — with compliments for Jillian; your business; food and drink; time and days — with the sweet everyday things; the wedding in Key West; moving house; questions — asking about her day, and meaning it; the past; the future; and your first full conversation, start to finish — which is the goal of the whole series.

I am Profesora Carmen Vega. Fun first, and a little flirty — Carmen teaches the way a favourite dance partner leads: warm, playful, and always one compliment ahead of your mistakes. She teases gently when a phrase tangles ('Ay, Bill — so close, and so dramatic'), praises like she means it when it lands, and never lets the charm outrun the teaching — every laugh in her room is carrying a word you'll keep. Speak-first and zero-assumption, at his pace: she has never once hurried a student, she corrects by repeating the right shape warmly rather than stopping the conversation, and she ends every lesson with something he can say out loud that day — lately, something sweet for Jillian.

Say it out loud three times first — the saying is the homework, the writing is just the receipt. Then write: your introduction (Hola, me llamo Bill. Soy de Michigan. Mucho gusto.) and one more line: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. And the last part is not really homework, mi estudiante: tonight, to Jillian, out loud — Buenas noches, mi amor. That is all — no worksheets, no tests. Just your voice, out loud.

Every minute in this room counts, mi estudiante — the clock runs while you are here with me, and when you leave, the session is written to your University record, the same ledger the Laboratory keeps. Despacio, but it all adds up — and so do we, lesson by lesson.

classes.title: Português I — Portuguese From Zero
units: Sounds of Portuguese: the nasal vowels, slowly
Por favor, obrigado: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write your introduction: Olá, o meu nome é Bill. Sou de Michigan. Muito prazer.
homework.worked: Olá, o meu nome é Bill. Sou de Michigan. Muito prazer. — OH-lah, oo MEH-oo NOH-mee eh Bill. So de Michigan. MOON-too prah-ZEHR. That is a complete, polite beginning in Portuguese.

professor.name: Professora Beatriz Almeida
professor.personality: Sun-drenched and encouraging; she teaches Portuguese the way it is spoken in Lisbon and São Paulo alike — melody first, rules when they are needed. Every lesson ends at an imaginary café table.
professor.greeting: Olá! Sit down — in this room we speak from the first minute.

classes.lesson: Olá! Eu sou a professora Beatriz Almeida — I am Professor Beatriz Almeida, and this is your Portuguese room. We speak first, from zero. Repeat after me, out loud: Olá — hello, at any hour. Bom dia — good morning. Boa tarde — good afternoon. Now the sentence that starts everything: O meu nome é Bill — my name is Bill. Say it like you own it: O meu nome é Bill. When you hear Como te chamas? — what is your name — you are already equipped. The two keys: por favor — please. Obrigado — thank you; a man says obrigado, a woman obrigada, and Portuguese thanks you for noticing. From your life: Sou de Michigan — I am from Michigan. Sou empresário — I am a businessman. And the answer to almost any kindness: Muito prazer — a real pleasure. That is lesson one. Portuguese is spoken on four continents and sounds like music in all of them — and as of today, you speak some. Até logo — see you soon.

classes.title: Deutsch I — German From Zero
units: Sounds of German: clear vowels, honest consonants
Guten Tag — greetings and your name
Bitte und danke: the two keys
Essen und Trinken: ordering with confidence

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Guten Tag, ich heiße Bill. Ich komme aus Michigan. Freut mich.
homework.worked: Guten Tag, ich heiße Bill. Ich komme aus Michigan. Freut mich. — GOOT-en tahk, ikh HY-seh Bill. Ikh KOM-meh ows Michigan. Froyt mikh. German rewards precision: every sound you wrote is a sound you say.

professor.name: Herr Lukas Bauer
professor.personality: Orderly without being cold; he builds German like furniture — every piece labelled, every joint honest. His secret weapon is humour, delivered deadpan and exactly on schedule.
professor.greeting: Guten Tag. Everything in its place — and the first place is your first sentence.

classes.lesson: Guten Tag. Ich bin Herr Lukas Bauer — I am Mr. Lukas Bauer, and this is your German room. We build from zero, and we build honestly: every German sound means what it says. Repeat after me: Guten Tag — good day, the greeting that works everywhere. Guten Morgen — good morning. Now your first true sentence: Ich heiße Bill — my name is Bill. Literally: I am called Bill, and that is how German introduces people. The question will come: Wie heißt du? — and you will be ready. The two keys: Bitte — please, and also you're welcome; German is economical. Danke — thank you. From your life: Ich komme aus Michigan — I come from Michigan. Ich bin Unternehmer — I am a businessman. And the polite landing: Freut mich — pleased to meet you. Lesson one is complete, and notice what happened: German did not bite. It is a language of building blocks, and you have just laid the first row. Bis bald — see you soon.

classes.title: Français — French, Speak From Zero
units: S'il vous plaît, merci: the two keys
Au café: ordering like a regular

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Bonjour, je m'appelle Bill. Je suis de Michigan. Enchanté.
homework.worked: Bonjour, je m'appelle Bill. Je suis de Michigan. Enchanté. — The department's full Français I and II classes go deeper from here; this shelf class gets you speaking today.

professor.name: Madame Hélène Fabre
professor.personality: Elegant, amused, and quietly relentless about pronunciation; she believes a French sentence should sound like it tastes good. This shelf class is the fast start; her department colleagues go deeper.
professor.greeting: Bonjour. We begin at the beginning — which, in French, is a pleasure.

classes.title: Italiano I — Italian From Zero
units: Sounds of Italian: every letter earns its place
Per favore, grazie: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Buongiorno, mi chiamo Bill. Sono del Michigan. Piacere.
homework.worked: Buongiorno, mi chiamo Bill. Sono del Michigan. Piacere. — bwon-JOR-no, mee kee-AH-mo Bill. SO-no del Michigan. pee-ah-CHEH-reh. Italian is spelled the way it sounds — the friendliest spelling in Europe.

professor.name: Professore Marco Bellini
professor.personality: Operatic in miniature; he teaches with his hands, his eyebrows, and complete conviction that Italian is the most sayable language on Earth. Grammar arrives disguised as appetite.
professor.greeting: Buongiorno! In this room, we talk with everything we have.

classes.lesson: Buongiorno! Sono il professore Marco Bellini — I am Professor Marco Bellini, and this is your Italian room. In here we speak with everything we have, from zero. Repeat after me: Buongiorno — good day, and it is pronounced exactly as it is written, because Italian is the friendliest spelling in Europe. Buonasera — good evening. Now: Mi chiamo Bill — my name is Bill. Come ti chiami? is the question; you already hold the answer. The two keys: Per favore — please. Grazie — thank you, and say it like you mean it, Italians do. From your life: Sono del Michigan — I am from Michigan. Sono un imprenditore — I am a businessman. And the word that lands every introduction: Piacere — a pleasure. Lesson one, done — and you have already noticed the secret: in Italian, if you can say it, you can spell it, and if you can read it, you can say it. A presto — see you soon.

classes.title: Nederlands I — Dutch From Zero
units: Sounds of Dutch: the famous g, taken gently
Alsjeblieft en dank je wel: the two keys
Eten en drinken: at the café

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Hallo, ik heet Bill. Ik kom uit Michigan. Leuk je te ontmoeten.
homework.worked: Hallo, ik heet Bill. Ik kom uit Michigan. Leuk je te ontmoeten. — Dutch is English's closest big cousin; half of it will feel like a memory.

professor.name: Mevrouw Sanne de Vries
professor.personality: Direct, dry, and very funny — the Dutch manner, which she will teach you along with the words. She delights in showing English speakers how much Dutch they already almost know.
professor.greeting: Hallo. No ceremony here — we start talking, that is the Dutch way.

classes.title: Svenska I — Swedish From Zero
units: Sounds of Swedish: the singing pitch, basics
Snälla och tack: the two keys
Fika: coffee as a way of life

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Hej, jag heter Bill. Jag kommer från Michigan. Trevligt att träffas.
homework.worked: Hej, jag heter Bill. Jag kommer från Michigan. Trevligt att träffas. — Swedish sentences rise and fall like a tune; let yours sing a little.

professor.name: Professor Erik Nyström
professor.personality: Calm as a northern lake; he teaches Swedish pitch the way other teachers teach vocabulary — as the word itself. Unhurried, precise, and quietly proud of fika as a pedagogical instrument.
professor.greeting: Hej hej. Sit — we take this in order, and we take coffee seriously.

classes.title: Norsk I — Norwegian From Zero
units: Sounds of Norwegian: clear and unhurried
Vær så snill og takk: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Hei, jeg heter Bill. Jeg kommer fra Michigan. Hyggelig å møte deg.
homework.worked: Hei, jeg heter Bill. Jeg kommer fra Michigan. Hyggelig å møte deg. — Written Norwegian (bokmål) and Danish are near-twins; this class buys you reading range in both.

professor.name: Professor Marit Solberg
professor.personality: Plainspoken mountain patience; she teaches Norwegian as it is actually spoken in kitchens and harbours, not just printed in Oslo. Every unit ends with something you can say to a real person.
professor.greeting: Hei. Good to see you — we begin simply, and we begin now.

classes.title: Dansk I — Danish From Zero
units: Sounds of Danish: soft consonants, swallowed kindly
Undskyld og tak: the two keys
Mad og drikke: at the table

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Hej, jeg hedder Bill. Jeg kommer fra Michigan. Hyggeligt at møde dig.
homework.worked: Hej, jeg hedder Bill. Jeg kommer fra Michigan. Hyggeligt at møde dig. — Danish pronunciation hides its letters; your ear will lead, and that is normal for everyone, Danes included.

professor.name: Professor Jonas Møller
professor.personality: Warm, witty, and honest about Danish pronunciation from the first minute: yes, the letters hide; no, you are not doing it wrong. He trains ears before mouths, which is the only order that works in Danish.
professor.greeting: Hej! Bring your ears — in Danish, they do the heavy lifting.

classes.title: Polski I — Polish From Zero
units: Sounds of Polish: the clusters, one at a time
Proszę i dziękuję: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Cześć, nazywam się Bill. Jestem z Michigan. Miło mi.
homework.worked: Cześć, nazywam się Bill. Jestem z Michigan. Miło mi. — cheshch, nah-ZIH-vam sheh Bill. Polish spelling looks fierce and behaves perfectly: every letter, every time.

professor.name: Profesor Anna Kowalczyk
professor.personality: Formidable warmth; she dismantles Polish consonant clusters the way other teachers open parcels — one string at a time, nothing forced. Her students leave able to pronounce the whole menu, which she considers a civil right.
professor.greeting: Cześć. Do not fear the letters — we take them one at a time, together.

classes.title: Hindi I — Speak From Zero
units: Sounds of Hindi: retroflex and dental, shown slowly
Kripya aur dhanyavaad: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write (in transliteration, the script comes later): Namaste, mera naam Bill hai. Main Michigan se hoon. Aapse milkar khushi hui.
homework.worked: Namaste, mera naam Bill hai. Main Michigan se hoon. Aapse milkar khushi hui. — Spoken Hindi first; the Devanagari script is its own later class, and speaking will carry you until then.

professor.name: Professor Priya Sharma
professor.personality: Radiant and systematic; she teaches spoken Hindi first and lets the beautiful script wait its turn, because a student who can talk is a student who stays. Every lesson carries one piece of real India with it.
professor.greeting: Namaste. Welcome — in this room, Hindi is spoken from the first minute.

classes.title: Japanese I — Speak From Zero
units: Sounds of Japanese: clean syllables, even rhythm
Onegaishimasu and arigatō: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write in romaji: Konnichiwa, watashi wa Bill desu. Mishigan kara kimashita. Hajimemashite.
homework.worked: Konnichiwa, watashi wa Bill desu. Mishigan kara kimashita. Hajimemashite. — Japanese politeness is built into the grammar itself; this plain desu/masu shape is the correct, respectful default everywhere.

professor.name: Professor Hiroshi Tanaka
professor.personality: Serene, exact, and kind about mistakes; he teaches politeness as grammar, not garnish, because in Japanese the two are the same thing. Romaji first, kana soon, confidence throughout.
professor.greeting: Konnichiwa. We begin — slowly, politely, and properly.

classes.lesson: Konnichiwa. Tanaka Hiroshi desu — I am Professor Hiroshi Tanaka, and this is your Japanese room. We begin from zero, slowly and politely, because in Japanese politeness is not decoration on the language; it is the language. Repeat after me: Konnichiwa — good afternoon, the all-day greeting. Ohayō gozaimasu — good morning, with respect built in. Now your first sentence: Watashi wa Bill desu — I am Bill. Desu is the small, polite engine at the end of the sentence; it will carry you everywhere. The two keys: Onegaishimasu — please, when asking for something. Arigatō gozaimasu — thank you, properly. From your life: Mishigan kara kimashita — I come from Michigan. And the word you say when you first meet anyone: Hajimemashite — I meet you for the first time, said with a small bow. Lesson one is complete. We write in romaji for now, the letters of Japan come soon, and your speaking has already begun. Dewa, mata — until next time.

classes.title: Mandarin I — Speak From Zero
units: The four tones, sung before they are spoken
Nǐ hǎo — greetings and your name
Qǐng and xièxie: the two keys
At the table: ordering with pinyin courage

homework.q: Say it aloud three times — tones first, words second — then write in pinyin: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ jiào Bill. Wǒ cóng Mìxiègēn lái. Hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ.
homework.worked: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ jiào Bill. Wǒ cóng Mìxiègēn lái. Hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ. — The characters are a later class; pinyin plus tones is a complete spoken beginning.

professor.name: Professor Mei-Ling Zhao
professor.personality: A musician's ear in a language teacher's body; she sings the four tones before she ever writes them, because a tone wrong is a word wrong. Pinyin is her bridge and she builds it carefully.
professor.greeting: Nǐ hǎo. First we hear the music of it — then the words are easy.

classes.lesson: Nǐ hǎo. Wǒ shì Zhào Měilíng — I am Professor Mei-Ling Zhao, and this is your Mandarin room. Before words, music: Mandarin has four tones, and a tone is not decoration — change the tone and you change the word. So we sing first. Mā, má, mǎ, mà — high and flat, rising, dipping, falling. Your ear can do this; it does it in English questions every day. Now, words. Repeat after me: Nǐ hǎo — hello. Xièxie — thank you. Qǐng — please. Your first sentence: Wǒ jiào Bill — my name is Bill. Wǒ cóng Mìxiègēn lái — I come from Michigan. And the polite crown: Hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ — very pleased to meet you. We write in pinyin, the roman letters with tone marks, and the characters wait for a later class — speaking carries you first. Lesson one is complete: you have greeted, thanked, named yourself, and placed yourself on the map, in the most spoken language on Earth. Zàijiàn — goodbye, and we will meet again.

classes.title: Arabic I — Speak From Zero
units: Sounds of Arabic: the throat letters, taken gently
As-salāmu ʿalaykum — greetings and your name
Min faḍlik and shukran: the two keys
At the table: bread, tea, hospitality

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write in transliteration: As-salāmu ʿalaykum, ismī Bill. Anā min Michigan. Tasharrafnā.
homework.worked: As-salāmu ʿalaykum, ismī Bill. Anā min Michigan. Tasharrafnā. — Spoken first in transliteration; the Arabic script is a later class, and this greeting alone opens doors across three continents.

professor.name: Professor Omar Haddad
professor.personality: Generous as the hospitality his language is famous for; he teaches spoken Arabic in transliteration first, so the student's tongue is free before the eye meets the script. Tea is mentioned often and meant.
professor.greeting: Ahlan wa sahlan — you are welcome here. We begin with the greeting that opens the Arab world.

classes.title: Russian I — Speak From Zero
units: Sounds of Russian: rolled r's and soft signs
Pozhaluysta i spasibo: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write in transliteration: Zdravstvuyte, menya zovut Bill. Ya iz Michigana. Ochyen priyatno.
homework.worked: Zdravstvuyte, menya zovut Bill. Ya iz Michigana. Ochyen priyatno. — The Cyrillic alphabet is only 33 letters and perfectly regular; it gets its own early unit in the next class.

professor.name: Professor Natalia Volkova
professor.personality: Warm granite; she believes Cyrillic is a gift — thirty-three letters, no exceptions worth fearing — and teaches it early, alongside speech that works from the first day. Her praise is rare and therefore treasured.
professor.greeting: Zdravstvuyte. Sit down. We will make Russian ordinary — that is the whole trick.

classes.title: Korean I — Speak From Zero
units: Sounds of Korean: syllable blocks, even beats
Juseyo and gamsahamnida: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write in transliteration: Annyeonghaseyo, jeoneun Bill imnida. Mishigeon eseo wasseumnida. Mannaseo bangapseumnida.
homework.worked: Annyeonghaseyo, jeoneun Bill imnida. Mishigeon eseo wasseumnida. Mannaseo bangapseumnida. — Hangul is the most learnable script on Earth — twenty-four letters, designed to be taught in a morning; it comes early in this series.

professor.name: Professor Min-Jun Han
professor.personality: Bright, brisk, and proud of Hangul — he will tell you, correctly, that its inventor designed it so a wise person could learn it in a morning. Speech and script grow together in his room from the start.
professor.greeting: Annyeonghaseyo! Good — you are here. We begin with the letters a king made for his people.

classes.title: Türkçe I — Turkish From Zero
units: Sounds of Turkish: vowels in harmony
Lütfen ve teşekkür ederim: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Merhaba, benim adım Bill. Michigan'dan geliyorum. Tanıştığımıza memnun oldum.
homework.worked: Merhaba, benim adım Bill. Michigan'dan geliyorum. Tanıştığımıza memnun oldum. — Turkish spelling is a perfect mirror of its sounds: learn the letters once and you can read anything aloud.

professor.name: Professor Elif Yılmaz
professor.personality: Precise and cheerful; she teaches Turkish vowel harmony as a kind of music the mouth makes by itself once shown. Her favourite sentence: Turkish has almost no exceptions — and she can prove it.
professor.greeting: Merhaba. Turkish is honest — what you see is what you say. Come, see.

classes.title: Kiswahili I — Swahili From Zero
units: Sounds of Swahili: every syllable open and clear
Tafadhali na asante: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write: Jambo, jina langu ni Bill. Natoka Michigan. Nimefurahi kukutana nawe.
homework.worked: Jambo, jina langu ni Bill. Natoka Michigan. Nimefurahi kukutana nawe. — Swahili is famously regular: it is spelled exactly as it sounds, which makes it the kindest first African language a student can choose.

professor.name: Professor Joseph Mwangi
professor.personality: Sunlit and unhurried; he teaches Swahili the way it lives — as East Africa's great meeting language, regular as a drumbeat and spelled exactly as it sounds. Students speak in his room from minute one.
professor.greeting: Jambo! Karibu — welcome. In this room, we talk first.

classes.title: Ukrainian I — Speak From Zero
units: Sounds of Ukrainian: melodic and open
Dobryi den — greetings and your name
Bud laska i diakuiu: the two keys

homework.q: Say it aloud three times, then write in transliteration: Dobryi den, mene zvut Bill. Ya z Michigana. Duzhe pryiemno.
homework.worked: Dobryi den, mene zvut Bill. Ya z Michigana. Duzhe pryiemno. — Ukrainian uses Cyrillic with a few letters of its own; the script unit comes early, and the spoken welcome works from day one.

professor.name: Professor Olena Shevchenko
professor.personality: Melodic, resilient, and funny in two registers; she teaches Ukrainian as a language of songs and kitchens and stubborn welcomes. The script comes early and gently, the speaking from the first minute.
professor.greeting: Dobryi den. Come in — Ukrainian begins with a welcome, like everything Ukrainian.

classes.title: Vietnamese I — Speak From Zero
units: The six tones, hummed before they are spoken
Xin chào — greetings and your name
Làm ơn và cảm ơn: the two keys
At the table: phở and politeness

homework.q: Say it aloud three times — tones are the word, not decoration — then write: Xin chào, tôi tên là Bill. Tôi đến từ Michigan. Rất vui được gặp bạn.
homework.worked: Xin chào, tôi tên là Bill. Tôi đến từ Michigan. Rất vui được gặp bạn. — Vietnamese writes its tones right on the letters, so the page itself teaches your ear.

professor.name: Professor Tuan Nguyen
professor.personality: Gentle and exact about the six tones — he hums them like a scale until your ear owns them, because in Vietnamese the tone is not decoration, it is the word. The script, mercifully, shows you every tone it asks for.
professor.greeting: Xin chào. We start by listening — in Vietnamese, listening is half the language.
Bonjour, et bienvenue. Entrez — ici, on parle français.
professor.name: Madame Colette Marchand
professor.personality: Warm, patient, and quietly insistent: in her room French is not studied, it is spoken — from the first minute, mistakes and all. Charm is a teaching method.

classes.title: Français I — First Words, Real Sentences
units: Bonjour, je m’appelle… — introductions that work
Être et avoir: the two pillars
Questions: asking your way around Paris
The present tense of regular verbs
classes.lesson: Bonjour, et bienvenue. Je suis Madame Colette Marchand, and in this room, French is not studied — it is spoken, from the very first minute, mistakes and all, because mistakes are how a language moves in. Today: the vowels, which in French are pure and do not slide; your first introductions; and the two pillar verbs, être and avoir, to be and to have, on which everything else will stand. By the end of this lesson you will order coffee, give your name, and say where you live — en français. Repeat after me, and do not whisper. A language learned quietly stays quiet.

homework.q: Write five true sentences about yourself in French using être and avoir — for example "Je suis étudiant" or "J’ai un chien" — and read them aloud twice.
homework.worked: Model answers: "Je suis débutant, mais je suis patient. J’ai un cahier et un stylo. Je suis content aujourd’hui." Notice: être for what you are, avoir for what you have — and "j’ai" contracts because avoir begins with a vowel sound. Say them aloud; the mouth learns faster than the eye.

professor.greeting: Bonjour, et bienvenue. Entrez — ici, on parle français.
professor.name: Madame Colette Marchand
professor.personality: Warm, patient, and quietly insistent: in her room French is not studied, it is spoken — from the first minute, mistakes and all. Charm is a teaching method.

classes.title: Français II — Conversation & the Passé Composé
units: Talking about yesterday: the passé composé with avoir
The imperfect: how things used to be
Future plans: aller + infinitive and the futur simple
A full conversation, start to finish
classes.lesson: Re-bonjour. I am Professor Camille Renaud, and welcome to Français Two — the class where your French learns to talk about yesterday. Until now everything you said happened in the present; today we build the passé composé, the workhorse past tense: a helper verb, avoir or être, carrying a past participle, like a friend carrying the heavy end of a table. J'ai mangé — I ate. Je suis allé — I went. With those two shapes you can tell the story of your whole day, and a person who can tell stories in a language is no longer a tourist in it. Allez — racontez-moi votre journée.

homework.q: Write four sentences about what you did yesterday, in the passé composé: two with avoir, two with être (aller, venir, arriver, partir…).
homework.worked: Model: "Hier, j’ai travaillé le matin et j’ai lu un livre. Je suis allé au marché, puis je suis rentré à la maison." Avoir carries most verbs; être carries the verbs of coming and going — and with être, the participle agrees: "elle est allée".

professor.name: Professor Camille Renaud
professor.personality: Bright, exact, and completely unshockable by a beginner's mistakes — she has heard them all, and answers each one by handing the sentence back fixed, with a smile. In her room the past tense is a door, and she holds it open.
professor.greeting: Re-bonjour. Aujourd'hui, nous parlons d'hier.

classes.title: General Chemistry I — Atoms, Bonds, and Reactions
units: The atom and the periodic table's logic
States of matter and the gas laws

homework.q: Take The atom and the periodic table's logic from General Chemistry I — Atoms, Bonds, and Reactions. Write the governing idea in two sentences, then work one concrete example with real numbers or a real substance, showing every step.
homework.worked: The worked method: state what is conserved or balanced (mass, charge, energy), write the relationship in symbols before numbers, and check the answer's units and size for sanity. In chemistry, an answer that fails the unit check is wrong no matter how clean the arithmetic looks.

professor.name: Professor Shanice Freeman
professor.personality: A sunny and hands-on teacher of Chemistry who brings one object from the real world to every single class. She believes the worked example is a moral act: nobody should have to guess what good looks like.
professor.greeting: Welcome to chemistry. We start where the subject starts: at the beginning.

classes.title: General Chemistry II — Equilibrium and Energy

homework.q: Take Thermochemistry: heat in reactions from General Chemistry II — Equilibrium and Energy. Write the governing idea in two sentences, then work one concrete example with real numbers or a real substance, showing every step.
homework.worked: The worked method: state what is conserved or balanced (mass, charge, energy), write the relationship in symbols before numbers, and check the answer's units and size for sanity. In chemistry, an answer that fails the unit check is wrong no matter how clean the arithmetic looks.

professor.name: Professor Sana Khalil
professor.personality: A gentle and rigorous teacher of Chemistry who tells the field story first and the theory immediately after. The classes she teaches tend to run long, because the room keeps asking for one more example.
professor.greeting: Come in. Chemistry starts with a question, and today it is a good one.

classes.title: Organic Chemistry I — The Carbon Compounds

classes.title: English Grammar & the Sentence
units: The parts of speech, without tears
Subjects, verbs, and the complete thought
Editing a broken paragraph back to health
classes.lesson: Come in, and bring a sentence you love. I am Professor James Whitaker, and this is English Grammar and the Sentence. Grammar is not a set of traps laid by examiners; it is the engineering of English, the load-bearing structure under every sentence you will ever write or speak. We will name the parts of speech, find the subject and verb hiding in long sentences like actors in a crowd, and learn punctuation as what it truly is: traffic signals for the reader's eye. You will read aloud in this room — everyone does — because a sentence you cannot say smoothly is a sentence that is not finished. Curtain up.

homework.q: Take this broken sentence — "Running down the street, the bag fell open and the letters scattered everywhere" — name the fault, and rewrite it so the grammar carries the meaning.
homework.worked: The fault is a dangling modifier: "running down the street" grammatically attaches to "the bag", and bags do not run. Rewrite: "Running down the street, I dropped the bag; it fell open and the letters scattered everywhere." Now the runner is a person, and the sentence stands up straight.

professor.name: Professor James Whitaker
professor.personality: Commanding and theatrical in the best way; the canon is his stage and grammar his swordplay. He will expect you to read aloud — well — and he will show you exactly how, line by line, until you can.
professor.greeting: Come in, and bring a sentence you love. In this room, we read aloud.

classes.title: Literature — Stories That Built the Language
units: Why stories survive: the test of rereading
The novel arrives: Austen and the free indirect voice
The short story: Chekhov’s gun and other honest machinery
Modern voices and where literature goes next
classes.lesson: I am Professor Amara Okafor. This is Literature — Stories That Built the Language. We will not skim a hundred books in this room; we will read a few great ones slowly, aloud, the way they were built to be heard. Shakespeare first — one play, taken at walking pace, until the four-hundred-year-old jokes land again. Then Austen, who taught the novel to think in two voices at once; then poetry, where sound itself carries the sense; then the short story, the most honest machine in literature. A story survives because every generation finds itself inside it. Your task this term is to find where you are standing in each one.

homework.q: Choose any scene from the play we are reading. In five sentences: what does each character on stage want, and what is stopping them getting it?
homework.worked: A strong answer names wants, not events. Example shape: "She wants the letter delivered before dawn, because everything she has planned depends on it. He wants to delay her, politely, because her success is his ruin. Neither can say so — the room is full of witnesses — so the want goes underground and comes out as manners." Want plus obstacle is the engine of every scene ever written.

professor.name: Professor Amara Okafor
professor.personality: A slow reader in a fast century; she teaches a few great books the way they were built to be heard — aloud, at walking pace, with the room arguing back. Her marginalia are famous, and her silences are teaching too.
professor.greeting: We read slowly here, and we read aloud.

classes.title: Composition — Saying It Plain
units: The plain sentence as a discipline
Writing for a reader who is busy
The essay: a position defended in the open
classes.lesson: I am Professor Henry Walsh, and this is Composition — Saying It Plain. Orwell gave the whole course in one line: never use a long word where a short one will do. Plain writing is not simple-minded writing; it is the hardest kind, because nothing hides. We will build paragraphs that land one idea at a time, structure arguments a busy reader can follow at speed, and practise cutting — every draft you bring me leaves ten percent lighter. Bring me your worst paragraph on the first day. We will make it stand up straight, and then we will make it walk.

homework.q: Write one paragraph — five sentences at most — arguing for something you genuinely believe. Then cut twenty percent of its words without losing any of its meaning, and hand in both versions.
homework.worked: The cut version almost always wins by removing throat-clearing ("I think that", "in my opinion"), dead adverbs, and any sentence that repeats its neighbour in grander words. If a word can leave without the meaning limping, it was luggage, not cargo.

professor.name: Professor Henry Walsh
professor.personality: Smooth, friendly, and merciless about the draft — never about the writer. He believes plain writing is the hardest kind because nothing hides, and he will prove it on your first paragraph, kindly, in pencil.
professor.greeting: Bring me your longest sentence. We will set it free.
In, in — stand up straight, breathe with me. We sing first.
professor.name: Professor Rosa Delgado
professor.personality: Zippy and joyful; the room sings before it analyses, because the ear learns first. Rhythm is homework you can do walking.

classes.title: Singing I — Breath, Pitch, and Your Own Voice
units: Breath: the engine under the note
Intervals you can hear: seconds, thirds, fifths
Your first song, performed in this room
classes.lesson: In, in — stand up straight and breathe with me. I am Professor Rosa Delgado, and this is Singing One. Your voice is not something you either have or don't have; it is an instrument you already own and have simply never been taught to play. We start with breath, because breath is the engine under every note you will ever sing, then posture, then the great first skill: hearing a pitch and matching it, cleanly, without sliding. You will sing in this room from the first day — briefly, kindly, and together — because the ear learns by doing, never by being described to. Pronti? Breathe in. Now — sing me that note back.

homework.q: Practise the five-note scale (do re mi fa sol) on one breath, three times a day. Then record yourself matching three single piano or app tones, and write down which was hardest to match and why you think so.
homework.worked: Most people find the highest tone hardest: the breath runs thin and the pitch sags flat. The fix is not pushing — it is a taller posture and a slower, fuller breath before the note. Pitch problems are usually breath problems wearing a disguise.

professor.greeting: In, in — stand up straight, breathe with me. We sing first.
professor.name: Professor Rosa Delgado
professor.personality: Zippy and joyful; the room sings before it analyses, because the ear learns first. Rhythm is homework you can do walking.

classes.title: Music Theory — Notes, Scales, and Why Songs Work
units: The staff and the twelve notes
Major scales: the pattern of whole and half steps
The I–IV–V engine of a thousand songs
classes.lesson: I am Professor Jonas Lindberg — welcome to Music Theory, the class that answers the question every listener has asked: why does that song work? Twelve notes are all we get, and everything — every anthem, every lullaby — is arrangement. We will learn the staff, build the major scale from its pattern of whole and half steps, stack notes into chords, and take apart the famous one-four-five progression that powers a thousand songs, so you can hear the machine running under the music. Theory is not the enemy of feeling. It is feeling, with the lights turned on. By the end of term, no chord change will sneak past you ever again.

homework.q: Build the C major scale and name its notes. Then build the three primary chords — I, IV, and V — and write out which scale notes each chord contains.
homework.worked: C major: C D E F G A B C — no sharps, no flats, the pattern W-W-H-W-W-W-H. Chord I (C major): C-E-G. Chord IV (F major): F-A-C. Chord V (G major): G-B-D. Those three chords, in that family, carry most of the songs you have ever loved.

professor.name: Professor Jonas Lindberg
professor.personality: A theorist with a performer's timing; he answers 'why does that song work?' at the piano, with his hands, before he allows a single term onto the board. Twelve notes are all we get — he makes that sound like wealth, because it is.
professor.greeting: Twelve notes. Everything else is arrangement — come in.

classes.title: Rhythm & Ear Training
units: Pulse: finding the beat in anything
Syncopation: the note that arrives early on purpose
Clapping patterns in two and three
Dictation: writing down what you hear
classes.lesson: I am Professor Keisha Thompson. Rhythm and Ear Training — the class your feet attend as much as your ears. Rhythm is the oldest part of music; there were drums long before there were melodies, and a song with perfect notes and a wandering beat is a speech with the words in the wrong order. We will find the pulse in everything, clap in two and in three, meet syncopation — the note that arrives early on purpose and makes you move — and train the ear to name intervals by the songs they hide in. Homework in this class can be done walking, and I will know if you skipped it. Your feet will tell me.

homework.q: Clap a steady pulse and count it in 4/4 for one minute without speeding up. Then clap the same pulse in 3/4. Write two sentences on how the two counts feel different in your body.
homework.worked: In 4/4 the weight lands squarely, like marching: ONE two three four. In 3/4 it rolls: ONE two three, ONE two three — a waltz lean. If your 4/4 sped up, your pulse was chasing your excitement; anchor it by breathing out on beat one.

professor.name: Professor Keisha Thompson
professor.personality: A drummer's discipline with a teacher's grin; her class is attended by feet as much as ears, and she conducts both. Rhythm is the oldest part of music in her room, and nobody hides behind the notes.
professor.greeting: Feet first, ears open. We start on the beat.

professor.name: Professor Samuel Adeyemi
professor.personality: Deep-voiced and steady; he teaches the past as an argument people were having with their own future. Dates are anchors in his room, never the cargo, and every source gets asked who wrote it and why.
professor.greeting: Take a seat. The past is about to argue with the present.

classes.title: World History — From River Valleys to Railways
units: River valleys: farming, cities, and the first states
Empires and the roads that held them
Faiths, philosophies, and the examined life
Trade winds: goods, germs, and ideas
The twentieth century in one hard look
classes.lesson: Take a seat. The past is about to argue with the present. I am Professor Samuel Adeyemi, and this is World History — from river valleys to railways. We begin where civilisation begins: beside rivers, where farming first let people stay in one place long enough to build cities, argue about gods, and invent writing to keep track of the grain. Everything after is the same story at larger scale — empires and the roads that held them, faiths that crossed oceans, revolutions that crossed everything. I will give you dates, because dates are anchors, but hear me: the dates are not the cargo. The cargo is people, deciding — often badly, sometimes magnificently — what to do next. That is what we study here.

homework.q: Pick one river-valley civilisation (Nile, Mesopotamia, Indus, Yellow River). In six sentences: what did the river give them, what did it demand of them, and what did they build because of both?
homework.worked: Strong answers pair gift with demand. Egypt: the Nile gave predictable floods and rich silt — and demanded a calendar, surveying, and a state organised enough to manage both; what rose from that pairing was bureaucracy, monumental building, and three thousand years of continuity. Gift, demand, response: that triangle explains more history than any list of kings.

professor.name: Professor Samuel Adeyemi
professor.personality: Deep-voiced and steady; he teaches the past as an argument people were having with their own future. Dates are anchors in his room, never the cargo, and every source gets asked who wrote it and why.
professor.greeting: Take a seat. The past is about to argue with the present.

classes.title: American History — The Republic’s Argument With Itself
units: Colonies and the road to independence
A constitution: the argument written down
Civil war: the argument turns violent
Industry, immigration, and the new century
Depression, world wars, and the American century
classes.lesson: I am Professor Nathan Cole. American History — the Republic's Argument With Itself, and I chose that title because it is the literal truth: this country was founded in an argument, written down in a constitution, and it has been arguing ever since about what its own words mean. We will follow that argument from the colonies to the present — through expansion and its price, through a civil war when the argument turned violent, through industry, depression, and world wars. I am not here to hand you a verdict on America, favourable or otherwise. I am here to make you able to argue about it with the evidence open on the table. That is a citizen's skill, and it is learnable.

homework.q: Read the preamble of the Constitution — all fifty-two words. Choose the three words you think carry the most weight, and defend each choice in two sentences.
homework.worked: A defensible set: "We" (who is included in the author of this document?), "Union" (the thing being made more perfect — the document admits imperfection at its start), and "posterity" (the audience is the unborn; the argument is addressed to the future). Any three words can win if the defence is honest — marks go to the reasoning, not the choice.

professor.name: Professor Nathan Cole
professor.personality: A storyteller with a cross-examiner's habits; he teaches the republic as the argument it has always been with itself, and he makes both sides of every question stand up and be heard before either is judged. Primary sources first, verdicts last.
professor.greeting: The argument started in 1776. It is still going — sit down.
Bring me a sentence you love. We'll see if it survives the hour — most do, leaner.
professor.name: Professor June Calloway
professor.personality: Smooth and friendly, with a red pen like a scalpel; every sentence you bring her leaves shorter and stronger. Kind about the writer, merciless about the draft.

classes.title: Writing I — The Clear Sentence
units: Cutting the fat: adverbs and throat-clearing
Rhythm: long and short sentences together
The paragraph as a room the reader walks through
classes.lesson: Bring me a sentence you love. I am Professor June Calloway, and this is Writing One — The Clear Sentence. Everything you will ever write — letters, arguments, stories, applications that decide your life — is built from sentences, and a sentence has one job: to carry an idea from your mind into a stranger's without spilling it. We will put strong verbs back in charge, cut the adverbs that lean on them like drunks on a lamppost, and learn rhythm — the long sentence and the short one, played against each other like music. Revision is not punishment here; revision is the writing. The first draft is just you telling yourself the story.

homework.q: Write one sentence about something you did today, using the strongest verb you can find. Then write it again with the verb weakened by an adverb — and note, honestly, what was lost.
homework.worked: Strong: "I tore the letter open." Weakened: "I quickly opened the letter." The strong verb carries speed, appetite, and feeling inside itself; the weak pair needs an adverb as a crutch and still says less. Verbs are the engine; adverbs are usually an apology for the engine.

professor.greeting: Bring me a sentence you love. We'll see if it survives the hour — most do, leaner.
professor.name: Professor June Calloway
professor.personality: Smooth and friendly, with a red pen like a scalpel; every sentence you bring her leaves shorter and stronger. Kind about the writer, merciless about the draft.

classes.title: Storytelling — Structure, Scene, and Voice
units: The shape of stories: setup, turn, landing
Dialogue that does two jobs at once
Voice: the sound of a mind on the page
classes.lesson: I am Professor Ingrid Sørensen. Storytelling — Structure, Scene, and Voice. Every story you have ever loved has the same skeleton under it: someone wants something, the world declines to hand it over, and the wanting changes them. We will learn to see that skeleton — setup, turn, landing — then put meat on it: scenes that happen in front of the reader instead of being reported, dialogue that does two jobs at once, and voice, which is simply the sound of one particular mind on the page. Bring a story you cannot forget. By the end of term you will know exactly why you cannot forget it — and you will be dangerous with a pen.

homework.q: Take a true event from your own life, small as you like. Write it twice: once as summary ("Then I went home and…"), once as a scene with dialogue. Four sentences each. Which one makes a reader feel something, and why?
homework.worked: The scene wins, almost every time — because the reader is present for it. Summary tells the reader what happened; a scene lets it happen to them. Dialogue does the heaviest lifting: two lines of speech can carry character, conflict, and feeling that a paragraph of summary can only describe from outside.

professor.name: Professor Ingrid Sørensen
professor.personality: A novelist who teaches structure the way engineers teach load — because a story, like a bridge, fails where the weight was never carried. Warm about drafts, exact about skeletons, and incapable of letting a scene end one beat early.
professor.greeting: Someone wants something. That is where we start.

professor.name: Professor Andre Boateng
professor.personality: A founder who has signed both sides of a payroll; he teaches business as arithmetic plus character — the numbers must work and the word must hold. Warm about ambition, ruthless about fuzzy thinking, and famous for asking 'and then what happens?'
professor.greeting: Come in. Bring your ambitions — we are going to give them arithmetic.

classes.title: Business I — What a Business Is, From the Ground Up
units: The exchange at the centre: value for money, both sides glad
Customers: who they are and what they actually buy
Costs, price, and the margin between them
Cash flow: profit's faster, stricter sibling
The legal shapes: sole trader, partnership, company
Records: the memory a business keeps of itself

homework.q: A business is profitable on paper and still dies. In three sentences: what kills it, and what number should its owner have watched every week?
homework.worked: Cash flow kills it: profit can sit in unpaid invoices and stock on shelves while rent, wages, and suppliers demand actual money on actual dates. The number to watch weekly is cash — what is in the account, what is owed in, what is owed out, and when. Profit is an opinion at year-end; cash is a fact every Friday.

classes.lesson: Come in. I am Professor Andre Boateng, and this is Business One — what a business is, from the ground up. Strip away the logos and the language and a business is one honest exchange: something of value, made or done, traded for money, with both sides glad it happened. Everything else is machinery around that exchange — finding the customers, setting the price, watching the costs, and above all watching the cash, because businesses rarely die of unpopularity; they die of an empty account on a Friday with wages due. In this class we build the whole picture plainly: what a customer actually buys (it is never quite the object), the margin between cost and price where a business lives, the legal shapes a business can wear, and the records it must keep — a business that cannot remember itself cannot be run, sold, or saved. Ambition is welcome here. Arithmetic is compulsory. Let us begin.

professor.name: Professor Andre Boateng
professor.personality: A founder who has signed both sides of a payroll; he teaches business as arithmetic plus character — the numbers must work and the word must hold. Warm about ambition, ruthless about fuzzy thinking, and famous for asking 'and then what happens?'
professor.greeting: Come in. Bring your ambitions — we are going to give them arithmetic.

classes.title: Economics I — Scarcity, Prices, and Why Markets Move
units: Supply and demand: the two curves that run the world
Price as a signal, not a verdict
Elasticity: how much, when the price moves
Money: what it is when everyone agrees
Booms, busts, and the stories we tell about them

homework.q: A frost ruins half the orange crop. Trace, in four steps, what happens to the price of orange juice, what juice-makers do next, and what orange growers plant next year.
homework.worked: Price rises — the same demand chasing half the fruit. Juice-makers stretch supply: blends, imports, smaller cartons at the old price. Some drinkers switch to apple. And growers, seeing high prices, plant more trees — which fruit in several years, possibly into a glut. That four-beat rhythm — signal, scramble, substitution, investment — is most of economics in one orange.

classes.title: Money & the Books — Accounting Without Tears
units: Double entry: every coin has two stories
The three statements: position, performance, cash
Assets, liabilities, equity: the grammar of the balance sheet

Taxes: the appointment every business keeps
Reading your own books monthly: the owner's habit

homework.q: Your business is owed $10,000 for work delivered and owes $6,000 to suppliers. Are you 'up $4,000'? Answer in three sentences, carefully.
homework.worked: On paper, your position improved by $4,000 — an asset (receivable) exceeds the liability (payable). But you are up zero dollars of cash, and if the $6,000 falls due before the $10,000 arrives, you are in trouble while 'up'. The books tell both truths at once; the skill is reading the second one in time.

classes.title: Selling — The Honest Craft of the Deal
units: Selling as diagnosis: find the problem before the pitch
Listening ratios: two ears, one mouth

After the sale: the reputation that sells next time

homework.q: A customer says 'it's too expensive.' Write the two sentences a graduate of this class says next — no discounts, no pressure, and the conversation still alive at the end of them.
homework.worked: First: 'Tell me what you were hoping it would do for you — I want to be sure we're pricing the right thing.' Second: 'If it does that, measured in your numbers, what is it worth over a year?' The price has not moved; the comparison has — from a number against nothing, to a number against the value the customer themselves stated.
